title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text: Preface

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
Why this book exists
Asset allocation is taught as a small set of ideas — a frontier, a risk measure, a constraint, a backtest — and practiced as a long chain of decisions about data, estimation, solvers and costs, in which the ideas are the shortest links. The gap between the two is where most of the difficulty lives. A student who can derive the tangency portfolio on paper is often unable to produce it from a return matrix, not because the mathematics is hard but because the implementation asks questions the derivation never did: in excess of what rate, on which window, under which constraint, with which solver, and did the solver actually do what it was told.
There is an excellent R package for this work. PortfolioAnalytics (Peterson and Carl 2026) has been under development for more than a decade, it supports nine solvers, fourteen constraint types and eleven risk measures, and almost nobody uses more than a tenth of it — partly because a reference manual answers what does this function do and never which of these constraints does my mandate need, and which solver will still honour it once I have added it, and partly because several of its defaults are wrong in ways that produce a plausible answer rather than an error. This book is a course text built on that package. It states each method in mathematics, attributes it to the literature, implements it in R on a market whose every property can be inspected, and then measures how much of the textbook answer survives contact with data the optimizer had not seen.
The model for how such a book should be built is Tidy Finance with R (Scheuch et al. 2023) and Machine Learning for Factor Investing (Coqueret and Guida 2020): explain what is being done, state it precisely, cite it, run it, and hand the reader takeaways and exercises. Where those books end — with a set of factors and a set of return forecasts — this one begins.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
Who this is for
This is a course text, written first for a master’s student meeting portfolio construction in a syllabus. Each chapter is meant to be teachable in one session: it opens with the question it answers and the work that first asked it, states the theory with the mathematics in the running text, implements it with code the student can run on the shipped data, and closes with takeaways and exercises whose solutions are in Appendix G — Solutions to Exercises. Nothing is assumed beyond an introductory course in finance and the R of Appendix E — A Short R Refresher.
It is also written for a practitioner who knows the theory and wants the working implementation, including the part the package makes hard. There is no separate track: the same text carries the derivation for the student and the callout for the practitioner, because in this subject the two are rarely far apart. The reader who wants only the machinery can read the implementation sections and the callouts and skip nothing that matters.
A doctoral student or a researcher is not the reader the prose is aimed at, but the references are complete enough that the book can be used as a route into the literature. Every method is attributed on first use, every empirical claim that the literature has settled carries the paper that settled it, and the bibliography has been checked entry by entry.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
How the chapters are built
Every chapter opens with the question it answers and the work that first asked it, states what we do, and then moves through theory, implementation and application. Each closes with key takeaways and exercises; solutions are in Appendix G — Solutions to Exercises.
Mathematics is in the running text, because a portfolio problem is easier to read as an optimization problem than as a paragraph. In Parts II to IV we state the problem and its solution and send the proof to Appendix B — Proofs. In Part VIII we derive in place, because there the theory is the subject.
Where PortfolioAnalytics defaults the wrong way, fails silently or accepts a constraint and then drops it, we say so in a callout placed where the reader would otherwise walk into it. That material is one of the reasons for this book, and it is not in any reference manual. Worked examples that the reader may want to skip on a first pass sit in collapsible boxes.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
How the book is organized
The parts follow the allocation hierarchy. Parts II to V work at the level of asset classes, because a sixteen-asset problem can be seen whole and a one-hundred-and-eighty-one-asset problem cannot. Part VI then goes inside a single class and asks which securities to hold. Part VII is about implementing and evaluating any of it, and Part VIII carries the theory behind the earlier intuitions.
Running across that hierarchy is a second distinction, between strategic allocation, which sets a long-run policy from unconditional assumptions, and tactical allocation, which departs from that policy using information available at the time. We define both in Returns, Horizons, and the Basis of Comparison and then say, chapter by chapter, which one is being done. The two ideas are often run together; they are not the same, and keeping them apart is worth the small effort it costs.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
The data
Every number in the book is computed on a modeled multi-asset market that ships with the companion package: five regions, sixteen risky asset-class series, 181 instruments, monthly and weekly over thirty-one model years, all in dollars, licensed to nobody. It is introduced in The Modeled Market, measured in Implementation and documented in full in Appendix A — Data Description. The market is modeled, not recorded — no series is the history of a real security — and that is what allows the whole book to reproduce on the reader’s machine without an account anywhere. Where a claim has to be about real markets, the free data reached through the companion package is used and the chapter says so.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
What you can skip
Parts I to VII are the course, and they are complete on their own. Part VIII gives the theory behind the intuition, the estimators behind the defaults, and the parts of the literature that have not yet reached the textbooks. Nothing in the earlier parts depends on it.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
What this book is not
It is not an introduction to R, and it is not an introduction to empirical asset pricing. Where those are needed, they are cited rather than reproduced:

For getting financial data into R and building factors from it, Scheuch et al. (2023) is better than anything this book would write, and its companion package is used here directly.
For the machine-learning algorithms behind return prediction, Coqueret and Guida (2020) is the reference. This book picks up where the prediction ends.
For the R language itself, Wickham et al. (2023) remains the standard, and Appendix E — A Short R Refresher offers a short refresher for readers who want one.

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
Conventions
Vectors are bold lower case, matrices bold capitals, and the symbols are fixed once in Notation. Returns are simple returns in decimal, and they enter every optimization in excess of the Treasury bill, for the reasons given in Returns, Horizons, and the Basis of Comparison. Code objects follow the mathematics: R is the return matrix, Re the excess-return matrix, rf the bill, w a weight vector.
Every chapter runs from the project root, sources one setup file, attaches the companion package tidypm, and loads the data in two lines. The boundary between the tidy long table the data ship as and the wide matrix the optimizer wants is crossed explicitly, once per chapter, with as_xts_pm() (The Tibble–xts Boundary). Wherever two objects have to line up — a weight vector and the columns of a return matrix, a group constraint and the groups it binds — the alignment is asserted in code rather than assumed, and every figure is built from a single data frame so that no coordinate can be paired with the wrong label.
Numbers in the prose are computed, never typed. The spelling is American in the text and follows the package in code, so ggplot2’s argument is colour. Functions are set in code font with their parentheses, optimize.portfolio().

title: Tidy Asset Allocation in R
text:
Reproducing this book

#> R version:          R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24 ucrt)
#> PortfolioAnalytics: 2.1.2
#> tidypm:             0.2.0

The full dependency set, pinned to the versions this book was built against, lives in renv.lock, and renv::restore() recreates it. Every deviation from the released package versions is listed in Appendix D — Package Notes, and Appendix I — Colophon and Changelog records how the book was built and what has changed.

title: 1  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
1.1 Two Data Models
What has to be installed, and in what shape must a return series arrive, before any portfolio in this book can be computed? The second question has two canonical answers that do not agree: Wickham (2014) defined a tidy table as one observation per row and one variable per column, and Zeileis and Grothendieck (2005) built the ordered, date-indexed matrix that zoo and xts carry and that every optimization function in PortfolioAnalytics expects. Both are used in every chapter of this book, and the boundary between them is crossed each time data are prepared for an optimizer or read back out of one, so we fix it here, once.
We first list what to install and what each package is for, then set out the two data models and why neither can be given up, then cross the boundary between them on the book’s own data and break it in the three ways it breaks, and finally read the data once in the way every later chapter will. On the horizon axis that Section 3.1 defines, this chapter is neither strategic nor tactical: it allocates nothing.
Three programs come first: R, of which the book was built on 4.6.1 and anything from 4.4 onward will do; an editor, RStudio or Visual Studio Code with the R extension; and Quarto (Allaire et al. 2022), needed only to render the book’s source, not to run its code. The packages install from CRAN in one call.
The companion package tidypm is not on CRAN. It holds the modeled market of Section 2.2, the two coercion functions this chapter is about, and the machinery that PortfolioAnalytics does not cover, recorded in Appendix D; it installs from GitHub.
renv.lock records every version the book was built against, and renv (Ushey and Wickham 2026) restores that record, so that the printed numbers reproduce to the last digit rather than to whatever CRAN offers on the day.
The tidyverse (Wickham et al. 2019) is the data-manipulation half of Table 1.1, with Wickham et al. (2023) as its reference; xts (Ryan and Ulrich 2026) on top of zoo (Zeileis and Grothendieck 2005) is the time-series half. PortfolioAnalytics (Peterson and Carl 2026b) and PerformanceAnalytics (Peterson and Carl 2026a) are the subject and its engine. The solvers are backends that PortfolioAnalytics dispatches to by name: ROI (Theußl et al. 2020) for quadratic and linear programs, CVXR (Fu et al. 2020) for convex problems ROI cannot express, and DEoptim (Ardia et al. 2011), GenSA and pso for problems that are not convex at all. Section 13.1 says which to use when, and Appendix C tables which constraint each supports.
A return panel is a set of numbers indexed by a date and an asset, and there are two ways to lay it out, each of which makes some operations natural and others awkward.
The tidy layout of Wickham (2014) stores one observation per row: a date, an asset identifier and a return. A panel of \(N\) assets over \(T\) periods is a table of \(TN\) rows and three columns, and every operation of relational algebra applies to it directly: a sub-period is a filter on the date, a universe is a filter on the asset, a currency return or a yield is a join on the keys, and a computation that runs asset by asset is a grouped mutate. That is how the real data sleeves of Section 2.3 are assembled, how the screens of Section 20.2 are applied, and how every figure in the book is prepared, since ggplot2 consumes long data and nothing else.
The wide layout stores the same panel as a \(T \times N\) matrix with the dates as an ordered index and the assets as named columns. In the notation that Section 2.1 fixes,
\[
\boldsymbol{R} =
\begin{pmatrix}
r_{1,1} & \cdots & r_{1,N} \\
\vdots  &        & \vdots  \\
r_{T,1} & \cdots & r_{T,N}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{r}_t' = (r_{t,1}, \dots, r_{t,N}),
\tag{1.1}\]
where \(\boldsymbol{r}_t\) is row \(t\), the cross-section of returns on date \(t\). A portfolio with weight vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\) earns
\[
r_{p,t} = \boldsymbol{r}_t'\boldsymbol{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\, r_{t,i},
\tag{1.2}\]
and the sample moments that Section 9.1 optimizes over are matrix expressions in \(\boldsymbol{R}\) and the vector of ones \(\boldsymbol{\iota}\):
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \frac{1}{T}\,\boldsymbol{R}'\boldsymbol{\iota},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \frac{1}{T-1}
  \left(\boldsymbol{R} - \boldsymbol{\iota}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\right)'
  \left(\boldsymbol{R} - \boldsymbol{\iota}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\right).
\tag{1.3}\]
zoo (Zeileis and Grothendieck 2005) made this layout a first-class object in R by attaching an ordered index to a matrix, and xts (Ryan and Ulrich 2026) specialized it to time, so that subsetting by date range, aligning two series, changing the frequency and rolling a window are each one call. Every function in PortfolioAnalytics and PerformanceAnalytics takes this object and nothing else; there is no method for a data frame.
Neither layout can be dropped: the long table is where data are built, because joining, filtering and grouping are relational operations and a matrix has no join, and the wide matrix is where portfolios are computed, because 1 through Equation 1.3 are matrix expressions. The boundary is therefore crossed in a fixed direction, long to wide once after the panel is built, wide to long whenever a result is to be drawn. timetk and tsibble hide the crossing; the book does not use them, because an explicit crossing can be checked.
The three equations also say what can go wrong, before any code does. In 1, \(T\) is one number shared by every column, so a panel in which one asset is missing a date has no matrix representation until the gap is filled or the date is dropped, and either choice changes Equation 1.3. In Equation 1.2, the \(i\) that indexes \(w_i\) and the \(i\) that indexes \(r_{t,i}\) must be the same asset, which a matrix product enforces by position and nothing else. And the map from \((t, i)\) to \(r_{t,i}\) must be a function: a panel in which some \((t, i)\) appears twice describes no matrix at all. These are the three failure modes of the boundary, and Section 1.2 produces each from the book’s data.

title: 1  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
1.2 The Tibble–xts Boundary
tidypm provides the crossing in both directions. as_xts_pm() takes a long table and the names of its date, identifier and value columns and returns the matrix of 1; as_pm() takes the matrix back to three columns. The book’s data ship in the long form.

sim_class_returns_monthly |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   date       class          return index
#>   <date>     <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2101-01-31 CH_credit     -0.0301  97.0
#> 2 2101-01-31 CH_equity     -0.0145  98.6
#> 3 2101-01-31 CH_government -0.0343  96.6
#> 4 2101-01-31 EU_credit     -0.0241  97.6


R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, nrow(R) == length(rf), !anyNA(R),
          all(zoo::index(R) == sim_riskfree_monthly$date))

The assertions state what the rest of the chapter assumes about R; if any of them were false the chunk would fail here, naming the condition, rather than three chapters later with a plausible number.

few <- c("US_equity", "US_government", "GLOBAL_commodity")
head(R[, few], 3)
#>            US_equity US_government GLOBAL_commodity
#> 2101-01-31  0.025013     -0.017372          0.02562
#> 2101-02-28  0.022790     -0.006756         -0.02290
#> 2101-03-31  0.005306     -0.003734         -0.02316

The reverse crossing returns a tibble with exactly three columns, and going round the loop changes nothing.

tb <- as_pm(R)
tb
#> # A tibble: 5,952 × 3
#>    date       asset               value
#>    <date>     <chr>               <dbl>
#>  1 2101-01-31 CH_credit        -0.0301 
#>  2 2101-01-31 CH_equity        -0.0145 
#>  3 2101-01-31 CH_government    -0.0343 
#>  4 2101-01-31 EU_credit        -0.0241 
#>  5 2101-01-31 EU_equity         0.0837 
#>  6 2101-01-31 EU_government    -0.0188 
#>  7 2101-01-31 GLOBAL_commodity  0.0256 
#>  8 2101-01-31 JP_credit         0.00347
#>  9 2101-01-31 JP_equity        -0.0388 
#> 10 2101-01-31 JP_government     0.0141 
#> # ℹ 5,942 more rows
stopifnot(identical(zoo::coredata(as_xts_pm(tb, date, asset, value)),
                    zoo::coredata(R)))


1.2.1 Three ways the boundary breaks
Each failure below is manufactured from sim_class_returns_monthly, so that the message the reader will meet in practice is printed here first.
A ragged panel. Drop one row, the EU_equity observation for 2101-01-31, and cross the boundary.

ragged <- sim_class_returns_monthly[-5, ]

R_ragged <- withCallingHandlers(
  as_xts_pm(ragged, date, class, return),
  warning = function(w) { cat(conditionMessage(w), "\n"); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }
)
#> Padded 1 missing return with "NA".
#> ℹ PortfolioAnalytics will not warn about these, but they change the effective
#>   sample of every moment estimate.
#> → Handle the gaps before crossing the boundary.

na_at <- which(is.na(R_ragged), arr.ind = TRUE)
c(row = as.character(zoo::index(R_ragged))[na_at[, "row"]],
  column = colnames(R_ragged)[na_at[, "col"]])
#>          row       column 
#> "2101-01-31"  "EU_equity"

The coercion pads rather than refuses, and says so. Two consequences follow. The first is that EU_equity has moved from column 5 to column 16, because as_xts_pm() orders columns by first appearance in the table and the dropped row was that asset’s first appearance. The second is what an optimizer does with the gap. For a variance objective, set.portfolio.moments() estimates the mean with na.rm = TRUE and the covariance with use = "pairwise.complete.obs", so one column is estimated on 371 months and the other fifteen on 372, and the matrix that results is the covariance of no sample that exists. The minimum-variance problem below is the one Section 9.2 builds up properly; here it only shows that the optimizer accepts the padded matrix without comment.

spec_of <- function(x) {
  portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(x)) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
}
w_full   <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(R,        spec_of(R),        optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_ragged <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(R_ragged, spec_of(R_ragged), optimize_method = "ROI"))

w_ragged <- w_ragged[names(w_full)]            # index by name: the columns moved
max_shift <- max(abs(w_ragged - w_full))
round(c(largest_weight_change = max_shift, cells_missing = sum(is.na(R_ragged))), 4)
#> largest_weight_change         cells_missing 
#>                0.0027                1.0000

The weights move by at most 0.0027, small because one month in 372 is small; the same gap in the sixty-month windows of Section 25.2 is one month in sixty, and a sleeve of instruments that list and delist, the setting of Section 21.1, is ragged by construction. The warning is the only notice the reader gets, and it comes from the coercion, not the optimizer. Handle the gap in the long table, before crossing.
Column order. The sort order of the long table becomes the column order of the matrix. Sort it differently, as a join or a dplyr::arrange() might, and the columns come out in a different order, from the same numbers.

reordered <- sim_class_returns_monthly |> dplyr::arrange(date, dplyr::desc(class))
R_rev     <- as_xts_pm(reordered, date, class, return)

c(same_set = setequal(colnames(R), colnames(R_rev)),
  same_order = identical(colnames(R), colnames(R_rev)))
#>   same_set same_order 
#>       TRUE      FALSE
colnames(R_rev)[1:3]
#> [1] "US_government" "US_equity"     "US_credit"

Now take a weight vector built in the original order, a 60/40 portfolio of US_equity and US_government, and apply it to the reordered matrix. Return.portfolio() pairs weights with columns by position.

w <- setNames(numeric(ncol(R)), colnames(R))
w[c("US_equity", "US_government")] <- c(0.6, 0.4)

rp <- merge(PerformanceAnalytics::Return.portfolio(R_rev, weights = w),
            PerformanceAnalytics::Return.portfolio(R_rev[, names(w)], weights = w))
colnames(rp) <- c("positional", "by_name")
PerformanceAnalytics::table.AnnualizedReturns(rp, Rf = rf)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   positional by_name
#>        <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1     0.0938   0.114
#> 2     0.150    0.130
#> 3     0.464    0.692

The positional column is a portfolio of CH_equity and CH_credit, because those are the series that now occupy the positions the weights were written for, and nothing reports that it is the wrong one. The guard is the condition of Equation 1.2, that the index of the weights and the index of the columns are the same index:

tryCatch(stopifnot(identical(colnames(R_rev), names(w))),
         error = function(e) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
#> Error: identical(colnames(R_rev), names(w)) is not TRUE

w <- w[colnames(R_rev)]                          # reindex by name, then assert
stopifnot(identical(colnames(R_rev), names(w)))

The same discipline applies coming out of the optimizer. extractWeights() returns a named vector in the column order of the matrix it was fitted on, and a vector fitted on one ordering and applied by position to another mis-pairs every entry.
Duplicate keys. If a date–asset pair appears twice, the table describes no matrix, and the failure surfaces in two steps.

dup <- dplyr::bind_rows(sim_class_returns_monthly,
                        dplyr::slice_head(sim_class_returns_monthly, n = 1))

tryCatch(
  withCallingHandlers(
    as_xts_pm(dup, date, class, return),
    warning = function(w) { cat("Warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n"); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }),
  error = function(e) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
#> Warning: Values from `return` are not uniquely identified; output will contain
#> list-cols.
#> • Use `values_fn = list` to suppress this warning.
#> • Use `values_fn = {summary_fun}` to summarise duplicates.
#> • Use the following dplyr code to identify duplicates.
#>   {data} |>
#>   dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(date, class)) |>
#>   dplyr::filter(n > 1L) 
#> Error: cannot convert lists to xts objects

The warning comes from tidyr::pivot_wider() and names the cause; the error comes from xts() and names only the symptom, and a reader who sees the error alone has no way back to the duplicated pair. The check belongs before the crossing, in the long table, where the keys are columns:

dup |> dplyr::count(date, class) |> dplyr::filter(n > 1)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   date       class         n
#>   <date>     <chr>     <int>
#> 1 2101-01-31 CH_credit     2
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(sim_class_returns_monthly[c("date", "class")]))

These three chunks are the first appearance of a rule the book applies wherever two objects have to line up and nothing in the language enforces it: state the invariant as an assertion that fails the render, not as a comment. Index by name, then assert that the names agree. The rule recurs in Section 9.2, where weight vectors are indexed against the columns of the return matrix and group limits against the output of split(), and in Section 25.2, where a rolling optimization that fails in one window must not enter the record as a portfolio that did not move.

title: 1  Setting Up Your Environment
section: 1.3 A First Pass Through the Data
text:
1.3 A First Pass Through the Data

1.3.1 How the code in this book is written
Every chapter opens with the same lines, run from the project root.

source("R/_common.R")                                              # seed, options, theme
library(tidypm)                                                    # the market, the boundary
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the Treasury bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns

R/_common.R attaches the tidyverse, xts and the two analytics packages, sets the seed to 1602, sets the printing options, registers theme_tidyaa() as the default ggplot2 theme with the palette tidyaa_colors and the scale scale_colour_tidyaa(), and warns if the installed PortfolioAnalytics is not the build the lockfile records (Appendix D). The data then load in two lines and a third subtracts the bill (Section 3.1); no chapter prepares data beyond this.
Three conventions follow. Every number in the prose is computed inline from an object a chunk created, never typed. Every figure is built from one long data frame, one row per plotted thing, so that an \(x\) cannot be paired with another row’s \(y\); that frame is usually the output of as_pm(). And ggplot2’s colour argument keeps its spelling in code while the prose is American. A reader who has not written R recently will find the language itself in Appendix E.

1.3.2 The shape of the data
The matrix built above is what Section 4.1 describes and every chapter after it consumes, so its dimensions are worth reading once.

p <- xts::periodicity(R)
c(months = nrow(R), assets = ncol(R),
  from = as.character(start(R)), to = as.character(end(R)), scale = p$scale)
#>       months       assets         from           to        scale 
#>        "372"         "16" "2101-01-31" "2131-12-31"    "monthly"

372 months of 16 series, from 2101-01 to 2131-12, 31 years on a monthly grid. A figure of three of them shows the reverse crossing in use: the matrix goes back to long form, a grouped mutate compounds each series, and the plot is drawn from that one frame.

growth <- as_pm(R[, few]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(asset) |>
  dplyr::mutate(growth = cumprod(1 + value)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

ggplot2::ggplot(growth, ggplot2::aes(date, growth, colour = asset)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "growth of one dollar, log scale", colour = NULL) +
  theme_tidyaa()






Figure 1.1: Growth of one dollar in three of the sixteen series, on a log scale. Built from one long data frame, one row per date and asset, the shape as_pm() returns.




Later chapters omit the call to theme_tidyaa(), which R/_common.R has already set. One dollar in US_equity at the start of the sample is 44.6 dollars at the end, against 4.0 in US_government and 4.1 in GLOBAL_commodity.

PerformanceAnalytics::table.AnnualizedReturns(R[, few], Rf = rf) |>
  kable(digits = 3)


Table 1.2: Annualized return, volatility and Sharpe ratio for three series, from PerformanceAnalytics on the wide matrix. The bill enters as a vector aligned with the rows.

The function annualizes the bill itself and prints the rate it used. The return in the first row is compounded and the Sharpe ratio divides the excess over the bill by the volatility; Section 4.1 fixes these conventions for the book and says where the arithmetic mean is used instead.

1.3.3 Reproducibility
Three things are pinned so that a reader’s numbers match the printed ones: the seed, set once in R/_common.R; the 299 package versions in renv.lock, with freeze: auto in _quarto.yml so that a chapter is re-executed only when its source changes; and the modeled market, at dataset version 6.2.0. The last pin is the one to respect most, because the source model redraws its idiosyncratic components on every run, so a regenerated dataset is a different realized path rather than a refresh; Section 2.2 explains why regenerating it is an event. The text is executed by knitr (Xie 2015) and assembled by Quarto (Allaire et al. 2022), the arrangement of the two books this one sits beside, Scheuch et al. (2023) and Coqueret and Guida (2020), and for the same reason: a number the reader cannot recompute is a number the reader cannot check.

title: 1  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
Key Takeaways

Two data models are unavoidable. The tidy long table of Wickham (2014) is where a return panel is built, filtered and joined; the date-indexed matrix of Zeileis and Grothendieck (2005) and xts is what every function in PortfolioAnalytics and PerformanceAnalytics consumes, and it is the \(\boldsymbol{R}\) of




The boundary is crossed in a fixed direction, one call each way: as_xts_pm() from long to wide, once, after the panel is built; as_pm() from wide to long whenever a result is to be drawn.
The boundary fails in three ways, none reported downstream: a ragged panel is padded and each moment is then estimated on a different sample; a differently sorted table gives a differently ordered matrix, so weights applied by position land on the wrong assets; a duplicated key fails with an error that names only the symptom.
The guard is the same in every case: index by name, then assert that the names agree, with a stopifnot() that fails the render.
The _v1 and _v2 exports of PortfolioAnalytics are legacy shims; the book uses the unsuffixed functions. The package fetches no data and optimizes what it is given.

title: 1  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
Exercises

The five money-market series ship beside the universe as sim_money_market_monthly. Bring them across the boundary and attach them to R with merge(), then confirm that the result has 21 columns, 372 rows and no NA. Do the same in the long form, with dplyr::bind_rows() before a single call to as_xts_pm(). Which route makes the alignment check unnecessary, and why?
Remove every JP_equity row from the first three model years from sim_class_returns_monthly and cross the boundary. Report the number of observations per column, then compute the covariance matrix with use = "complete.obs" and with use = "pairwise.complete.obs" and count the entries that differ. Check whether the pairwise matrix is positive definite from its smallest eigenvalue. Which of the two would PortfolioAnalytics have used?
For each of the legacy exports listed in the callout above, determine whether an unsuffixed function of the same name exists in the namespace. Which shims have no modern counterpart, and what does the name update_constraint_v1tov2() say about how the constraint interface changed?

title: 2  Notation and Data
text:
2.1 Notation
What do the symbols mean, and where do the numbers come from? Every chapter of this book manipulates the same handful of objects, a matrix of returns, a vector of weights, a mean vector and a covariance matrix, and Markowitz (1952) needed all four before he could state the problem the rest of the book solves. Following Coqueret and Guida (2020) and Scheuch et al. (2023), whose books open the same way, we fix the notation once here so that no later chapter redefines a symbol, and we describe the two sources of data once so that no later chapter has to explain what it is computing on.
We first fix the notation and the conventions for annualizing, then describe the modeled market on which every chapter runs, its calendar and the choices that went into building it, then the real-data layer the book reaches for when a claim has to be about real markets, and finally the vocabulary that maps the names in the data onto the names the industry uses. This chapter sits on neither side of the strategic–tactical distinction that Section 3.1 defines; it is the ground both stand on.
Vectors are bold lower case, matrices are bold capitals, and a prime denotes the transpose. There are \(N\) assets observed over \(T\) periods. The object everything else is computed from is the \(T \times N\) matrix of simple returns \(\boldsymbol{R}\), whose element \(r_{t,i}\) is the return on asset \(i\) over period \(t\),
\[
r_{t,i} = \frac{P_{t,i} + D_{t,i}}{P_{t-1,i}} - 1,
\tag{2.1}\]
with \(P\) the price and \(D\) whatever the asset paid out during the period, so that every return in this book is a total return. Simple returns rather than log returns, because a portfolio’s simple return is the weighted average of its constituents’ simple returns and that linearity is what makes Equation 2.2 below true; log returns aggregate over time and not across assets, and the book aggregates across assets far more often.
The risk-free rate over period \(t\) is \(r_{f,t}\), the return on a Treasury bill bought at the start of the period and held to its end, and it is the only return in the book that is known at the start of the period it applies to. Excess returns, \(r_{t,i} - r_{f,t}\), are the default basis throughout. Every mean, covariance, Sharpe ratio and optimizer input is computed on excess returns unless a chapter says otherwise, and the risk-free asset enters an optimization as the origin of the return axis rather than as a column of the return matrix. Section 3.1 argues why: a constant column makes the covariance matrix singular, a tangency portfolio exists only relative to a risk-free rate in the sense of Tobin (1958), and only the excess formulation stays coherent when weights are allowed to sum to less than one. Here we only state the convention.
The portfolio is the vector \(\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathbb{R}^N\) of weights, one per asset, and \(\boldsymbol{\iota}\) is the vector of \(N\) ones, so that \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1\) says the portfolio is fully invested. The vector of expected excess returns is \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and the covariance matrix of excess returns is \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). Both are population quantities; an estimate of either carries a hat, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), and the distinction matters more in this book than in most, because Part III is about the gap between the two. The portfolio’s expected excess return and variance are
\[
\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad
\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
\tag{2.2}\]
and their ratio \(\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} / \sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}\) is the Sharpe ratio of Sharpe (1966), which on the excess basis needs no rate subtracted from it. Section 9.1 takes Equation 2.2 as its starting point.

title: 2  Notation and Data
text:
2.1.1 Annualizing
Returns arrive monthly and are reported annually, and the book uses two conventions for the conversion, each in its place. Under the first, a monthly mean is multiplied by twelve and a monthly standard deviation by \(\sqrt{12}\), so that a monthly Sharpe ratio is multiplied by \(\sqrt{12}\); this is exact for the mean and for the variance when returns are uncorrelated over time, and Lo (2002) gives the correction when they are not. It is the convention for anything that enters or leaves an optimizer, because \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) are arithmetic objects. Under the second, the annual return over a sample of \(T\) months is the compounded one,
\[
\bar{r}_{\text{ann}} = \Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1 + r_t)\Big)^{12/T} - 1,
\tag{2.3}\]
which is what an investor who held the series actually earned per year. It is the convention for any table describing what a series did over the sample, and for cumulative returns over an episode. Per period the compounded mean falls short of the arithmetic one by roughly half the variance, and on a volatile series that gap is not a rounding artifact: it is the variance drag, and Section 9.2 returns to it. We say which convention a number follows wherever it could matter.

The right-hand column of Table 2.1 is a convention too. Every chapter’s first code block builds the same three objects and nothing else, because universe decisions are taken once, at import, and the excess-return basis is argued once, in chapter 3. A reader who has seen the block below has seen every data-preparation step the book performs:

R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # total returns
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, nrow(R) == length(rf), !anyNA(R))

as_xts_pm() is the boundary between the tidy world, where the data are stored one row per asset per date in the sense of Wickham et al. (2023), and the wide xts matrix PortfolioAnalytics requires; Section 1.2 explains the crossing and the three ways it fails. The stopifnot() is the book’s habit rather than decoration: wherever two objects must line up and nothing in the language enforces it, the invariant is stated in code, so that a mismatch fails the render rather than producing a plausible number.
As code, the two conventions are two lines, and every table in the book uses them:

ann_ret <- function(x, p = 12) prod(1 + x)^(p / length(x)) - 1   # compounded
ann_vol <- function(x, p = 12) stats::sd(x) * sqrt(p)             # sqrt-of-time







NoteWorked: annualizing one series three ways





Take US_equity. Its monthly sample mean and standard deviation are

x   <- as.numeric(R[, "US_equity"])
m   <- mean(x)
s   <- stats::sd(x)
g   <- prod(1 + x)^(1 / length(x)) - 1          # compounded monthly mean
round(c(monthly_mean = m, monthly_sd = s, months = length(x)), 5)
#> monthly_mean   monthly_sd       months 
#>      0.01128      0.04514    372.00000

so the arithmetic annual mean is \(12 \times 0.01128 =
0.1354\), the annual volatility is \(\sqrt{12} \times 0.04514 = 0.1564\), and the compounded return of Equation 2.3 is
\[
\bar{r}_{\text{ann}}
= \Big(\prod_{t=1}^{372}(1 + r_t)\Big)^{12/372} - 1
= 44.6152^{\,0.03226} - 1
= 0.1303 .
\]
Per month, the arithmetic mean exceeds the compounded mean, \(44.6152^{\,1/372} - 1 = 0.01026\), by 0.00102, which is half the monthly variance, \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.04514^2 = 0.00102\). That is the variance drag. Between the two annual figures the gap is smaller, 0.0051 against half the annual variance of 0.0122, because the compounded figure also earns return on return within the year, 0.0072, and twelve times a monthly mean does not. The same arithmetic in code:

round(c(arithmetic = 12 * m, compounded = ann_ret(x), volatility = ann_vol(x),
        monthly_gap = m - g, half_monthly_variance = 0.5 * s^2,
        annual_gap = 12 * m - ann_ret(x), half_annual_variance = 0.5 * ann_vol(x)^2,
        return_on_return = (1 + g)^12 - 1 - 12 * g), 5)
#>            arithmetic            compounded            volatility 
#>               0.13541               0.13034               0.15638 
#>           monthly_gap half_monthly_variance            annual_gap 
#>               0.00102               0.00102               0.00507 
#>  half_annual_variance      return_on_return 
#>               0.01223               0.00719

title: 2  Notation and Data
text:
2.2 The Modeled Market
The default data of this book is a modeled market, and it contains no real data. Factor models for government bonds, credit, equities and commodities were estimated by historical simulation on market data from 1992 to 2022; the factors were replayed, the idiosyncratic components drawn afresh, and the asset paths reassembled, so that no series is the history of a real security. The market therefore runs on its own calendar, model years 1 to 31. Its stress episodes are named for what happens in them and ship as the table sim_episodes. And because every series is the output of a factor model, the market can be re-run with its factors shocked, which a history cannot, and Appendix H does so.
Because it contains no real data, the whole market ships inside tidypm and every number in this book reproduces offline, for every reader. The risk-free rate, a three-month Treasury bill, and the exchange rates enter the model as inputs. What the estimation on market data buys is realism of structure: the stress episodes arrive in the right places and with the right relative magnitudes, which Section 4.3 relies on.

2.2.1 The model calendar
Because the data are modeled rather than recorded, a date in this market is a position on the model’s own calendar, not a point in history. The dates are stored as ordinary Date objects, so that xts needs no special cases, but their years are not calendar years. Four tools translate them, the same four in every chapter: model_year() and in_episode() from tidypm, and fmt_model() and scale_x_model() from the book’s setup script, R/_common.R.
model_year() turns a date into its model year, and fmt_model() writes a date the way the prose does:

d <- zoo::index(R)                                   # the month ends of the sample
range(d)                                             # as stored
#> [1] "2101-01-31" "2131-12-31"
range(model_year(d))                                 # as read
#> [1]  1 31
fmt_model(range(d))                                  # as written
#> [1] "January of model year 1"   "December of model year 31"
worst <- d[which.min(as.numeric(R[, "US_equity"]))]  # a position is derived, never typed
fmt_model(worst)
#> [1] "March of model year 29"

The sample is thus 372 months, model years 1 to 31, and a point in it is named the way the worst month of US_equity is: March of model year 29, or simply model year 29. The stress episodes are the rows of sim_episodes, shown in Table 2.2, and the text calls each by its label.

2.2.2 The class universe
The allocation spine of the book is the table sim_class_returns_monthly: sixteen risky class series, five currencies (US, UK, EU, CH, JP) times three classes (government, credit, equity) plus one global commodity index, over 372 complete months, the 31 model years, everything in US dollars and unhedged. A weekly counterpart, sim_class_returns_weekly, holds the same market at the model’s native frequency, on 1618 weekly dates.

colnames(R)
#>  [1] "CH_credit"        "CH_equity"        "CH_government"    "EU_credit"       
#>  [5] "EU_equity"        "EU_government"    "GLOBAL_commodity" "JP_credit"       
#>  [9] "JP_equity"        "JP_government"    "UK_credit"        "UK_equity"       
#> [13] "UK_government"    "US_credit"        "US_equity"        "US_government"

Five money-market series, one per region, ship beside the universe as sim_money_market_monthly and are deliberately not in it. Each is the 0.25-year point on a curve fitted to that region’s two, five and ten-year yields, marked to market: a short-duration bond rather than a bill held to maturity, and so not the risk-free rate either. One calculation settles the point:

M  <- as_xts_pm(sim_money_market_monthly, date, class, return)
stopifnot(all(as.Date(zoo::index(M)) == as.Date(zoo::index(R))))
mm <- as.numeric(M[, "US_money_market"])

round(c(negative_months_money_market = mean(mm < 0),
        negative_months_bill         = mean(rf < 0),
        correlation                  = stats::cor(mm, rf)), 3)
#> negative_months_money_market         negative_months_bill 
#>                        0.188                        0.003 
#>                  correlation 
#>                        0.930

US_money_market tracks the bill at a correlation of 0.93, and is negative in 19% of months against the bill’s 0.3%. A risk-free rate has to be riskless over the holding period. The four foreign money markets have almost no duration and are, unhedged in dollars, nearly pure currency positions. The money markets are there for the chapters that need a short-duration asset or a currency exposure; sim_riskfree_monthly is the risk-free rate everywhere.

2.2.3 How the class series are built
Each equity class is the value-weighted return of its constituent securities, weighted on their market capitalization at the previous weekly observation, never the contemporaneous one, so no portfolio is formed on information it could not have had; the capitalizations are sim_marketcap_weekly, which reaches back before model year 1 so that a prior week exists even for the first return date. Government, credit and commodity classes are equally weighted, because no capitalization exists for a constant-maturity bond or a commodity index. The weekly frequency is the model’s own, and a monthly class return is the compounded weekly return within the month: every monthly date is a month end, every week lies in the month it compounds into, and the monthly series is the weekly-rebalanced portfolio observed at month ends, not a monthly-rebalanced one. That can be checked rather than believed:

weekly_compounded <- sim_class_returns_weekly |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(class, month) |>
  dplyr::summarise(compounded = prod(1 + return) - 1, .groups = "drop")

both <- sim_class_returns_monthly |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(weekly_compounded, by = c("class", "month"))

stopifnot(nrow(both) == nrow(sim_class_returns_monthly),
          all(both$date == lubridate::ceiling_date(both$month, "month") - 1),   # month ends
          min(sim_marketcap_weekly$date) < min(sim_class_returns_weekly$date)) # a prior week
max(abs(both$return - both$compounded))
#> [1] 0.0000000000000007945

2.2.5 Exchange rates, curves, capitalizations and rating changes
Three further tables let a chapter show what moved a series rather than only its return, and a fourth carries sustainability information. sim_fx_monthly and sim_fx_weekly hold the exchange rate of each of the four non-dollar currencies, quoted as dollars per unit of the local currency, so that a positive fx_return means the local currency appreciated and an unhedged dollar investor gained. Because every series is unhedged in dollars, a foreign holding carries its local return and its currency’s move together, and the hedged return is one subtraction away:
\[
r^{\text{hedged}}_{t} = r^{\text{unhedged}}_{t} - f_{t},
\tag{2.4}\]
with \(f_t\) the matching fx_return. That is the whole of currency hedging as this book implements it; whether to hedge, and how much, is the question of Perold and Schulman (1988) and Campbell et al. (2010), which Section 4.3 opens and Section 15.2 settles for the strategic portfolio.

fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedged_vol <- function(series, region) {
  f <- fx[fx$region == region, ]
  stopifnot(all(f$date == as.Date(zoo::index(R))))      # same grid, same order
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  c(unhedged = ann_vol(u), hedged = ann_vol(u - f$fx_return))
}
regions <- c("UK", "EU", "CH", "JP")
gov <- t(sapply(regions, function(r) hedged_vol(paste0(r, "_government"), r)))
rownames(gov) <- paste0(regions, "_government")
jp_equity <- hedged_vol("JP_equity", "JP")
round(rbind(gov, JP_equity = jp_equity), 3)
#>               unhedged hedged
#> UK_government    0.095  0.048
#> EU_government    0.098  0.039
#> CH_government    0.109  0.033
#> JP_government    0.107  0.031
#> JP_equity        0.196  0.212

Hedging takes JP_government from 10.7% to 3.1% and does not lower JP_equity at all, which moves from 19.6% to 21.2%; Section 4.3 explains why the two differ.
sim_curve_weekly holds the drivers of the bond block: for each region the level, slope and curvature of a Nelson and Siegel (1987) yield curve, in the dynamic form of Diebold and Li (2006) which Section 22.2 takes up, plus an investment-grade and a high-yield credit spread per region, ten spreads in all.

sort(unique(sim_curve_weekly$series))
#>  [1] "CH_Curvature" "CH_HY_Spread" "CH_IG_Spread" "CH_Level"     "CH_Slope"    
#>  [6] "EU_Curvature" "EU_HY_Spread" "EU_IG_Spread" "EU_Level"     "EU_Slope"    
#> [11] "JP_Curvature" "JP_HY_Spread" "JP_IG_Spread" "JP_Level"     "JP_Slope"    
#> [16] "UK_Curvature" "UK_HY_Spread" "UK_IG_Spread" "UK_Level"     "UK_Slope"    
#> [21] "US_Curvature" "US_HY_Spread" "US_IG_Spread" "US_Level"     "US_Slope"

sim_marketcap_weekly holds the weekly market capitalization of the 123 equities, which is what a capitalization-weighted benchmark needs and what Section 21.2 builds one from.
sim_esg_changes_quarterly records changes in an ESG rating of the equities, one row per change, dated at the quarter end: 1113 integer changes on 122 of the 123 equities, from model year 11 on. The table carries changes only and no starting level, so cumulating them gives a rating up to an unknown constant, and the changes have no effect on the returns; Section 20.2 works with them.

2.2.6 Three caveats, one departure, and a frozen version
Three properties of the market are consequences of how it is built, and a reader should know them before modeling on it.
Currency dominates foreign bonds. Hedging removes on average 63% of a foreign government bond’s dollar volatility, as the calculation above shows, and a foreign money market is almost entirely currency. Only US and GLOBAL series are free of it.
The bond block is nearly rank-deficient at instrument level. Three maturities per region are priced off a three-factor curve, and the two credit grades at each maturity share one credit factor, so some bond combinations are near-exact replicas of others. The covariance matrix of the 181 instruments is technically invertible and practically not:

A <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly, date, asset, return)
stopifnot(ncol(A) == nrow(sim_assets), setequal(colnames(A), sim_assets$asset_id))

log10_condition <- function(X) {
  e <- eigen(stats::cov(X), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  log10(max(e) / min(e))
}
round(c(sixteen_classes = log10_condition(R), instruments = log10_condition(A)), 1)
#> sixteen_classes     instruments 
#>             4.1            12.2

A condition number of \(10^{12.2}\) means that unconstrained mean-variance at instrument level produces nonsense, which is worth demonstrating rather than preventing, and it is why the sleeve chapters shrink the matrix in the manner of Ledoit and Wolf (2004) or constrain the weights. At class level the number is \(10^{4.1}\) and the problem does not exist; Section 7.1 is about the difference.
Equity series are single securities. The median annualized volatility of the 123 names is 31%, which is realistic for one security, but a portfolio of these names diversifies more readily than a real index would, because the names are few and their idiosyncratic components are drawn independently of one another.
One departure from the estimated model is deliberate and is stated as a parameter rather than hidden. Every euro-area equity carries an expected-return overlay of three percentage points a year, added as a constant drift. It is a capital-market assumption, not a measurement, and the sample says why it was needed:

overlay <- 0.03
eq      <- classes[classes$kind == "equity", ]
vol     <- setNames(eq$vol, eq$class)
without <- setNames(eq$ret - ifelse(eq$class == "EU_equity", overlay, 0), eq$class)
sharpe_without <- (without - ann_ret(rf)) / vol
eu      <- as.numeric(R[, "EU_equity"])
se_mean <- ann_vol(eu) / sqrt(nrow(R) / 12)     # sigma / sqrt(years)
stopifnot(overlay < se_mean,
          names(which.max(vol)) == "EU_equity",
          all(sharpe_without[c("US_equity", "UK_equity", "CH_equity")] >
                sharpe_without[["EU_equity"]]))

# The long-only tangency portfolio of chapter 9, with the overlay and without.
spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")
tangency <- function(X) {
  extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE))
}
Re_without <- Re
Re_without[, "EU_equity"] <- Re[, "EU_equity"] - overlay / 12
w_eu <- c(with    = tangency(Re)[["EU_equity"]],
          without = tangency(Re_without)[["EU_equity"]])
stopifnot(w_eu[["with"]] > 0.01, w_eu[["without"]] < 0.001)

round(c(return_without    = without[["EU_equity"]],
        sharpe_without    = sharpe_without[["EU_equity"]],
        cor_with_UK       = stats::cor(eu, as.numeric(R[, "UK_equity"])),
        cor_with_CH       = stats::cor(eu, as.numeric(R[, "CH_equity"])),
        tangency_with     = w_eu[["with"]],
        tangency_without  = w_eu[["without"]],
        se_of_annual_mean = se_mean,
        overlay_in_se     = overlay / se_mean), 2)
#>    return_without    sharpe_without       cor_with_UK       cor_with_CH 
#>              0.11              0.42              0.75              0.72 
#>     tangency_with  tangency_without se_of_annual_mean     overlay_in_se 
#>              0.09              0.00              0.04              0.79

Without the overlay, EU_equity earns 11.2% a year at the highest volatility of the five equity markets, a Sharpe ratio of 0.42 where the United States, Britain and Switzerland have 0.69, 0.50 and 0.46, and it correlates at 0.75 with Britain and 0.72 with Switzerland. The long-only tangency portfolio of Section 9.1 then holds none of it, against 9% with the overlay, and every chapter that trades return against risk would have carried a dead column. The overlay is 0.8 standard errors of the sample mean, so within one; by the argument of Merton (1980) that standard error depends only on the span of the sample in years, and 31 model years cannot distinguish a three-point assumption from the measured mean. No other series carries an overlay, and Appendix A records this one beside every other modeling choice.
Finally, the dataset is frozen at version 6.2.0. The idiosyncratic components are one draw, so a regenerated export is a different realized path rather than an update, and the drift is uneven across moments. Regenerating it is an event, not a refresh: every printed number in this book is pinned to 6.2.0, and the book’s repository carries a script that recomputes the load-bearing ones and names those a new export has moved. The full description of every series, its construction, its units and its known limitations is Appendix A.

title: 2  Notation and Data
text:
2.3 The Real Data Sleeves
The modeled market is the default because every number reproduces offline for every reader. It cannot, by construction, support a claim about real markets, and some chapters have to make one: Section 21.2 measures factor premia on Kenneth French’s portfolios, and Section 25.3 notes that every asset in the modeled market survives to the end of the sample, a survivorship bias by construction that the real sleeves do not share. For those, tidypm carries a small data layer built the way Scheuch et al. (2023) build theirs, from free public sources, with two additions: a pinned cutoff date and a manifest.
The layer begins with a registry. pm_sources() is a list with one entry per sleeve, naming its source and carrying the function that fetches it. The registry is data rather than state; calling it downloads nothing.



Table 2.5: The sleeve registry of pm_sources(). A sleeve with no fetch function is declared so that the gap is visible rather than implied.

8 of the 12 sleeves are built. Three equity sleeves and the cash sleeve come from Kenneth French’s data library, the market returns and risk-free rate behind Fama and French (1993); two government sleeves and an investment-grade credit sleeve are constructed from FRED yields by pricing a constant-maturity bond, which is the calculation Section 22.1 sets out; and high yield is a long-running mutual fund, because every free high-yield index history has been withdrawn behind a rolling window. Two caveats on that last sleeve belong here rather than in a footnote: a managed fund holding higher-quality high yield understates drawdowns, the wrong direction for the one sleeve whose reason to exist is its left tail, and its source is undocumented and could disappear, so the cache protects a reader who has already built the panel and not one arriving in ten years.
pm_init() walks the registry, downloads each implemented sleeve, joins them on the month-end date and writes the result, together with a manifest, to a single file in pm_cache_dir(), a directory in the user’s R cache outside any project and overridable through the environment variable TIDYPM_CACHE. It stops at a pinned cutoff, exported as a constant so that a chapter can name it rather than repeat a literal:

PM_CUTOFF
#> [1] "2025-12-31"

The cutoff is a calendar year end so that every annual table is a complete year and no chapter carries a stub year in which the sources, which publish at different speeds, have not all arrived. Run once, and read forever after:

pm_init()                       # downloads once, writes the panel and its manifest
panel <- pm_data()              # a disk read: no network, no recomputation
pm_data(sleeves = c("us_equity", "gov_long"), from = "1990-07-01")
pm_check()                      # your build against the manifest the book was built on

pm_data() never reaches the network. If no panel has been cached it stops and says to run pm_init(), because a function that silently downloads behaves differently on a plane. The panel it returns is deliberately ragged: a sleeve whose source starts later than the others is NA until it begins, and nothing pads or fills those rows, because a filled gap is an estimate dressed as an observation, and a covariance matrix estimated across one silently changes its effective sample, which is the failure as_xts_pm() warns about in Section 1.2.
The manifest is the honest version of reproducibility for data that is not ours to redistribute. French and FRED both revise history, so a panel rebuilt today need not equal the one the book’s numbers were computed on. pm_init() records an observation count and a hash per sleeve; pm_check() compares a reader’s manifest against the book’s and names the sleeves that moved, rather than leaving the difference to surface as an unexplained mismatch three chapters later. No downloaded file is committed to the book’s repository, and Appendix D records the version of every package the pipeline depends on.

The data uses one set of names and the industry another, and both appear in this book. Table 2.6 maps one onto the other. The rule is that code uses the data’s names, because a column is called what it is called, and prose uses whichever is clearer, which is usually the industry’s.

One word in the table deserves a sentence. Alternatives usually covers real estate, hedge funds, private equity and commodities together; this market carries only the last, so the word appears only where the industry’s usage is being quoted.
The class level of Table 2.3 is where Parts III to V of the book work, and it is the level at which the allocation literature since Brinson et al. (1986) locates most of the variation in a diversified portfolio’s return; the instrument level of Table 2.4 belongs to Part VI. Which of the two an allocation is set at is a question of granularity. Whether it is set from long-run assumptions or from conditioning information is a different question, that of horizon, and the words for its two answers, strategic and tactical, are defined in Section 3.1 rather than here.

title: 2  Notation and Data
text:
Key Takeaways

Vectors are bold lower case, matrices bold capitals, estimates carry hats. \(\boldsymbol{R}\) is the \(T \times N\) matrix of simple total returns, \(\boldsymbol{w}\) the weights, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) the moments of excess returns, and Equation 2.2 gives the portfolio’s mean and variance. Excess over the bill is the default basis everywhere; chapter 3 says why.
Arithmetic annualizing, mean \(\times 12\) and volatility \(\times\sqrt{12}\), is for anything that enters an optimizer. The compounded return of Equation 2.3 is for what a series earned. Per period, the gap is half the variance.
The modeled market contains no real data, so no series is the history of a real security, and it runs on model years 1 to


model_year(), in_episode(), fmt_model() and scale_x_model() are how every chapter reads a date, and the four stress episodes are the rows of sim_episodes.


The market is sixteen risky class series over 372 months, five currencies times government, credit and equity plus a global commodity index, all in dollars and unhedged, with 181 instruments beneath them. The five money markets ship beside the universe and are neither cash nor the risk-free rate; the bill is.
Currency dominates foreign bonds, the bond block is nearly rank-deficient at instrument level, and equities are single names. Euro-area equity carries a deliberate three-point overlay, within one standard error of its sample mean. The dataset is frozen at version 6.2.0 because regenerating it redraws the idiosyncratic components.
Real data enters through pm_sources(), pm_init(), pm_data() and pm_check(): a registry, one download to a cache with a pinned cutoff, an offline read, and a manifest that names the sleeves that have moved since the book was built. It is used where a claim has to be about real markets.

title: 2  Notation and Data
text:
Exercises

Apply Equation 2.4 to all twelve non-US series in R, using sim_fx_monthly, and tabulate the unhedged and hedged annualized volatility with the share of variance the hedge removes. Group the result by asset class. Why does hedging remove most of a bond’s volatility and almost none of an equity market’s, and what does that say about treating currency as one decision per country?
Rebuild GLOBAL_commodity at weekly frequency as the equally weighted mean of its eight instruments in sim_asset_returns_weekly, then compound to months and compare with sim_class_returns_monthly. How close do you get, and what does the answer tell you about how the non-equity classes are constructed?
Rebuild US_equity at weekly frequency two ways: equally weighted across its instruments, and value-weighted on the previous week’s capitalization from sim_marketcap_weekly. Confirm that the second reproduces the shipped series, then compare the annualized return and the correlation of the two. Which one should a benchmark use, and why does the choice move the return by as much as it does?

title: 3  Return, Risk, and the Investor’s Problem
text:
3.1 Returns, Horizons, and the Basis of Comparison
What does an investor want from a portfolio, and in which units should the answer be measured? Markowitz (1952) reduced the first question to two numbers per portfolio, an expected return and a variance, and the reduction has held up well enough that most of this book is built on it. The second question is older and is usually skipped. Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) gave the criterion that ranks risky prospects by their expected utility, and every mean-variance objective is an approximation to that criterion whose quality depends on how a return is defined, over which horizon, in which currency, and relative to which riskless alternative. Those definitions are fixed here once, so that no later chapter has to revisit them.
We first fix the return conventions: simple against log returns, arithmetic against geometric means, annualization, and how a Sharpe ratio aggregates over a horizon. We make excess returns the book’s basis and say what nominal, real and currency mean for it. We state the investor’s problem as expected utility, derive the mean-variance criterion and the certainty equivalent from it, and say what the risk-aversion parameter \(\gamma\) means in basis points. We define mean-variance dominance and the northwest rule, show where \(\gamma\) enters PortfolioAnalytics and what raising it does on the sixteen class series, and close by defining strategic and tactical allocation for the rest of the book. On that horizon axis this chapter is neither strategic nor tactical: it is where the terms are defined, and the last part of Section 3.1 says which later chapters are which.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, loaded as every chapter loads them, in the symbols of Section 2.1: \(\boldsymbol{R}\) for the matrix of total returns, \(r_f\) for the Treasury bill, \(\boldsymbol{R}^e\) for the difference. The environment is the one Section 1.2 builds.
crumbs: 3  Return, Risk, and the Investor's Problem

title: 3  Return, Risk, and the Investor’s Problem
text:
3.1.1 Simple returns, log returns, and compounding
A simple return over one period is the change in value relative to the value at the start, income included, and a log return is its logarithm:
\[
R_t = \frac{P_t + D_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1,
\qquad
r_t = \log\left(1 + R_t\right).
\tag{3.1}\]
The two aggregate in opposite directions. Simple returns add across assets: the return on a portfolio with weights \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{R}_t\), which is why every weight vector in this book multiplies a matrix of simple returns. Log returns add across time. Over \(T\) periods,
\[
1 + R_{0,T} = \prod_{t=1}^{T}\left(1 + R_t\right) = \exp\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t\right),
\tag{3.2}\]
so a multi-period simple return is a product and the matching log return is a sum. The shipped data are simple monthly returns, and they stay simple wherever a portfolio is formed. Log returns appear only where a horizon is aggregated.

3.1.2 Averages, annualization, and the variance drag
There are two averages of a return series and they answer different questions. The arithmetic mean \(\hat\mu = T^{-1}\sum_t R_t\) is the expected one-period return and the quantity \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) that enters every objective in this book, because variance is defined around it. The geometric mean \(g = \left(\prod_t (1 + R_t)\right)^{1/T} - 1\) is the constant return that would have produced the same terminal wealth, and it is what an investor who held the asset actually earned per period. To second order,
\[
\log(1 + g) \approx \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2},
\tag{3.3}\]
where \(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the simple return. The gap is the variance drag, half the variance lost to compounding. It is small for a government bond and not small for an equity market, and it lets a series have the higher arithmetic mean and the lower geometric one, a case Section 3.3 meets on this data.
Monthly moments are annualized by
\[
\mu_{\text{a}} = 12\,\mu_{\text{m}},
\qquad
\sigma_{\text{a}} = \sqrt{12}\,\sigma_{\text{m}},
\qquad
1 + g_{\text{a}} = \left(1 + g_{\text{m}}\right)^{12}.
\tag{3.4}\]
The first two follow from independence across months: the mean of a sum is the sum of the means, and so is the variance, so the standard deviation grows with the square root of the horizon. The third is compounding. Two mistakes follow from mixing them. Multiplying a geometric monthly mean by twelve understates the compounded annual return, and multiplying a monthly standard deviation by \(\sqrt{12}\) is wrong whenever monthly returns are autocorrelated, because the variance of a sum then carries covariance terms that independence set to zero.

3.1.3 The Sharpe ratio and its horizon
The ratio of expected excess return to standard deviation was introduced by Sharpe (1966) as a measure of fund performance and restated by Sharpe (1994) in the form the industry uses:
\[
\text{SR} = \frac{\mu - r_f}{\sigma} = \frac{\mu^e}{\sigma^e}.
\tag{3.5}\]
Under independence the numerator scales with \(T\) and the denominator with \(\sqrt{T}\), so the ratio over \(q\) periods is \(\sqrt{q}\) times the one-period ratio, and \(\sqrt{12}\) turns a monthly Sharpe ratio into an annual one. Lo (2002) derived the general case. With autocorrelations \(\rho_k\) at lags \(k = 1, \ldots, q - 1\),
\[
\text{SR}_q = \text{SR}_1 \cdot
\frac{q}{\sqrt{q + 2\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}(q - k)\,\rho_k}},
\tag{3.6}\]
which reduces to \(\sqrt{q}\,\text{SR}_1\) when every \(\rho_k\) is zero. Positive autocorrelation makes the naive \(\sqrt{q}\) overstate the annual ratio, negative autocorrelation makes it understate it, and Section 3.2 measures the error on this data.

3.1.4 Excess returns as the basis
Every return this book optimizes over is measured in excess of the Treasury bill,
\[
R^e_{it} = R_{it} - r_{f,t},
\tag{3.7}\]
for four reasons, in increasing order of consequence.
First, the objects the theory talks about are defined relative to a riskless rate. Tobin (1958) showed that when a riskless asset exists, every investor holds the same portfolio of risky assets and differs only in how much of it is held against the riskless asset; the tangency portfolio at the center of that result is the point where a ray from \(r_f\) touches the frontier, and it moves when \(r_f\) moves. Sharpe (1964) builds the market equilibrium on the same portfolio. Neither exists without a riskless rate to measure from.
Second, PortfolioAnalytics has no argument for one. optimize.portfolio() takes a return matrix and a specification, and its maximum-Sharpe objective maximizes the ratio of mean to standard deviation over zero. Handing it excess returns is the only way to make that ratio the Sharpe ratio of Equation 3.5.
Third, when the weights may sum to less than one, the objective treats the balance as earning exactly zero. With total returns that is false, because the balance earns the bill. With excess returns it is true, because the balance earns zero excess return. Section 3.3 shows by how much the difference raises the invested fraction at the same risk aversion.
Fourth, the bill moves. Under rebalancing the riskless rate is a different number in every period, so a total-return objective compares each period’s assets against a different alternative, while the excess formulation subtracts each period’s own bill and is the only one consistent through time.

rate <- sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual
c(first = rate[1], lowest = min(rate), highest = max(rate), last = rate[length(rate)])
#>   first  lowest highest    last 
#>  0.0384 -0.0001  0.0619  0.0430

The bill paid 3.8% a year in January of model year 1 and -0.01% at its lowest, in September of model year 24; an objective that compares risky assets against zero in both periods is wrong in at least one.
The riskless rate is sim_riskfree_monthly, the three-month Treasury bill, and not any of the five money-market series. Those are marked-to-market quarter-year bonds, they carry duration, and they lose money in far more months than the bill does; Section 4.2 measures the difference. A riskless asset has to be riskless over the holding period, and only the bill is.

3.1.5 Nominal and real
Every return above is nominal. A real return removes inflation \(\pi\) through the relation of Fisher (1930),
\[
1 + i = (1 + r)(1 + \pi), \qquad r \approx i - \pi,
\tag{3.8}\]
with \(i\) the nominal and \(r\) the real rate. The modeled market carries no inflation series, so this book works in nominal dollars throughout, and the bill is riskless in nominal terms only. An investor whose liabilities are real, a pension fund or an endowment spending a fixed share of purchasing power, would measure every return in excess of realized inflation, would find the bill risky over any horizon longer than its maturity, and would treat an inflation-indexed bond as the riskless asset. Campbell and Viceira (2002) develop that investor’s problem in full, and Campbell and Viceira (2001) show that for a long-horizon investor the indexed bond, not the bill, is the safe asset. Nothing in the machinery of later chapters changes for such an investor; only the series handed to it does.

3.1.6 Currency
Every series in the modeled market is a dollar return, unhedged. A foreign asset’s dollar return compounds its local return with the return \(f_t\) on its currency, quoted as dollars per unit of local currency so that a positive \(f_t\) means the local currency appreciated:
\[
1 + R^{\$}_t = \left(1 + R^{\text{loc}}_t\right)\left(1 + f_t\right),
\qquad
R^{\text{hedged}}_t = R^{\$}_t - f_t \approx R^{\text{loc}}_t .
\tag{3.9}\]
Hedging in this book is therefore a subtraction: the matching fx_return from sim_fx_monthly is removed from the unhedged series, to first order. A forward hedge also earns the interest differential between the two currencies, which the data do not carry, so the convention is the spot return alone, and Section 15.2 and Section 22.1 keep it. Perold and Schulman (1988) argued that hedging removes volatility at no expected cost, a free lunch; Black (1989) derived a single universal hedge ratio for every investor; Campbell et al. (2010) found that the answer differs between bonds, which should be fully hedged, and equities, whose currencies covary with the local market in ways that sometimes hedge them for free. Section 4.3 decomposes the variance of a foreign series into its local and currency parts, and Section 3.2 shows what the subtraction does to a foreign government bond.

3.1.7 The investor’s objective
Write \(W_0\) for initial wealth, \(\boldsymbol{w}\) for the weights on the risky assets, and \(1 - \boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w}\) for the balance in the bill. The investor of Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) chooses the weights that maximize the expected utility of terminal wealth,
\[
\max_{\boldsymbol{w}} \; \mathbb{E}\!\left[U(W_1)\right],
\qquad
W_1 = W_0\left(1 + r_f + \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{R}^e\right),
\tag{3.10}\]
for a utility function \(U\) that is increasing and concave. Concavity is risk aversion, and Pratt (1964) and Arrow (1965) measured it: the coefficient of absolute risk aversion is \(A(W) = -U''(W)/U'(W)\), the coefficient of relative risk aversion is \(\gamma(W) = W A(W)\), and an investor with relative risk aversion \(\gamma\) facing a return with variance \(\sigma^2\) demands a premium, as a fraction of wealth, of approximately
\[
\text{premium} \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,\gamma\,\sigma^2 .
\tag{3.11}\]
A second-order expansion of Equation 3.10 around expected terminal wealth turns it into a function of two moments. Dropping the terms that do not depend on \(\boldsymbol{w}\), the investor maximizes
\[
U(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}}
= \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
\tag{3.12}\]
with \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) the mean vector and covariance matrix of the excess returns. This is the mean-variance criterion of Markowitz (1952), and Markowitz (1959) gave the two conditions under which the expansion is exact: \(U\) is itself quadratic, or returns are normal so that every higher moment is a function of the first two. Neither holds for the series of this book, and the question is what that costs. Levy and Markowitz (1979) compared the expected utility of the mean-variance optimum with that of the true optimum across utility functions and historical returns and found the two almost perfectly correlated; Markowitz (2014) revisited the evidence with thirty more years of data and reached the same conclusion. The approximation fails where returns are far from normal, and Section 11.1 takes up that case by adding skewness and kurtosis to Equation 3.12 rather than abandoning it.
Two readings of Equation 3.12 are worth having. First, \(U(\boldsymbol{w})\) is a certainty equivalent: the riskless excess return the investor would accept in place of the portfolio, the expected return less the premium of Equation 3.11 applied to the portfolio’s own variance. Second, \(\gamma\) is a price. Along an indifference curve \(U(\boldsymbol{w})\) is constant, so an increase in expected return of \(\Delta\mu\) buys an increase in variance of
\[
\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_0^2 = \frac{2\,\Delta\mu}{\gamma},
\tag{3.13}\]
and the price has units. With \(\Delta\mu\) one percentage point and \(\sigma_0 = 0\), an investor with \(\gamma = 2\) accepts a volatility of \(\sqrt{0.02 / 2} = 10.0%\) for one point of expected return; one with \(\gamma = 10\) accepts \(\sqrt{0.02 / 10} = 4.5%\). Read the other way, ten percent of volatility costs an investor with \(\gamma = 4\) a certainty equivalent of \(\tfrac{4}{2} \times 0.10^2 =
200\) basis points a year.



Table 3.1: What the risk-aversion parameter means in units an investor recognizes. Each row is computed from Equation 3.13 with one percentage point of expected return on one side, from cash and from a portfolio with ten percent volatility, and from Equation 3.12 for the certainty-equivalent cost of ten percent volatility.
