Table 3.1 is the table to keep in mind whenever a chapter reports a \(\gamma\). The customary range in the literature runs from about two to about ten, and the data give one more anchor: an investor who holds the US equity market and nothing else, and is at an optimum, has \(\gamma = \mu^e / \sigma^2\) by the first-order condition of Equation 3.12 with one asset.

mu_us <- mean(Re[, "US_equity"]) * 12
sd_us <- stats::sd(Re[, "US_equity"]) * sqrt(12)
c(excess_return = mu_us, volatility = sd_us, implied_gamma = mu_us / sd_us^2)
#> excess_return    volatility implied_gamma 
#>        0.1130        0.1562        4.6332

On this sample that investor has \(\gamma = 0.113 /
0.156^2 = 4.6\).
The alternative to quadratic utility that the rest of the literature uses is constant relative risk aversion, \(U(W) = W^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\), under which the premium of Equation 3.11 is the same fraction of wealth at every level of wealth. When returns are lognormal, maximizing expected power utility is equivalent to maximizing \(\mu - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2\) in log returns with the same \(\gamma\), so the two objectives agree exactly on that distribution and approximately on any distribution close to it. The disagreements are in the tails, and Section 11.1 measures them on the credit series where they matter.

3.1.8 The horizon of the problem
Equation 3.10 is a one-period problem, and a reader may object that the investor lives for many. Samuelson (1969) in discrete time and Merton (1969) in continuous time solved the multi-period problem for a power-utility investor and found that when returns are independent across periods and the investment opportunities do not change, the optimal weights are the same in every period and at every horizon: the long-lived investor behaves myopically, and the one-period rule is exact. When opportunities do change, because the riskless rate or the expected returns move, the long-horizon investor holds additional positions that hedge those changes, which is the case Campbell and Viceira (2002) treat and the reason their safe asset is the indexed bond. This book solves the one-period problem throughout and re-solves it at each rebalancing date, which is the myopic policy; the chapters on the horizon axis, defined below, are about how the inputs to that policy are formed rather than about intertemporal hedging.

3.1.9 Dominance, efficiency, and the northwest rule
Two moments per portfolio make comparison a matter of geometry. In the plane with volatility on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical, portfolio \(A\) dominates portfolio \(B\) if it offers at least as much return for at most as much risk, with strictly more of one or strictly less of the other:
\[
A \succ B
\iff
\mu_A \ge \mu_B \;\text{ and }\; \sigma_A \le \sigma_B,
\;\text{ with at least one inequality strict.}
\tag{3.14}\]
The relation has a direction. A dominating portfolio lies above, to the left, or both: a better allocation always lies to the northwest. A portfolio or asset that no feasible alternative dominates is efficient, and the set of efficient portfolios is the efficient frontier that Section 9.1 derives. Equation 3.14 is weaker than Equation 3.12, because it ranks only pairs one of which is northwest of the other and says nothing about a pair where one has more return and more risk; the utility function settles those by choosing a point on the frontier. It is also stronger in one respect: a dominated portfolio is rejected by every investor with any \(\gamma > 0\), so the vocabulary applies before a risk aversion is chosen, and every chapter from here on uses dominated and efficient in this sense.

3.1.10 Strategic and tactical allocation
Two distinct cuts run through the book and are easily confused. The first is granularity: allocate across asset classes, then select within a class, which is the order of the parts. The second is horizon, and it needs two terms that are defined here once.
Strategic allocation is the long-run policy: the portfolio an investor would hold given unconditional beliefs about the assets, with \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) estimated over the whole available history and no attempt to time anything. Tactical allocation is a deviation from that policy using conditioning information available at the time: a signal, a regime, a view. The two are orthogonal to granularity, because a tactical tilt can be taken across classes and a permanent tilt inside a sleeve is strategic. Brinson et al. (1986) and Brinson et al. (1991) measured how much of the variation in a set of pension funds’ returns the policy alone explained and found most of it; Ibbotson and Kaplan (2000) clarified what that number does and does not mean, in particular that it says nothing about the level of return the policy earns. Sharpe (1987) gave the framework in which the two are stages of one decision, the policy set from capital-market assumptions and the tactical position from the same assumptions updated with current information, and Ang (2014) organizes an entire treatment of asset management around the strategic question of which bad times an investor can bear. The strategic policy is itself an estimate from a finite history, and DeMiguel et al. (2009) measured what that costs out of sample.
The chapters of this book sort as follows. Chapters 9 to 14 and chapter 15 are strategic: they solve Equation 3.12 and its relatives from full-sample moments, and Section 9.1 opens by saying so. Chapters 16 to 19 are tactical: they condition the inputs on information available at the time, beginning with Section 16.1. Chapters 23 to 25 are about implementation and evaluation of either, and Section 25.3 is where the strategic policies of Part IV are finally run as they would have been run. Each chapter says which it is doing in its opening paragraph.
One rule follows from the objective and applies on either axis. The measure a portfolio is judged by must be the measure it was chosen by. A portfolio that minimizes expected shortfall and is then reported on its Sharpe ratio has been misreported: it was never asked to maximize that ratio, and its shortfall, the quantity it was built for, has gone unmentioned. Artzner et al. (1999) and Acerbi and Tasche (2002) give the properties a risk measure should have; Section 10.1 chooses among them, and Section 25.3 reports every strategy on every measure so that the reader can see which portfolio won on which criterion.

title: 3  Return, Risk, and the Investor’s Problem
text:
3.2 Implementation

3.2.1 Return conventions in PerformanceAnalytics

PerformanceAnalytics implements every convention above, and the point of showing them is to see which convention each function defaults to. The class tables ship a total-return index, so a price series can be rebuilt and Equation 3.1 checked against the shipped return.

us <- dplyr::filter(sim_class_returns_monthly, class == "US_equity")
P  <- xts::xts(us$index, order.by = us$date)

simple <- Return.calculate(P, method = "discrete")
logret <- Return.calculate(P, method = "log")
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(simple[-1]), as.numeric(R[-1, "US_equity"])))
head(merge(simple, logret, shipped = R[, "US_equity"]), 3)
#>              simple   logret US_equity
#> 2101-01-31       NA       NA  0.025013
#> 2101-02-28 0.022790 0.022534  0.022790
#> 2101-03-31 0.005306 0.005292  0.005306

The first observation is NA, because a return needs two prices. The log return is smaller than the simple one when the simple return is positive and larger in absolute value when it is negative, which is Equation 3.1.
Return.annualized() with scale = 1 returns the per-period geometric mean, because it evaluates \(\left(\prod (1 + R_t)\right)^{\text{scale}/T} - 1\), so the two averages and the drag between them come from one series.

x    <- R[, "US_equity"]
mu_m <- mean(x)                                          # arithmetic, monthly
g_m  <- as.numeric(Return.annualized(x, scale = 1))      # geometric, monthly
s2_m <- stats::var(as.numeric(x))
c(arithmetic = mu_m, geometric = g_m, gap = mu_m - g_m, half_variance = s2_m / 2)
#>    arithmetic     geometric           gap half_variance 
#>      0.011284      0.010262      0.001022      0.001019







NoteWorked: the drag of Equation 3.3 on US_equity





With the sample numbers substituted, the drag is
\[
\mu - g
= 0.011284 - 0.010262
= 0.001022,
\qquad
\frac{\sigma^2}{2} = \frac{0.002038}{2} = 0.001019,
\]
and the two agree to 3.0e-06, which is the third-order term Equation 3.3 drops. The drag is 10.2 basis points a month, or 1.23 percentage points a year on a series with 15.6% annualized volatility.



Annualizing the same series under the three conventions of Equation 3.4 gives three different numbers, and the package’s default is the compounded one.

c(arithmetic_x12    = as.numeric(Return.annualized(x, scale = 12, geometric = FALSE)),
  compounded        = as.numeric(Return.annualized(x, scale = 12)),          # the default
  cumulative        = as.numeric(Return.cumulative(x)),
  volatility_sqrt12 = as.numeric(StdDev.annualized(x, scale = 12)))
#>    arithmetic_x12        compounded        cumulative volatility_sqrt12 
#>            0.1354            0.1303           43.6152            0.1564

A dollar in US_equity at the start of the sample became 44.6 dollars by its end, which is \(\left(1 + 0.1303\right)^{31}\) to rounding and not \(1 + 31 \times 0.1354\). The arithmetic figure is the right input to Equation 3.12 and the wrong answer to the question of what the asset paid.

3.2.2 The Sharpe ratio, in two conventions
Return.excess() implements Equation 3.7 and reproduces the subtraction of the data block exactly, so the two routes to Re cannot drift apart.

bill  <- xts::xts(rf, order.by = zoo::index(R)); colnames(bill) <- "bill"
Re_pa <- Return.excess(R, Rf = bill)
stopifnot(all.equal(zoo::coredata(Re_pa), zoo::coredata(Re), check.attributes = FALSE))

table.AnnualizedReturns() reports the compounded return, the annualized volatility and a Sharpe ratio per series; SharpeRatio.annualized() reports the last of these on its own. On the same series they disagree.

three <- c("US_equity", "US_credit", "US_government")
table.AnnualizedReturns(R[, three], scale = 12, Rf = bill)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   US_equity US_credit US_government
#>       <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1     0.130    0.063         0.0454
#> 2     0.156    0.0725        0.0478
#> 3     0.676    0.545         0.469
SharpeRatio.annualized(R[, three], Rf = bill, scale = 12)
#>                                           US_equity US_credit US_government
#> Annualized Sharpe Ratio (Rf=2.2%, p=95%):    0.7236    0.5726        0.4882







NoteTwo functions, two defaults for the same ratio



table.AnnualizedReturns() defaults to geometric = TRUE and divides the compounded excess return by the annualized volatility. SharpeRatio.annualized() defaults to geometric = FALSE and divides twelve times the arithmetic monthly excess return by the same volatility, which is \(\sqrt{12}\) times the monthly ratio of Equation 3.5. The gap is the drag of Equation 3.3 divided by the volatility, so it grows with the volatility of the series, and it can reorder a ranking. Either convention is defensible; mixing them across a table is not. When this book reports the Sharpe ratio of a series it uses the compounded convention, as Section 4.2 does; when it optimizes, the objective contains the arithmetic mean, because that is what Equation 3.12 is a function of.


The reordering is visible on the sixteen series, and both rankings come from one function with the convention as an argument.

sr_compounded <- SharpeRatio.annualized(R, Rf = bill, scale = 12, geometric = TRUE)[1, colnames(R)]
sr_arithmetic <- SharpeRatio.annualized(R, Rf = bill, scale = 12, geometric = FALSE)[1, colnames(R)]
rank_of <- function(s, a) as.integer(rank(-s)[[a]])

sr_rank <- tibble::tibble(
  asset           = colnames(R),
  volatility      = unname(StdDev.annualized(R, scale = 12)[1, asset]),
  rank_arithmetic = as.integer(rank(-sr_arithmetic[asset])),
  rank_compounded = as.integer(rank(-sr_compounded[asset]))
)
moved <- dplyr::filter(sr_rank, rank_arithmetic != rank_compounded)

# Pairs that trade places under compounding: one series falls, one rises.
swaps <- dplyr::inner_join(
  dplyr::filter(moved, rank_compounded > rank_arithmetic),
  dplyr::filter(moved, rank_compounded < rank_arithmetic),
  by = c(rank_arithmetic = "rank_compounded", rank_compounded = "rank_arithmetic"),
  suffix = c("_falls", "_rises"))
stopifnot(2L * nrow(swaps) == nrow(moved), nrow(swaps) > 0L,       # every move is a swap
          all(swaps$volatility_falls > swaps$volatility_rises),
          names(which.max(sr_compounded)) == names(which.max(sr_arithmetic)),
          rank_of(sr_compounded, "US_credit") == rank_of(sr_arithmetic, "US_credit"))
dplyr::select(swaps, asset_falls, asset_rises, rank_arithmetic, rank_compounded)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   asset_falls      asset_rises   rank_arithmetic rank_compounded
#>   <chr>            <chr>                   <int>           <int>
#> 1 CH_equity        US_government               5               6
#> 2 GLOBAL_commodity CH_government              11              12
#> 3 JP_equity        EU_credit                   9              10
#> 4 UK_credit        CH_credit                   7               8

The two conventions agree on the top of the ranking: US_equity is first under both, and US_credit ranks 3 of sixteen under both. Elsewhere 8 series change rank, always two at a time trading places: under compounding CH_equity falls behind US_government, GLOBAL_commodity falls behind CH_government, JP_equity falls behind EU_credit, UK_credit falls behind CH_credit. In each of the 4 pairs the series that falls is the more volatile one, whose drag is larger, and the stopifnot() asserts it.

3.2.3 Aggregation over horizons
Equation 3.6 says when \(\sqrt{12}\) is the right factor. The direct test is to compound the monthly series to quarters and years and compute the ratio at each horizon.

sr <- function(v) mean(v) / stats::sd(v)
by_horizon <- function(series) {
  z <- Re[, series]
  q <- xts::apply.quarterly(z, function(v) prod(1 + v) - 1)
  y <- xts::apply.yearly(z,    function(v) prod(1 + v) - 1)
  c(monthly_x_sqrt12 = sr(z) * sqrt(12), quarterly_x_2 = sr(q) * 2, annual = sr(y))
}
horizons  <- rbind(US_equity = by_horizon("US_equity"),
                   US_government = by_horizon("US_government"))
shortfall <- 1 - horizons[, "annual"] / horizons[, "monthly_x_sqrt12"]
rho1      <- apply(Re, 2, function(v) stats::acf(as.numeric(v), lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
stopifnot(shortfall[["US_government"]] > shortfall[["US_equity"]], shortfall[["US_equity"]] > 0,
          rho1[["US_government"]] > 0.1, abs(rho1[["US_equity"]]) < 0.05)
round(cbind(horizons, shortfall, rho1 = rho1[rownames(horizons)]), 3)
#>               monthly_x_sqrt12 quarterly_x_2 annual shortfall   rho1
#> US_equity                0.724         0.663  0.652     0.098 -0.004
#> US_government            0.488         0.417  0.379     0.224  0.147

For US_government the annual ratio is 22% below the \(\sqrt{12}\) figure, because its monthly returns have a first-order autocorrelation of 0.147: the variance of a twelve-month sum exceeds twelve monthly variances, and the annual ratio falls short of \(\sqrt{12}\) times the monthly one. For US_equity the annual ratio is 10% below it, and a first-order autocorrelation of -0.004 does not explain that. The correction of Equation 3.6, applied to every series, says how far the naive factor is off on account of autocorrelation at every lag.

lo_factor <- function(v, q = 12) {
  rho <- stats::acf(as.numeric(v), lag.max = q - 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
  q / sqrt(q + 2 * sum((q - seq_len(q - 1)) * rho))
}
lo_ratio  <- apply(Re, 2, lo_factor) / sqrt(12)   # 1 means sqrt(12) was right
lo_sorted <- sort(lo_ratio)
round(lo_sorted, 3)
#>    US_government        EU_credit        JP_credit        US_credit 
#>            0.867            0.870            0.875            0.876 
#>    EU_government    JP_government        UK_credit        JP_equity 
#>            0.894            0.913            0.936            0.937 
#> GLOBAL_commodity        US_equity        CH_credit        UK_equity 
#>            0.947            0.970            1.020            1.022 
#>        EU_equity        CH_equity    UK_government    CH_government 
#>            1.033            1.033            1.047            1.068

# The largest overstatements lead with bond and credit series.
n_lead <- which(!grepl("_(government|credit)$", names(lo_sorted)))[1] - 1L
stopifnot(n_lead >= 5L, all(lo_sorted[seq_len(n_lead)] < 1),
          all(rho1[names(lo_sorted)[seq_len(n_lead)]] > 0),
          all(1 - lo_ratio[names(shortfall)] < shortfall))

The naive factor overstates the annual Sharpe ratio of 10 of the sixteen series, US_government most, by 15%, and understates that of the other 6, CH_government most, by 6%; the median correction across the sixteen is 7%. The 7 largest overstatements are all on government and credit series, whose monthly returns are positively autocorrelated. The correction puts the annual ratio of US_government 13% below the \(\sqrt{12}\) figure, where the direct calculation had it 22% below, and that of US_equity 3% below against 10%. The rest is not autocorrelation: the direct figure rests on 31 annual observations and is itself imprecise. \(\sqrt{12}\) is the convention this book uses, with that caveat attached.

3.2.4 The bill is not a seventeenth asset
A reader who has just been told that the riskless rate is essential will be tempted to add it to the return matrix as another column. With the actual bill as a seventeenth column, a minimum-variance optimizer buys almost nothing else; with a constant riskless rate, the covariance matrix loses rank and cannot be inverted, which is why Tobin (1958) treats the riskless asset separately in the algebra rather than as one more row of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\).

gmv_of <- function(X) {
  spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(X)) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
  w[colnames(X)]
}
R_bill  <- merge(R, bill)
R_const <- merge(R, constant = xts::xts(rep(mean(rf), nrow(R)), order.by = zoo::index(R)))

w_bill <- gmv_of(R_bill)
round(w_bill[w_bill > 0.001], 4)
#> CH_credit JP_equity      bill 
#>    0.0034    0.0021    0.9941
c(rank_with_bill = qr(stats::cov(R_bill))$rank, rank_with_constant = qr(stats::cov(R_const))$rank)
#>     rank_with_bill rank_with_constant 
#>                 17                 16

The optimizer puts 99.4% into the bill, and the constant column leaves a 17-by-17 covariance matrix of rank 16. The riskless asset enters through the excess-return basis and the budget constraint, not through the covariance matrix.

3.2.5 Hedging a foreign government bond
Equation 3.9 is one subtraction per series, and the four foreign government bonds are where it matters most, because a government bond has little local volatility to begin with.

fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedge_stats <- function(series, region) {
  f <- fx$fx_return[fx$region == region]
  stopifnot(all(fx$date[fx$region == region] == zoo::index(R)))   # same months
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  c(unhedged = stats::sd(u) * sqrt(12), hedged = stats::sd(u - f) * sqrt(12))
}
govs <- tibble::tibble(region = c("EU", "UK", "CH", "JP"),
                       series = paste0(region, "_government"))
hedged_govs <- govs |>
  dplyr::mutate(stats = purrr::map2(series, region, hedge_stats),
                unhedged = purrr::map_dbl(stats, "unhedged"),
                hedged   = purrr::map_dbl(stats, "hedged"),
                removed  = 1 - hedged / unhedged) |>
  dplyr::select(series, unhedged, hedged, removed)
hedged_govs
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   series        unhedged hedged removed
#>   <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 EU_government   0.0981 0.0390   0.603
#> 2 UK_government   0.0951 0.0475   0.500
#> 3 CH_government   0.109  0.0335   0.693
#> 4 JP_government   0.107  0.0312   0.709

Hedging removes between 50% and 71% of a foreign government bond’s volatility. JP_government goes from 10.7% to 3.1%: 71% of what a dollar investor experiences as bond volatility in that series is exchange rate. Whether the same holds for an equity market is a different question with a different answer, and Section 4.3 gives it.

3.2.6 Where risk aversion enters the package
PortfolioAnalytics states Equation 3.12 as two objectives on one specification: a return objective named mean and a risk objective named var carrying a risk_aversion argument. quadratic_utility_objective() builds the same pair in one call, to be assigned to the specification’s objectives slot. Before either is used, one thing about the argument has to be known.






Warningrisk_aversion is \(\gamma/2\), not \(\gamma\)



The package builds \(\boldsymbol{Q} = 2\lambda\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) from risk_aversion =\(\lambda\) and hands it to ROI, whose quadratic program is stated as \(\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{x}\). The two factors of two do not cancel: the coefficient on \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\) in the solved problem is \(\lambda\), where Equation 3.12 puts \(\gamma/2\). To solve the problem a textbook writes with \(\gamma\), pass risk_aversion =\(\gamma/2\). The behavior is undocumented upstream, the derivation is in Section B.5, and the check below verifies it numerically on this data. Every \(\gamma\) in this book is the textbook one, and every call halves it.



base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

qu_spec <- function(spec, gamma) {
  spec |>
    add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = gamma / 2)
}

pa_weights <- function(spec, gamma) {
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, qu_spec(spec, gamma), optimize_method = "ROI"))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

# The same objective through the package's own constructor.
spec_qu <- base_spec
spec_qu$objectives <- quadratic_utility_objective(risk_aversion = 10 / 2)
w_ctor <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_qu, optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(all.equal(pa_weights(base_spec, gamma = 10), w_ctor))
round(w_ctor[w_ctor > 0.005], 4)
#>     EU_equity     US_credit     US_equity US_government 
#>        0.1499        0.0611        0.2838        0.5038

The check is a second solver that takes \(\gamma\) literally. quadprog minimizes \(\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{d}'\boldsymbol{x}\), so \(\boldsymbol{D} = \gamma\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) and \(\boldsymbol{d} = \boldsymbol{\mu}\) is exactly the negative of Equation 3.12. The weights may sum to anything between zero and one, because a budget that binds would hide the scale on which the two conventions differ.

mu <- colMeans(Re)
S  <- stats::cov(Re)

relaxed_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0, max_sum = 1) |>   # 0 <= sum(w) <= 1
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

qp_weights <- function(gamma) {
  n <- ncol(Re)
  w <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = gamma * S, dvec = mu,
                          Amat = cbind(-rep(1, n), diag(n)),        # -sum(w) >= -1, w >= 0
                          bvec = c(-1, rep(0, n)))$solution
  setNames(w, colnames(Re))
}

gamma0 <- 10
w_pa   <- pa_weights(relaxed_spec, gamma0)                  # passes risk_aversion = 5
c(gap_if_argument_is_half_gamma = max(abs(w_pa - qp_weights(gamma0))),
  gap_if_argument_is_gamma      = max(abs(w_pa - qp_weights(gamma0 / 2))))
#> gap_if_argument_is_half_gamma      gap_if_argument_is_gamma 
#>          0.000000000000000451          0.400563221028796157

The package’s answer at risk_aversion = 5 matches the textbook problem at \(\gamma = 10\) to machine precision and misses the one at \(\gamma = 5\) by 0.40 in the largest weight. The claim of the callout is measured rather than asserted.

title: 3  Return, Risk, and the Investor’s Problem
section: 3.3 What the Objective Does on Sixteen Assets
text:
3.3 What the Objective Does on Sixteen Assets

3.3.1 The northwest rule applied
The application opens with the picture. Each series is one point in the plane of Equation 3.14, with the arithmetic excess mean on the vertical axis because that is what \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is, and every coordinate is assembled into one data frame before anything is drawn, so that a volatility can never be paired with another asset’s return.

mom <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = colnames(Re),
  mu    = as.numeric(colMeans(Re)) * 12,                # arithmetic excess, annualized
  sigma = as.numeric(apply(Re, 2, stats::sd)) * sqrt(12)
)
n_dominating <- function(i) sum(mom$mu >= mom$mu[i] & mom$sigma <= mom$sigma[i]) - 1L
mom$dominated_by <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(mom)), n_dominating, integer(1))
mom$kind         <- ifelse(mom$dominated_by > 0L, "dominated", "efficient")
mom <- dplyr::arrange(mom, dplyr::desc(mu))
stopifnot(setequal(mom$asset, colnames(Re)))

Figure 3.1: The sixteen series in the volatility-return plane. Filled points are efficient: nothing lies to their northwest. Hollow points are dominated by at least one other series. The shaded rectangle is the northwest quadrant of one of the most-dominated series, and every point inside it dominates that series.




12 of the sixteen series are dominated by at least one other, and EU_equity, US_equity, US_credit, US_government are efficient. GLOBAL_commodity is one of 3 series dominated by 4 others, each offering more excess return at less volatility over this sample. This is a statement about one sample and carries no test, but it needs no optimizer, and it is the first thing to look at before one runs. An investor with any \(\gamma\) prefers each efficient series to every series it dominates; which efficient series, or which combination of them, is what Equation 3.12 decides and what Section 9.2 computes.
The basis matters even here. Repeating the count on compounded total returns, which is how Section 9.2 draws the same picture, leaves the efficient set as it is and changes which series dominates which.

mom_comp <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = colnames(R),
  mu    = Return.annualized(R, scale = 12)[1, colnames(R)],
  sigma = StdDev.annualized(R, scale = 12)[1, colnames(R)]
)
dominators <- function(m) {                    # the series northwest of each series
  lapply(setNames(seq_len(nrow(m)), m$asset), function(i)
    setdiff(m$asset[m$mu >= m$mu[i] & m$sigma <= m$sigma[i]], m$asset[i]))
}
dom_arith <- dominators(mom)[colnames(R)]
dom_comp  <- dominators(mom_comp)[colnames(R)]

efficient_comp <- names(dom_comp)[lengths(dom_comp) == 0L]
stopifnot(all(lengths(dom_arith)[mom$asset] == mom$dominated_by),
          setequal(efficient_comp, mom$asset[mom$kind == "efficient"]))   # same efficient set

gained <- Map(setdiff, dom_comp, dom_arith)                 # dominators only once compounded
lost   <- Map(setdiff, dom_arith, dom_comp)
stopifnot(all(lengths(lost) == 0L), all(lengths(gained) <= 1L), any(lengths(gained) == 1L))

changed <- tibble::tibble(asset  = names(gained)[lengths(gained) == 1L],
                          gained = unname(unlist(gained))) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(mom, asset, mu, sigma), by = "asset") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sigma))
changed
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   asset         gained            mu sigma
#>   <chr>         <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>

#> 2 EU_credit     CH_credit     0.0357 0.125
#> 3 JP_credit     EU_government 0.0180 0.112
#> 4 CH_government US_government 0.0246 0.109

flip      <- changed[1, ]                                   # the largest drag
flip_lead <- flip$mu - mom$mu[mom$asset == flip$gained]
flip_comp <- setNames(mom_comp$mu, mom_comp$asset)[c(flip$asset, flip$gained)]
stopifnot(flip_lead > 0, flip$sigma^2 / 2 > flip_lead, flip_comp[[1]] < flip_comp[[2]])

The same 4 series are efficient on both bases. Beneath them the relation moves: JP_equity, EU_credit, JP_credit, CH_government are each dominated by one more series on the compounded basis than on the arithmetic one, and no series by fewer. JP_equity is the case with the largest drag. Its arithmetic excess mean is 1.5 percentage points above that of US_credit, and its volatility of 19.6% costs it a drag of about 1.9 percentage points a year under Equation 3.3, which is more than its lead: compounded, it returned 6.1% a year against 6.3%, and US_credit dominates it. Both statements are true; they answer different questions, and a chapter has to say which one it is asking.

3.3.2 Raising \(\gamma\) under full investment
With the weights forced to sum to one, raising \(\gamma\) walks the solution along the efficient frontier toward its left end and stops there. It does not reach cash, because there is no cash to reach: the whole portfolio must be in the sixteen risky series, and the least risky thing they can form is the minimum-variance portfolio of Section 9.1.

p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12

w_gmv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(
  Re, base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
  optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]

gammas <- c(1, 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, 100, 1000, 10000)
sweep_full <- purrr::map_dfr(gammas, function(g) {
  w <- pa_weights(base_spec, g)
  tibble::tibble(gamma = g, rule = "fully invested", invested = sum(w),
                 vol = p_vol(w), ret = p_ret(w), largest = max(w),
                 to_gmv = sum(abs(w - w_gmv)) / 2)
})

Volatility falls from 20.0% at \(\gamma = 1\) to 4.13% at \(\gamma = 10{,}000\), against 4.13% for the minimum-variance portfolio, and the distance between the two portfolios is 0.0004 at the top of the range. A very risk-averse investor who must be fully invested holds the minimum-variance portfolio, the one portfolio that needs no estimate of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), and Jagannathan and Ma (2003) explain why that is an advantage rather than a limitation. At the other end the solution approaches the single highest-return series, the corner every long-only frontier ends in.

3.3.3 Relaxing full investment
Let the weights sum to anything between zero and one, so that the balance sits in the bill at zero excess return. Without the budget constraint the first-order condition of Equation 3.12 is \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = \gamma\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\), so that
\[
\boldsymbol{w}^\ast(\gamma) = \frac{1}{\gamma}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w}^\ast(\gamma) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\gamma}:
\tag{3.15}\]
the composition of the risky holdings does not depend on \(\gamma\), and the invested fraction is proportional to \(1/\gamma\). That is Tobin (1958)’s separation with the algebra written out, and it survives the long-only constraint, because scaling a feasible long-only vector keeps it feasible. The cap at one adds only a range of small \(\gamma\) over which the investor would borrow and is not allowed to.

sweep_relaxed <- purrr::map_dfr(c(gammas, 1e5), function(g) {
  w <- pa_weights(relaxed_spec, g)
  tibble::tibble(gamma = g, rule = "budget relaxed", invested = sum(w),
                 vol = p_vol(w), ret = p_ret(w), largest = max(w), to_gmv = NA_real_)
})

# Composition is invariant once the cap stops binding: same risky portfolio, rescaled.
comp <- lapply(c(50, 1000), function(g) { w <- pa_weights(relaxed_spec, g); w / sum(w) })
stopifnot(all.equal(comp[[1]], comp[[2]], tolerance = 1e-6))

k <- with(dplyr::filter(sweep_relaxed, invested < 0.999), invested * gamma)
stopifnot(diff(range(k)) < 1e-6)                       # invested * gamma is a constant
sweep_relaxed |>
  dplyr::transmute(gamma, invested_x_gamma = round(invested * gamma, 2),   # before rounding
                   invested = round(invested, 4), vol = round(vol, 5)) |>
  as.data.frame()
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>     gamma invested_x_gamma invested     vol
#>     <dbl>            <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1      1              1     1      0.200  
#>  2      2              2     1      0.167  
#>  3      4              4     1      0.145  
#>  4     10             10     1      0.0707 
#>  5     20             19.4   0.967  0.0495 
#>  6     50             19.4   0.387  0.0198 
#>  7    100             19.4   0.194  0.00991
#>  8   1000             19.4   0.0193 0.00099
#>  9  10000             19.4   0.0019 0.0001 
#> 10 100000             19.4   0.0002 0.00001

The cap binds up to \(\gamma\) of about 19; beyond it the invested fraction is exactly 19.35\(/\gamma\): 19.3% at \(\gamma = 100\) and 0.019% at \(\gamma = 100{,}000\). The risky part of the portfolio is the same at every one of those levels, which the stopifnot() asserts rather than assumes, and it is the long-only portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio, the one Section 9.2 reads off the frontier. The very risk-averse investor who may hold the bill holds almost nothing else; the one who may not holds the minimum-variance portfolio. Same \(\gamma\), different budget rule, different answer, and Figure 3.2 shows both.







Figure 3.2: What raising the risk aversion does under the two budget rules, from one data frame. Left: annualized volatility, with the minimum-variance level dashed. Right: the invested fraction. Under full investment the volatility stops at the minimum-variance level; with the budget relaxed it falls without limit and the invested fraction goes as one over gamma.





3.3.4 The basis, once more, in the invested fraction
The third argument for excess returns in Section 3.1 can now be measured. Hand the same relaxed problem total returns instead of excess returns and the optimizer believes the alternative to the risky series earns zero rather than the bill.

invested_on <- function(X, gamma) {
  spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(X)) |>
    add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0, max_sum = 1) |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only")
  sum(extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, qu_spec(spec, gamma), optimize_method = "ROI")))
}
basis <- tibble::tibble(gamma = c(50, 100, 200)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(excess = purrr::map_dbl(gamma, invested_on, X = Re),
                total  = purrr::map_dbl(gamma, invested_on, X = R),
                ratio  = total / excess)
stopifnot(all(basis$ratio > 1), diff(range(basis$ratio)) < 1e-4)   # one ratio at every gamma
basis
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   gamma excess total ratio
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    50 0.387  0.636  1.64
#> 2   100 0.193  0.318  1.64
#> 3   200 0.0967 0.159  1.64

At every \(\gamma\) the total-return problem invests 64% more of the portfolio in risky assets than the excess-return problem, because it credits each risky series with the bill’s 2.2% a year as if that were a reward for bearing risk. The extra holding is not a view about the assets; it is an arithmetic error about the alternative, and it is why the data block of every chapter subtracts the bill before anything else is done.

title: 3  Return, Risk, and the Investor’s Problem
text:
Key Takeaways

Simple returns add across assets and log returns add across time. The arithmetic mean is the input to every objective, the geometric mean is what was earned, and the gap is half the variance Equation 3.3. Annualizing a Sharpe ratio by \(\sqrt{12}\) assumes independence across months, and Equation 3.6 says by how much autocorrelation breaks it (Lo 2002).
Returns enter every optimizer in excess of the Treasury bill: the tangency portfolio is defined relative to a riskless rate (Tobin 1958), PortfolioAnalytics has no argument for one, an uninvested fraction then earns exactly what the objective assumes, and the bill moves. The money-market series are not the bill.

\(\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}}\) is a second-order approximation to expected utility (Neumann and Morgenstern 1944; Markowitz 1959) whose value is a certainty equivalent and whose \(\gamma\) is a price: at \(\gamma = 4\), ten percent of volatility costs 200 basis points a year Table 3.1.
A portfolio dominates another if it has at least as much expected return and at most as much volatility, with one inequality strict; a better allocation lies to the northwest, and an asset nothing dominates is efficient. On this sample 12 of the sixteen series are dominated before any optimizer runs.

risk_aversion in PortfolioAnalytics is \(\gamma/2\). Under full investment a rising \(\gamma\) converges to the minimum-variance portfolio, not to cash; with the budget relaxed the risky composition is fixed and the invested fraction is proportional to \(1/\gamma\), which is two-fund separation.
Strategic allocation is the long-run policy from unconditional moments; tactical allocation deviates from it on conditioning information. Chapters 9 to 15 are strategic, 16 to 19 tactical, 23 to 25 about implementing and evaluating either, and the measure a portfolio is judged by must be the one it was chosen by.

Exercises

Recompute Table 3.2 on the weekly data, sim_class_returns_weekly in excess of sim_riskfree_weekly, annualizing with 52 in place of 12. Which series change status between the monthly and the weekly count, and what property of Equation 3.4 is responsible?
Apply the correction of Equation 3.6 at \(q = 3\) and \(q = 12\) to all sixteen series and compare it with the Sharpe ratios computed directly from quarterly and annual compounded returns, as by_horizon() does. Where the two disagree, say which of Lo’s assumptions the series violates.
Repeat the hedging calculation of hedge_stats() for the four foreign equity markets. Hedging removes most of a government bond’s volatility; what does it do to JP_equity, and what sign must the covariance between the local return and the currency have for that to happen?
Find the \(\gamma\) at which the relaxed-budget solution has the same annualized volatility as a portfolio with sixty percent in the five equity series and forty percent in the five government series, equally weighted within each block. Report the invested fraction at that \(\gamma\) and read the corresponding row of Table 3.1. What does the answer say about the risk aversion of a 60/40 investor on this sample?

title: 4  Descriptive Analysis of Asset Returns
text:
4.1 What Can Be Estimated
Every later chapter takes a return series and does something to it: estimates a moment, imposes a constraint, holds a portfolio through a crisis. None of that is interpretable without knowing what the series are, and none of it is trustworthy without knowing which of their properties can be estimated at all. Since Mandelbrot (1963) and Fama (1965) it has been understood that financial returns are not Gaussian, and Cont (2001) collects the regularities that survive across markets and periods. This chapter asks which of those regularities hold in the market this book uses, and which of the numbers we are about to rely on are worth relying on.
We first set out what the moments of a return series are and how precisely each can be estimated, then compute them, then examine the two properties of this market that shape every portfolio result that follows: its tails arrive as events rather than as a distribution, and its currency exposure is a property of the asset rather than of the country.
The data are the modeled market of Section 2.2: five regions, the United States, Europe, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and Japan, each with equities, government bonds and credit, plus a global commodity index, which makes sixteen risky class series over 372 months, model years 1 to 31, all in US dollars and unhedged, with a money-market series per region beside them and the US Treasury bill as the risk-free rate. No series in it is the history of a real security, so it ships with the package, and every number below reproduces on the reader’s machine without an account anywhere.
Let \(r_t\) denote the return on an asset in period \(t\), observed for \(t = 1, \dots, T\). The four sample moments in universal use are
\[
\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t,
\qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r_t - \hat{\mu})^2,
\tag{4.1}\]
\[
\hat{S} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{r_t - \hat{\mu}}{\hat{\sigma}}\right)^{3},
\qquad
\hat{K} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{r_t - \hat{\mu}}{\hat{\sigma}}\right)^{4} - 3 .
\tag{4.2}\]
They are conventionally reported side by side, in one table, as though they were four facts of the same kind. They are not, and the difference is the single most consequential thing in this chapter.

title: 4  Descriptive Analysis of Asset Returns
text:
4.1.1 The mean is the moment that does not improve
Suppose returns are independent with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) per unit of time, observed over a calendar span \(\tau\) at intervals of length \(\Delta\), so that \(T = \tau / \Delta\). The standard errors of the first two moments behave quite differently:
\[
\operatorname{se}(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}},
\qquad
\operatorname{se}(\hat{\sigma}^2) \approx \sigma^2\sqrt{\frac{2}{T}}
= \sigma^2\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta}{\tau}}.
\tag{4.3}\]
The precision of the mean depends only on the calendar span \(\tau\). Sampling the same thirty years weekly rather than monthly multiplies \(T\) by roughly four and does nothing whatever to the standard error of \(\hat{\mu}\), because each observation carries proportionally less of the drift. The precision of the variance depends on the number of observations, so the same change cuts its standard error in half. This is the point of Merton (1980), and it is why expected returns remain the hard problem while volatility modeling has made steady progress. Section 6.1 and Section 7.1 are the two chapters this asymmetry splits the book into.
Higher moments are worse still. \(\hat{S}\) and \(\hat{K}\) depend on third and fourth powers of standardized returns, so a single extreme observation can move them by more than the rest of the sample combined.

4.1.2 Testing normality rather than assuming it
Jarque and Bera (1980) combine the two shape moments into a single statistic,
\[
\mathrm{JB} = \frac{T}{6}\left(\hat{S}^2 + \frac{\hat{K}^2}{4}\right)
\;\xrightarrow{\;d\;}\; \chi^2_2
\tag{4.4}\]
under the null of normality. It is a specification test, not a model, and a rejection says only that some combination of skewness and excess kurtosis is larger than sampling error allows.
Whether normality matters depends on what is being computed. For a portfolio variance it hardly does. For a tail quantile it decides the answer. Write \(\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha\) for the \(\alpha\)-quantile of the loss distribution and
\[
\mathrm{ES}_\alpha = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\, r \mid r \leq \mathrm{VaR}_\alpha \right]
\tag{4.5}\]
for the expected shortfall, the average loss conditional on being in the tail. Expected shortfall is preferred to value at risk because it is coherent in the sense of Artzner et al. (1999), in particular subadditive, so that combining two positions can never make the measured risk larger than the sum of its parts (Acerbi and Tasche 2002). Value at risk fails that test, which matters precisely when portfolios are being built.
Equation 4.5 can be estimated directly from the sample tail, or from a normal quantile corrected for the observed skewness and kurtosis using the Cornish-Fisher expansion,
\[
z_{\mathrm{CF}} = z + \frac{(z^2-1)\hat{S}}{6}
  + \frac{(z^3-3z)\hat{K}}{24} - \frac{(2z^3-5z)\hat{S}^2}{36},
\tag{4.6}\]
with \(z\) the standard normal quantile. The resulting modified expected shortfall was brought into portfolio work by Favre and Galeano (2002) and refined by Boudt et al. (2008), and it is what PerformanceAnalytics computes by default. The gap between the two estimates measures how much the normal approximation is costing.

title: 4  Descriptive Analysis of Asset Returns
text:
4.2 Implementation
Three tables carry the whole book, and their shape is the shape everything else expects.

returns  <- sim_class_returns_monthly     # date, class, return, index
money    <- sim_money_market_monthly      # the five money markets, beside them
bill     <- sim_riskfree_monthly          # date, rate_annual, return
assets   <- sim_assets                    # one row per instrument

dplyr::glimpse(returns, width = 72)
#> Rows: 5,952
#> Columns: 4
#> $ date   <date> 2101-01-31, 2101-01-31, 2101-01-31, 2101-01-31, 2101-0…
#> $ class  <chr> "CH_credit", "CH_equity", "CH_government", "EU_credit",…
#> $ return <dbl> -0.030113, -0.014463, -0.034335, -0.024132, 0.083737, -…
#> $ index  <dbl> 96.99, 98.55, 96.57, 97.59, 108.37, 98.12, 102.56, 100.…

16 risky class series, 372 complete months, no gaps. Underneath them sit 181 individual instruments in sim_asset_returns_monthly, the same market at a finer grain and the universe the sleeve chapters of Part VI use.
PortfolioAnalytics, which occupies most of this book, wants none of this shape. It wants a wide xts matrix, and it will not convert on the reader’s behalf.

R  <- as_xts_pm(returns, date, class, return)
M  <- as_xts_pm(money,   date, class, return)
rf <- bill$return
stopifnot(identical(zoo::index(R), zoo::index(M)), length(rf) == nrow(R))
dim(R)
#> [1] 372  16

That is the boundary between the tidy world and the matrix world that Section 1.2 establishes, and this book crosses it explicitly every time rather than letting a helper do it invisibly.

4.2.1 The moments

moments <- tibble::tibble(
  series   = colnames(R),
  ret      = apply(R, 2, ann_ret),
  vol      = apply(R, 2, ann_vol),
  sharpe   = (apply(R, 2, ann_ret) - ann_ret(rf)) / apply(R, 2, ann_vol),
  skew     = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::skewness(R)),
  exkurt   = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::kurtosis(R, method = "excess")),
  maxdd    = apply(R, 2, function(x) { i <- cumprod(1 + x); min(i / cummax(i)) - 1 })
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sharpe))

Three features of Table 4.1 matter for what follows.
The return ranking is not the Sharpe ranking. US_credit earns 6.3% a year against US_equity’s 13.0%, less than half, and on Sharpe ratio it ranks 3 of 16, at 0.56 against 0.69 for US_equity and above 3 of the 5 equity markets, because its volatility is under half that of US_equity. Whether that makes it the better holding depends on whether variance is the right measure of its risk, which Section 4.3 takes up and Section 10.1 settles.
The money market is not the risk-free rate. The five money-market series are kept outside the risky universe, and the reason is worth one calculation. US_money_market is a three-month instrument marked to market off a fitted curve rather than a bill held to maturity.

mm <- as.numeric(M[, "US_money_market"])
c(mm_negative_months   = mean(mm < 0),
  bill_negative_months = mean(rf < 0),
  correlation          = stats::cor(mm, rf),
  mm_drawdown          = { i <- cumprod(1 + mm); min(i / cummax(i)) - 1 })
#>   mm_negative_months bill_negative_months          correlation 
#>             0.188172             0.002688             0.930009 
#>          mm_drawdown 
#>            -0.009095

It tracks the bill, at a correlation of 0.93, but it carries duration: it loses money in 19% of months against the bill’s 0.3%. A risk-free rate has to be riskless over the holding period, and this series is not. We treat the money markets as short-duration assets and use sim_riskfree_monthly as the risk-free rate; every risk-free figure in this book comes from there.
Currency is a first-order driver. The four foreign money markets have volatilities near ten percent.

round(apply(M, 2, ann_vol), 3)
#> CH_money_market EU_money_market JP_money_market UK_money_market US_money_market 
#>           0.104           0.096           0.101           0.092           0.007

A three-month instrument has almost no duration, so unhedged in dollars it is very nearly a pure currency position, and the same currency sits inside every foreign bond and equity series in Table 4.1. Section 4.3 takes that apart.







Figure 4.1: Every class series in mean-volatility space. The dashed line runs from the bill through the highest Sharpe ratio available; series below it earn less per unit of risk than the best single holding did.





4.2.2 Testing the distribution
Applying Equation 4.4 to each series gives one verdict and sixteen very different statistics, and their order is not the one intuition suggests.

jb_stat <- vapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  x <- as.numeric(R[, s]); n <- length(x)
  s3 <- mean((x - mean(x))^3) / stats::sd(x)^3
  s4 <- mean((x - mean(x))^4) / stats::sd(x)^4 - 3
  n / 6 * (s3^2 + s4^2 / 4)
}, numeric(1))
jb <- stats::pchisq(jb_stat, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)

sum(jb < 0.05)                      # of 16
#> [1] 16
round(sort(jb_stat), 1)             # the statistic, closest to Gaussian first
#>    US_government        JP_equity    EU_government        CH_credit 
#>              8.0             18.5             23.2             31.7 
#> GLOBAL_commodity    CH_government        CH_equity        US_equity 
#>             39.7             48.1             68.3             74.0 
#>    UK_government        JP_credit        EU_equity        UK_equity 
#>            120.1            131.7            165.1            181.7 
#>    JP_government        EU_credit        US_credit        UK_credit 
#>            205.0            825.0           2420.7           2480.3

16 of 16 series reject normality at the five percent level, and the statistic runs from 8 to 2480. JP_equity, at 19.6% volatility the second most volatile series in the set, is the second closest to Gaussian, with a statistic of 18: its skewness is -0.28 and its excess kurtosis 0.96, against -1.45 and 12.24 for US_credit, whose statistic is 2421 at less than half the volatility. Volatility and non-normality are different properties, and this is the cleanest demonstration of it in the book.
The three largest statistics belong to credit series rather than to equity, and Equation 4.6 puts a number on what that costs.


Table 4.2: Expected shortfall at 95%, computed two ways. The Gaussian-corrected figure is the Cornish-Fisher expansion, which adjusts a normal quantile for skewness and kurtosis; the historical figure simply averages the realized tail.

tails <- tibble::tibble(
  series = colnames(R),
  es_hist = apply(R, 2, function(x)
    as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "historical"))),
  es_mod  = apply(R, 2, function(x)
    as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "modified")))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(ratio = es_mod / es_hist) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(ratio))

head(tails, 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   series    es_hist  es_mod ratio
#>   <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 US_credit -0.0431 -0.0946  2.20
#> 2 UK_credit -0.0891 -0.179   2.01
#> 3 EU_credit -0.0765 -0.129   1.68
#> 4 UK_equity -0.103  -0.140   1.36



For US_credit the two estimates disagree by a factor of 2.2. For US_equity they disagree by a factor of 1.11. A Gaussian risk model is roughly right for equities and roughly half right for credit, and US_credit is the series that ranked 3 of 16 on Sharpe ratio in Table 4.1.






NoteES() does not default to the historical estimate



PerformanceAnalytics::ES() defaults to method = "modified", so a call without that argument returns the Cornish-Fisher figure of Equation 4.6 rather than the sample tail. It is the better default, given how few observations a 95% tail contains, and it is rarely noticed. Whenever a reported expected shortfall is compared against another source, check which estimator produced it.



4.2.3 How well each moment is estimated
Equation 4.3 is a statement about standard errors under independence. Its practical counterpart is what a rolling window would have told an investor at each point in the sample.

win <- 60L
risky <- colnames(R)

roll_stat <- function(x, f) zoo::rollapply(x, win, f, align = "right")

instab <- lapply(risky, function(s) {
  x <- as.numeric(R[, s])
  full <- c(mean = mean(x), vol = stats::sd(x),
            skew = mean((x - mean(x))^3) / stats::sd(x)^3)
  rw <- list(mean = roll_stat(x, mean), vol = roll_stat(x, stats::sd),
             skew = roll_stat(x, function(z)
               mean((z - mean(z))^3) / stats::sd(z)^3))
  tibble::tibble(
    series = s, moment = names(full),
    rel_iqr   = vapply(names(full), function(m)
      as.numeric(stats::IQR(rw[[m]]) / abs(full[[m]])), numeric(1)),
    sign_flip = vapply(names(full), function(m)
      mean(sign(rw[[m]]) != sign(full[[m]])), numeric(1))
  )
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

instab_med <- instab |>
  dplyr::group_by(moment) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_rel_iqr = median(rel_iqr),
                   median_sign_flip = median(sign_flip))
instab_med
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   moment median_rel_iqr median_sign_flip
#>   <chr>           <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 mean            1.18             0.107
#> 2 skew            1.48             0.342
#> 3 vol             0.289            0

Read the second column first. Across 16 risky series and 313 overlapping sixty-month windows, the rolling volatility never once disagrees in sign with its full-sample value, which it cannot, being a positive quantity, and for the median series its interquartile range is 29% of its own level. The rolling mean wanders by more than its own level, 118% of it. The rolling skewness disagrees in sign with the full-sample skewness in 34% of all windows.
That is Equation 4.3 made concrete, and it is the statement this book leans on repeatedly: volatility is estimable, the mean is not, and skewness will regularly report the opposite of the truth.







Figure 4.2: Rolling sixty-month estimates against the full-sample value, for four representative series. The dashed horizontal line is the whole-sample answer; the solid line is what a sixty-month window would have told an investor at each point in the sample.





4.2.4 Drawdowns are episodes, not a number
Maximum drawdown is the summary an investor asks for first. PerformanceAnalytics will return it in one call, and that call discards most of what the reader needs.

deepest <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {

title: 4  Descriptive Analysis of Asset Returns
section: 4.3 Two Properties That Shape Every Portfolio
text:
4.3 Two Properties That Shape Every Portfolio
Neither is visible in a table of moments, and both decide what the optimizers of Part IV can achieve.

4.3.1 Fat tails are events, not a distribution
Table 4.1 reports an excess kurtosis for each series separately, which invites the reading that each series independently has a fat tail. That reading is wrong, and the error matters for a portfolio, because independent fat tails diversify and shared ones do not.

Rr  <- R[, risky]
z   <- scale(Rr)
hit <- rowSums(abs(z) > 2.5)
p   <- mean(abs(z) > 2.5)

obs <- table(factor(hit, levels = 0:ncol(Rr)))
exp <- stats::dbinom(0:ncol(Rr), ncol(Rr), p) * nrow(Rr)

tibble::tibble(k = 0:ncol(Rr), observed = as.integer(obs), expected = round(exp, 2)) |>
  dplyr::filter(k >= 3, observed > 0)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>       k observed expected
#>   <int>    <int>    <dbl>
#> 1     3        9     1.91
#> 2     4        4     0.15
#> 3     5        2     0.01
#> 4     7        1     0   
#> 5     9        1     0   
#> 6    13        1     0

Months in which five or more of the 16 risky series moved beyond two and a half standard deviations number 5 observed against 0.01 expected under independence. The excess is not marginal; it is a different phenomenon.

d <- zoo::index(Rr)
w <- d[which.max(hit)]
stopifnot(in_episode(w, "credit_crisis"))   # the text below places it there
c(month = fmt_model(w), series_beyond_2.5sd = max(hit), of = ncol(Rr))
#>                      month        series_beyond_2.5sd 
#> "October of model year 17"                       "13" 
#>                         of 
#>                       "16"

In October of model year 17, a month of the credit crisis described below, 13 of the 16 risky series moved beyond two and a half standard deviations at once. The fat tail in this market is not sixteen fat tails. It is 5 months in which a large part of the market moves together, which is the joint counterpart of the marginal non-normality Equation 4.4 detected, and the reason Longin and Solnik (2001) study correlation in the tails rather than on average.







Figure 4.3: Standardized monthly returns of the risky series. Each row is a series, each column a month; the dark vertical stripes are the events in which the whole market moved at once.





4.3.2 The crises are not one crisis
We keep four episodes apart throughout the book, because they are economically different and a lesson learned from one is false in another. They ship with the data as sim_episodes, each named for what happens in it, and Appendix A tabulates them.

ep  <- sim_episodes                 # episode, label, start, end, description
cum <- vapply(ep$episode, function(e) {
  apply(Rr[in_episode(d, e), ], 2, function(x) prod(1 + x) - 1)
}, numeric(ncol(Rr)))
round(100 * cum[c("US_equity", "US_government", "JP_government",
                  "US_credit", "EU_credit", "GLOBAL_commodity"), ], 1)
#>                  equity_bear credit_crisis liquidity_shock rates_shock
#> US_equity              -33.6         -27.9           -10.0       -13.8
#> US_government           34.0           8.2             6.2       -10.7
#> JP_government           -6.9          14.6             2.3       -15.9
#> US_credit               28.1          -8.5            -2.0       -15.1
#> EU_credit               17.3         -13.1            -8.4       -23.3
#> GLOBAL_commodity        20.7         -19.6            -1.9        11.8

In the credit crisis the safest government bonds did what the textbook says they do: US_government gained 8.2% while US_equity lost 27.9%, and credit fell with equity, US_credit by 8.5%. The equity bear market was a different decline. US_equity lost 33.6% over 30 months while US_credit gained 28.1% beside a government bond that gained 34.0%, so credit sided with bonds in one equity decline and with equities in the other. In the 3 months of the liquidity shock 14 of the 16 series fell. In the rates shock the government bond that had gained in each of the other three episodes lost 10.7%, every government bond and credit series lost with it, and only 2 of the 16 series gained.

names(which(cum[, "rates_shock"] > 0))
#> [1] "GLOBAL_commodity" "UK_equity"

One of them, GLOBAL_commodity, had lost 19.6% in the credit crisis. A book that teaches diversification from the credit crisis alone teaches a rule that reverses in the rates shock, which is why every backtest in Section 25.3 reports these episodes separately rather than averaging over them.
The correlation matrix says the same thing in the form an optimizer will feel.

mean_cor <- function(idx) {
  C <- stats::cor(Rr[idx, ]); mean(C[upper.tri(C)])
}
in_ep <- vapply(ep$episode, function(e) in_episode(d, e), logical(nrow(Rr)))
calm  <- rowSums(in_ep) == 0

regime <- tibble::tibble(
  regime   = c("calm", ep$episode),
  months   = c(sum(calm), unname(colSums(in_ep))),
  mean_cor = c(mean_cor(calm), unname(apply(in_ep, 2, mean_cor)))
)
regime
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   regime          months mean_cor
#>   <chr>            <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 calm               320    0.297
#> 2 equity_bear         30    0.219
#> 3 credit_crisis        7    0.509
#> 4 liquidity_shock      3    0.719
#> 5 rates_shock         12    0.612

Average pairwise correlation rises from 0.30 in calm months to 0.51 through the credit crisis and 0.61 through the rates shock. In the equity bear market it falls to 0.22, because bonds rose while equities fell. The diversification an optimizer found in the calm sample is not the diversification available when it is needed. Longin and Solnik (2001) and Ang and Chen (2002) document the same asymmetry in real equity markets: correlations rise in falling markets and not in rising ones.
One caution about the numbers themselves. The credit crisis is 7 months and the liquidity shock 3, and a correlation matrix estimated on so few observations is a description rather than an estimate. Forbes and Rigobon (2002) show further that measured correlation rises mechanically with volatility even when the underlying dependence is unchanged, so a rise of this kind is not by itself evidence of contagion. The cumulative returns above carry far more weight than the correlations do.

4.3.3 Currency is not one decision
Everything here is unhedged in dollars, so a foreign holding carries its local return and its currency’s move together. How much of it is currency depends on the asset rather than on the country, and that is the non-obvious part.

fx <- sim_fx_monthly
share <- function(series, region) {
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  f <- fx$fx_return[fx$region == region][
        match(zoo::index(R), fx$date[fx$region == region])]
  c(unhedged  = ann_vol(u),
    hedged    = ann_vol(u - f),
    fx_share  = 1 - stats::var(u - f) / stats::var(u),
    if_indep  = stats::var(f) / stats::var(u))
}
round(rbind(
  JP_government = share("JP_government", "JP"),
  JP_equity     = share("JP_equity", "JP"),
  CH_equity     = share("CH_equity", "CH"),
  EU_credit     = share("EU_credit", "EU")
), 3)
#>               unhedged hedged fx_share if_indep
#> JP_government    0.107  0.031    0.916    0.882
#> JP_equity        0.196  0.212   -0.175    0.265
#> CH_equity        0.182  0.179    0.034    0.318
#> EU_credit        0.125  0.066    0.717    0.584

Hedging JP_government takes its volatility from 10.7% to 3.1%. Hedging JP_equity takes it from 19.6% to 21.2%, which is to say it removes nothing and adds a little.
The if_indep column explains why. Writing \(r^{\text{usd}} = r^{\text{loc}} + f\) for the unhedged return of a foreign asset, where \(f\) is the currency return, the variance decomposes as
\[
\operatorname{Var}(r^{\text{usd}})
= \operatorname{Var}(r^{\text{loc}}) + \operatorname{Var}(f)
+ 2\operatorname{Cov}(r^{\text{loc}}, f).
\tag{4.7}\]
If the local return and the currency were unrelated the covariance term would vanish and the currency’s share of variance would be \(\operatorname{Var}(f)/\operatorname{Var}(r^{\text{usd}})\), which is the if_indep column. For JP_equity that benchmark is 26% and the measured share is -18%. The gap is a negative covariance: the Japanese market rises when the yen falls, so the hedge is supplied by the economics rather than by a forward contract. For EU_credit the covariance runs the other way and hedging removes more than the currency’s own share.
The practical conclusion matches Campbell et al. (2010), who find that the optimal currency hedge differs systematically between bonds and equities because currencies covary differently with each. Whether to hedge is therefore not one question with one answer per currency. It is a different question for the bond sleeve and the equity sleeve of the same country, and Section 15.2 treats it as such. Perold and Schulman (1988) and Black (1989) are the two classic and opposed statements of the general case.

title: 4  Descriptive Analysis of Asset Returns
text:
Key Takeaways

The four moments of Equation 4.1 and Equation 4.2 are not four facts of the same kind. By Equation 4.3 the mean’s precision depends only on the calendar span, while the variance improves with the number of observations, so sampling more finely helps one and not the other (Merton 1980).
Measured on sixty-month rolling windows, volatility never changes sign and moves by 29% of its level, the mean moves by 118% of its own level, and skewness reverses sign in 34% of windows.
Non-normality and volatility are unrelated. All 16 series reject the normality test of Equation 4.4, but JP_equity, the second most volatile, is the second closest to Gaussian, while US_credit, at less than half its volatility, has two estimates of expected shortfall that differ by a factor of 2.2.
Fat tails in this market are events rather than a distribution. 5 months show joint exceedances of a kind that independence would produce once in 114 samples of this length. Independent fat tails diversify; shared ones do not.
The four episodes of sim_episodes are not one crisis. Average correlation rises in the credit crisis and the rates shock and falls in the equity bear market, and a correlation estimated on a 7-month window is a description, part of whose rise is mechanical (Forbes and Rigobon 2002).
The currency share of a foreign holding is a property of the asset, not of the country. Hedging a Japanese government bond removes most of its volatility; hedging Japanese equity removes none (Campbell et al. 2010).

title: 4  Descriptive Analysis of Asset Returns
text:
Exercises


sim_class_returns_weekly holds the same market at the model’s native frequency. Recompute Table 4.1 on it, annualizing by \(\sqrt{52}\) instead of \(\sqrt{12}\). Which of the six columns change materially and which do not? Explain the pattern using Equation 4.3.
The exceedance count above used a threshold of 2.5 standard deviations. Repeat it at 2, 3 and 4. At which threshold does the excess over independence first appear, and what does that tell you about where in the distribution the dependence lives?
Pick two series with similar volatility but opposite skewness, for example US_credit and JP_government. Construct the equally weighted combination and compute its skewness. Is it the average of the two? Explain why not.
Using sim_fx_monthly, build the fully hedged version of all sixteen risky series and recompute the average pairwise correlation in calm months and in each of the four episodes. Does hedging change the diversification of the set, or only its volatility?
Verify Equation 4.3 by simulation. Draw 30 years of returns at monthly and at weekly frequency from the same process, estimate the mean and the variance from each, repeat 1,000 times, and compare the two sets of standard errors against the formula.

title: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation
text:
5.1 The Single-Factor Model
Section 4.3 described the market one series at a time. This chapter asks what the series have in common. That question has a canonical answer, the single-factor model of Sharpe (1964), Lintner (1965) and Black (1972), in which an asset’s expected excess return is proportional to its covariance with the market. The regression form of it, due to Jensen (1968), is what every risk report still prints: a beta that is the input to a hedge, and an alpha that is the claim an active manager makes.
We first set out the model and what its components mean, then estimate it on this market, and then examine how much of the resulting explanation survives being measured properly. The finding worth stating in advance is that most of it does not. Outside equity the typical beta changes sign in about a third of all estimation windows, an apparent asymmetry between rising and falling markets survives inference in two cases out of sixteen, and a factor that appears to add explanatory power turns out to be sorting on something other than its name.
Write \(r_{it}\) for the return on asset \(i\) in period \(t\), \(r_{ft}\) for the risk-free rate, and \(r_{mt}\) for the return on the market. Returns enter in excess of the bill throughout, for the reasons set out in Section 3.1. The regression is
\[
r_{it} - r_{ft} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\left(r_{mt} - r_{ft}\right) + \varepsilon_{it},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{it}] = 0,
\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, r_{mt}) = 0,
\tag{5.1}\]
with the population slope
\[
\beta_i = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(r_i, r_m)}{\operatorname{Var}(r_m)} .
\tag{5.2}\]
Under the asset pricing theory, \(\alpha_i = 0\) for every asset. Under the regression read as a statistical description, \(\alpha_i\) is whatever the market does not account for, and Equation 5.1 splits the variance of each asset into a part the market explains and a part it does not:
\[
\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(r_i)}_{\text{total}}
= \underbrace{\beta_i^2 \operatorname{Var}(r_m)}_{\text{systematic}}
+ \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)}_{\text{idiosyncratic}},
\qquad
R^2_i = \frac{\beta_i^2\operatorname{Var}(r_m)}{\operatorname{Var}(r_i)} .
\tag{5.3}\]
The \(R^2\) is therefore not a goodness-of-fit statistic in the usual decorative sense. It is the share of an asset’s risk that the model claims to describe, and an asset with a low \(R^2\) is one the model has nothing to say about.
Two extensions matter here. The first allows the slope to differ in rising and falling markets, in the spirit of the lower partial moment framework of Bawa and Lindenberg (1977) and the downside betas of Ang et al. (2006):
\[
r_{it} - r_{ft} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\,\tilde{r}_{mt}
  + \gamma_i\,\tilde{r}_{mt}\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{r}_{mt} < 0\} + \varepsilon_{it},
\tag{5.4}\]
where \(\tilde{r}_{mt} = r_{mt} - r_{ft}\), so that \(\beta_i\) is the beta in up markets and \(\beta_i + \gamma_i\) the beta in down markets. The second allows the slope to move over time, which is the conditional CAPM of Ferson and Harvey (1991) and Jagannathan and Wang (1996) and which we approach here descriptively, through rolling windows.

title: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation
text:
5.1.1 Inference is where these models are usually lost
Monthly returns are serially dependent and heteroskedastic, so the textbook standard error of an ordinary least squares slope is wrong. Throughout this chapter we use the heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent estimator of Newey and West (1987), which replaces \(\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}\) with
\[
(X'X)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j=-L}^{L} w_j \hat{\Gamma}_j\right)(X'X)^{-1},
\qquad
w_j = 1 - \frac{|j|}{L+1},
\tag{5.5}\]
where \(\hat{\Gamma}_j\) is the sample autocovariance of the score at lag \(j\) and \(L\) the bandwidth, six lags here.
The reason to insist on this is that Equation 5.4 is estimated sixteen times, once per series, and any procedure repeated sixteen times will produce significant-looking differences whether or not any exist. Harvey et al. (2016) make the case at scale for the cross-section of expected returns; the same arithmetic applies to a table of sixteen betas.
crumbs: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation

title: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation
text:
5.2 Implementation
A factor model needs a factor. The obvious one here is the market, and it has to be built rather than assumed. We build it from the instrument universe described in Section 2.2, not from the class series, because a capitalization weight only exists at instrument level.

returns <- sim_class_returns_monthly
R  <- as_xts_pm(returns, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
risky <- colnames(R)
stopifnot(length(risky) == 16L)

# Capitalization-weighted global equity, from all 123 equity instruments. The
# weight in month t is the last capitalization observed on or before the end of
# t-1: a weight an investor could actually have held.
eq  <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
Ra  <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly[sim_asset_returns_monthly$asset %in% eq, ],
                 date, asset, return)
cap <- sim_marketcap_weekly[sim_marketcap_weekly$asset %in% eq, ]
d   <- zoo::index(Ra)
stopifnot(ncol(Ra) == 123L, identical(d, zoo::index(R)))

W <- t(vapply(seq_along(d), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) d[1] - 40 else d[i - 1]
  cc   <- cap[cap$date <= cutoff, ]
  last <- cc[!duplicated(cc$asset, fromLast = TRUE), ]
  w <- last$market_cap[match(colnames(Ra), last$asset)]
  w[is.na(w)] <- 0
  if (sum(w) == 0) rep(1 / ncol(Ra), ncol(Ra)) else w / sum(w)
}, numeric(ncol(Ra))))

MKT   <- rowSums(W * zoo::coredata(Ra))
mkt_e <- MKT - rf

The weights are lagged by one period deliberately. A capitalization weight observed at the end of month \(t\) is not available for investing during month \(t\), and using it would give the proxy a return no investor could have earned.

c(annualized = ann_ret(MKT), volatility = ann_vol(MKT))
#> annualized volatility 
#>     0.1234     0.1488

# Which region is this "global" market, really?
usm <- sim_assets$region[match(colnames(Ra), sim_assets$asset_id)] == "US"
us_share <- rowSums(W[, usm])
c(first = us_share[1], mean = mean(us_share), last = us_share[length(us_share)])
#>  first   mean   last 
#> 0.4889 0.5696 0.6998

The second line deserves attention before any beta in this chapter is used. The proxy is on average 57% United States by weight and ends the sample at 70%. It is global in construction and American in effect. Every beta below is largely a beta on the United States market, and Roll (1977) is the standing reminder that a test of Equation 5.1 is a joint test of the model and of whatever proxy stands in for the market.

5.2.1 One factor, sixteen series

fit1 <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  y <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
  m <- stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e)
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 alpha_ann = 12 * stats::coef(m)[1],
                 alpha_t   = stats::coef(m)[1] / sqrt(nw[1, 1]),
                 beta      = stats::coef(m)[2],
                 r2        = summary(m)$r.squared)
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
