Read Table 5.1 through Equation 5.3. The model explains 4 series and fails on the rest. Above an \(R^2\) of one half sit CH_equity, EU_equity, UK_equity, US_equity. JP_equity reaches 0.321, 9 of the 16 fall below 0.10, and the extreme is JP_government at 0.000950, a regression that accounts for nothing whatsoever.
The median \(R^2\) across all 16 is 0.077. A single-factor model is a model of equities that happens to be applied to everything else.







Figure 5.1: How much of each series the market explains. The four bars above one half are equity blocks; everything else is a regression that has not been told what drives it.




Of the 16 alphas only one clears a t-statistic of two, that of US_government at +2.92% a year with t = 2.73. US_credit comes next, at +2.79% with t = 1.76, and both return later. A government bond carrying significant alpha against an equity market is not a mispricing. It is the model reporting that it has the wrong factors, exactly as Fama and French (1993) argued when adding a term structure and a default factor for precisely these assets.

5.2.2 Splitting the beta, and then testing the split
A single beta assumes Equation 5.2 is the same on the way up and on the way down. PerformanceAnalytics estimates the two halves of Equation 5.4 in one call.

Rm <- xts::xts(MKT, order.by = d)
rfx <- xts::xts(rf, order.by = d)

cond <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  tibble::tibble(
    series = s,
    beta   = PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta(R[, s], Rm, rfx),
    bull   = PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta.bull(R[, s], Rm, rfx),
    bear   = PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta.bear(R[, s], Rm, rfx)
  )
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap = bear - bull)

cond |> dplyr::arrange(gap) |> head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   series           beta  bull    bear    gap
#>   <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 JP_government -0.0223 0.159 -0.120  -0.279
#> 2 UK_government  0.186  0.283  0.138  -0.145
#> 3 JP_credit      0.0953 0.227  0.105  -0.121
#> 4 CH_government  0.0642 0.163  0.0424 -0.121

JP_government has an unconditional beta of -0.0223, indistinguishable from zero and the sort of number that files a series under uncorrelated and forgets it. It is not uncorrelated. It rises with the market when the market rises, at +0.159, and rises against it when the market falls, at -0.120. The single number is the average of two opposite behaviors and destroys the only interesting property of the series.
Now the step that is usually skipped. An apparent asymmetry has to survive a test, because splitting a sample in two and comparing the halves is a machine for producing differences.

asym <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  y  <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
  dn <- as.numeric(mkt_e < 0)
  m  <- stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e + I(mkt_e * dn))
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 gap = stats::coef(m)[3],
                 t   = stats::coef(m)[3] / sqrt(nw[3, 3]),
                 p   = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(stats::coef(m)[3] / sqrt(nw[3, 3]))))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

asym |> dplyr::filter(p < 0.05) |> dplyr::arrange(p)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   series           gap     t      p
#>   <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 JP_government -0.283 -2.37 0.0177
#> 2 US_government -0.121 -2.30 0.0213

This is Equation 5.4 with the standard errors of Equation 5.5, and 2 of 16 survive, both of them government bonds. The Japanese bond asymmetry is real, at t = -2.37. The credit asymmetry, which is the one an allocator would most like to believe in, is not: US_credit has a gap of +0.098 with t = 0.66 and p = 0.51.
There are 130 down months in this sample. Estimating a separate beta on them, for sixteen series, will produce differences whether or not any exist. Report the split as a diagnostic; do not build a hedge on it without the test.







Figure 5.2: Beta when the market rises against beta when it falls. Points below the diagonal fall less than they rise; points above it fall more. Only the filled points survive a Newey-West test of the difference; the rest of the spread is what splitting 372 months into two piles will produce on its own.





5.2.3 What a factor is actually sorting on
Size is the second factor everyone reaches for, following Fama and French (1992) and Fama and French (1993), and here it is a trap worth walking into deliberately.

capW <- W
reg  <- sim_assets$region[match(colnames(Ra), sim_assets$asset_id)]

# Global sort: bottom half by capitalization minus top half.
smb_global <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(Ra)), function(i) {
  w <- capW[i, ]; ok <- w > 0; med <- median(w[ok])
  mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, ok & w <= med]) - mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, ok & w > med])
}, numeric(1))

# Region-neutral: rank within each region, then average the five spreads.
smb_neutral <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(Ra)), function(i) {
  w <- capW[i, ]
  mean(vapply(unique(reg), function(g) {
    j <- reg == g & w > 0; med <- median(w[j])
    mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, j & w <= med]) - mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, j & w > med])
  }, numeric(1)))
}, numeric(1))

Before using either, look at what the global sort placed in each leg.

legs <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(Ra)), function(i) {
  w <- capW[i, ]; ok <- w > 0; med <- median(w[ok])
  c(big_us   = sum(w[ok & w > med & reg[ok] == "US"]) / sum(w[ok & w > med]),
    small_us = sum(w[ok & w <= med & reg[ok] == "US"]) / sum(w[ok & w <= med]))
}, numeric(2))
round(rowMeans(legs), 3)
#>   big_us small_us 
#>    0.628    0.152

The big leg is 63% United States. The small leg is 15%. A global capitalization sort in a five-region universe does not sort on size. It sorts on region, and since region carries a currency, it sorts on currency too.
The consequence is measurable.

med_r2 <- function(f = NULL) {
  median(vapply(risky, function(s) {
    y <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
    summary(if (is.null(f)) stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e) else stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e + f))$r.squared
  }, numeric(1)))
}
c(market_only  = med_r2(),
  plus_global  = med_r2(smb_global),
  plus_neutral = med_r2(smb_neutral))
#>  market_only  plus_global plus_neutral 
#>      0.07726      0.09156      0.07894

# The premium of each construction, with its Newey-West t-statistic.
nw_t <- function(x) {
  m <- stats::lm(x ~ 1)
  unname(stats::coef(m)[1] / sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)[1, 1]))
}
c(global_premium  = ann_ret(smb_global),  global_t  = nw_t(smb_global),
  neutral_premium = ann_ret(smb_neutral), neutral_t = nw_t(smb_neutral),
  correlation     = cor(smb_global, smb_neutral))
#>  global_premium        global_t neutral_premium       neutral_t     correlation 
#>         0.02395         1.99148         0.03393         3.24015         0.61953

Adding the global size factor lifts the median \(R^2\) from 0.077 to 0.092. Constructing the same factor region-neutrally lifts it only to 0.079, an improvement of 0.002. The explanatory power was not size. It was the regional composition of the legs.
The premium runs the other way. The region-neutral factor earns 3.4% a year with a t-statistic of 3.24, the global sort 2.4% with 1.99: the construction that explains less variance carries the more reliable premium. The lesson is not that size does not exist. It is that a factor is defined by its construction, and a sort nobody has inspected is a bet nobody has chosen. Griffin (2002) makes the empirical case that the size and value factors are country-specific rather than global, and Hou et al. (2011) reach a similar conclusion on a wider cross-section. A practitioner building a global factor without neutralizing the country dimension is, on this evidence, building a country factor.






Notetable.CAPM() computes most of this chapter in one call



PerformanceAnalytics::table.CAPM() returns alpha and beta with their p-values, the bull and bear betas, \(R^2\), tracking error, the information ratio, Treynor’s ratio and the appraisal ratio, for as many series as it is handed. Most readers compute these one function at a time, and several never learn that the conditional betas are in there.



PerformanceAnalytics::table.CAPM(R[, c("US_credit", "JP_government", "US_equity")],
                                 Rm, Rf = rfx)

#>    `US_credit to ` `JP_government to ` `US_equity to `
#>              <dbl>               <dbl>           <dbl>

#>  2          0.129              -0.0223          0.985 
#>  3          0.0031             -0.0013          0.0001

title: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation
text:
5.3 How Much of This Survives

5.3.1 A beta is a time series
Equation 5.2 is written as though \(\beta_i\) were a constant. The conditional asset pricing literature starting with Ferson and Harvey (1991) and Jagannathan and Wang (1996) assumes it is not, and a rolling window shows directly how much it moves.

win <- 60L
roll_beta <- function(s) {
  y <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
  zoo::rollapply(cbind(y, mkt_e), win,
                 function(z) stats::cov(z[, 1], z[, 2]) / stats::var(z[, 2]),
                 by.column = FALSE, align = "right")
}

travel <- lapply(risky, function(s) {
  b <- roll_beta(s)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 full = stats::cov(as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf, mkt_e) / stats::var(mkt_e),
                 min = min(b), max = max(b), travel = diff(range(b)),
                 sign_flips = mean(sign(b) != sign(stats::cov(as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf, mkt_e))))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(travel))

Two patterns emerge, and the second is the one to carry forward.
The betas that travel furthest are not the largest. UK_credit moves 0.96 across the sample, from -0.13 to +0.82, while US_equity, with a beta near one, travels only 0.33 and never changes sign. Blume (1971) documented the same regularity in individual stocks: extreme betas are the unreliable ones, and they revert.
The largest full-sample beta outside equity is 0.40 in absolute value, and every one of the 11 changes sign, the median in 31% of all windows. JP_government, whose beta is closest to zero, does so in 47% and US_credit in 31%; US_government, at 7%, is the one small beta that is reliably negative. The five equity series flip in none.







Figure 5.3: Sixty-month rolling betas for six series. The dashed line is the full-sample estimate. An equity beta moves without changing sign; a beta near zero crosses it repeatedly, which means the sign of the hedge it implies is not known.




A small beta is not a stable beta. It is a beta whose sign is unknown. That is why Section 8.1 exists, and why a hedge ratio needs an error bar before it needs a decimal place.

5.3.2 Measuring the instability itself
If the moments move, the movement is itself a quantity. A turbulence index measures it as the Mahalanobis distance of a period’s returns from their recent mean, scaled by the covariance structure,
\[
d_t = \left(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right)'
      \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
      \left(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right),
\tag{5.6}\]
so that an unusual pattern of returns counts as turbulent even when no single series is extreme. Chow et al. (1999) introduced the construction for portfolio work and Kritzman and Li (2010) developed it as a risk-management signal. The implementation used here is Stöckl (2020), which is not on CRAN; see Appendix D.

library(uncertaintymeasures)

R_risky <- R[, risky]
turb <- OSturbulence(R_risky, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)

OSturbulence() estimates \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) from data strictly before each observation, so the index never sees the month it is scoring. An in-sample variant exists, and the gap between them is a clean picture of what look-ahead buys.

tb  <- as.numeric(turb$turb)
top <- order(tb, decreasing = TRUE, na.last = NA)[1:5]

# Which of the named episodes, if any, each month belongs to.
episode_of <- rep("none", length(d))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(sim_episodes))) {
  episode_of[in_episode(d, sim_episodes$episode[i])] <- sim_episodes$label[i]
}

data.frame(month = fmt_model(d[top]), turbulence = round(tb[top], 2),
           episode = episode_of[top])
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   month                     turbulence episode        
#>   <chr>                          <dbl> <chr>          
#> 1 October of model year 17        1.93 credit crisis  
#> 2 November of model year 17       0.99 credit crisis  
#> 3 December of model year 17       0.83 credit crisis  
#> 4 January of model year 18        0.82 credit crisis  
#> 5 March of model year 29          0.81 liquidity shock

The highest reading in the sample is October of model year 17, in the credit crisis, at 1.93, 1.95 times the next one, and 4 of the 5 highest readings fall in that episode. The peak is the same month Section 4.3 identified by counting exceedances, arrived at independently, expressed as one number rather than a count, and available on the day rather than in hindsight.
The component that makes Equation 5.6 more than a volatility measure is the ratio of the full distance to the one computed from variances alone.

ct <- as.numeric(turb$cturb)
c(median     = median(ct, na.rm = TRUE),
  peak_month = ct[peak],
  max        = max(ct, na.rm = TRUE))
#>     median peak_month        max 
#>      1.569      1.631      9.580

This isolates how much of a turbulent month is correlations breaking rather than volatilities rising, which is the distinction Forbes and Rigobon (2002) showed is easy to confuse. In the peak month the ratio is 1.63 against a median of 1.57: the most turbulent month of the sample was a month of extreme moves in an ordinary correlation structure. Section 4.3 found average pairwise correlation higher in the credit crisis than in calm months, but only by choosing the windows by hand and knowing the answer first. This is the same question asked continuously and without hindsight, and it is what a regime-aware allocation in Section 19.1 would have to react to.







Figure 5.4: Out-of-sample turbulence, estimated from a sixty-month trailing window. The first five model years are consumed by the window and are not shown.

title: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation
text:
Key Takeaways

The \(R^2\) of Equation 5.1 is not decoration. By Equation 5.3 it is the share of an asset’s risk the model claims to describe, and the median across these sixteen series is 0.08. A one-factor model is an equity model applied to everything else.
A market proxy has a composition, and this one is on average 57% United States and 70% at the end of the sample. Every beta computed against it is largely a United States beta (Roll 1977).
Conditional betas are worth computing and are rarely worth believing. Of sixteen asymmetries estimated with Equation 5.4, 2 survive Newey-West inference, and the one an allocator would most want is not among them.
A factor is defined by its construction. A global size sort in a multi-region universe puts 63% United States in one leg and 15% in the other, so it is a region bet wearing a size label (Griffin 2002; Hou et al. 2011).
Betas move. Equity betas do so without changing sign; outside equity the median beta has the wrong sign in 31% of all sixty-month windows and the one closest to zero in 47% (Blume 1971).
The instability is itself measurable without hindsight. The Mahalanobis turbulence of Equation 5.6 picks out October of model year 17, in the credit crisis, from a trailing window, and its correlation component separates dependence breaking down from volatility merely rising (Chow et al. 1999; Kritzman and Li 2010).

title: 5  Factor Models and Beta Estimation
text:
Exercises

Rebuild the market proxy with equal rather than capitalization weights. Which betas move most, and does the ranking in Table 5.2 survive? Explain what that says about the phrase “the market”.
The asymmetry test uses a single interaction term. Replace it with separate regressions on the up and down months, and confirm that the point estimates agree while the standard errors do not. Which is the honest one, and why?
Take the two series with the highest sign_flips in Table 5.2 and plot their rolling betas against the turbulence index. Does the beta move because the market is turbulent, or independently of it?

OSturbulence() has an s.k argument controlling the length of the short window whose mean is compared with the long-run mean. Vary it from 1 to 12 and describe what the index measures at each end.

Harvey et al. (2016) argue that a t-statistic of two is too low a bar once many hypotheses have been tested. Sixteen asymmetries were tested here. Apply a Bonferroni correction and a Benjamini-Hochberg correction to the p-values in asym, and report how many survive each.

title: 6  Expected Returns
text:
6.1 How Precisely a Mean Can Be Known
Every optimizer in this book consumes a vector of expected returns, and nothing in the data pins that vector down as well as the covariance matrix beside it. Merton (1980) established why: the standard error of a mean estimated over a span of \(\tau\) years is \(\sigma/\sqrt{\tau}\) whatever the sampling frequency, so only a longer history helps, and thirty years of it leaves an annual risk premium known to within several percentage points. That is a property of the object rather than of any estimator, and it is the reason expected returns are the hard input of Section 9.1 while the covariance matrix of Section 7.1 is merely a large one.
This chapter is about strategic expected returns in the sense of Section 3.1: the unconditional vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) a long-run policy is set on, with no information about where in the cycle we stand. Conditional forecasts are the tactical work of Section 16.1, and turning an opinion into a return is the subject of Section 17.1. We first measure how imprecisely each of the sixteen means is known and what that does to a return target, then set out the two alternatives to the sample mean, shrinkage toward a common value and reverse optimization from market weights, then implement both and show how PortfolioAnalytics takes a mean vector it did not compute, and finally feed the three vectors to the same tangency problem to see what each buys and how much each moves when the sample changes.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill for the reasons given in Section 3.1.
Write \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) for the vector of sample means of the excess returns and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) for their sample covariance, as in Section 9.1. Each element of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) is an average of \(T\) monthly observations, and if those observations are independent with volatility \(\sigma\) per year, the standard error of the annualized mean is
\[
\operatorname{se}(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}},
\tag{6.1}\]
where \(\tau\) is the calendar span in years. Equation 4.3 derived this alongside the standard error of the variance, and the contrast between the two is the point of Merton (1980): the sampling interval does not appear in Equation 6.1, so nothing short of more calendar time improves it. A 95 percent interval for the mean is
\[
\hat{\mu} \pm 1.96\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}},
\tag{6.2}\]
and setting its half-width equal to the mean itself gives the span of history needed before the interval excludes zero:
\[
\tau^{*} = \left(\frac{1.96\,\sigma}{\mu}\right)^{2}.
\tag{6.3}\]
Both quantities are computable for every series, and the table they produce is the right way to begin a chapter on expected returns.
mu_s <- colMeans(Re)                 # monthly sample means, the mu of chapter 9
S    <- stats::cov(Re)               # the sample covariance of chapter 7

precision <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = colnames(Re),
  mean  = mu_s * 12,
  vol   = apply(Re, 2, stats::sd) * sqrt(12)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(se    = vol / sqrt(years),                 # @eq-06-se
                t     = mean / se,
                lower = mean - 1.96 * se,                  # @eq-06-interval
                upper = mean + 1.96 * se,
                years_needed = (1.96 * vol / mean)^2) |>   # @eq-06-years
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(t))

n_straddle <- sum(precision$lower < 0)
c(series = nrow(precision), interval_includes_zero = n_straddle,
  median_se = median(precision$se), median_years_needed = median(precision$years_needed))
#>                 series interval_includes_zero              median_se 
#>               16.00000               10.00000                0.02184 
#>    median_years_needed 
#>               45.32200

Take the series whose mean is furthest from zero relative to its standard error, US_equity. Its annualized volatility is 0.156 and the sample spans 31 model years, so by Equation 6.1
\[
\operatorname{se}(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{0.156}{\sqrt{31}}
= 0.0280,
\]
a standard error of 2.8 percentage points on a mean of 11.3%, and an interval from 5.8% to 16.8%. That is the best case. For 10 of the 16 series the interval of Equation 6.2 includes zero: the data do not reject the hypothesis that the asset carries no risk premium at all. The median series would need 45 years of history before it did, and JP_government, with a mean of 0.6% against a standard error of 1.9 points, would need 1263. Fama and French (2002) make the same point on a century and a quarter of United States data: the realized equity premium is estimated with a standard error that leaves its level open to debate by several percentage points, which is why they estimate it from dividend and earnings growth instead. Section 4.2 measured the practical counterpart on this market, a rolling sixty-month mean that wanders by more than its own level, and Figure 4.2 shows it. Nothing in this chapter improves on Equation 6.1; the estimators below manage the imprecision rather than remove it.

title: 6  Expected Returns
text:
NoteSampling more finely helps the variance and not the mean



The obvious response to an imprecise mean is more observations, and the weekly panel sim_class_returns_weekly holds the same 31 model years at more than four times the resolution. Equation 4.3 says what to expect: the standard error of the variance falls with \(\sqrt{T}\), and the standard error of the mean does not move.

Rw   <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_weekly, date, class, return)
# The weekly bill series starts one week before the return panel: align by date.
rf_w <- sim_riskfree_weekly$return[match(zoo::index(Rw), sim_riskfree_weekly$date)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(rf_w), identical(colnames(Rw), colnames(Re)))
Rew  <- Rw - rf_w

freq <- tibble::tibble(
  asset     = colnames(Re),
  se_mean_m = apply(Re,  2, stats::sd) * sqrt(12) / sqrt(nrow(Re) / 12),
  se_mean_w = apply(Rew, 2, stats::sd) * sqrt(52) / sqrt(nrow(Rew) / 52),
  se_var_m  = apply(Re,  2, stats::var) * 12 * sqrt(2 / nrow(Re)),
  se_var_w  = apply(Rew, 2, stats::var) * 52 * sqrt(2 / nrow(Rew))
)
c(months = nrow(Re), weeks = nrow(Rew),
  mean_se_ratio     = median(freq$se_mean_w / freq$se_mean_m),
  variance_se_ratio = median(freq$se_var_w / freq$se_var_m),
  sqrt_T_ratio      = sqrt(nrow(Re) / nrow(Rew)))
#>            months             weeks     mean_se_ratio variance_se_ratio 
#>          372.0000         1618.0000            1.0309            0.5115 
#>      sqrt_T_ratio 
#>            0.4795

Going from 372 months to 1618 weeks leaves the standard error of the mean where it was, at a median ratio of 1.03, and cuts the standard error of the variance to 0.51 of its monthly value, against the 0.48 that \(\sqrt{T}\) predicts. This is why Section 7.2 can estimate its input from the same history that leaves this chapter’s input undetermined.



6.1.1 A target set on a sample mean
Equation 9.2 fixes a return target \(\bar{\mu}\) and asks for the least variance that attains it, and Section 9.2 solves that program with \(\bar{\mu}\) set at the upper quartile of the sample means. The constraint \(\boldsymbol{w}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \bar{\mu}\) is then satisfied to the solver’s tolerance, on an input known to the precision of Table 6.1.

target_m <- as.numeric(quantile(mu_s, 0.75))      # the target chapter 9 imposes
se_med   <- median(precision$se)
c(target_annual = target_m * 12, median_se = se_med,
  target_lower = target_m * 12 - 1.96 * se_med,
  target_upper = target_m * 12 + 1.96 * se_med)
#> target_annual     median_se  target_lower  target_upper 
#>       0.06650       0.02184       0.02370       0.10930

The target is 6.65% a year, held to eight decimal places. The inputs that define it carry a median standard error of 2.2 percentage points, so a mean of that size is itself known only to somewhere between 2.4% and 10.9%. A constraint set on a sample mean is a constraint set on noise, and the optimizer honors it exactly.
The literature on what follows is old and consistent, and one sentence each suffices here because Section 9.1 has already used it. Jobson and Korkie (1980) showed that the sampling distribution of the estimated tangency weights is so wide that the portfolio’s expected Sharpe ratio falls far short of the one the estimate promises. Best and Grauer (1991) traced the mechanism to Equation 9.5: the weights are \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\) applied to \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), so an error in a mean is magnified by the condition number of the covariance matrix on its way into the portfolio. Chopra and Ziemba (1993) priced the two inputs against each other and found errors in means roughly an order of magnitude more costly than errors in variances. Michaud (1989) named the consequence, an optimizer that systematically overweights whatever the sample flattered. Kan and Zhou (2007) derived the expected out-of-sample loss of the plug-in rule, showed that the term due to \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) dominates, and proposed holding the sample tangency portfolio alongside the minimum-variance portfolio of Equation 9.3, which is exactly what the shrinkage estimator below turns out to do. DeMiguel et al. (2009) supplied the empirical verdict with fourteen rules on seven datasets: none that estimates the mean was consistently better than equal weighting out of sample. 1 measures the cost on this market and Section 26.1 derives it.

6.1.2 Shrinkage of the mean
The response from statistics predates all of that. Stein (1956) showed that for three or more means estimated jointly, the vector of sample means is inadmissible under quadratic loss: an estimator that pulls every element toward a common value has lower expected error whatever the true means are. James and Stein (1961) gave the estimator its form, a shrinkage factor that depends on how far the sample means sit from their target, and Efron and Morris (1975) the intuition, that a set of estimates spread by sampling error is always spread too far. Jorion (1985) brought the argument to portfolios and Jorion (1986) gave it the form that is still used. The target is the expected return of the minimum-variance portfolio, the one number about \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) that \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) alone pins down, and the estimator is
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\text{BS}}
= (1-v)\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} + v\,\mu_0\,\boldsymbol{\iota},
\qquad
\mu_0 = \frac{\boldsymbol{\iota}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}
             {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}},
\qquad
v = \frac{N+2}
         {(N+2) + T\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\mu_0\boldsymbol{\iota})'
                     \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}
                     (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\mu_0\boldsymbol{\iota})}.
\tag{6.4}\]
The intensity \(v\) is set by the data rather than chosen. The quadratic form in its denominator is \(T\) times the squared distance of the sample means from their target, measured in the metric of the covariance matrix; when the means are far apart relative to their sampling error, \(v\) is small and the sample is trusted, and when they are indistinguishable, \(v\) approaches one and every asset is assigned the same expected return. As \(T\) grows, \(v\) falls to zero, so the estimator is consistent. This is the same construction as Equation 7.6 for the covariance matrix, where Ledoit and Wolf (2004) derive the analogous intensity, and it has the same character: a biased estimator with lower total error than the unbiased one.
What shrinkage does to the portfolio is visible from Equation 9.5. Because the map from means to unconstrained tangency weights is linear,
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\text{BS}}
= (1-v)\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
+ v\,\mu_0\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota},
\tag{6.5}\]
a combination of the sample tangency direction and the minimum-variance direction of Equation 9.3. Shrinking the means toward \(\mu_0\) therefore moves the tangency portfolio toward the minimum-variance portfolio, which is the three-fund rule of Kan and Zhou (2007) arrived at from the estimator’s side. Other targets are possible and each carries an argument: Pástor (2000) and MacKinlay and Pástor (2000) shrink toward the means a factor model such as that of Section 5.2 implies, Tu and Zhou (2011) combine the sample rule with equal weighting, and Garlappi et al. (2007) reach a shrinkage form from ambiguity aversion rather than from loss. The target used here is the one that needs no model beyond \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\).

6.1.3 Equilibrium returns by reverse optimization
The third route asks a different question. Rather than estimating \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) from the history of returns, it asks what \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) would have to be for a portfolio someone actually holds to be optimal. Sharpe (1974) posed the problem in that form, and Black and Litterman (1992) chose the portfolio: the market, weighted by capitalization, which is the portfolio the equilibrium of Sharpe (1964) and Lintner (1965) says every investor holds. An investor who maximizes \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\delta}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\) has the first-order condition \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = \delta\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\), derived in Section B.5, and if the aggregate investor holds the market, the expected returns consistent with that are
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}} = \delta\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}.
\tag{6.6}\]
The scalar \(\delta\) is the market’s risk aversion, and premultiplying Equation 6.6 by \(\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\) shows how to read it from the market’s own history:
\[
\delta = \frac{\mu_{\text{mkt}}}{\sigma^{2}_{\text{mkt}}}
       = \frac{\text{SR}_{\text{mkt}}}{\sigma_{\text{mkt}}},
\tag{6.7}\]
the market’s expected excess return divided by its variance, which is the same number whether computed from monthly or from annual moments. He and Litterman (1999) give the intuition for what the resulting vector does inside an optimizer, Satchell and Scowcroft (2000) the Bayesian derivation, and Idzorek (2007) a step-by-step account of the full model with views attached; the views are Section 17.1’s subject, and only the prior is used here.
Three properties of Equation 6.6 matter here. It is not a forecast: it is the vector for which the market portfolio is the tangency portfolio of Equation 9.5, by construction, so an optimizer handed \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) returns \(\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}\), a portfolio that is held, diversified and consistent with the covariance matrix. \(\delta\) scales every element alike, and the tangency portfolio is invariant to scale, so \(\delta\) sets how much of the portfolio is risky rather than what the risky part holds; it matters for position size and, in Section 17.1, for how heavily a view is weighed against the prior. And the package’s risk_aversion argument is \(\gamma/2\) in the notation of Section B.5, so reproducing the market portfolio requires risk_aversion set to \(\delta/2\), verified numerically below.
The weakness of the method is the weight vector. Roll (1977) is the reminder that the market portfolio is not observable, and on this market the problem is concrete: sim_marketcap_weekly carries capitalizations for the 123 equity instruments and for nothing else. No capitalization exists for the government or credit series or for the commodity index, so a full class-level equilibrium cannot be read from the data as shipped. We do the two things that can be done: a clean demonstration on the five equity classes, whose weights are their capitalizations, and a class-level version on a stated proxy for the rest, kept in a box and labelled as the assumption it is.

title: 6  Expected Returns
text:
6.2 Three Estimators in Code

6.2.1 Bayes-Stein in a few lines
Equation 6.4 is a function of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), \(N\) and \(T\), and nothing else. Jorion (1986) scales the sample covariance by \((T-1)/(T-N-2)\) before inverting it, which makes the inverse unbiased; on 372 observations and 16 assets the factor is 1.048 and changes \(v\) at the second decimal.

bayes_stein <- function(R) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu   <- colMeans(X)
  S    <- stats::cov(X) * (T - 1) / (T - N - 2)   # Jorion's unbiased scaling
  Sinv <- solve(S); iota <- rep(1, N)
  mu0  <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% mu) / as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% iota)
  d    <- mu - mu0
  v    <- (N + 2) / ((N + 2) + T * as.numeric(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d))
  list(mu = setNames((1 - v) * mu + v * mu0, colnames(X)), mu0 = mu0, v = v)
}

bs <- bayes_stein(Re)
stopifnot(bs$v > 0.5, bs$v < 0.6)    # "more than half" and "roughly halved" below
c(v = bs$v, mu0_annual = bs$mu0 * 12)
#>          v mu0_annual 
#>    0.52768    0.03234

The intensity is \(v = 0.528\) and the target is \(\mu_0 = 3.23%\) a year, the expected return of the minimum-variance portfolio. For US_equity the estimator of Equation 6.4 reads
\[
\hat{\mu}_{\text{BS}}
= (1 - 0.528) \times 0.1130
+ 0.528 \times 0.0323
= 0.0704,
\]
so more than half of the distance between the sample mean and the common value is removed. The same happens to every series, in both directions.

mu_long <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = rep(colnames(Re), 2),
  kind  = rep(c("sample mean", "Bayes-Stein"), each = N),
  value = c(mu_s, bs$mu) * 12
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(asset = factor(asset, levels = names(sort(mu_s))))
stopifnot(nrow(mu_long) == 2 * N, !anyNA(mu_long$value))

# The ordering is untouched: the same ranks, asset by asset.
stopifnot(identical(names(mu_s), names(bs$mu)), identical(rank(mu_s), rank(bs$mu)))
c(spread_sample = diff(range(mu_s)) * 12, spread_shrunk = diff(range(bs$mu)) * 12,
  rank_correlation = stats::cor(mu_s, bs$mu, method = "spearman"))
#>    spread_sample    spread_shrunk rank_correlation 
#>          0.12818          0.06054          1.00000








Figure 6.1: Sample means and Bayes-Stein estimates for the sixteen series, annualized. Each segment joins an asset’s two estimates; the dashed line is the common target, the expected return of the minimum-variance portfolio. The ordering is untouched and the spread is roughly halved.




The spread between the highest and the lowest expected return falls from 12.8 to 6.1 percentage points, and the rank correlation between the two vectors is 1.00, because Equation 6.4 is a linear map with a positive slope. Shrinkage changes how different the assets look, not which looks better.

6.2.2 Equilibrium returns for the five equity classes
The clean case first. Each regional equity class is the capitalization-weighted sum of its instruments, so its weight in the world equity market is the sum of their capitalizations. As in Section 5.2 the weight used in month \(t\) is the last one observed on or before the end of month \(t-1\), a weight that could have been held.

eq_ids     <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
region_of  <- setNames(sim_assets$region, sim_assets$asset_id)
eq_classes <- grep("_equity$", colnames(Re), value = TRUE)

# Capitalization of each region's listed equities, week by week.
cap_region <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% eq_ids) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = paste0(region_of[asset], "_equity")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(cap = sum(market_cap), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = class, values_from = cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
stopifnot(setequal(setdiff(names(cap_region), "date"), eq_classes), !anyNA(cap_region))
cap_mat <- as.matrix(cap_region[, eq_classes])      # columns in class order, by name

d <- zoo::index(Re)
W_eq <- t(vapply(seq_along(d), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) d[1] - 31 else d[i - 1]     # last week of the previous month
  j <- max(which(cap_region$date <= cutoff))
  cap_mat[j, ] / sum(cap_mat[j, ])
}, numeric(length(eq_classes))))
colnames(W_eq) <- eq_classes
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W_eq) - 1) < 1e-10), identical(colnames(W_eq), eq_classes))

round(rbind(first = W_eq[1, ], average = colMeans(W_eq), last = W_eq[nrow(W_eq), ]), 3)
#>         CH_equity EU_equity JP_equity UK_equity US_equity
#> first       0.034     0.161     0.185     0.123     0.497
#> average     0.075     0.175     0.095     0.085     0.570
#> last        0.059     0.142     0.056     0.044     0.700

The composition drifts, from 50% United States at the start to 70% at the end, which Section 5.2 found for the same proxy. An unconditional \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is matched to an unconditional weight vector, so we use the average composition over the sample; the last month’s weights are an exercise. The market’s own excess return calibrates \(\delta\) through Equation 6.7.

mkt_e  <- rowSums(W_eq * zoo::coredata(Re[, eq_classes]))   # the market's excess return
delta  <- mean(mkt_e) / stats::var(mkt_e)                    # @eq-06-delta
w_mkt5 <- colMeans(W_eq)
S5     <- S[eq_classes, eq_classes]
mu_eq5 <- setNames(delta * as.numeric(S5 %*% w_mkt5), eq_classes)   # @eq-06-equilibrium
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_mkt5 * mu_eq5) - delta * as.numeric(t(w_mkt5) %*% S5 %*% w_mkt5)) < 1e-12)

c(market_return = mean(mkt_e) * 12, market_vol = stats::sd(mkt_e) * sqrt(12),
  market_sharpe = mean(mkt_e) / stats::sd(mkt_e) * sqrt(12), delta = delta)
#> market_return    market_vol market_sharpe         delta 
#>        0.1058        0.1486        0.7117        4.7886

With an annualized excess return of 0.1058 and a variance of 0.0221, Equation 6.7 gives
\[
\delta = \frac{0.1058}{0.0221}
= 4.79,
\]
and Equation 6.6 then produces one expected return per class.

prem_eq <- sum(w_mkt5 * mu_eq5)               # the market's own equilibrium premium
beta5   <- mu_eq5 / prem_eq                     # (Sigma w) / (w' Sigma w), asset by asset

cmp5 <- tibble::tibble(
  asset       = eq_classes,
  weight      = w_mkt5,
  beta        = beta5,
  sample      = mu_s[eq_classes] * 12,
  se          = precision$se[match(eq_classes, precision$asset)],
  equilibrium = mu_eq5 * 12
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap_in_se = (equilibrium - sample) / se)
stopifnot(identical(cmp5$asset, eq_classes), !anyNA(cmp5),
          abs(sum(w_mkt5 * beta5) - 1) < 1e-12)
# The two revisions the text reads off the table: JP_equity up, US_equity down.
stopifnot(cmp5$gap_in_se[cmp5$asset == "JP_equity"] > 0,
          cmp5$gap_in_se[cmp5$asset == "US_equity"] < 0)




Table 6.2: Sample means and equilibrium returns for the five equity classes, annualized. Beta is the class’s beta on the market portfolio; the last column is the gap between the two estimates in units of the sample mean’s standard error.

Dividing Equation 6.6 by the market’s own equilibrium premium \(\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\) shows what the vector is: each element is the asset’s beta on the market times that premium,
\[
\mu_{\text{eq},i}
= \frac{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}})_i}
       {\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}}
  \times \boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}}'\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}
= \beta_i \times 10.28%,
\]
which is the CAPM of Equation 5.1 read as a prior rather than tested as a model. Every equilibrium return sits within 0.6 standard errors of the corresponding sample mean, so the two vectors are not in conflict; they answer different questions. The sample mean says what each market paid. The equilibrium says what each would have to pay for investors to hold it in the proportion they do, and it pays a beta of 0.75 for JP_equity at the market premium where the sample paid less, and revises US_equity, with a beta of 1.00, down from a sample mean the market premium does not support.






NoteWorked: a class-level equilibrium on a stated proxy





The application below needs \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\) for all sixteen classes, and eleven of them have no capitalization. What follows is a placeholder, and it should be read as one. Assumption: world investable wealth is split 40 percent equity, 40 percent government bonds, 15 percent credit and 5 percent commodities, and within the equity, government and credit blocks each region’s share is its share of equity capitalization. Nothing in the data supports the block split; it is a round-number stand-in for a figure that a real allocation would take from a global market-capitalization survey.


# ASSUMPTION, not data: the split of world wealth across the four blocks.
block <- c(equity = 0.40, government = 0.40, credit = 0.15, commodity = 0.05)
stopifnot(abs(sum(block) - 1) < 1e-12)

W16 <- matrix(0, nrow(Re), N, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Re)))
for (r in sub("_equity$", "", eq_classes)) {
  s <- W_eq[, paste0(r, "_equity")]                 # the region's share of equity capitalization
  W16[, paste0(r, "_equity")]     <- block[["equity"]]     * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_government")] <- block[["government"]] * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_credit")]     <- block[["credit"]]     * s
}
W16[, "GLOBAL_commodity"] <- block[["commodity"]]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W16) - 1) < 1e-10), identical(colnames(W16), colnames(Re)))

mkt16_e <- rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re))
delta16 <- mean(mkt16_e) / stats::var(mkt16_e)                       # @eq-06-delta
w_mkt   <- colMeans(W16)
mu_eq   <- setNames(delta16 * as.numeric(S %*% w_mkt), colnames(Re))  # @eq-06-equilibrium

c(proxy_return = mean(mkt16_e) * 12, proxy_vol = stats::sd(mkt16_e) * sqrt(12),
  proxy_sharpe = mean(mkt16_e) / stats::sd(mkt16_e) * sqrt(12), delta = delta16)
#> proxy_return    proxy_vol proxy_sharpe        delta 
#>      0.05841      0.07325      0.79746     10.88695

round(cbind(weight = w_mkt, sample = mu_s * 12, equilibrium = mu_eq * 12)[order(-w_mkt), ], 3)
#>                  weight sample equilibrium
#> US_equity         0.228  0.113       0.099
#> US_government     0.228  0.023       0.007
#> US_credit         0.085  0.042       0.032
#> EU_equity         0.070  0.134       0.127
#> EU_government     0.070  0.018       0.041
#> GLOBAL_commodity  0.050  0.033       0.039
#> JP_equity         0.038  0.056       0.074
#> JP_government     0.038  0.006       0.021
#> UK_equity         0.034  0.099       0.103
#> UK_government     0.034  0.020       0.042
#> CH_equity         0.030  0.097       0.102
#> CH_government     0.030  0.025       0.037
#> EU_credit         0.026  0.036       0.065
#> JP_credit         0.014  0.018       0.037
#> UK_credit         0.013  0.041       0.071
#> CH_credit         0.011  0.035       0.051

A bond-heavy proxy with a Sharpe ratio of 0.80 at a volatility of 7.3% implies, by Equation 6.7, \(\delta = 10.9\), more than twice the equity-only figure. The vector it produces disagrees with the sample in one place that matters: US_government is assigned 0.7% a year against a sample mean of 2.3%, because it covaries negatively with the equity block and so carries almost no risk in the market portfolio. Whether that is right depends entirely on whether the block split is, which is what reverse optimization can and cannot do without a market weight.




6.2.3 The moments as PortfolioAnalytics sees them
PortfolioAnalytics (Peterson and Carl 2026) computes every moment an objective needs through one function, set.portfolio.moments(), whose method argument selects the estimator.

spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

eval(formals(set.portfolio.moments)$method)
#> [1] "sample"          "boudt"           "black_litterman" "meucci"

m_sample <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, spec, method = "sample")
str(m_sample, give.attr = FALSE)
#> List of 2
#>  $ mu   : num [1:16, 1] 0.00291 0.00808 0.00205 0.00298 0.01118 ...
#>  $ sigma: num [1:16, 1:16] 0.001164 0.000666 0.001026 0.000987 0.000568 ...
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(m_sample$mu), unname(mu_s)))

sample returns the moments of Table 6.1. boudt cleans the higher moments through a factor structure and belongs to Section 11.1; black_litterman and meucci blend a prior with views and belong to Section 17.1. None of the four is Bayes-Stein, and none accepts a market weight. The route in is the one Section 7.2 used for a shrunk covariance matrix: optimize.portfolio() takes a momentFUN argument, and a function of (R, portfolio, ...) returning the named list the package expects can supply any mean vector at all.

bayes_stein_moments <- function(R, portfolio, ...) {
  m <- bayes_stein(R)$mu
  S <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(R))
  list(mu = m, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = m, var = S)
}

opt_bs <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                             momentFUN = bayes_stein_moments)
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(opt_bs$moment_values$mu), unname(bs$mu)))
names(opt_bs$moment_values)
#> [1] "momentFun" "mu"        "sigma"
round(extractWeights(opt_bs)[extractWeights(opt_bs) > 0.005], 4)
#>        EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity        JP_equity        UK_equity 
#>           0.0558           0.0425           0.0190           0.0055 
#>        US_equity    US_government 
#>           0.1191           0.7581

The stopifnot() confirms that the moments the solver used are the shrunk ones, and maxSR = TRUE asks for the tangency portfolio directly.






ImportantOn the CRAN release, maxSR ignores the mean you supplied



optimize.portfolio(maxSR = TRUE) on PortfolioAnalytics 2.1.2 as released recomputes the mean from R inside the Sharpe-ratio search and discards the one momentFUN returned, so the three estimators of this chapter would all produce the sample-mean tangency portfolio, without a message. This book runs on the patched build recorded in Appendix D, and R/_common.R warns if it is not installed. On the release, the portable route is the one Section 9.2 used, reading the highest Sharpe ratio off create.EfficientFrontier(), which does honor momentFUN. Either way, assert that the answers differ, as the application below does; a stopifnot() is the only thing that distinguishes a solved problem from the wrong one solved quietly.


The package also ships the Black-Litterman formula as black.litterman(). Called with the prior alone, it should return the prior, and it does, together with a second object that needs care.

bl <- black.litterman(Re, P = diag(N), Mu = mu_eq, Views = mu_eq)
str(bl, give.attr = FALSE)
#> List of 2
#>  $ BLMu   : num [1:16, 1] 0.00426 0.00851 0.00308 0.00544 0.01062 ...
#>  $ BLSigma: num [1:16, 1:16] 0.000582 0.000333 0.000513 0.000494 0.000284 ...
c(posterior_equals_prior = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(bl$BLMu), unname(mu_eq))),
  variance_ratio = unique(round(diag(bl$BLSigma) / diag(S), 6)))
#> posterior_equals_prior         variance_ratio 
#>                    1.0                    0.5







Warningblack.litterman() is the blending formula, not the model



Four things about this function are measured rather than documented, and a reader who expects Black and Litterman (1992) will walk into each of them.

bl_default <- black.litterman(Re, P = diag(N))                   # Mu and Views left at their defaults
bl_moments <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, spec, method = "black_litterman")
c(default_view_shift_pp   = mean(as.numeric(bl_default$BLMu) - mu_s) * 1200,
  moments_shift_min_pp    = min(as.numeric(bl_moments$mu) - mu_s) * 1200,
  moments_shift_max_pp    = max(as.numeric(bl_moments$mu) - mu_s) * 1200,
  moments_variance_ratio  = min(diag(bl_moments$sigma) / diag(S)))
#>  default_view_shift_pp   moments_shift_min_pp   moments_shift_max_pp 
#>                20.0752                 1.3329                21.4745 
#> moments_variance_ratio 
#>                 0.6705

First, there is no market-weight argument and no \(\delta\): Mu defaults to colMeans(R), so the prior is the sample mean unless Equation 6.6 is computed and passed in, as above. Second, there is no \(\tau\): the prior’s uncertainty is \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) itself and the view uncertainty is fixed at \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\). Third, Views = NULL is not the absence of a view. The default view is the standard deviation of each view portfolio, a bullish opinion on everything, and with P = diag(N) it lifts every mean by 20 percentage points a year on average; set.portfolio.moments(method = "black_litterman") inherits this with one default view on the plain sum of the assets’ returns and shifts the means by between 1 and 21 points. Fourth, BLSigma is the posterior covariance of the mean, not of returns: with the prior alone it is exactly \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/2\), and set.portfolio.moments() hands it to the optimizer as sigma, which then optimizes on half the risk. Supply Mu yourself, set Views to P %*% Mu when you want the prior alone, and never let BLSigma reach a risk objective.


One more trap, this time in how arguments travel. set.portfolio.moments() recovers Mu, P and Views through match.call(), which returns the expression a caller typed rather than its value.

try(set.portfolio.moments(Re, spec, method = "black_litterman",
                          Mu = mu_eq, P = diag(N), Views = mu_eq))
#> Error in black.litterman(R = tmpR, P = P, Mu = Mu, Sigma = Sigma, Views = Views) : 
#>   length of Mu must equal number of columns of R

opt_bl <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
                             momentFUN = "set.portfolio.moments",
                             method = "black_litterman",
                             Mu = mu_eq, P = diag(N), Views = mu_eq)
c(mu_honored  = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(opt_bl$moment_values$mu), unname(mu_eq))),
  sigma_ratio = unique(round(diag(opt_bl$moment_values$sigma) / diag(S), 6)))
#>  mu_honored sigma_ratio 
#>         1.0         0.5

Called directly with a variable, the function sees the symbol mu_eq, a vector of length one, and stops. Called through optimize.portfolio(), which assembles the call with do.call(), the values arrive intact and the mean is honored; the covariance arrives halved, which is the fourth point of the callout. The custom momentFUN of the previous chunk has neither problem, and it is what the rest of this chapter uses.
Finally, the \(\gamma/2\) convention. The equilibrium vector was built so that the market portfolio maximizes \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\delta}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\), and the package’s quadratic utility objective puts risk_aversion where \(\delta/2\) stands. Feeding \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\) back in is therefore a test of both the vector and the convention.

make_moments <- function(mu, S) {
  force(mu); force(S)
  function(R, portfolio, ...) list(mu = mu, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = mu, var = S)
}

base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

qu_weights <- function(lambda) {
  s <- base_spec |>
    add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = lambda)
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, s, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                         momentFUN = make_moments(mu_eq, S)))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

gamma_check <- c(at_delta_over_2 = max(abs(qu_weights(delta16 / 2) - w_mkt)),
                 at_delta        = max(abs(qu_weights(delta16)     - w_mkt)))
stopifnot(gamma_check[["at_delta_over_2"]] < 1e-8)
gamma_check
#>     at_delta_over_2            at_delta 
#> 0.00000000000001023 0.35987017381783498

At risk_aversion = delta16 / 2 the optimizer returns the proxy market portfolio to within 1e-14; at risk_aversion = delta16 it returns a portfolio that differs by up to 36 percentage points in a single weight. The first number is Equation 6.6 working. The second is what a reader who takes the argument’s name at face value gets.

title: 6  Expected Returns
text:
6.3 What the Three Vectors Buy

6.3.1 Three tangency portfolios
The same long-only tangency problem that Section 9.2 solved on the sample mean is now solved three times, on the sample mean, on the Bayes-Stein vector and on the class-level equilibrium, with the sample covariance matrix held fixed throughout so that only \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) changes.

mus <- list(sample = mu_s, `Bayes-Stein` = bs$mu, equilibrium = mu_eq)

W3 <- sapply(mus, function(m) {
  o <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                          momentFUN = make_moments(m, S))
  w <- extractWeights(o)
  w[colnames(Re)]
})
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W3), colnames(Re)),
          !isTRUE(all.equal(W3[, "sample"], W3[, "Bayes-Stein"])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(W3[, "equilibrium"], w_mkt, tolerance = 1e-6)))

round(W3[rowSums(W3 > 0.005) > 0, ], 4)

The second assertion is the guard the callout asked for: the sample and Bayes-Stein answers differ, so the supplied means were used. The third is Equation 6.6’s defining property observed: the tangency portfolio of the equilibrium vector is the market portfolio it was read from, to solver precision.






NoteWorked: the long-only tangency portfolio in one quadratic program





A Sharpe ratio is invariant to the scale of the weight vector, and so is a sign constraint. The long-only tangency portfolio can therefore be found by minimizing variance at a unit expected return with no budget constraint, and rescaling the answer to sum to one; this is one quadratic program rather than a search over a frontier, and it makes the rolling exercise below cheap.

tangency_lo <- function(mu, S) {
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(mu)), names(mu)))  # no long-only tangency
  N <- length(mu)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, N),
                            Amat = cbind(mu, diag(N)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, N)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), names(mu))
}

W3_qp <- sapply(mus, tangency_lo, S = S)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W3_qp), rownames(W3)), max(abs(W3 - W3_qp)) < 1e-6)
c(max_abs_difference_from_package = max(abs(W3 - W3_qp)))
#> max_abs_difference_from_package 
#>                   0.00000001737

The two routes agree to 2e-08 in every weight, which is the check that maxSR = TRUE on the patched build solves the problem it is asked.




p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w, m = mu_s) sum(m[names(w)] * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w, m = mu_s) p_ret(w, m) / p_vol(w)
eff_bets <- function(w) 1 / sum(w^2)
turnover <- function(w1, w2) sum(abs(w1[names(w2)] - w2)) / 2

summ <- tibble::tibble(
  estimator    = names(mus),
  held         = colSums(W3 > 0.005),
  eff_bets     = apply(W3, 2, eff_bets),
  largest      = apply(W3, 2, max),
  promised_sr  = mapply(function(j, m) p_sr(W3[, j], m), seq_along(mus), mus),
  in_sample_sr = apply(W3, 2, p_sr),
  vol          = apply(W3, 2, p_vol),
  from_sample  = apply(W3, 2, function(w) turnover(W3[, "sample"], w))
)
stopifnot(identical(summ$estimator, colnames(W3)))

Figure 6.2: Weights of the long-only tangency portfolio under the three mean vectors, from one data frame. The sample and Bayes-Stein answers hold a handful of series; the equilibrium answer is the market portfolio and holds all sixteen.




Read Table 6.3 across. The sample-mean portfolio holds 4 series with 2.0 effective bets and 68% in US_government, and promises a Sharpe ratio of 0.99, the highest of the three by construction, since it is scored on the vector it maximized. The Bayes-Stein portfolio is more concentrated still, with 76% in the same series. That is Equation 6.5 at work: shrinking the means toward \(\mu_0\) mixes the tangency direction with the minimum-variance direction, and the minimum-variance portfolio of Section 9.2 is 82% US_government. Shrinkage did not make the portfolio more diversified. It made it lean on the one input that is estimated well.
The equilibrium portfolio is different in kind. It holds all 16 series with 7.6 effective bets, because it is the market, and its in-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.82 gives up 18% of the sample tangency’s 0.99. That is the wrong yardstick, because the number the sample tangency is scored on here is the one it was fitted to. Table 9.5 reads the same rule out of sample from the register of Section 25.3: on a sixty-month rolling window rebalanced monthly it earns a Sharpe ratio of 0.55, 55% of the fitted figure and the lowest of the three portfolios compared there. What matters for a strategic allocation is how much each answer moves when the sample does.

6.3.2 Which vector moves least
We re-estimate each of the three vectors on every rolling sixty-month window, the window Section 25.3 uses, and solve the same tangency problem on each. Two things are measured: how far the mean vector itself moves from one window to the next, and the turnover of the portfolio it implies. The equilibrium’s inputs re-estimated each window are \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) and the average market weights over the window; \(\delta\) is held at its full-sample value, because it is a preference parameter rather than a forecast and, by the scale invariance noted above, it does not affect the tangency weights.

win    <- 60L
starts <- seq_len(T - win + 1L)

roll <- lapply(starts, function(s) {
  idx <- s:(s + win - 1L)
  X   <- Re[idx, ]
  Sw  <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X))
  wm  <- colMeans(W16[idx, , drop = FALSE])
  m   <- cbind(sample        = colMeans(X),
               `Bayes-Stein` = bayes_stein(X)$mu,
               equilibrium   = delta16 * as.numeric(Sw %*% wm))
  rownames(m) <- colnames(Re)
  list(mu = m, w = apply(m, 2, tangency_lo, S = Sw))
})
stopifnot(length(roll) == T - win + 1L,
          identical(rownames(roll[[1]]$w), colnames(Re)))

roll_stats <- sapply(colnames(roll[[1]]$mu), function(e) {
  MU <- sapply(roll, function(r) r$mu[, e]) * 12       # N x windows, annualized
  W  <- sapply(roll, function(r) r$w[, e])
  stopifnot(!anyNA(W))                                  # every window had a tangency
  to <- vapply(2:ncol(W), function(j) turnover(W[, j - 1], W[, j]), numeric(1))
  c(mean_abs_change_pp  = mean(abs(MU[, -1] - MU[, -ncol(MU)])) * 100,
    mean_turnover       = mean(to),
    p95_turnover        = as.numeric(quantile(to, 0.95)),
    mean_effective_bets = mean(1 / colSums(W^2)))
})

# The order the text reports, in the vectors and in the portfolios they imply.
est <- c("sample", "Bayes-Stein", "equilibrium")
stopifnot(identical(colnames(roll_stats), est),
          all(diff(roll_stats["mean_abs_change_pp", est]) < 0),
          all(diff(roll_stats["mean_turnover", est]) < 0))
to_ratio <- roll_stats["mean_turnover", c("sample", "Bayes-Stein")] /
  roll_stats["mean_turnover", "equilibrium"]

On 313 windows, a sample mean moves by 0.83 percentage points a year between one window and the next, the Bayes-Stein estimate by 0.51 and the equilibrium return by 0.21. The tangency portfolios move accordingly: the sample-mean answer turns over 8.2% of the portfolio in an average month and 23% in the worst twentieth, Bayes-Stein about 23 percent less, and the equilibrium answer 0.1%, which is the rate at which capitalizations drift. The last row is no trick: the tangency portfolio of Equation 6.6 is the market portfolio in every window, whatever that window’s covariance matrix says, so its turnover is the market’s. The two estimated vectors move the portfolio 68 and 52 times as much as the one that was not estimated, and Section 23.3 puts a price on the difference.

6.3.3 What the book carries forward
The sample mean is the input every closed form in Section 9.1 assumes and the one Table 6.1 shows is not known: 10 of 16 intervals include zero, and the portfolio it implies is rebuilt every month. Bayes-Stein keeps the ordering, halves the spread and cuts the turnover, and by Equation 6.5 does so by leaning on the minimum-variance portfolio, the part of the problem \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) pins down. The equilibrium vector returns a portfolio that is held, diversified and consistent with the covariance matrix, and is only as good as the weights it is read from, which on this market exist for five classes and are assumed for eleven.
The book therefore carries two of the three. Where market weights exist, the equilibrium return of Equation 6.6 is the anchor: it is the prior that Section 17.1 blends views into and the strategic policy its tactical portfolios deviate from. Where they do not, the Bayes-Stein estimator of Equation 6.4 is the default, because it asks nothing of the data beyond \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) and moves the portfolio in the direction Jagannathan and Ma (2003) and Frost and Savarino (1988) showed a constraint moves it anyway. The sample mean is carried as the benchmark: it is the input whose cost 1 measures and the forecast without a signal that the predictors of Section 16.1 have to improve on.

title: 6  Expected Returns
text:
Key Takeaways

By Equation 6.1 the precision of a mean depends on the calendar span alone, and on 31 model years of data 10 of the 16 intervals of Equation 6.2 include zero. Sampling weekly instead of monthly leaves that unchanged and halves the standard error of the variance (Merton 1980).
A return target set on a sample mean is honored to machine precision on an input known to a few percentage points, and the optimizer amplifies the difference (Best and Grauer 1991; Michaud 1989). The cost is measured in




Bayes-Stein shrinks every mean toward the expected return of the minimum-variance portfolio with an intensity the data set at \(v = 0.53\) here, preserves the ordering, and by Equation 6.5 moves the tangency portfolio toward the minimum-variance portfolio (Jorion 1986; Kan and Zhou 2007).
Reverse optimization returns the vector for which the market portfolio is the tangency portfolio. \(\delta\) scales it without changing the weights, and the package’s risk_aversion is \(\delta/2\), verified by feeding the vector back in (Sharpe 1974; Black and Litterman 1992).

black.litterman() is the blending formula only: no market weights, no \(\tau\), a default view that is bullish on everything, and a posterior covariance that halves the variances. Supply Mu and Views yourself and keep BLSigma away from a risk objective.
On rolling windows the sample tangency turns over about 8% of the portfolio a month, Bayes-Stein 6%, and the equilibrium 0.1%. The book carries the equilibrium as its anchor where market weights exist and Bayes-Stein where they do not.

title: 6  Expected Returns
text:
Exercises

Replace the target \(\mu_0\) in Equation 6.4 with the plain average of the sixteen sample means, recompute \(v\) and the long-only tangency portfolio, and compare it with Table 6.3. Does the new target still move the portfolio toward the minimum-variance portfolio, and what does Equation 6.5 say about why?
Reverse-optimize the five equity classes with the last month’s weights, W_eq[nrow(W_eq), ], in place of the average composition. Report how far each equilibrium return moves in units of the standard error in Table 6.2, and say which region’s revision is largest and why.
Change the block split in the worked box to 60 percent equity, 25 percent government, 10 percent credit and 5 percent commodities and recompute the class-level equilibrium. Which entries of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\) move most, does the tangency portfolio still equal the proxy weights, and what does that say about what reverse optimization can be trusted for?
Recompute Table 6.4 on one-hundred-and-twenty-month windows. Does the ranking of the three estimators change, and does the sample-mean turnover fall by the factor that Equation 6.1 predicts for a doubled span?
