title: 7  The Covariance Matrix
text:
7.1 What the Optimizer Requires
Suppose we have an equity sleeve to fill. There are one hundred and twenty-three names in the eligible universe, thirty-one model years of monthly returns are available, and we want the combination of them with the lowest risk. That is the most modest request anyone makes of a portfolio optimizer: no view, no forecast, no tilt, just the low-volatility end of the frontier of Section 9.1.
We will not get it. Not because the data are poor and not because the optimizer is badly written, but because the object it requires cannot be estimated from the data available. Michaud (1989) named the consequence and Chopra and Ziemba (1993) priced it, but the failure here is not one of degree: on a realistic universe the sample covariance matrix is singular, and a singular matrix does not give a noisy answer, it gives a meaningless one.
We first set out what the optimizer is asking for and why the request cannot be met, then work through the four available responses in order of what they cost, then ask which of them actually pays out of sample. The answer to that last question is less flattering than the literature on shrinkage usually suggests.
A minimum-variance portfolio is the weight vector minimizing \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\) subject to the constraints, and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the entire input. Nothing else about the assets enters: not their names, not their sectors, not their expected returns. Whatever the matrix says about risk is risk as far as the optimizer is concerned.
Being symmetric, it holds \(N(N+1)/2\) distinct numbers, estimated from \(T\) observations by
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
  (\boldsymbol{r}_t - \bar{\boldsymbol{r}})(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \bar{\boldsymbol{r}})' .
\tag{7.1}\]
Written this way the difficulty is immediate. Equation 7.1 is a sum of \(T\) outer products, each of rank one, so
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) \leq \min(N,\, T-1).
\tag{7.2}\]
Whenever \(N > T-1\) the estimate is singular, whatever the data look like. This is arithmetic, not a property of markets: it would hold if the returns were coin flips.
The sixteen asset classes of Section 4.2 need 136. The 123 equities need 7,626, from 372 months of history. That asks the data to pin down more parameters than it has observations, and at some point the answer stops being an estimate.

title: 7  The Covariance Matrix
text:
7.1.1 What singularity claims about portfolios
Equation 7.2 is a statement about a matrix. Its consequence is a statement about money. If \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) is singular, there exists a weight vector \(\boldsymbol{w} \neq \boldsymbol{0}\) with
\[
\boldsymbol{w}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\boldsymbol{w} = 0,
\tag{7.3}\]
a portfolio the estimate says cannot lose money, and there are as many independent such portfolios as the matrix is short of full rank. An optimizer told to minimize variance will find them, because that is exactly its job, and will put everything there.
They are not real. They are long-short cancellations that happened to net out over the particular months used for estimation, and they will not net out again. This is the mechanism behind the familiar complaint that mean-variance optimization produces absurd weights. Michaud (1989) called the optimizer an error maximizer for this reason, and the label is exact rather than rhetorical: among all portfolios consistent with the constraints, the procedure selects the one the estimate is most optimistic about, which is the one the estimate is most wrong about.
Even short of singularity, the inverse is what the optimizer uses, and the quantity governing how much an error in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) is magnified on its way into the weights is the condition number
\[
\kappa(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
= \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}},
\tag{7.4}\]
the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue. Laloux et al. (1999) showed that most of the small eigenvalues of a financial correlation matrix are indistinguishable from those of a random matrix of the same dimensions, a comparison made precise by the limiting spectrum of Marčenko and Pastur (1967). The directions the optimizer most wants to exploit are the ones carrying the least information.
Chopra and Ziemba (1993) measured how the cost divides. Errors in expected returns hurt an order of magnitude more than errors in variances, which in turn hurt more than errors in covariances, which is why Section 6.1 is the harder chapter. It is also why this one is unavoidable: a singular matrix is not an error of degree.

7.1.2 Diagnosing it before the solver does
Two numbers, neither of which requires inverting anything.

covariance_health <- function(X) {
  S  <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X))
  ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  c(assets = ncol(X), observations = nrow(X), rank = qr(S)$rank,
    riskless_directions = sum(ev < 1e-12),
    condition = if (min(ev) <= 0) Inf else max(ev) / min(ev))
}

h_ins <- covariance_health(ins)             # all instruments, the whole sample
rbind(classes     = covariance_health(cls[1:60, ]),
      equities    = covariance_health(eq[1:60, ]),
      instruments = h_ins)
#>             assets observations rank riskless_directions     condition
#> classes         16           60   16                   0         12297
#> equities       123           60   59                  64           Inf
#> instruments    181          372  178                   3 1570624508843

rank below assets means the matrix is singular, and riskless_directions counts the portfolios it believes are free. Five years of data on 123 equities produces 64 of them.
condition is the subtler warning. It is the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to the smallest, and it bounds how much the inverse magnifies an error in the input. A finite but very large value is more dangerous than an infinite one, because everything still runs: the matrix inverts, weights come back, and they are a magnified copy of the sampling noise. Past roughly \(10^{8}\) the computation is reading noise with double precision arithmetic.
The third row is that case. All 181 instruments on the full 372 months have \(N < T - 1\), so Equation 7.2 does not bind and every eigenvalue is positive, yet qr() reports rank 178 at its default tolerance, 3 eigenvalues lie below \(10^{-12}\) and the condition number is \(10^{12.2}\). No longer sample cures it: the cause is the bond block of Section 2.2, where some instruments nearly replicate others.

rank_report <- function(X, label) {
  vapply(c(60L, 120L, 180L), function(W) {
    S  <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X[seq_len(W), ]))
    ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
    c(T = W, N = ncol(X), rank = qr(S)$rank, min_eigen = min(ev),
      condition = if (min(ev) <= 0) Inf else max(ev) / min(ev))
  }, numeric(5)) |> t() |> as.data.frame() |> dplyr::mutate(universe = label)
}

dplyr::bind_rows(rank_report(cls, "16 classes"),
                 rank_report(eq,  "123 equities")) |>
  dplyr::select(universe, T, N, rank, min_eigen, condition)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   universe         T     N  rank min_eigen condition
#>   <chr>        <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 16 classes      60    16    16  5.45e- 7    12297.
#> 2 16 classes     120    16    16  8.77e- 7     7921.
#> 3 16 classes     180    16    16  8.33e- 7     8061.
#> 4 123 equities    60   123    59 -2.59e-17      Inf 
#> 5 123 equities   120   123   119 -5.55e-18      Inf 
#> 6 123 equities   180   123   123  1.34e- 4     1317.

Look at min_eigen on the two singular rows. It is negative. A covariance matrix cannot have a negative eigenvalue; that is floating-point noise around an eigenvalue which is exactly zero. The matrix is not imprecise. It describes a world in which some portfolio has negative variance.

7.1.3 Why this book has not needed the chapter until now
Every allocation up to here happened across asset classes, and at that level the problem does not arise.

bad <- sum(vapply(seq.int(61L, nrow(cls)), function(i) {
  qr(stats::cov(zoo::coredata(cls[(i - 60L):(i - 1L), ])))$rank < ncol(cls)
}, logical(1)))

c(rolling_windows = nrow(cls) - 60L, rank_deficient = bad)
#> rolling_windows  rank_deficient 
#>             312               0

Not one sixty-month window in the sample is rank deficient at class level. The moment Section 21.1 descends into individual securities it becomes the only question that matters, and nothing about the data has changed. What changed is how many things the portfolio was asked to hold.

title: 7  The Covariance Matrix
text:
7.2 Four Routes
There are four routes. Two change what may be owned, two change how it is estimated. We take them in order of what they cost.

7.2.1 Route one: hold fewer things
The cheapest fix is not to have the problem. Allocating across sixteen classes rather than 123 securities, or across sector sleeves rather than names, leaves a matrix comfortably estimable on five years.
This is not a dodge. Most institutional mandates are set at exactly this level for exactly this reason, and Section 15.1 treats the sleeve structure as a decision rather than a convenience. It does not help when the mandate names 123 securities, which is what a stock selection process hands its allocator.

7.2.2 Route two: impose a structure
If 7,626 free parameters cannot be estimated, the answer is to stop trying to. Assert instead that returns are driven by \(k\) common factors plus asset-specific noise, so that
\[
\boldsymbol{r}_t = \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{B}' + \boldsymbol{D},
\tag{7.5}\]
with \(\boldsymbol{B}\) the \(N \times k\) loadings, \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) the covariance of the factors and \(\boldsymbol{D}\) a diagonal matrix of residual variances. That is \(Nk + N\) numbers rather than \(N(N+1)/2\): for three factors on 123 assets, 492 rather than several thousand. Because \(\boldsymbol{D}\) is positive by construction, Equation 7.5 cannot be singular whatever \(T\) is. Fan et al. (2008) give the conditions under which it converges where Equation 7.1 does not, and Bai and Ng (2002) and Connor and Korajczyk (1993) the machinery for choosing \(k\) rather than asserting it.
The factors can be economic, as in Section 5.2, or purely statistical, the principal components of the returns themselves. The second is six lines.

factor_covariance <- function(X, k = 3L) {
  x  <- zoo::coredata(X)
  pc <- prcomp(x)
  B  <- pc$rotation[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE]      # loadings, N x k
  f  <- x %*% B                                      # factor realizations
  e  <- x - f %*% t(B)                               # residuals
  e  <- sweep(e, 2, colMeans(e))
  B %*% stats::cov(f) %*% t(B) + diag(colSums(e^2) / (nrow(x) - k - 1L))
}

S_fac <- factor_covariance(eq[1:120, ], k = 3L)
e_fac <- eigen(S_fac, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
c(rank = qr(S_fac)$rank, min_eigen = min(e_fac),
  condition = max(e_fac) / min(e_fac))
#>       rank  min_eigen  condition 
#> 123.000000   0.001926  98.592045

Full rank on a window where the sample matrix has 4 riskless directions, and a condition number of 99 where the sample matrix’s is infinite. The structure does the work: because every asset’s risk runs through three shared factors, no combination can cancel to zero unless the residuals do, and those are positive by construction.
PortfolioAnalytics ships this as statistical.factor.model(), with one constraint worth knowing about in the released version.

sapply(c(60L, 120L, 180L), function(W) {
  tryCatch({ statistical.factor.model(eq[seq_len(W), ], k = 3L); "accepted" },
           error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
})
#> [1] "fewer observations than assets" "fewer observations than assets"
#> [3] "accepted"

It requires at least as many observations as assets, which is precisely the condition under which it is not needed. The body of the function does not: principal components need enough components, not enough columns, which is why the six lines above run on the same window. Appendix D records the patch that relaxes the check and where it stands.

7.2.3 Route three: shrink the matrix
Keep every asset and keep the sample estimate, but pull it part of the way towards a target that is well conditioned by construction:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\text{shrunk}}
= (1-\lambda)\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} + \lambda\,\boldsymbol{F},
\qquad \lambda \in [0, 1],
\tag{7.6}\]
with \(\boldsymbol{F}\) commonly a scaled identity and sometimes a constant-correlation or factor matrix. The construction descends from Stein (1956), who showed that shrinking a multivariate estimate towards a fixed point can dominate the sample estimate in mean squared error despite being biased. Ledoit and Wolf (2003) and Ledoit and Wolf (2004) derive the \(\lambda\) minimizing expected loss and show that it can be estimated from the data, so it is not a tuning parameter anyone has to guess; Schäfer and Strimmer (2005) give the analytic form corpcor implements, and Ledoit and Wolf (2017) extend it to shrink each eigenvalue by a different amount.
This is the workhorse. It needs no assumption about what drives returns, it cannot fail, and Equation 7.6 is invertible whenever \(\boldsymbol{F}\) is and \(\lambda > 0\).

S_shr <- corpcor::cov.shrink(zoo::coredata(eq[1:120, ]), verbose = FALSE)
c(lambda = attr(S_shr, "lambda"),
  rank = qr(S_shr)$rank,
  min_eigen = min(eigen(as.matrix(S_shr), symmetric = TRUE,
                        only.values = TRUE)$values))
#>      lambda        rank   min_eigen 
#>   0.2329951 123.0000000   0.0009555

lambda is the weight on the target rather than on the data, 23% of the way towards independence here.

7.2.4 Route four: estimate robustly
The three routes above address a matrix badly conditioned because the sample is short. A robust estimator addresses one badly centered because a few observations dominate it. That is a different problem, and it is taken up below.

7.2.5 Getting any of this into the optimizer
PortfolioAnalytics routes every moment estimate through one function, and the released version of that function does not offer shrinkage.

eval(formals(set.portfolio.moments)$method)
#> [1] "sample"          "boudt"           "black_litterman" "meucci"

sample is the sample matrix, boudt a factor-based cleaning of the higher moments, black_litterman and meucci view-blending machinery belonging in Section 17.1. None of them is route three.
This is the point at which many users give up and compute weights outside the package, discarding every constraint and diagnostic it provides. That is unnecessary. optimize.portfolio() takes a momentFUN argument, and it accepts a function object rather than merely the name of one.

shrinkage_moments <- function(R, portfolio) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R)
  S <- corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE)
  S <- matrix(as.numeric(S), ncol(X), ncol(X),
              dimnames = list(colnames(X), colnames(X)))
  list(mu = colMeans(X), sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL,
       mean = colMeans(X), var = S)
}

spec <- portfolio.spec(colnames(eq)) |>
  add.constraint("full_investment") |> add.constraint("long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

opt <- optimize.portfolio(eq[1:120, ], spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
                          momentFUN = shrinkage_moments)
w <- extractWeights(opt)
c(holdings = sum(w > 1e-6), sum = sum(w), max_weight = max(w))
#>   holdings        sum max_weight 
#>   42.00000    1.00000    0.07059

Because it is a function rather than a name, it can be built on the fly with its settings baked in: one per shrinkage intensity to be compared, or one closing over a factor model fitted elsewhere. Nothing has to live in the global environment.






ImportantA moment function must set both pairs of names



The returned list carries mu and sigma, and also mean and var. Different code paths inside the package read different names, so a moment function that sets only one pair works until the objective changes and then fails in a way that points nowhere near the cause. The matrix must also be a plain matrix carrying dimnames, because cov.shrink() returns attributes that some downstream code does not expect.



7.2.6 When the package function is the thing in the way
There is a third option beyond using a function and working around it, and on an open source package it is usually the right one: fix it and send the fix back. The constraint in statistical.factor.model() is one line, the reason it is wrong is demonstrable in a paragraph, and a patch with a test is less work than the workaround it replaces. Appendix D lists the patches this book contributed and their state, which is also the only honest way to tell a reader which behavior to expect.

7.2.7 Route four in full: robust estimation
PortfolioAnalytics ships a family of robust covariance estimators that almost nobody uses and that no textbook of this generation covers.

grep("covRob", ls("package:PortfolioAnalytics"), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "custom.covRob.Mcd"   "custom.covRob.MM"    "custom.covRob.Rocke"
#> [4] "custom.covRob.TSGS"  "MycovRobMcd"         "MycovRobTSGS"

These answer route four. Shrinkage repairs a matrix badly conditioned because the sample is short; a robust estimator repairs one badly centered because a few months dominate it, whether a flash crash, a redenomination or a bad print in a vendor file. The minimum covariance determinant estimator behind custom.covRob.Mcd() searches for the subset of \(h\) observations whose sample covariance has the smallest determinant and estimates from that subset alone, discarding the rest (Rousseeuw 1984; Rousseeuw and Van Driessen 1999).
They plug in exactly where route three did.

robust_moments <- function(R, portfolio) {
  m <- custom.covRob.Mcd(zoo::coredata(R))
  list(mu = m$mu, sigma = m$sigma, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL,
       mean = m$mu, var = m$sigma)
}

rb <- robust_moments(cls[1:120, ])
sb <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(cls[1:120, ]))
c(robust_mean_vol = mean(sqrt(diag(rb$sigma))) * sqrt(12),
  sample_mean_vol = mean(sqrt(diag(sb))) * sqrt(12))
#> robust_mean_vol sample_mean_vol 
#>          0.1061          0.1244

The robust estimate of volatility is lower, because it has judged part of what the sample matrix calls risk to be a few unusual months rather than the process. Whether that is an improvement is a judgment about the world rather than about the estimator: right if those months were contamination, wrong if they were the tail an investor is paid to bear. Section 4.3 found that this market’s extreme months arrive together across series, which argues for the second reading. Section 28.1 makes the case properly, and Section 10.1 is where discarding the tail stops being defensible.

title: 7  The Covariance Matrix
section: 7.3 What the Routes Do to the Matrix
text:
7.3 What the Routes Do to the Matrix

7.3.1 Scoring the routes out of sample
This is not a question the matrix can answer. Every estimator reports a flattering number about itself in sample. The only honest test is to estimate on one window, hold the resulting portfolio for a month, and score what happened.
R/ch05-estimator-race.R does that for four estimators and three window lengths, long only and fully invested, rebalanced monthly. All three windows are scored on the same months, so a longer window earns no credit for starting later.

FIRST_OOS <- 181L
oos    <- seq.int(FIRST_OOS, nrow(eq))
stopifnot(all(sim_riskfree_monthly$date == zoo::index(eq)))   # the bill lines up
ew_ret <- rowMeans(zoo::coredata(eq[oos, ]))
ew_ex  <- ew_ret - sim_riskfree_monthly$return[oos]

ew <- c(ann_vol = stats::sd(ew_ret) * sqrt(12),
        ann_ret = mean(ew_ret) * 12,
        sharpe  = mean(ew_ex) / stats::sd(ew_ex) * sqrt(12))
round(ew, 4)
#> ann_vol ann_ret  sharpe 
#>  0.1829  0.1182  0.5993

Read failed first. At sixty and at one hundred and twenty months, two of the four estimators produce nothing at all, not a poor portfolio but no portfolio, on every one of the 192 rebalancing dates. That is Equation 7.2 arriving as an empty result. Route three and the diagonal target reach a weight vector; the sample matrix and the released factor model do not.
Where the sample matrix fails, shrinkage gives the lower volatility of the two estimators that run: 12.2% at a hundred and twenty months against 15.9% for the diagonal and 18.3% for holding everything equally.

At a hundred and eighty months the sample matrix is finally estimable and shrinkage stops buying anything: 0.1196 against 0.1192 is a dead heat, and the factor model is marginally behind both on volatility and further behind on Sharpe ratio. Shrinkage is not a better estimator in general. It is the estimator that exists when the others do not, which is a different and more useful property.
The lambda column says so from the inside: it falls from 0.281 to 0.105 as the window lengthens. The procedure asks for less help as it needs less, which is the practical content of the Ledoit-Wolf result.

7.3.2 Lower volatility is not a better portfolio
sharpe is not ann_vol, and the ordering is not the same. At a hundred and eighty months the sample matrix has the lowest volatility and shrinkage the highest Sharpe ratio, and the factor model, within a tenth of a point of both on volatility, trails them by 0.11 on Sharpe ratio. Volatility was the objective, and it does not rank the results.
Minimum variance did what it was asked. It cut annualized volatility from 18.3% to 12.2%, about a third, and gave up 1.0 percentage points of annual return for it, so on this market it finished ahead of equal weighting on Sharpe ratio as well, 0.812 against 0.599. That is not the general finding: DeMiguel et al. (2009) report that across their universes no optimized rule, minimum variance included, is reliably ahead of equal weighting, and whether the advantage here belongs to the method or to this sample is the subject of Section 8.1.
Every route is one operation on the eigenvalues of Equation 7.1, and it is easier to see than to derive.

X   <- zoo::coredata(eq[1:120, ])
ev  <- function(S) pmax(eigen(as.matrix(S), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values, 0)
e_s <- ev(stats::cov(X))
e_h <- ev(corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE))

tibble::tibble(
  matrix      = c("sample", "shrunk"),
  largest     = c(e_s[1], e_h[1]),
  smallest    = c(min(e_s), min(e_h)),
  zero_eigens = c(sum(e_s < 1e-12), sum(e_h < 1e-12)),
  condition   = c(e_s[1] / max(min(e_s), .Machine$double.eps), e_h[1] / min(e_h)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   matrix largest smallest zero_eigens condition
#>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 sample   0.183 0                  4   8.25e14
#> 2 shrunk   0.141 0.000956           0   1.48e 2

4 eigenvalues of the sample matrix are zero. Those are the riskless portfolios of Equation 7.3 seen from the other side, and they are not a property of these particular equities. They would be there if the returns were coin flips, because 120 observations cannot pin down 123 directions, by Equation 7.2.







Figure 7.1: The eigenvalue spectrum before and after shrinkage, on a log scale. The sample matrix runs off the bottom of the plot: several of its eigenvalues are exactly zero. Shrinkage compresses the range from fifteen orders of magnitude to two.




The largest falls by 23.0% and the smallest non-zero one rises by a factor of 301, which is Equation 7.4 brought back into a range where the inverse means something. That is what a shrinkage target is: not a better guess at any individual covariance, but a statement that the extremes of a sample spectrum are mostly sampling error and belong nearer the middle, which is the reading Laloux et al. (1999) gave them. A factor model reaches the same place by another road, building Equation 7.5 from a few directions plus a positive residual for every asset, so that small eigenvalues cannot be zero to begin with.

7.3.3 Shrink towards what, when the target moves?
The usual \(\boldsymbol{F}\) in Equation 7.6 is a scaled identity: equal variances, no correlations. It is chosen for being maximally unlike the noisy thing it corrects, not for being true. How untrue it is depends on when the question is asked.

d      <- zoo::index(cls)
in_ep  <- vapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) in_episode(d, e),
                 logical(length(d)))
crisis <- in_ep[, "credit_crisis"]
calm   <- rowSums(in_ep) == 0               # outside all four episodes

regime_shape <- function(keep) {
  e <- ev(stats::cov(zoo::coredata(cls[keep, ])))
  C <- stats::cor(cls[keep, ])
  data.frame(months = sum(keep), pc1_share = e[1] / sum(e),
             directions = sum(e)^2 / sum(e^2),
             mean_correlation = mean(C[upper.tri(C)]))
}

# A short sample concentrates its spectrum whatever the market does, so score
# every run of calm months of the crisis's length as well.
n_c   <- sum(crisis)
runs  <- which(vapply(seq_len(length(d) - n_c + 1L),
                      function(i) all(calm[i + seq_len(n_c) - 1L]), logical(1)))
short <- do.call(rbind, lapply(runs, function(i) {
  regime_shape(seq_along(d) %in% (i + seq_len(n_c) - 1L))
}))

shape <- rbind(calm       = regime_shape(calm),
               calm_short = as.data.frame(lapply(short, stats::median)),
               crisis     = regime_shape(crisis))
shape$regime <- rownames(shape)
shape[, c("regime", "months", "pc1_share", "directions", "mean_correlation")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   regime     months pc1_share directions mean_correlation
#>   <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 calm          320     0.368       4.81            0.297
#> 2 calm_short      7     0.556       2.60            0.295
#> 3 crisis          7     0.760       1.66            0.509

The calm sample is the 320 months outside the four episodes of sim_episodes, the crisis the 7 months of the credit crisis. In calm months the first principal component carries 37% of the variance and the matrix behaves like roughly 4.8 independent directions; through the credit crisis the same sixteen series carry 76% and collapse to 1.7. Part of that is arithmetic, since by Equation 7.2 a 7-month matrix has at most 6 non-zero eigenvalues and the median calm window of that length already shows 56% and 2.6, but the crisis lies beyond 97% of those windows, and average pairwise correlation, which no rank bound touches, rises from 0.30 to 0.51, above 92% of them.
A diagonal target asserts that the assets are unrelated. In calm months that is wrong by some margin; in the credit crisis it is wrong by far more, and precisely when the portfolio depends on it. Shrinking towards independence is least defensible exactly when it does the most work, which is the honest reason to prefer a factor target where one is available. Section 19.1 is where this choice stops being a footnote.

7.3.4 The shrinkage already in place
One last connection, because it reframes much of this book. Every optimization so far has been long only. Jagannathan and Ma (2003) showed that a non-negativity constraint is not merely a restriction: it acts on the solution the way Equation 7.6 acts on the matrix, because it forbids exactly the large offsetting long-short positions that Equation 7.3 invites. Their finding is that imposing the constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when it is known to be false, which is why a constrained optimization on a sample matrix behaves far better than the unconstrained arithmetic suggests. Frost and Savarino (1988) reach the same conclusion from the Bayesian side.
That is worth holding next to Table 7.1. Route three took about a third off the volatility of an equal-weighted sleeve. The long-only constraint, imposed for reasons of mandate rather than of statistics, had already done a comparable amount of work for nothing.

title: 7  The Covariance Matrix
text:
Key Takeaways

By Equation 7.2 the sample covariance matrix is singular whenever there are more assets than observations, regardless of the data. On 123 equities and five years of monthly returns it is short of full rank by more than sixty.
A singular estimate does not merely give a noisy answer. By Equation 7.3 it asserts that some portfolio has zero variance, and a minimizer will find it and hold it.
Even without singularity, the condition number of Equation 7.4 measures how much an input error is magnified in the weights, and the smallest eigenvalues of a financial covariance matrix are largely indistinguishable from noise (Laloux et al. 1999; Marčenko and Pastur 1967).
There are four responses: hold fewer assets, impose the factor structure of Equation 7.5, shrink towards a well-conditioned target as in Equation 7.6, or estimate robustly. The first three address conditioning; the fourth addresses contamination, which is a different complaint.
Shrinkage is not a better estimator in general. Scored out of sample it wins where the sample matrix cannot be computed at all, and ties with it once the window is long enough. Its own \(\lambda\) falls as the window grows, which is the procedure reporting that it is needed less.
Minimum variance did what it was asked and cut volatility by about a third, and on this market it finished ahead of equal weighting on Sharpe ratio as well. Whether that survives on other universes is Section 8.1’s subject.
The long-only constraint is itself a form of shrinkage and was already doing comparable work before any estimator was changed (Jagannathan and Ma 2003).

title: 7  The Covariance Matrix
text:
Exercises

Apply covariance_health() to the government and credit instruments of sim_assets alone, on the full sample. There are far more observations than assets, so Equation 7.2 does not bind, and the matrix is nearly singular all the same. Identify the reason from the eigenvectors of the smallest eigenvalues rather than from the asset names.

corpcor::cov.shrink() chooses lambda analytically. Fix it instead at 0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 and plot realized out-of-sample volatility against it. Where is the minimum, and is the analytic choice near it?
Replace shrinkage_moments() with one built on factor_covariance() and compare them on the same rolling windows. At which window length does the factor structure stop helping, and does that coincide with the point where the sample matrix becomes estimable?
Repeat the unconstrained minimum-variance optimization of Section 9.1 on the 123 equities with the shrunk matrix, once long only and once with weights free to go negative. Quantify the Jagannathan and Ma (2003) effect on this data.





Bai, Jushan, and Serena Ng. 2002. “Determining the Number of Factors in Approximate Factor Models.” Econometrica 70 (1): 191–221. https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0262.00273.


Chopra, Vijay K., and William T. Ziemba. 1993. “The Effect of Errors in Means, Variances, and Covariances on Optimal Portfolio Choice.” Journal of Portfolio Management 19 (2): 6–11. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1993.409440.


Connor, Gregory, and Robert A. Korajczyk. 1993. “A Test for the Number of Factors in an Approximate Factor Model.” Journal of Finance 48 (4): 1263–91. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1993.tb04754.x.


DeMiguel, Victor, Lorenzo Garlappi, and Raman Uppal. 2009. “Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient Is the 1/n Portfolio Strategy?” Review of Financial Studies 22 (5): 1915–53.


Fan, Jianqing, Yingying Fan, and Jinchi Lv. 2008. “High Dimensional Covariance Matrix Estimation Using a Factor Model.” Journal of Econometrics 147 (1): 186–97. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2008.09.017.


Frost, Peter A., and James E. Savarino. 1988. “For Better Performance: Constrain Portfolio Weights.” Journal of Portfolio Management 15 (1): 29–34. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1988.409181.


Jagannathan, Ravi, and Tongshu Ma. 2003. “Risk Reduction in Large Portfolios: Why Imposing the Wrong Constraints Helps.” Journal of Finance 58 (4): 1651–83. https://doi.org/10.1111/1540-6261.00580.


Laloux, Laurent, Pierre Cizeau, Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, and Marc Potters. 1999. “Noise Dressing of Financial Correlation Matrices.” Physical Review Letters 83 (7): 1467–70. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.83.1467.


Ledoit, Olivier, and Michael Wolf. 2003. “Improved Estimation of the Covariance Matrix of Stock Returns with an Application to Portfolio Selection.” Journal of Empirical Finance 10 (5): 603–21. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0927-5398(03)00007-0.

title: 8  Estimation Error and Its Cost
text:
8.1 The Plug-In Rule and the Price of Its Inputs
How much is a better forecast worth, in Sharpe ratio? DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) asked the question the other way round: they ran fourteen optimizing rules against the portfolio that forecasts nothing, equal weighting, on seven datasets, and found that none of them beat it reliably out of sample. The estimation window a mean-variance investor would need before optimization paid was measured in thousands of months, about three thousand for twenty-five assets and six thousand for fifty. That paper is the end of a line that runs through most of modern portfolio theory. Jobson and Korkie (1980) derived the sampling distribution of estimated efficient portfolios and showed that the estimated tangency portfolio can be outperformed by equal weighting; Jobson and Korkie (1981) gave the test for whether two Sharpe ratios differ at all. Michaud (1989) named the mechanism: an optimizer is an error maximizer, because it allocates most to whatever the sample happened to flatter. Best and Grauer (1991) showed analytically that small changes in the mean vector move the weights by large amounts while barely moving the portfolio’s own mean and variance. Chopra and Ziemba (1993) priced the inputs, finding errors in means roughly eleven times as costly as errors in variances and twice as costly again as errors in covariances. Broadie (1993) separated the true, the estimated and the actual frontier and showed that the estimated one lies above both. Frost and Savarino (1988) found that constraining the weights improves realized performance, and Jagannathan and Ma (2003) explained why: a short-sale constraint is a shrinkage of the covariance matrix in disguise. Kan and Zhou (2007) gave the expected loss in closed form under normality, and Ledoit and Wolf (2004) gave the estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) that works when the sample one does not.
This chapter is about strategic allocation: the inputs are unconditional moments, and the question is what estimating them costs. We first define the two naive benchmarks and state what is known about the loss, then measure the gap between the Sharpe ratio a rolling window promises and the one the next month delivers, for four rules on the sixteen risky class series, then simulate under a known truth to split the loss between the mean and the covariance and to find the window length at which optimization overtakes equal weighting.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill for the reasons of Section 3.1.

title: 8  Estimation Error and Its Cost
text:
8.1.1 What the estimator is asked to do
The objective of Markowitz (1952), stated in Section 3.1 and solved in Section 9.1, consumes a mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and a covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). Neither is observed. From \(T\) months of excess returns \(\boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{r}_T\) the sample estimates are
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\boldsymbol{r}_t,
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
  (\boldsymbol{r}_t - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})' ,
\tag{8.1}\]
and the plug-in rule substitutes them into the solution as though they were the truth. For the tangency portfolio of Equation 9.5 that gives
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\text{tan}}
= \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\text{mv}}
= \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}} ,
\tag{8.2}\]
with the minimum-variance portfolio of Equation 9.3 beside it. The two differ in one respect that decides this chapter: the second needs no \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\). Section 4.1 showed, following Merton (1980), that the precision of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) depends on the calendar span of the sample and not on how often it is observed, while the precision of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) improves with every observation. A rule that uses only \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) therefore uses only the input that can be estimated. Section 6.1 and Section 7.1 treat the two estimation problems separately; this chapter measures what they cost together, and which of them costs more.
Under a long-only constraint neither expression in Equation 8.2 has a closed form and both become quadratic programs, as Section 9.1 explains. Everything computed below is long only, and Section 8.3 shows that the constraint is not a detail.

8.1.2 Two rules that estimate almost nothing
The benchmarks against which every optimizing rule is judged are two portfolios that require no optimizer. Equal weighting holds
\[
\boldsymbol{w}_{1/N} = \frac{\boldsymbol{\iota}}{N},
\tag{8.3}\]
and estimates nothing at all: it is the same portfolio on every window, of every length, on every history. Inverse-volatility weighting holds
\[
w_i = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_i^{-1}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\hat{\sigma}_j^{-1}},
\tag{8.4}\]
and estimates one moment per asset, the volatility, ignoring the means and every correlation. Section 14.1 treats Equation 8.4 as a risk-based allocation in its own right, the one-line approximation to equal risk contribution; here it is a benchmark, the rule that sits one estimated moment away from \(1/N\). Both are estimators in the statistical sense, with Equation 8.3 the degenerate one whose variance is zero, and that is the correct way to read the comparison that follows: not naive against sophisticated, but a sequence of rules that estimate zero, one, or all of the moments the objective asks for.

8.1.3 Why the promise is inflated and the delivery is not
The mechanism of Best and Grauer (1991) is visible in Equation 8.2. The unconstrained weights are linear in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) with coefficient matrix \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\), so an error in the mean vector is multiplied by the inverse covariance matrix before it reaches the portfolio, and Section 7.1 showed how large the entries of that inverse become as the matrix approaches singularity. The error in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) is not small: from Equation 4.3 its standard error over sixty months is of the order of the volatility divided by \(\sqrt{5}\), which for an equity market is a few percent a year, comparable to the premium being estimated.
Two consequences follow, and both can be written down. First, the Sharpe ratio a plug-in portfolio reports on its own estimation window is biased upward. With \(\theta^2 = \boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}\) the true squared maximum Sharpe ratio and \(\hat{\theta}^2\) its sample counterpart, Kan and Zhou (2007) show, under independent normal returns and with \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) scaled by \(T\) rather than \(T-1\), that
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\theta}^2\big] = \frac{T\,\theta^2 + N}{T - N - 2} ,
\tag{8.5}\]
which exceeds \(\theta^2\) for every finite \(T\) and does so by a term of order \(N/T\) that is present even when \(\theta^2 = 0\). A window of \(T\) months on \(N\) assets manufactures a squared Sharpe ratio of roughly \(N/T\) from noise alone. Second, the portfolio built on those estimates is expected to do worse than the true optimum. For an investor with quadratic utility \(U(\boldsymbol{w}) = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\), whose unconstrained optimum \(\boldsymbol{w}^* = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/\gamma\) attains \(U(\boldsymbol{w}^*) = \theta^2/(2\gamma)\), Kan and Zhou (2007) derive the expected utility of the plug-in rule \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\gamma\) in closed form:
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[U(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})\big]
= \frac{\theta^2}{\gamma}\,\frac{T}{T-N-2}
\;-\;\frac{T^2 (T-2)}{2\gamma\,(T-N-1)(T-N-2)(T-N-4)}
   \left(\theta^2 + \frac{N}{T}\right).
\tag{8.6}\]
The derivation is theirs and we do not repeat it; what matters is the shape. The first term is the expected return of the plug-in portfolio, inflated by \(T/(T-N-2)\) because \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\) is biased upward. The second is its expected variance, and it carries the same \(N/T\) as Equation 8.5: the noise in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) is converted into positions, and positions taken on noise have variance but no return. The loss \(U(\boldsymbol{w}^*) - \mathbb{E}[U(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})]\) falls with \(T\) and rises with \(N\), and for small enough \(T\) relative to \(N\) the expected utility is negative, meaning that the plug-in investor is expected to end up worse off than one holding the bill. Klein and Bawa (1976) had reached the qualitative conclusion three decades earlier by treating the parameters as uncertain in a Bayesian predictive distribution; Kan and Zhou (2007) put numbers on it, and the box below puts this universe’s numbers in.






NoteWorked: Equation 8.6 on the sixteen series





The only quantity in Equation 8.6 that belongs to the data is \(\theta^2\). On the full sample of 372 months,

theta2 <- as.numeric(t(mu) %*% solve(S, mu))     # squared maximum Sharpe ratio, monthly

# gamma = 1. Both terms scale with 1 / gamma, so the ratio to the optimum does not.
kz_utility <- function(theta2, N, T) {
  theta2 * T / (T - N - 2) -
    T^2 * (T - 2) / (2 * (T - N - 1) * (T - N - 2) * (T - N - 4)) * (theta2 + N / T)
}

kz <- tibble::tibble(T = c(60L, 120L, 240L, nrow(Re), 1000L)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(expected = kz_utility(theta2, N, T),
                optimum  = theta2 / 2,
                share    = expected / optimum)
round(c(theta2 = theta2, max_sharpe_annualized = sqrt(12 * theta2)), 4)
#>                theta2 max_sharpe_annualized 
#>                0.1012                1.1018

so \(\theta^2 = 0.1012\) a month, an unconstrained maximum Sharpe ratio of 1.10 a year. Substituting \(N = 16\) and \(T = 60\) into Equation 8.6 with \(\gamma = 1\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[U(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})\big]
= \frac{60}{42} \times 0.1012
- \frac{60^2 \times 58}{2 \times 43 \times 42 \times 40}
   \left(0.1012 + \frac{16}{60}\right)
= 0.1445 - 0.5316
= -0.3871 ,
\]
against \(U(\boldsymbol{w}^*) = \theta^2 / 2 = 0.0506\). The expected utility of the plug-in investor is negative: on sixty months of sixteen assets, an unconstrained mean-variance investor is expected to do worse than holding cash. The sample this book uses, 372 months, recovers 45% of the optimum, and a thousand months 81%.

The formula assumes normality and independence, which Section 4.3 showed this market violates. Whether that matters at the first decimal can be checked by drawing sixty months from a normal distribution with these moments, forming the plug-in portfolio and scoring it under the truth, two thousand times.

set.seed(1602)
L <- chol(S)                                   # X = Z L has covariance L'L = S
mc <- vapply(seq_len(2000L), function(b) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(60L * N), 60L) %*% L + matrix(mu, 60L, N, byrow = TRUE)
  m <- colMeans(X); V <- stats::cov(X) * 59 / 60         # scaled by T, as in @eq-08-kz
  w <- solve(V, m)                                       # gamma = 1
  c(utility    = sum(w * mu) - 0.5 * as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w),
    theta2_hat = sum(m * solve(V, m)))
}, numeric(2))

round(c(utility_simulated    = mean(mc["utility", ]),
        utility_formula      = kz_utility(theta2, N, 60L),
        theta2_hat_simulated = mean(mc["theta2_hat", ]),
        theta2_hat_formula   = (60 * theta2 + N) / (60 - N - 2)), 4)
#>    utility_simulated      utility_formula theta2_hat_simulated 
#>              -0.3914              -0.3871               0.5295 
#>   theta2_hat_formula 
#>               0.5255

Both expectations agree with Equation 8.5 and Equation 8.6 to the second decimal, which is the algebra working. The promised squared Sharpe ratio on a sixty-month window is 0.53 against a true 0.1012: an annualized promise of 2.52 for a truth of 1.10.




8.1.4 The Sharpe gap
Equation 8.5 and Equation 8.6 make two statements about the same portfolio: it promises more than the truth, and it delivers less. The distance between the two is what this book measures, and it needs a definition that can be computed on data where the truth is unknown. On a rolling window ending at \(t\), with estimates \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_t\) and a rule producing \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t\), the promised Sharpe ratio is the one the window itself reports,
\[
\widehat{SR}^{\,\text{promised}}_t
= \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t'\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t}
       {\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_t\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t}} ,
\tag{8.7}\]
and the realized Sharpe ratio is the one earned by the sequence of held portfolios, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t'\boldsymbol{r}_{t+1}\), over every month of the out-of-sample period. The Sharpe gap is the average promise minus the realization,
\[
\text{gap} = \overline{\widehat{SR}^{\,\text{promised}}} - SR^{\,\text{realized}} ,
\tag{8.8}\]
annualized as in Sharpe (1966) by \(\sqrt{12}\). The gap is a property of a rule on a universe, not of a single window, and it aggregates over the same rolling scheme that Section 25.1 formalizes as Equation 25.1. For equal weighting the promise is not zero: Equation 8.3 estimates no weights, but the Sharpe ratio it reports on a window is still computed from that window’s \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_t\), so its gap measures how much a window flatters even a portfolio that did not look at it. That is what makes it the control.
The gap is not the same thing as the loss in Equation 8.6. The loss compares a rule with the optimum under a truth; the gap compares a rule with itself across time and needs no truth. Broadie (1993)’s three frontiers are the picture: the promise is a point on the estimated frontier, the realization is a point on the actual one, and the true frontier between them is what a simulation can supply and a backtest cannot. Section 8.2 measures the gap; Section 8.3 supplies a truth and measures the loss, which is also where forecast error is put into the investor’s own units.

title: 8  Estimation Error and Its Cost
section: 8.2 Measuring the Gap on Rolling Windows
text:
8.2 Measuring the Gap on Rolling Windows

8.2.1 The naive rules in PortfolioAnalytics

Both benchmarks are exported functions, documented, and almost never used. They take a return matrix and a portfolio specification, exactly like optimize.portfolio(), and return an object of the same class.

base <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

args(equal.weight)
#> function (R, portfolio, ...) 
#> NULL

ew <- equal.weight(Re, base)
iv <- inverse.volatility.weight(Re, base)
c(class(ew)[1], class(iv)[1])
#> [1] "optimize.portfolio.eqwt"  "optimize.portfolio.invol"
names(ew)
#> [1] "R"                  "weights"            "out"               
#> [4] "objective_measures" "call"               "portfolio"

The object carries the weights, the returns it was handed and the specification, so extractWeights() and everything downstream of it work unchanged.

w_ew <- extractWeights(ew)[colnames(Re)]
w_iv <- extractWeights(iv)[colnames(Re)]
vols <- apply(Re, 2, stats::sd)
stopifnot(all.equal(sum(w_ew), 1), all.equal(sum(w_iv), 1),
          all.equal(unname(w_iv), unname((1 / vols) / sum(1 / vols))))   # @eq-08-iv
round(sort(w_iv, decreasing = TRUE)[1:4], 4)
#> US_government     US_credit UK_government EU_government 
#>        0.1489        0.0975        0.0746        0.0721

The stopifnot() confirms that inverse.volatility.weight() computes Equation 8.4 and nothing else: US_government, the least volatile series, receives 14.9% against the 6.2% of Equation 8.3.






NoteThe naive rules cannot be passed to the rebalancing loop



Since both functions have the signature of an optimizer, it is natural to expect optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(optimize_method = "equal.weight") to run the rule on every window. It does not, and it does not say so.

bt_naive <- suppressWarnings(optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re, base, optimize_method = "equal.weight",
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = 60L, rolling_window = 59L))

as_function <- try(optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re, base, optimize_method = equal.weight,
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = 60L, rolling_window = 59L), silent = TRUE)

tibble::tibble(
  route   = c("name, rebalancing", "function, rebalancing", "name, single call"),
  result  = c(class(bt_naive$opt_rebalancing[[1]])[1], class(as_function)[1],
              class(optimize.portfolio(Re, base, optimize_method = "equal.weight"))[1]),
  usable  = c(sum(!is.na(extractWeights(bt_naive))), NA,
              !is.null(extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, base, optimize_method = "equal.weight")))))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   route                 result                          usable
#>   <chr>                 <chr>                            <int>
#> 1 name, rebalancing     optimize.portfolio.equal.weight      0
#> 2 function, rebalancing try-error                           NA
#> 3 name, single call     optimize.portfolio.equal.weight      0

Passing the name completes normally: 313 periods, each an object of class optimize.portfolio.equal.weight, and every one of them with NA weights, because the dispatch inside optimize.portfolio() matches the string against its solver list, finds nothing, and builds the class name from the string anyway. Passing the function object fails at the first subscript. The only route is to call the functions directly on each window, which is what the loop below does and what pm_backtest() in Section 25.3 does through its weight_fun argument. One further detail: equal.weight() reads max_sum off the specification, so under the relaxed budget that Section 9.2 describes as a workaround for the full_investment trap it returns \(1/N\) scaled by the relaxation.



8.2.2 The two optimized rules as quadratic programs
The loop solves 624 optimizations and the simulation in Section 8.3 solves several thousand more, so the two long-only problems are written directly as the quadratic programs that optimize.portfolio(optimize_method = "ROI") hands to quadprog in any case. The minimum-variance problem is Equation 9.2 without its return constraint. The long-only tangency portfolio uses a standard change of variable: minimize \(\boldsymbol{y}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{y}\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{y}'\boldsymbol{\mu} = 1\) and \(\boldsymbol{y} \geq \boldsymbol{0}\), then rescale \(\boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{y}/\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{y}\); the rescaling leaves the Sharpe ratio unchanged and the constraint makes it the maximum. The trick needs one asset with a positive estimated mean, and the function records when there is none.

# Long-only minimum variance: min w'Sw subject to w'i = 1, w >= 0. Percent scaling
# keeps quadprog's matrix well away from its positive-definiteness tolerance.
gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}

# Long-only maximum Sharpe: min y'Sy subject to y'mu = 1, y >= 0, then w = y / sum(y).
# With no positive estimated mean the ratio has no maximum worth holding; the rule
# then holds the minimum-variance portfolio and says so through an attribute.
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(structure(gmv_qp(S), fallback = TRUE))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  structure(setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu)), fallback = FALSE)
}

# Annualized Sharpe ratio of w under the moments (mu, S); returns are excess already.
sharpe_of <- function(w, mu, S) {
  as.numeric(sum(w * mu) / sqrt(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
}

Before either function is trusted on four thousand problems it is checked against the package on one.

w_gmv_roi <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(
  Re, base |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
  optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]

w_tan_roi <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(
  Re, base |> add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
              add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev"),
  optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE))[colnames(Re)]

w_gmv <- gmv_qp(S)
w_tan <- tan_qp(mu, S)
stopifnot(sum(abs(w_gmv - w_gmv_roi)) / 2 < 1e-4,
          sum(abs(w_tan - w_tan_roi)) / 2 < 1e-4)

round(w_tan[w_tan > 0.005], 4)
#>        EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity        US_equity    US_government 
#>           0.0945           0.0309           0.1860           0.6841

The two agree to a turnover below one basis point. maxSR = TRUE locates the tangency correctly here because the installed build is the patched one of Appendix D; Section 9.2 explains why the book does not rely on it and reads the point off a computed frontier instead. The full-sample tangency portfolio places 68% in US_government and 19% in US_equity, and its Sharpe ratio under the full-sample moments is 0.991; that number is the promise every shorter window will be compared with.

8.2.3 Three hundred and twelve windows
Each window of 60 months estimates Equation 8.1, forms the four portfolios, records the Sharpe ratio each promises by Equation 8.7 and the total return each earns in the month that follows. Weights are indexed by name and asserted against the columns before any return is multiplied by them.

win  <- 60L
ends <- seq.int(win, nrow(Re) - 1L)           # every window forecasts the month after it
rf_by_month <- setNames(rf, as.character(zoo::index(R)))
oos_start   <- zoo::index(R)[121]             # the first month the register scores
stopifnot(model_year(oos_start) == 11L, model_year(zoo::index(R)[120]) == 10L)

roll <- lapply(ends, function(e) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(Re)[(e - win + 1L):e, , drop = FALSE]
  m <- colMeans(X)
  V <- stats::cov(X)
  rules <- list(
    max_sharpe   = tan_qp(m, V),
    min_variance = gmv_qp(V),
    equal_weight = setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re)),
    inverse_vol  = setNames((1 / sqrt(diag(V))) / sum(1 / sqrt(diag(V))), colnames(Re))
  )
  stopifnot(all(vapply(rules, function(w) identical(names(w), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))
  nxt <- zoo::coredata(R)[e + 1L, ]           # total return in the month held
  tibble::tibble(
    date     = zoo::index(R)[e + 1L],
    rule     = names(rules),
    promised = vapply(rules, sharpe_of, numeric(1), mu = m, S = V),
    realized = vapply(rules, function(w) sum(w * nxt), numeric(1)),
    fallback = isTRUE(attr(rules$max_sharpe, "fallback"))
  )
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

c(windows = length(ends), no_positive_mean = sum(roll$fallback[roll$rule == "max_sharpe"]))
#>          windows no_positive_mean 
#>              312                0

The realized Sharpe ratio is computed the way the register of Section 25.3 computes it, compounding the held returns and the bill separately and dividing their difference by the annualized volatility, so that the two chapters can be compared to the third decimal. The register scores every configuration on the same months, from January of model year 11, so that a longer window earns no credit for starting later; the same start is used here.

sharpe_realized <- function(r, rf) {
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}

summarise_gap <- function(d) {
  d |>
    dplyr::group_by(rule) |>
    dplyr::summarise(months   = dplyr::n(),
                     promised = mean(promised),
                     realized = sharpe_realized(realized, rf_by_month[as.character(date)]),
                     .groups  = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(gap = promised - realized, kept = realized / promised) |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(realized))
}

gap     <- summarise_gap(dplyr::filter(roll, date >= oos_start))
gap_all <- summarise_gap(roll)


sweep_all <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>      # every window of the register
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
sr_sweep <- function(s, w = win) {
  sweep_all$sharpe[match(paste(s, w), paste(sweep_all$strategy, sweep_all$window))]
}
sweep <- dplyr::filter(sweep_all, window == win)                    # the sixty-month rows

check <- gap |>
  dplyr::mutate(register = sr_sweep(rule), difference = realized - register)
stopifnot(!anyNA(check$register),
          all(abs(check$difference[check$rule %in% c("equal_weight", "max_sharpe")]) < 5e-5),
          all(abs(check$difference) < 1e-3))
check |> dplyr::select(rule, realized, register, difference)

Two independent implementations of a rolling backtest agreeing to within a thousandth is not a formality; Section 25.1 lists the conventions on which they could have differed.

Read Table 8.2 from the bottom. The tangency portfolio promises 1.50 on the average window and delivers 0.55, keeping 36% of its promise and finishing last of the four. Its gap of 0.96 is 17.4 times the gap of equal weighting, whose own gap of 0.06 is the control: that much of a promise is manufactured by the window on a portfolio that never looked at it. Minimum variance, which estimates only \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), has the highest realized Sharpe ratio, 0.83, and keeps 78% of what it promised. Inverse volatility keeps 84%. Starting the scoring in January of model year 6 instead, with all 312 windows, moves every number and lifts the tangency portfolio from last to rank 2 of 4: it realizes 0.53 against equal weighting’s 0.52. What the scoring period does not change is the gap. At 1.05 the tangency portfolio’s remains the largest of the four, and the four gaps keep their order.







Figure 8.1: The Sharpe gap of Equation 8.8 for four rules. Each segment runs from the Sharpe ratio realized out of sample to the one promised on the estimation window; its length is the gap. Rules are ordered by what they realized.




Figure 8.1 is the chapter’s first result. The ordering of the gaps is the ordering of how much each rule estimates: equal weighting, which estimates nothing, has the shortest segment, inverse volatility with its 16 volatilities the next, minimum variance with the whole of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) the third, and the one rule that estimates \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and maximizes over it the longest, 4.2 times the third. The realizations are ordered differently: the rule with the highest promise realizes least, and the rule that estimates only \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) realizes most. Whether the differences in realized Sharpe ratios are statistically distinguishable is a separate question, answered by the test of Jobson and Korkie (1981) with the correction of Memmel (2003) and by the error bar of Lo (2002) that Section 25.3 puts on the register; the differences in promise are not in doubt, because they are computed rather than sampled.

title: 8  Estimation Error and Its Cost
text:
8.3 Where the Loss Comes From

8.3.1 A truth to score against
A backtest cannot say which input caused the gap, because the truth against which the estimates erred is never observed. A simulation can. We take the full-sample moments of the sixteen series as the truth, draw \(T\) months from a normal distribution with those moments, estimate Equation 8.1 on the draw, form the long-only tangency portfolio, and score it under the truth. Repeating this a few hundred times per \(T\) gives the expected Sharpe ratio a \(T\)-month investor actually earns, against which the promise and the naive rules can be placed. A twelve-month block bootstrap of the actual returns, as in Section 9.3, would preserve the tails that a normal draw loses; exercise 2 asks what changes.

draw_months <- function(T, mu, L) {
  matrix(rnorm(T * length(mu)), T) %*% L + matrix(mu, T, length(mu), byrow = TRUE)
}

w_star  <- tan_qp(mu, S)                       # the long-only tangency under the truth
sr_star <- sharpe_of(w_star, mu, S)
sr_gmv  <- sharpe_of(gmv_qp(S), mu, S)
sr_ew   <- sharpe_of(w_ew, mu, S)
round(c(tangency = sr_star, min_variance = sr_gmv, equal_weight = sr_ew), 3)
#>     tangency min_variance equal_weight 
#>        0.991        0.795        0.617

Under the truth the long-only tangency portfolio has a Sharpe ratio of 0.99, equal weighting 0.62, and minimum variance 0.80. The first number is the ceiling: no estimated portfolio can exceed it under the truth, so every draw lands at or below it, and the average distance is the loss.

8.3.2 The mean channel and the covariance channel
The decomposition is Chopra and Ziemba (1993)’s, done by substitution rather than by perturbation. Three portfolios are formed on every draw: the plug-in rule with both moments estimated, the rule with the estimated mean and the true covariance, and the rule with the true mean and the estimated covariance. The second isolates what estimating \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) costs, the third what estimating \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) costs.

set.seed(1602)
Ts <- c(60L, 120L, 240L, 372L, 1000L)
B  <- 300L

one_draw <- function(T) {
  X <- draw_months(T, mu, L); m <- colMeans(X); V <- stats::cov(X)
  w_hat <- tan_qp(m, V)
  c(plug_in   = sharpe_of(w_hat, mu, S),             # both estimated
    mean_only = sharpe_of(tan_qp(m, S), mu, S),      # estimated mean, true covariance
    cov_only  = sharpe_of(tan_qp(mu, V), mu, S),     # true mean, estimated covariance
    promised  = sharpe_of(w_hat, m, V),              # what the draw itself claims
    fallback  = as.numeric(isTRUE(attr(w_hat, "fallback"))))
}

sim <- lapply(Ts, function(T) {
  d <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) one_draw(T), numeric(5))
  tibble::tibble(T = T, channel = rownames(d), mean = rowMeans(d), sd = apply(d, 1, stats::sd))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

sim_wide <- sim |>
  dplyr::select(-sd) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = channel, values_from = mean) |>
  dplyr::mutate(loss = sr_star - plug_in,
                loss_mean = sr_star - mean_only,
                loss_cov  = sr_star - cov_only)
stopifnot(all(sim_wide$fallback == 0), all(sim_wide$plug_in <= sr_star))

At sixty months the plug-in portfolio delivers 0.76 against a promise of 1.38 and a ceiling of 0.99. Of the loss of 0.23, estimating the mean alone accounts for 0.22 and estimating the covariance alone for 0.04: the mean channel costs 6 times as much. That is Chopra and Ziemba (1993)’s finding reproduced on this universe by substitution. At sixty months the ratio is smaller than their eleven, because the long-only constraint caps what an error in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) can do to the weights, which is Jagannathan and Ma (2003)’s point again; it rises with the window and reaches 12 at a thousand months, because the covariance channel closes faster. That channel is nearly closed at every \(T\) in the table; on sixteen series a sixty-month window already has nearly four observations per asset, the matrix is well conditioned by the measure of Section 7.1, and the shrinkage of Ledoit and Wolf (2004) has little to shrink. The mean channel is still open at a thousand months, where it costs 0.027, and Equation 4.3 says why: a thousand months is eighty-three years, and the standard error of a mean falls with the square root of the span.







Figure 8.2: Sharpe ratio under the truth against the length of the estimation window. Solid lines are the three estimated portfolios; dashed lines are the true tangency, true minimum-variance and equally weighted portfolios, which need no window. The mean channel accounts for almost the whole distance between the plug-in rule and its ceiling.




One feature of Figure 8.2 deserves a sentence, because it is not what DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) would lead a reader to expect. Under this truth the estimated tangency portfolio is above equal weighting at every window in the table, including 60 months: the crossover on the sixteen series is at or below the shortest window shown, and the subsection after the next one locates it. The reason is the ceiling. The true tangency portfolio’s Sharpe ratio exceeds equal weighting’s by 0.37 on this universe, because bonds and equities sit side by side and \(1/N\) cannot tell them apart, and a long-only estimate that loses 0.23 of that is still 0.14 ahead.

8.3.3 Forecast error in the investor’s units
A forecast of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is conventionally scored by its mean squared error, and the score is in the wrong units. It says how far the numbers were from the truth; it does not say what being that far cost, because the cost depends on \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), on the constraint set and on the rule that turned the forecast into positions. The idea behind the risk-adjusted forecast error is to measure the error in the units the investor cares about: the Sharpe ratio the portfolio built on the forecast gives up relative to the portfolio built on the truth. Table 8.3 contains that number for the plug-in tangency rule on sixty months: 0.22 of annualized Sharpe ratio lost to the forecast of the mean alone, with the covariance held at its true value. No mean squared error can produce it, and two forecasts with the same mean squared error can produce very different values of it, which is the whole of the argument (Salcher et al. 2026b, 2026a). Section 26.1 derives the measure and shows which channel it charges, and Section 27.1 asks the question that follows from it, whether a forecaster should be trained on mean squared error at all.

8.3.4 When \(1/N\) stops winning
DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) derive from Equation 8.6 the window length at which the unconstrained plug-in rule overtakes equal weighting in expected utility, holding the Sharpe ratios of the tangency portfolio and of \(1/N\) fixed at values typical of their datasets, and obtain the thousands of months quoted at the start of this chapter. In that calculation the benefit of optimizing is held fixed and the cost of estimating grows with \(N\) through Equation 8.6, so the required window grows with \(N\). On this universe nothing is held fixed. We draw sub-universes of four, eight and all sixteen series, and for each one and each window length score the long-only plug-in rule, the unconstrained plug-in rule and equal weighting under that sub-universe’s own truth. The unconstrained rule’s Sharpe ratio is that of the direction \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\); leverage does not change a Sharpe ratio, so no budget normalization is needed and none of the sign reversals that plague the normalized version arise.

set.seed(1602)
Ns <- c(4L, 8L, 16L)
Tg <- c(24L, 36L, 48L, 60L, 120L, 240L, 372L, 600L, 1000L, 2000L)

one_universe <- function(n, T) {
  idx  <- if (n == N) seq_len(N) else sort(sample.int(N, n))
  mu_n <- mu[idx]; S_n <- S[idx, idx]
  X <- draw_months(T, mu_n, chol(S_n)); m <- colMeans(X); V <- stats::cov(X)
  c(long_only     = sharpe_of(tan_qp(m, V), mu_n, S_n),
    unconstrained = sharpe_of(solve(V, m), mu_n, S_n),
    equal_weight  = sharpe_of(rep(1 / n, n), mu_n, S_n),
    ceiling       = sharpe_of(tan_qp(mu_n, S_n), mu_n, S_n),
    ceiling_unc   = sqrt(12 * sum(mu_n * solve(S_n, mu_n))))
}

cells  <- tidyr::expand_grid(n_assets = Ns, T = Tg)
region <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(i) {
  n <- cells$n_assets[i]; T <- cells$T[i]
  d <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) one_universe(n, T), numeric(5))
  tibble::tibble(n_assets = n, T = T,
                 long_only     = mean(d["long_only", ]     - d["equal_weight", ]),
                 unconstrained = mean(d["unconstrained", ] - d["equal_weight", ]),
                 share_long_only = mean(d["long_only", ] > d["equal_weight", ]),
                 benefit       = mean(d["ceiling", ]       - d["equal_weight", ]),
                 benefit_unc   = mean(d["ceiling_unc", ]   - d["equal_weight", ]))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

cross <- region |>
  dplyr::group_by(n_assets) |>
  dplyr::summarise(T_long_only     = min(T[long_only > 0]),
                   T_unconstrained = min(T[unconstrained > 0]),
                   benefit         = mean(benefit),
                   benefit_unc     = mean(benefit_unc),
                   .groups = "drop")

Figure 8.3: Expected Sharpe ratio of the estimated tangency portfolio minus equal weighting’s, under the truth, by window length and universe size. Above the line optimization pays. The left panel is the long-only rule; the right is the unconstrained rule of Equation 8.2, whose loss is what Equation 8.6 prices.




Two things in Figure 8.3 and Table 8.4 are consistent with DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) and one is not, and the one that is not is instructive. The unconstrained rule loses to \(1/N\) at every short window and by a wide margin: at twenty-four months on sixteen series it is 0.38 of Sharpe ratio behind, which is Equation 8.6 in Sharpe units. The long-only rule crosses far earlier than the unconstrained one at every \(N\), at 24 rather than 120 months on the sixteen, which is the constraint acting as the shrinkage Jagannathan and Ma (2003) describe and DeMiguel, Garlappi, Nogales, et al. (2009) generalize to a bound on the norm of the weights. What differs is the direction in \(N\). The unconstrained crossover is 240 months at four series and 120 at sixteen, and the long-only one falls from 60 to 24: the required window does not grow with \(N\) here, because the benefit of optimizing grows with it. The true tangency portfolio’s advantage over \(1/N\) rises from 0.15 at four series to 0.48 at sixteen, since a larger draw from this universe is more likely to hold government bonds beside equities, which is exactly the heterogeneity that equal weighting cannot exploit. The mechanism is the same in both calibrations: the cost of estimating is of order \(N/T\), and the benefit is whatever the universe offers. DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) hold the benefit at the level of a typical equity universe; on a multi-asset universe it is larger, and the crossover moves accordingly. Tu and Zhou (2011) show that a combination of the two rules dominates both, and Kirby and Ostdiek (2012) that much of \(1/N\)’s advantage in the original comparison came from the turnover of the rules it was set against, which Section 23.3 prices on this universe.
The simulation says that on sixty months the long-only tangency portfolio beats equal weighting under this truth in 82% of draws. The rolling backtest of Table 8.2 says it did not: 0.55 against 0.63. On 120-month windows the register has the order the simulation expects, 0.70 against 0.63, so in the backtest the tangency portfolio overtakes \(1/N\) between sixty and 120 months and not at the 24 of Table 8.4. At both windows the tangency portfolio realizes less than the 0.76 and 0.83 that Table 8.3 expects of it. Part of that shortfall is sampling error in the realized figure, which Equation 25.2 puts at about 0.22 of Sharpe ratio over 252 months. The rest is that \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) are not constants: Section 5.3 measured the betas of these series drifting through the sample, Section 4.3 measured the average correlation rising in the credit crisis and the rates shock, and Section 19.1 takes the drift as its subject. Estimation error under a fixed truth is therefore a lower bound on what estimating costs, and the mean-based rule is the one that pays the rest, because it is the one whose positions depend on the input that moves most. Garlappi et al. (2007) and Section 28.1 treat that as uncertainty about the model rather than about its parameters.

8.3.5 The register line
Every construction chapter in this book ends by reading its strategy off the register that Section 25.3 computes with pm_backtest(), so that no chapter carries a number another chapter could contradict.

reg     <- sweep |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sharpe))
reg_120 <- sweep_all |> dplyr::filter(window == 120) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sharpe))
rank_of <- function(s, r = reg) match(s, r$strategy)
reg |> dplyr::select(label, sharpe, ann_vol, ann_turnover)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   label              sharpe ann_vol ann_turnover
#>   <chr>               <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Minimum CVaR        0.893  0.0479        0.478
#> 2 Minimum variance    0.829  0.0412        0.336
#> 3 Equal weight        0.626  0.0875        0.159
#> 4 Inverse volatility  0.573  0.0740        0.166
#> 5 Maximum Sharpe      0.546  0.0610        0.836

Out of sample on sixty-month windows the order is Minimum CVaR, Minimum variance, Equal weight, Inverse volatility, Maximum Sharpe. The rules that estimate no mean occupy the first four places and the one that does is last, which is the ordering of Table 8.2 with minimum conditional value at risk, the strategy of Section 10.3, added at the top. That order holds on thirty-six-month windows as well and not on 120-month ones, where it is Minimum variance, Minimum CVaR, Maximum Sharpe, Equal weight, Inverse volatility, with the tangency portfolio ranking 3 of 5, ahead of both naive rules. Of this chapter’s four rules minimum variance is the strongest at every window, ranking 2 of 5 here, and that is Jagannathan and Ma (2003)’s result: it estimates only \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), the input that can be estimated, and its short-sale constraint shrinks that estimate further.
Equal weighting is not the winner here, ranking 3 of 5, behind two rules that estimate risk alone. That differs from what DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) report, and the two findings are consistent. Their claim is about the mean: no rule that estimates \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) beat \(1/N\) reliably, and none does here. The tangency portfolio is behind \(1/N\) on thirty-six- and sixty-month windows and ahead of it on 120-month ones, each time by less than the standard error of 0.22 that Equation 25.2 attaches to its Sharpe ratio. Whether \(1/N\) also beats a rule that estimates \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) alone is a different question, about how well the covariance matrix is estimated, and on sixteen series with 372 months it is estimated well: Section 7.3 showed shrinkage buying nothing once the sample matrix becomes estimable, and Table 8.3 showed the covariance channel costing a few hundredths of a Sharpe ratio. On the larger universes of DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009) the matrix is the problem and the ranking is theirs, and on the one-hundred-and-eighty-one instruments of Section 21.1 the matrix is the problem again. The lesson is not that optimization fails. It is that the cost of an input is set by how well it can be estimated, and that the mean cannot.

title: 8  Estimation Error and Its Cost
text:
Key Takeaways

A plug-in portfolio promises more than the truth and delivers less. Under normality Equation 8.5 gives the size of the promise’s inflation and Equation 8.6 the expected shortfall, both driven by \(N/T\) (Kan and Zhou 2007). On sixty months of sixteen series the unconstrained rule’s expected utility is negative.
The Sharpe gap of Equation 8.8, promised minus realized on rolling windows, is computable without a truth. On this universe the tangency portfolio keeps 36% of its promise; minimum variance keeps 78%; equal weighting’s own gap of 0.06 is what a window manufactures on a portfolio that never used it.
Splitting the loss by substitution, the mean channel costs 6 times the covariance channel at sixty months and is still open at a thousand (Chopra and Ziemba 1993). The covariance channel is nearly closed on sixteen series.
The window at which optimization overtakes \(1/N\) depends on the cost, of order \(N/T\), and on the benefit, which the universe sets. A long-only constraint shortens it several-fold (Jagannathan and Ma 2003), and on a multi-asset universe the benefit grows with \(N\), so the window does not lengthen with \(N\) the way it does in the calibration of DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009).
Estimation error under a fixed truth is a lower bound. The simulated sixty-month tangency portfolio beats \(1/N\) in 82% of draws; the actual one trailed \(1/N\) on sixty-month windows and overtook it only on 120-month ones, realizing less than the simulation expects at both.
Out of sample on sixty-month windows the register reads Minimum CVaR, Minimum variance, Equal weight, Inverse volatility, Maximum Sharpe: the rules that estimate no mean lead. On 120-month windows the tangency portfolio ranks 3 of 5, ahead of both naive rules, and minimum variance, which estimates only \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), is the strongest of this chapter’s four rules at every window.

equal.weight() and inverse.volatility.weight() are exported, take a return matrix and a specification, and return an optimize.portfolio object. Passed to optimize.portfolio.rebalancing() by name they produce 313 periods of NA weights and no error.

Exercises

Rerun the rolling loop with a window of 120 months and recompute Table 8.2, scoring from the first month of model year 11 as before. Compare the realized Sharpe ratios with the window == 120 rows of output/tables/oos-sweep.csv. Does the longer window close the tangency portfolio’s gap, and by how much relative to the other three rules?
Replace draw_months() with a twelve-month block bootstrap of Re, as in the bootstrap of Section 9.3, and recompute the channel split at \(T = 60\) with the full-sample moments still serving as the truth. Does the mean channel still dominate, and does the plug-in portfolio still beat equal weighting?
Using Equation 8.6 with \(\theta^2\) fixed at this universe’s value, find the \(T\) at which the expected utility of the unconstrained plug-in rule turns positive and the \(T\) at which it reaches ninety percent of the optimum, for \(N = 16\) and for \(N = 50\). How do the two thresholds scale with \(N\)?
In the rolling loop, replace \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t\) by \((1 - \delta)\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t + \delta\,\bar{\mu}_t\boldsymbol{\iota}\) with \(\bar{\mu}_t\) the cross-sectional average and \(\delta = 0.5\), a crude version of the shrinkage of Jorion (1986) that Section 6.1 develops properly. Remeasure the gap of the tangency portfolio. Does shrinking the mean help more than the long-only constraint already did?
