title: 10  Risk Measures Beyond Variance
text:
10.1 Coherence, Tails, and What Variance Assumes
Every optimizer in Section 9.1 measured risk by the variance of the portfolio, and nothing in the data required it: Markowitz (1959) himself proposed the semi-variance, which counts only the returns below the mean, as the measure an investor who fears losses rather than dispersion should prefer. Artzner et al. (1999) turned the question around and asked which properties a number must have before it can be called a measure of risk at all, and found that the industry’s standard, value at risk, lacks the one that matters most for building portfolios. This chapter asks what changes when variance is replaced by a measure that has that property.
We first set out the coherence axioms, value at risk and why it fails them, expected shortfall and the linear program that makes it as easy to optimize as variance, its Cornish-Fisher extension, and the downside and drawdown measures that sit beside them; then show which of these PortfolioAnalytics can solve, with which solver, and where its defaults do something other than what the specification says; then solve one long-only problem on the sixteen class series under four objectives and read what each bought. The allocation is strategic in the sense of Section 3.1: full-sample moments, no timing, and the out-of-sample check read from the register of Section 25.3 rather than recomputed.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill for the reasons of Section 3.1, loaded as Section 9.1 loads them.

title: 10  Risk Measures Beyond Variance
text:
10.1.1 Four properties of a risk measure
Write \(X\) for the random excess return of a position over one period and \(\rho(X)\) for the number a risk measure assigns to it, in the units of a loss. Artzner et al. (1999) call \(\rho\) coherent if it satisfies four axioms: monotonicity, so that a position which pays at least as much as another in every state is not riskier; translation invariance, so that adding a sure amount \(c\) reduces the measured risk by exactly \(c\); positive homogeneity, so that \(\rho(\lambda X) = \lambda\rho(X)\) for \(\lambda > 0\); and subadditivity,
\[
\rho(X + Y) \;\leq\; \rho(X) + \rho(Y).
\tag{10.1}\]
The last axiom is the one that matters here. It says that combining two positions can never make the measured risk larger than the sum of the two measured separately, which is what diversification means; a measure that violates it can rank a diversified portfolio as riskier than its concentrated parts, and an optimizer built on it will act on that ranking. Variance is not coherent, since it scales with \(\lambda^2\) rather than \(\lambda\), and the standard deviation fails monotonicity. They are used anyway because, when returns are elliptical, every translation-invariant and positively homogeneous measure is an increasing function of the standard deviation at a given mean (McNeil et al. 2015), so the choice of measure changes no ranking. Whether returns are elliptical is a question Section 4.2 answered for this market: they are not.

10.1.2 Value at risk
The value at risk at level \(\alpha\) is the loss that is exceeded with probability \(\alpha\): writing \(q_\alpha(X)\) for the \(\alpha\)-quantile of the return,
\[
\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha(X) = -\,q_\alpha(X),
\tag{10.2}\]
with \(\alpha = 0.05\) for the 95% level that this chapter uses throughout, and which PortfolioAnalytics writes as p = 0.95. It is the regulatory standard of Jorion (2007); it is monotone, translation invariant and homogeneous; and it fails Equation 10.1, not only in contrived examples: a quantile ignores everything beyond itself, so two positions whose losses each sit inside the 5% tail can, combined, produce a loss outside it.






NoteWorked: where value at risk fails subadditivity on this data





Equation 10.1 can be tested on every pair of the sixteen series. For an equally weighted pair, homogeneity turns the axiom into \(\rho\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}X + \tfrac{1}{2}Y\right) \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\rho(X) + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho(Y)\), which is one comparison per pair. PerformanceAnalytics reports both as negative numbers by default; invert = FALSE returns the loss as a positive one, the convention of Equation 10.2.

loss_var <- function(x) as.numeric(VaR(x, p = 0.95, method = "historical", invert = FALSE))
loss_es  <- function(x) as.numeric(ES(x,  p = 0.95, method = "historical", invert = FALSE))

pairs <- utils::combn(colnames(Re), 2)
mix <- apply(pairs, 2, function(p) {
  a <- as.numeric(Re[, p[1]]); b <- as.numeric(Re[, p[2]]); m <- (a + b) / 2
  c(var_mix = loss_var(m), var_avg = (loss_var(a) + loss_var(b)) / 2,
    es_mix  = loss_es(m),  es_avg  = (loss_es(a)  + loss_es(b))  / 2)
}) |>
  t() |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::mutate(a = pairs[1, ], b = pairs[2, ],
                var_fails = var_mix > var_avg + 1e-12,
                es_fails  = es_mix  > es_avg  + 1e-12)

c(pairs = nrow(mix), var_violations = sum(mix$var_fails), es_violations = sum(mix$es_fails))
#>          pairs var_violations  es_violations 
#>            120              3              0
mix |> dplyr::filter(var_fails) |> dplyr::select(a, b, var_mix, var_avg)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   a         b             var_mix var_avg
#>   <chr>     <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 CH_credit CH_government  0.0449  0.0441
#> 2 EU_credit EU_government  0.0467  0.0457
#> 3 US_credit US_government  0.0225  0.0223

Value at risk fails on 3 of the 120 pairs, CH_credit with CH_government, EU_credit with EU_government, and US_credit with US_government, each a credit series combined with the government bond of its own currency. Expected shortfall, defined below, fails on none. The violations are small, at most 0.10 percentage points of monthly loss, because at a 5% tail on 372 months most pairs are close to elliptical, and they are exactly where Section 4.3 located the non-normality of this market: in credit.




10.1.3 Expected shortfall and the linear program
The expected shortfall at level \(\alpha\) is the expected loss given that the loss exceeds the value at risk, Equation 4.5 of Section 4.1, also called conditional value at risk and expected tail loss; PortfolioAnalytics accepts all three names. It is coherent (Acerbi and Tasche 2002) and the smallest coherent measure that dominates value at risk at the same level, which is why it is the tail measure this book uses.
What made expected shortfall usable in an optimizer is a representation due to Rockafellar and Uryasev (2000). For a portfolio \(\boldsymbol{w}\) with return \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}\),
\[
\mathrm{ES}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{w})
= \min_{\zeta \in \mathbb{R}}
  \left\{\, \zeta + \frac{1}{\alpha}\,
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(-\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r} - \zeta\right)_+\right] \right\},
\tag{10.3}\]
where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\), and the minimizing \(\zeta\) is the value at risk. The expression inside the braces is convex in \((\boldsymbol{w}, \zeta)\) jointly, so minimizing it over both at once minimizes the expected shortfall over \(\boldsymbol{w}\) without ever computing a quantile. With the expectation replaced by the average over \(T\) observed return vectors \(\boldsymbol{r}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{r}_T\) and one auxiliary variable \(z_t\) per observation, the minimum-ES problem under full investment and no short sales is the linear program
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol{w},\,\zeta,\,\boldsymbol{z}} \;
  \zeta + \frac{1}{\alpha T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} z_t
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
  z_t \geq -\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}_t - \zeta,\;
  z_t \geq 0,\;
  \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,\;
  \boldsymbol{w} \geq \boldsymbol{0},
\tag{10.4}\]
with \(N + T + 1\) variables, here 389, and one inequality per month. Rockafellar and Uryasev (2002) extend the representation to distributions with atoms, which the empirical distribution is. Every constraint in Equation 10.4 is linear, so the problem is convex and a local minimum is the global one (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004), as for the quadratic program of Equation 9.2; Section 13.1 is about that distinction. A mean-ES frontier adds the row \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} \geq \bar{\mu}\) and traces \(\bar{\mu}\), and the ratio of mean excess return to expected shortfall, which the package calls STARR, is the tail analog of the Sharpe ratio, maximized by the same normalization that turns the maximum-Sharpe problem into a quadratic program in Section 13.1.






NoteWorked: the expected shortfall of US_credit by hand





The sample version of Equation 4.5 is an average over the tail. With \(T\) months and \(\alpha = 0.05\) the tail holds the \(\alpha T\) worst observations, which is not an integer, and PerformanceAnalytics averages every return strictly below the \(\alpha\)-quantile.

x  <- as.numeric(Re[, "US_credit"])
q  <- stats::quantile(x, 0.05)              # the quantile; its negative is the VaR
tail_months <- x[x < q]
es_hand <- -mean(tail_months)

stopifnot(all.equal(es_hand, loss_es(x)))
c(months = length(x), alpha_T = 0.05 * length(x), in_tail = length(tail_months),
  VaR = as.numeric(-q), ES = es_hand,
  ES_modified = as.numeric(ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "modified", invert = FALSE)))
#>      months     alpha_T     in_tail         VaR          ES ES_modified 
#>   372.00000    18.60000    19.00000     0.02509     0.04470     0.09405

The 19 months below the quantile run from -16.4% to -2.5%, and
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{ES}}_{0.05}
= -\frac{1}{19}\sum_{t \in \text{tail}} r_t
= -\frac{-0.8493}{19}
= 0.0447,
\]
against a value at risk of 0.0251: the average month in the tail loses 1.8 times the loss at its edge. The Cornish-Fisher figure of 0.0941 is the estimate Section 4.2 reported as roughly twice the historical one, and the two disagree because the excess-return skewness of -1.36 pushes the expansion further out than 19 observed months reach.




10.1.4 The modified expected shortfall
The historical estimator uses \(\alpha T\) observations, 18.6 of them here, and Yamai and Yoshiba (2005) show that expected shortfall is estimated with a larger standard error than value at risk from the same sample precisely because it depends on the few observations beyond the quantile. The alternative of Favre and Galeano (2002) and Boudt et al. (2008) replaces the sample tail by a normal quantile corrected for skewness and kurtosis through the Cornish-Fisher expansion, Equation 4.6, and the resulting modified expected shortfall is a function of the portfolio’s first four moments. Each is a polynomial in \(\boldsymbol{w}\) through the coskewness and cokurtosis tensors that Section 11.1 sets out, so the modified measure responds to the asymmetry of every asset and every pair, and Boudt et al. (2008) also decompose it into the contribution of each position, which is the quantity Section 14.1 budgets. But it is not convex in \(\boldsymbol{w}\), and no linear program computes its minimum. PortfolioAnalytics reaches it by search, which Section 10.2 shows and Section 13.3 measures. One default from Section 4.2 carries over: ES() in PerformanceAnalytics returns this modified figure unless method = "historical" is asked for.

10.1.5 Downside measures, drawdowns, and two more coherent measures
Three further families deserve a place. The oldest is the safety-first criterion of Roy (1952), which minimizes the probability of falling below a disaster level, and the semi-variance of Markowitz (1959), which Bawa and Lindenberg (1977) generalized to the lower partial moment of order \(n\) around a target \(\tau\),
\[
\mathrm{LPM}_n(\tau) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\tau - \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}\right)_+^{\,n}\right],
\tag{10.5}\]
whose square root at \(n = 2\) is the downside deviation and the denominator of the ratio of Sortino and Meer (1991). Drawdown measures ask about the path rather than the distribution: Chekhlov et al. (2005) define the conditional drawdown at risk as the average of the worst \(\alpha\) share of drawdowns and show that it, too, is minimized by a linear program of the form of Equation 10.4, with drawdowns in place of losses. The third family is the one Krokhmal (2007) built by replacing the average in Equation 10.3 with a higher norm. At the second order,
\[
\mathrm{CSM}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{w})
= \min_{\zeta}
  \left\{\, \zeta + \frac{1}{\alpha}\,
  \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(-\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r} - \zeta\right)_+^{2}\right]} \right\},
\tag{10.6}\]
which is coherent, penalizes the shape of the tail beyond its average, and is a second-order cone program rather than a linear one; PortfolioAnalytics names it CSM. The package also offers EQS, an “expected quadratic shortfall” documented only by its code, which minimizes over \(\zeta\) the expression of Equation 10.3 with a squared positive part in place of the loss; which tail it squares is a question Section 10.2 measures rather than assumes.

10.1.6 What the choice of measure assumes
Each measure encodes a belief about what the investor of Section 3.1 dislikes. Variance treats a gain of ten percent and a loss of ten percent as the same event, and by Equation 3.12 that is right only if utility is quadratic or every higher moment is a function of the first two, the two cases Markowitz (1959) identified; Levy and Markowitz (1979) and Markowitz (2014) find the approximation good across most utility functions and return histories, and poor where returns are far from normal. A tail measure asks about one side of the distribution only, and so responds to skewness and kurtosis, which Section 4.3 showed to live in credit rather than in equity: US_credit has the third-best Sharpe ratio of the sixteen and a total-return skewness of -1.45, the most negative of them. Markets appear to price downside risk separately from variance (Ang et al. 2006), so the choice is not only a matter of taste; and it has a cost in estimation, since the historical tail uses a twentieth of the sample and the modified one inherits the sample skewness, which Section 4.2 found to change sign in a third of rolling windows. Section 11.1 takes the comoments as inputs; here they enter only through the measure.
One rule from Section 3.1 governs what follows: the measure a portfolio is judged by must be the measure it was chosen by, and a comparison across objectives has to show every portfolio on every measure so that the mismatch is visible. Section 10.3 does that.

title: 10  Risk Measures Beyond Variance
text:
10.2 Implementation

10.2.1 The objectives the package knows
A risk objective in PortfolioAnalytics is named for the function that computes it. "var" or "StdDev" is the variance of Equation 9.1; "ES", with the aliases "ETL" and "CVaR", is Equation 4.5, taking its level and estimator as arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "historical"); "VaR" is Equation 10.2, which no convex solver accepts, since a quantile is not convex in the weights, so it is reachable only through the search methods of Section 13.1; "CSM" and "EQS" are solved by CVXR only. Four specifications on one constraint set carry the chapter: minimum variance, minimum historical expected shortfall, quadratic utility at risk_aversion = 2, which by the \(\gamma/2\) convention of Section B.5 is \(\gamma = 4\), and minimum modified expected shortfall.

base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

spec_var <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
spec_es  <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES",
                                       arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "historical"))
spec_mes <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES",
                                       arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "modified"))
spec_qu  <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = 2)   # lambda = 2, i.e. gamma = 4

The first three are convex and go to ROI: a quadratic program for the two variance objectives, as in Section 9.2, and the linear program of Equation 10.4 for the shortfall.

w_of <- function(opt) extractWeights(opt)[colnames(Re)]      # always index by name

o_var <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_var, optimize_method = "ROI")
o_es  <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_es,  optimize_method = "ROI")
o_qu  <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_qu,  optimize_method = "ROI")
w_var <- w_of(o_var); w_es <- w_of(o_es); w_qu <- w_of(o_qu)
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_es) - 1) < 1e-6, all(w_es >= -1e-8))

W3   <- rbind(`minimum variance` = w_var, `minimum ES` = w_es, `quadratic utility` = w_qu)
keep <- colnames(Re)[apply(W3, 2, max) > 0.005]
round(W3[, keep], 3)
#>                   EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity JP_equity JP_government UK_equity
#> minimum variance      0.014            0.051     0.042         0.000     0.022
#> minimum ES            0.000            0.044     0.021         0.019     0.039
#> quadratic utility     0.312            0.000     0.000         0.000     0.000
#>                   US_credit US_equity US_government
#> minimum variance      0.000     0.051         0.821
#> minimum ES            0.000     0.029         0.849
#> quadratic utility     0.098     0.589         0.000

The risk numbers come back two ways. extractObjectiveMeasures() reports what the solver minimized, and extract_risk() recomputes the mean, the standard deviation and all three tail measures for any weight vector, so a portfolio chosen by one measure can be read on the others.

extractObjectiveMeasures(o_es)
#> $ES
#> [1] 0.02394
unlist(extract_risk(Re, w_es)[c("StdDev", "ES", "CSM")])
#>  StdDev      ES     CSM 
#> 0.01215 0.02394 0.03516

The two ES figures agree, and both are the value of Equation 10.4, which with \(\alpha T = 18.6\) interpolates between the eighteenth and nineteenth worst months, rather than the sample-tail average of ES(); the two differ at the fourth decimal, 0.0239 against 0.0238.






NoteUnder ROI the method argument is not read



The linear program of Equation 10.4 is the sample formulation, and it is the only formulation ROI has. Asking for method = "modified" on an ES objective and then solving with ROI returns the historical solution without a message.

o_mes_roi <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mes, optimize_method = "ROI")
c(same_weights_as_historical = isTRUE(all.equal(w_of(o_mes_roi), w_es)))
#> same_weights_as_historical 
#>                       TRUE

The modified measure needs a solver that evaluates the objective as a black box, which means differential evolution (Storn and Price 1997; Ardia et al. 2011), particle swarm, simulated annealing or random portfolios, none of which carries an optimality guarantee. We use differential evolution with a small budget, and Section 10.3 shows what the budget bought.



set.seed(1602)
invisible(utils::capture.output(
  o_mes <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mes, optimize_method = "DEoptim",
                              search_size = 2000, itermax = 50, traceDE = 0)
))
w_mes <- w_of(o_mes)
c(modified_ES = as.numeric(extractObjectiveMeasures(o_mes)$ES),
  US_credit = w_mes[["US_credit"]], positions = sum(w_mes > 0.005),
  seconds = round(as.numeric(o_mes$elapsed_time, units = "secs"), 1))
#> modified_ES   US_credit   positions     seconds 
#>     0.02546     0.01200     9.00000    19.90000







WarningA mean plus a risk objective is a ratio problem by default, but only for the tail measures



optimize.portfolio() decides what one return objective plus one risk objective means, and decides differently for different measures. With mean and StdDev the default maxSR = FALSE makes it a quadratic-utility problem at the default risk_aversion = 1, and the tangency portfolio needs maxSR = TRUE. With mean and ES the default is maxSTARR = TRUE, as it is for CSMratio and EQSratio: the package maximizes the ratio unless told not to, and maxSTARR = FALSE turns the specification into a minimum-ES problem in which the return objective is merely reported.

spec_mean_es <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95))
spec_mean_sd <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

starr  <- function(w) { x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w); mean(x) / loss_es(x) }
sharpe <- function(w) { x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w); mean(x) / stats::sd(x) }

asked <- list(
  `mean + ES, defaults`         = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_es, optimize_method = "ROI"),
  `mean + ES, maxSTARR = FALSE` = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_es, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                                     maxSTARR = FALSE),
  `mean + StdDev, defaults`     = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_sd, optimize_method = "ROI"),
  `mean + StdDev, maxSR = TRUE` = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_sd, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                                     maxSR = TRUE)
)

# What each default actually solved, checked rather than asserted.
w_qu1 <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = 1), optimize_method = "ROI"))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(w_of(asked[[2]]), w_es,  tolerance = 1e-4)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(w_of(asked[[3]]), w_qu1, tolerance = 1e-4)))

ratios <- tibble::tibble(
  specification = names(asked),
  solves  = c("maximum STARR", "minimum ES", "quadratic utility, risk_aversion = 1",
              "maximum Sharpe"),
  STARR   = vapply(asked, function(o) starr(w_of(o)),  numeric(1)),
  Sharpe  = vapply(asked, function(o) sharpe(w_of(o)), numeric(1)),
  largest = vapply(asked, function(o) {
    w <- w_of(o); sprintf("%s %.0f%%", names(which.max(w)), 100 * max(w)) }, character(1))
)




Table 10.1: Four two-objective specifications and what each solved. STARR is the monthly mean excess return over the 95% expected shortfall; the Sharpe ratio is monthly.











specification

The two default rows of Table 10.1 have 27% of their weight in common: one maximizes a tail ratio and holds mostly US_government, the other a utility whose risk penalty is almost switched off and holds only equity, EU_equity first. Nothing in the returned object says which was solved beyond the name of the objective measure. State the ratio arguments explicitly in every call, in both directions.



10.2.2 The mean-ES frontier
create.EfficientFrontier() with type = "mean-ETL" calls meanetl.efficient.frontier(), which solves Equation 10.4 for the minimum-ES portfolio, for the maximum return, and then for n.portfolios return targets between them. chart.EfficientFrontier() draws it in one call, its default match.col = "ES" locating the horizontal axis; the mean-variance frontier of Section 9.2 is computed beside it on the same constraints.

ef_es <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, spec_mean_es, type = "mean-ETL",
                                  n.portfolios = 50, optimize_method = "ROI")
ef_sd <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, spec_mean_sd, type = "mean-StdDev",
                                  n.portfolios = 50, optimize_method = "ROI")

# `unclass()` before `as.data.frame()`, for the reason given in chapter 9.
fr_es <- as.data.frame(unclass(ef_es$frontier))
fr_sd <- as.data.frame(unclass(ef_sd$frontier))

# The direct call returns the same matrix, without the wrapper object.
fr_direct <- meanetl.efficient.frontier(spec_mean_es, Re, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                        n.portfolios = 10)
c(es_points = nrow(fr_es), sd_points = nrow(fr_sd), direct_points = nrow(fr_direct),
  min_ES_on_frontier = fr_es$ES[1], min_ES_solved = extractObjectiveMeasures(o_es)$ES)
#>          es_points          sd_points      direct_points min_ES_on_frontier 
#>           50.00000           50.00000           10.00000            0.02394 
#>      min_ES_solved 
#>            0.02394


chart.EfficientFrontier(ef_es, match.col = "ES", rf = 0, tangent.line = TRUE,
                        RAR.text = "STARR", main = "")






Figure 10.1: The package’s own mean-ES frontier chart. The tangent is drawn to a zero rate, which is correct here because the returns are already in excess of the bill, and the point it touches is the maximum-STARR portfolio.




Two frontiers under two measures are compared on a common axis, and there are two of them. Every coordinate goes into one data frame first, one row per frontier portfolio and per asset, with the realized volatility and expected shortfall of each, so that a point cannot be paired with another portfolio’s return.

weights_of <- function(fr) {
  W <- as.matrix(fr[, grep("^w[.]", colnames(fr))])
  colnames(W) <- sub("^w[.]", "", colnames(W))
  stopifnot(setequal(colnames(W), colnames(Re)))
  W[, colnames(Re)]
}
p_stats <- function(w) {
  x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w)
  c(ret = mean(x) * 12, vol = stats::sd(x) * sqrt(12), es = loss_es(x))
}
frontier_frame <- function(fr, label) {
  W <- weights_of(fr)
  s <- t(apply(W, 1, p_stats))
  tibble::tibble(kind = label, label = NA_character_,
                 ret = s[, "ret"], vol = s[, "vol"], es = s[, "es"],
                 w_credit = W[, "US_credit"])
}
assets <- tibble::tibble(
  kind = "asset", label = colnames(Re),
  ret  = as.numeric(colMeans(Re)) * 12,
  vol  = as.numeric(apply(Re, 2, stats::sd)) * sqrt(12),
  es   = as.numeric(apply(Re, 2, loss_es)),
  w_credit = NA_real_
)
pts <- dplyr::bind_rows(frontier_frame(fr_es, "mean-ES frontier"),
                        frontier_frame(fr_sd, "mean-variance frontier"),
                        assets)
dplyr::count(pts, kind)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   kind                       n
#>   <chr>                  <int>
#> 1 asset                     16
#> 2 mean-ES frontier          50
#> 3 mean-variance frontier    50








Figure 10.2: The two frontiers in two planes, from one data frame: realized 95% expected shortfall, monthly, on the left; annualized volatility on the right. Each is the envelope in its own plane, and the two are almost indistinguishable as curves. Grey points are the sixteen series.





gap_at <- function(ret_target, col) {
  f <- function(k) stats::approx(pts$ret[pts$kind == k], pts[[col]][pts$kind == k],
                                 xout = ret_target)$y
  f("mean-variance frontier") - f("mean-ES frontier")
}
grid <- seq(0.04, 0.12, by = 0.005)
credit_gap  <- gap_at(grid, "w_credit")             # variance frontier minus ES frontier
peak_credit <- vapply(c("mean-variance frontier", "mean-ES frontier"),
                      function(k) max(pts$w_credit[pts$kind == k]), numeric(1))

# What the text below states: the two curves lie within a tenth of a percentage
# point of each other in either risk, the gap in `US_credit` runs both ways, and
# the higher peak is on the expected-shortfall frontier.
stopifnot(!anyNA(credit_gap),
          max(abs(gap_at(grid, "es"))) < 0.001, max(abs(gap_at(grid, "vol"))) < 0.001,
          max(credit_gap) > 0, min(credit_gap) < 0,
          peak_credit[["mean-ES frontier"]] > peak_credit[["mean-variance frontier"]])

c(largest_ES_saved        = max(gap_at(grid, "es")),
  largest_vol_paid        = -min(gap_at(grid, "vol")),
  credit_more_on_variance = max(credit_gap),
  credit_more_on_ES       = -min(credit_gap))
#>        largest_ES_saved        largest_vol_paid credit_more_on_variance 
#>               0.0004475               0.0006075               0.0624938 
#>       credit_more_on_ES 
#>               0.0960000

Read Figure 10.2 as two statements. As curves, the frontiers nearly coincide: at any target return the mean-ES portfolio saves at most 0.04 percentage points of monthly expected shortfall and pays at most 0.06 percentage points of annualized volatility for it, both within the width of the line. As portfolios, they differ, and Figure 10.3 shows where.







Figure 10.3: The weight of US_credit along the two frontiers, against the target excess return. On the variance frontier the weight rises to a single peak and falls back to zero; on the expected-shortfall frontier it is zero at low targets and irregular above them, with the higher peak.




The variance frontier holds US_credit at up to 17.2% of the portfolio and the expected-shortfall frontier at up to 25.4%; at a matched target return the variance frontier holds up to 6 percentage points more of it and the expected-shortfall frontier up to 10 more. The tail measure did not sell the asset whose risk is in its third moment rather than its second, the holding Section 9.3 traced to a measure that cannot see a left tail: once a return target has to be met, both measures buy the series. The reason is what a 5% historical tail registers.

x_credit <- as.numeric(Re[, "US_credit"])
i_worst  <- which.min(x_credit)
d_worst  <- zoo::index(Re)[i_worst]                    # the worst month of the series
per_sd   <- function(method) apply(Re, 2, function(x)
  as.numeric(ES(as.numeric(x), p = 0.95, method = method, invert = FALSE)) / stats::sd(x))
tail_sd  <- list(historical = per_sd("historical"), modified = per_sd("modified"))
tail_rank <- vapply(tail_sd, function(v) rank(-v)[["US_credit"]], numeric(1))

credit_tail <- c(skewness            = as.numeric(skewness(x_credit)),
                 without_worst_month = as.numeric(skewness(x_credit[-i_worst])),
                 worst_month_in_sd   = (x_credit[i_worst] - mean(x_credit)) / stats::sd(x_credit),
                 ES_per_sd           = tail_sd$historical[["US_credit"]],
                 modified_ES_per_sd  = tail_sd$modified[["US_credit"]])
stopifnot(in_episode(d_worst, "credit_crisis"),
          abs(credit_tail[["without_worst_month"]]) < 0.25 * abs(credit_tail[["skewness"]]),
          tail_rank[["historical"]] > 4, tail_rank[["modified"]] <= 3)
round(credit_tail, 2)
#>            skewness without_worst_month   worst_month_in_sd           ES_per_sd 
#>               -1.36               -0.03               -8.01                2.13 
#>  modified_ES_per_sd 
#>                4.49
tail_rank
#> historical   modified 
#>          8          2

The skewness of US_credit is the work of one month, October of model year 17 in the credit crisis, a return 8.0 standard deviations below the mean: without it the excess-return skewness is -0.03 rather than -1.36. A 5% tail averages that month with 18 others, so the historical expected shortfall of the series is 2.13 times its standard deviation, rank 8 of the sixteen, where the Cornish-Fisher figure, which is built from the skewness, is 4.49 times, rank 2. The frontier holdings that differ by so much are separated by the few hundredths of a percentage point of risk reported above, which is the statement of McNeil et al. (2015) made on sixteen assets: series that are close to elliptical are ranked the same way by both measures, and the weights on which the two frontiers disagree are weakly determined by either.

10.2.3 Two coherent measures that need a cone solver
CSM and EQS are solved by CVXR alone, through the formulation of Equation 10.6 and its squared counterpart; meancsm.efficient.frontier() and meaneqs.efficient.frontier() trace their frontiers the way meanetl.efficient.frontier() does. Their minimum-risk portfolios sit beside the minimum-ES one.

spec_csm <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "CSM", arguments = list(p = 0.95))
spec_eqs <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "EQS", arguments = list(p = 0.95))

w_csm <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_csm, optimize_method = "CVXR"))
w_eqs <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_eqs, optimize_method = "CVXR"))

W_tail <- rbind(`minimum ES` = w_es, `minimum CSM` = w_csm, `minimum EQS` = w_eqs)
round(W_tail[, colnames(Re)[apply(W_tail, 2, max) > 0.005]], 3)
#>             CH_equity CH_government EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity JP_equity
#> minimum ES      0.000         0.000      0.00            0.044     0.021
#> minimum CSM     0.016         0.205      0.00            0.000     0.000
#> minimum EQS     0.018         0.000      0.03            0.043     0.070
#>             JP_government UK_equity UK_government US_equity US_government
#> minimum ES          0.019     0.039         0.000     0.029         0.849
#> minimum CSM         0.000     0.030         0.000     0.090         0.660
#> minimum EQS         0.000     0.000         0.084     0.000         0.756







ImportantCSM is unavailable to the search methods



Every objective a metaheuristic evaluates passes through constrained_objective(), and that function’s branch for CSM is empty: it sets no function, so the objective contributes nothing to the score (upstream issue #51, recorded in Appendix D). A random-portfolio or differential-evolution run on a CSM objective does not fail; it scores every candidate at zero and returns the first one it looked at.

set.seed(1602)
rp <- random_portfolios(base_spec, permutations = 2000, rp_method = "simplex")
o_csm_rp <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_csm, optimize_method = "random", rp = rp, trace = TRUE)

scores <- vapply(o_csm_rp$random_portfolio_objective_results, function(z) z$out, numeric(1))
c(candidates = nrow(rp), distinct_scores = length(unique(scores)), score = unique(scores)[1],
  returned_first_candidate = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(w_of(o_csm_rp)),
                                              unname(rp[1, colnames(Re)]))))
#>               candidates          distinct_scores                    score 
#>                     1606                        1                        0 
#> returned_first_candidate 
#>                        1
length(extractObjectiveMeasures(o_csm_rp))
#> [1] 0

The returned object has weights, an empty list of objective measures, and no warning. Use CVXR for CSM, and treat an empty extractObjectiveMeasures() as the signature of an objective that was never evaluated.








ImportantTwo things to check before trusting an EQS number



The ratio problems are solved in a normalized form, mean fixed at one and box and group limits scaled by the weight sum, and the weights are rescaled to sum to one afterwards. Earlier builds skipped the rescaling, so that a box or group limit on a ratio problem did not bind in the returned weights; on the build recorded in Appendix D it does, and we measure it rather than assume it. What does not survive the rescaling is the objective value: expected shortfall and CSM are homogeneous and divide through, while EQS is quadratic in the weights, so the figure reported for a ratio solution is not the EQS of the weights reported with it.

# split() orders groups alphabetically; the limit vectors are built by name and
# the assertion fails the render if they ever drift apart.
grp  <- split(seq_len(ncol(Re)), dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", colnames(Re))     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", colnames(Re)) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", colnames(Re))     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                                ~ "commodity"))
gmin <- c(commodity = 0.00, credit = 0.05, equity = 0.20, government = 0.10)
gmax <- c(commodity = 0.15, credit = 0.40, equity = 0.60, government = 0.50)
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(gmin)), identical(names(grp), names(gmax)))

spec_eqs_ratio <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.25) |>
  add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp,
                 group_min = unname(gmin), group_max = unname(gmax)) |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "EQS", arguments = list(p = 0.95))

o_eqs_ratio <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_eqs_ratio, optimize_method = "CVXR")  # EQSratio = TRUE
w_r     <- w_of(o_eqs_ratio)
group_w <- vapply(grp, function(g) sum(w_r[g]), numeric(1))

c(sum = sum(w_r), largest = max(w_r),
  box_binds    = all(w_r <= 0.25 + 1e-6),
  groups_bind  = all(group_w >= gmin - 1e-6 & group_w <= gmax + 1e-6),
  reported_EQS = as.numeric(extractObjectiveMeasures(o_eqs_ratio)$EQS),
  EQS_of_weights = extract_risk(Re, w_r)$EQS)
#>            sum        largest      box_binds    groups_bind   reported_EQS 
#>       1.000000       0.250000       1.000000       1.000000       0.416255 
#> EQS_of_weights 
#>       0.002253

The second check concerns the measure itself. In both optimize.portfolio() and extract_risk() the quantity squared is the positive part of the portfolio return, where the ES and CSM branches of the same functions take the positive part of its negative. The number the package calls EQS is therefore the tail average of squared gains, and only on negated returns does it become the tail average of squared losses.

# The empirical version of the minimization in @eq-10-ru for a nonnegative
# series v: the average of its largest alpha share, interpolated at the edge.
tail_mean <- function(v, alpha = 0.05) {
  v <- sort(v, decreasing = TRUE); m <- alpha * length(v); k <- floor(m)
  (sum(v[seq_len(k)]) + (m - k) * v[k + 1]) / m
}
r_es <- as.numeric(Re %*% w_es)
eqs_check <- c(package_EQS            = extract_risk(Re, w_es)$EQS,
               tail_of_squared_gains  = tail_mean(pmax(r_es, 0)^2),
               tail_of_squared_losses = tail_mean(pmax(-r_es, 0)^2),
               package_EQS_on_negated = extract_risk(-Re, w_es)$EQS)
stopifnot(all.equal(eqs_check[["package_EQS"]], eqs_check[["tail_of_squared_gains"]],
                    tolerance = 1e-3))
signif(eqs_check, 4)
#>            package_EQS  tail_of_squared_gains tail_of_squared_losses 
#>              0.0008126              0.0008126              0.0006052 
#> package_EQS_on_negated 
#>              0.0006052

skew_of <- function(w) as.numeric(skewness(as.numeric(Re %*% w)))
stopifnot(skew_of(w_eqs) < skew_of(w_es))        # the order the next sentence states

Minimizing the package’s EQS therefore penalizes large gains, which is why its minimum-risk portfolio above has a more negative skewness than the minimum-ES one, -0.44 against -0.10. Until the sign is corrected upstream, an EQS objective should be posed on -Re, and every EQS figure read from the returned weights rather than from the returned object.

title: 10  Risk Measures Beyond Variance
text:
10.3 Four Objectives on One Universe

10.3.1 What each objective bought
The four portfolios of Section 10.2 solve the same long-only, fully invested problem and differ only in what they call risk. Each is reported here on every measure, with the tail measures computed on the excess returns that were optimized and the drawdown on the total-return wealth path.

portfolios <- list(`minimum variance` = w_var,
                   `minimum ES` = w_es,
                   `quadratic utility, lambda = 2` = w_qu,
                   `minimum modified ES (search)` = w_mes)

measures_of <- function(w) {
  x  <- as.numeric(Re %*% w)                                       # excess, what was optimized
  xt <- xts::xts(as.numeric(R %*% w), order.by = zoo::index(R))    # total, for the wealth path
  c(US_credit = w[["US_credit"]], positions = sum(w > 0.005),
    ret = mean(x) * 12, vol = stats::sd(x) * sqrt(12),
    ES = loss_es(x),
    modified_ES = as.numeric(ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "modified", invert = FALSE)),
    utility = (mean(x) - 2 * stats::var(x)) * 12,                   # mu - lambda sigma^2, lambda = 2
    skewness = as.numeric(skewness(x)),
    max_drawdown = as.numeric(maxDrawdown(xt)))
}

title: 10  Risk Measures Beyond Variance
text:
Key Takeaways

A risk measure is coherent if it is monotone, translation invariant, positively homogeneous and subadditive (Artzner et al. 1999). Value at risk fails subadditivity on 3 of the 120 pairs in this market; expected shortfall never does (Acerbi and Tasche 2002); variance is not coherent either, but ranks portfolios correctly when returns are elliptical.
The representation of Rockafellar and Uryasev (2000), Equation 10.3, turns minimum expected shortfall into the linear program Equation 10.4, convex and solved exactly by ROI; the modified expected shortfall of Favre and Galeano (2002) and Boudt et al. (2008) depends on the third and fourth moments, is not convex, and is reached only by search.
In PortfolioAnalytics a mean plus ES, CSM or EQS specification is a ratio problem unless maxSTARR, CSMratio or EQSratio is FALSE, while mean plus StdDev is a quadratic-utility problem unless maxSR = TRUE; ROI ignores method = "modified"; CSM is silently unevaluated by the search methods; and EQS squares the gains.
On the sixteen class series the two frontiers are almost the same curve and not the same portfolios: at a matched return their US_credit weights differ by up to 10 percentage points, and in both directions. A 5% historical tail does not register the skewness of that series, which is the work of one month; the Cornish-Fisher estimate does. Of the four objectives only quadratic utility holds it in size, and the minimum-ES portfolio is the closest to symmetric of the convex solutions.
Report each portfolio by the measure it optimized, and show all on all measures. Out of sample the minimum-ES rule realizes a higher expected shortfall than minimum variance at every window: a 5% tail on sixty months is three observations, and a thirty-six-month window’s Sharpe ratio rests on two.

title: 10  Risk Measures Beyond Variance
text:
Exercises

Re-solve the minimum-ES problem at p = 0.90 and p = 0.99. Report the number of months in each tail, the weight of US_credit and the largest holding. How does the distance to the minimum-variance portfolio change as p rises, and why does Equation 10.4 become harder to trust as it does?
Rebuild the two frontiers of Figure 10.2 on sim_class_returns_weekly in excess of sim_riskfree_weekly, matched by date, where the tail holds about four times as many observations. Does the largest gap in the US_credit weight between the frontiers widen or narrow, and what changed: the estimator or the quantity estimated?
Locate the maximum-STARR portfolio on the mean-ES frontier by scanning mean / ES, as Section 9.2 located the tangency portfolio, and compare it with the maxSTARR = TRUE solution of Table 10.1 and with the tangency portfolio. How much US_credit does each hold, which would the investor of Section 3.1 with \(\gamma = 4\) prefer under full investment, and why?
Run the modified-ES search with random portfolios from rp and with differential evolution at itermax = 25 and itermax = 100, seeded, and record the modified expected shortfall each reaches against that of the minimum-ES portfolio from Equation 10.4. Relate the gaps to the fraction of the attainable optimum that Section 13.3 reports.

title: 11  Higher Moments
text:
11.1 Expected Utility Beyond Two Moments
What does an investor lose by describing an asset class with two moments when its returns are skewed and fat-tailed? Kraus and Litzenberger (1976) extended the capital asset pricing model to a third moment and showed that investors pay for positive skewness and demand compensation for negative coskewness with the market; Harvey and Siddique (2000) confirmed on the cross-section of equity returns that conditional skewness carries a price of its own, and Dittmar (2002) extended the argument to kurtosis. If the market prices these moments, a portfolio built on \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) alone is leaving something on the table, and the question of this chapter is how much, on the sixteen asset classes of this book.
The allocation is strategic in the sense of Section 3.1: the moments are unconditional, estimated once on the full sample, and nothing is timed. We first extend the expected-utility expansion of Equation 3.12 to four moments and define the comoment tensors that a portfolio’s skewness and kurtosis are built from, then implement them in PortfolioAnalytics, including the structured estimator, the moment interface and a custom objective, and then compare on the sixteen classes what a two-moment investor, a four-moment investor and a minimum-modified-shortfall investor hold.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill as in Section 9.1.
The case for the chapter is one series. Section 4.2 computed the shape moments of Equation 4.2 for every class, and US_credit stood out; here we recompute the two numbers that matter and the weight a mean-variance investor gives the series.
US_credit has a skewness of -1.45, the most negative of the 16 series, and an excess kurtosis of 12.2, the second highest. A mean-variance investor with relative risk aversion \(\gamma = 5\), solving Equation 3.12 on these sixteen series exactly as Section 9.3 did, holds 15.2% of it. The tangency portfolio of Section 9.2 holds less, and the middle of the frontier holds more; we return to both in Section 11.3. The weight is not a mistake of the optimizer. Equation 9.2 sees a volatility of 7.3% a year and nothing else, and the question is what changes once it sees the rest.

title: 11  Higher Moments
text:
11.1.1 The four-moment expansion
Take the investor of Equation 3.10 with initial wealth normalized to one and returns measured in excess of the bill, so that terminal wealth is \(W = 1 + r_{\boldsymbol{w}}\) with \(r_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{R}^e\) the portfolio’s excess return. Write \(\bar{W} = 1 + \mu_{\boldsymbol{w}}\) for its expectation and \(m_{k,\boldsymbol{w}} = \mathbb{E}[(r_{\boldsymbol{w}} - \mu_{\boldsymbol{w}})^k]\) for the \(k\)-th central moment of the portfolio return. A Taylor expansion of \(U(W)\) around \(\bar{W}\), taken through the fourth order and then averaged, gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[U(W)\right] \approx
U(\bar{W})
+ \frac{U''(\bar{W})}{2}\, m_{2,\boldsymbol{w}}
+ \frac{U'''(\bar{W})}{6}\, m_{3,\boldsymbol{w}}
+ \frac{U''''(\bar{W})}{24}\, m_{4,\boldsymbol{w}} .
\tag{11.1}\]
Stopping after the second term is Equation 3.12, and Markowitz (1959) gave the two conditions under which stopping there is exact. Samuelson (1970) gave the reason it is usually close: for distributions that become compact as the holding period shrinks, the \(k\)-th moment is of order \(\Delta t^{k/2}\), so each further term is smaller than the last by a factor that vanishes with the horizon. That is a statement about monthly returns of moderate size, and it is why Levy and Markowitz (1979) and Markowitz (2014) found the two-moment approximation almost exact on historical equity data. It says nothing about a series whose fourth moment is dominated by a handful of months, which is what Section 4.3 found for credit.
The signs of the derivatives are not free. Scott and Horvath (1980) showed that any investor with positive marginal utility, risk aversion and decreasing absolute risk aversion has \(U''' > 0\) and \(U'''' < 0\): a preference for skewness and an aversion to kurtosis follow from the same properties that produce an aversion to variance. Equation 11.1 is therefore a four-moment objective with signs fixed by economics; Jondeau and Rockinger (2006) developed its portfolio-choice form, Athayde and Flôres (2004) the maximum-skewness problem, and Mitton and Vorkink (2007) show that an investor who values the right tail deliberately under-diversifies to keep it.

11.1.2 Coskewness and cokurtosis
The portfolio moments in Equation 11.1 are polynomials in the weights whose coefficients are moments of the joint distribution. Let \(\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{R}^e - \boldsymbol{\mu}\) be the vector of centered excess returns. The coskewness matrix and the cokurtosis matrix are
\[
\boldsymbol{M}_3 = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\boldsymbol{r}\,\boldsymbol{r}' \otimes \boldsymbol{r}'\right]
\;\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N^2},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{M}_4 = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\boldsymbol{r}\,\boldsymbol{r}' \otimes \boldsymbol{r}' \otimes \boldsymbol{r}'\right]
\;\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N^3},
\tag{11.2}\]
with \(\otimes\) the Kronecker product, so that the element of \(\boldsymbol{M}_3\) in row \(i\) and column \((j-1)N + k\) is \(m_{ijk} = \mathbb{E}[r_i r_j r_k]\), and \(\boldsymbol{M}_4\) holds \(m_{ijkl}\) in the same unfolded arrangement. They are the third- and fourth-order analogues of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), flattened into two dimensions so that the portfolio moments are matrix products,
\[
m_{3,\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{M}_3\,(\boldsymbol{w}\otimes\boldsymbol{w}),
\qquad
m_{4,\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{M}_4\,(\boldsymbol{w}\otimes\boldsymbol{w}\otimes\boldsymbol{w}),
\tag{11.3}\]
and the standardized skewness and excess kurtosis of the portfolio are \(s_{\boldsymbol{w}} = m_{3,\boldsymbol{w}} / \sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}^3\) and \(\kappa_{\boldsymbol{w}} = m_{4,\boldsymbol{w}} / \sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}^4 - 3\), the portfolio versions of Equation 4.2. This is the representation of Jondeau and Rockinger (2006) and of Boudt et al. (2008), whose modified expected shortfall consumes exactly these objects, and it is the one PerformanceAnalytics and PortfolioAnalytics use.
The price of the representation is its size. By symmetry \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) has \(N(N+1)/2\) distinct elements, \(\boldsymbol{M}_3\) has \(N(N+1)(N+2)/6\) and \(\boldsymbol{M}_4\) has \(N(N+1)(N+2)(N+3)/24\).

params <- c(covariance = N * (N + 1) / 2,
            coskewness = N * (N + 1) * (N + 2) / 6,
            cokurtosis = N * (N + 1) * (N + 2) * (N + 3) / 24)
c(params, observations = n_months)
#>   covariance   coskewness   cokurtosis observations 
#>          136          816         3876          372

With \(N = 16\) the sample coskewness matrix has 816 free parameters and the cokurtosis matrix 3876, against 372 months of data: 10.4 parameters per observation for the fourth moment alone, each estimated from a fourth power that a single month can dominate. Section 7.1 found structure necessary for 136 covariances; here it is unavoidable. Martellini and Ziemann (2010) supplied it: impose a constant-correlation or a single-factor model on the comoments, and shrink the sample tensor toward it as Ledoit and Wolf (2004) shrink a covariance matrix. Under a single factor, \(r_i = \beta_i f + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i\) independent of \(f\) and of each other, the coskewness reduces to
\[
m_{ijk} = \beta_i \beta_j \beta_k\, \mathbb{E}[f^3]
        + \mathbb{1}\{i = j = k\}\, \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i^3],
\tag{11.4}\]
so that \(2N + 1\) numbers replace 816, and the cokurtosis has an analogous form in the loadings and the second and fourth moments of the factor and of the residuals. Boudt et al. (2015) extend this to \(k\) factors in closed form; it is what PortfolioAnalytics computes under method = "boudt", with the factors taken from principal components of the returns. What the structure assumes is worth stating before it is used: the cross terms \(\mathbb{E}[f^2 \varepsilon_i]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[f \varepsilon_i^2]\) are set to zero, so an asset whose residual is large precisely when the factor is large has its skewness removed by the structure. Section 11.2 shows that this is the case for credit.

11.1.3 The CRRA investor
The utility function the rest of the literature uses, introduced in Section 3.1, is constant relative risk aversion, \(U(W) = W^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\). Its derivatives are \(U' = W^{-\gamma}\), \(U'' = -\gamma W^{-\gamma-1}\), \(U''' = \gamma(\gamma+1)W^{-\gamma-2}\) and \(U'''' = -\gamma(\gamma+1)(\gamma+2)W^{-\gamma-3}\), with the sign pattern of Scott and Horvath (1980). Substituting into Equation 11.1 gives the objective we write into PortfolioAnalytics below,
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[U(W)\right] \approx
\frac{\bar{W}^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}
- \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bar{W}^{-\gamma-1}\, m_{2,\boldsymbol{w}}
+ \frac{\gamma(\gamma+1)}{6}\,\bar{W}^{-\gamma-2}\, m_{3,\boldsymbol{w}}
- \frac{\gamma(\gamma+1)(\gamma+2)}{24}\,\bar{W}^{-\gamma-3}\, m_{4,\boldsymbol{w}} ,
\tag{11.5}\]
with the portfolio moments from Equation 11.3. Truncated after the second term it is Equation 3.12 up to the wealth factors, which are close to one for monthly returns; the third and fourth terms are what this chapter adds. Brandt et al. (2005) use this fourth-order expansion to make a dynamic CRRA problem tractable, Jondeau and Rockinger (2006) measure when the last two terms move the allocation, and Harvey et al. (2010) treat the same objective with uncertain comoments. Because expected utility has no units an investor recognizes, we report it through the certainty equivalent, the riskless excess return that gives the same utility,
\[
\mathrm{CE}_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \big((1-\gamma)\,\mathbb{E}[U(W)]\big)^{1/(1-\gamma)} - 1 ,
\tag{11.6}\]
which is in return units and can be annualized and compared across portfolios.

11.1.4 The modified expected shortfall as a four-moment objective
The other four-moment objective, and the one PortfolioAnalytics uses most, is the modified expected shortfall of Favre and Galeano (2002) and Boudt et al. (2008). It takes the Cornish-Fisher quantile of Equation 4.6 with the portfolio’s own \(s_{\boldsymbol{w}}\) and \(\kappa_{\boldsymbol{w}}\) substituted in, and reads the expected shortfall of Equation 4.5 off the corrected normal. Its inputs are therefore \((\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \boldsymbol{M}_3, \boldsymbol{M}_4)\) and the weights, nothing else, which is why the estimator of the tensors decides the answer. Section 10.1 treats expected shortfall as a risk measure, its coherence and its historical estimator; here we use only the fact that its modified form is a function of the same four moments as Equation 11.5.

11.1.5 Dependence that no moment describes
Coskewness and cokurtosis summarize a joint distribution; they are not the joint distribution. A copula is: by Sklar’s theorem any joint distribution is its marginals composed with a function on the unit cube that carries the dependence and nothing else (see McNeil et al. 2015, ch. 7). The property of that function a portfolio investor cares about is tail dependence,
\[
\lambda_L = \lim_{q \to 0}\; \Pr\!\left(U_1 \leq q \mid U_2 \leq q\right),
\tag{11.7}\]
the probability that one asset is in its worst \(q\) fraction of months given that the other is. Embrechts et al. (2002) showed why correlation cannot carry this: a Gaussian copula has \(\lambda_L = 0\) for every correlation below one, whereas a \(t\) copula has \(\lambda_L > 0\), rising as its degrees of freedom fall. Longin and Solnik (2001) and Ang and Chen (2002) documented on equity markets that dependence is stronger in the lower tail than in the upper, and Patton (2004) measured what modeling the asymmetry is worth out of sample. The cross terms that Equation 11.4 discards are the moment-based shadow of this asymmetry, and Section 11.3 measures both on the same pairs.

title: 11  Higher Moments
text:
11.2 Comoment Tensors and Custom Objectives

11.2.1 The sample tensors and their shape
set.portfolio.moments() computes every moment a specification’s objectives need, in one call, and returns them as a named list. Which moments it computes depends on the objectives, so the same returns and the same method yield different lists for different specifications.

var_spec <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
mes_spec <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES",
                arguments = list(method = "modified", p = 0.95))

mom_var <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, var_spec, method = "sample")
mom_s   <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, mes_spec, method = "sample")

list(variance_objective = names(mom_var), modified_ES_objective = names(mom_s))
#> $variance_objective
#> [1] "mu"    "sigma"
#> 
#> $modified_ES_objective
#> [1] "mu"    "sigma" "m3"    "m4"
vapply(mom_s, function(x) paste(dim(x), collapse = " x "), character(1))
#>          mu       sigma          m3          m4 
#>    "16 x 1"   "16 x 16"  "16 x 256" "16 x 4096"

A variance objective produces mu and sigma; a modified expected shortfall objective adds m3 of dimension \(16 \times 256\) and m4 of \(16 \times 4096\), which are Equation 11.2 computed by PerformanceAnalytics::M3.MM() and M4.MM() with the \(1/T\) convention. The tensors carry no dimnames, so every element is addressed by position, and the first thing to do with them is confirm that the contraction of Equation 11.3 returns the moment of the portfolio’s return series.

r_qu5 <- as.numeric(Re %*% w_qu5)
m3_w  <- PerformanceAnalytics::portm3(w_qu5, mom_s$m3)
m4_w  <- PerformanceAnalytics::portm4(w_qu5, mom_s$m4)

stopifnot(all.equal(m3_w, mean((r_qu5 - mean(r_qu5))^3)),
          all.equal(m4_w, mean((r_qu5 - mean(r_qu5))^4)))

sd_ml <- sqrt(mean((r_qu5 - mean(r_qu5))^2))      # the 1/T standard deviation
stopifnot(m3_w / sd_ml^3 < min(shape$skew[shape$kind == "equity"]))   # as the text says
c(skew_from_tensor = m3_w / sd_ml^3,
  skew_from_series = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::skewness(r_qu5)),
  exkurt_from_tensor = m4_w / sd_ml^4 - 3)
#>   skew_from_tensor   skew_from_series exkurt_from_tensor 
#>            -0.7948            -0.7948             3.3409

portm3() and portm4() are the PerformanceAnalytics implementations of Equation 11.3, and the stopifnot() is the guard that the tensor and the series agree to machine precision. The quadratic-utility portfolio at \(\gamma = 5\) has a skewness of -0.79, more negative than any equity market in Table 4.1, which is the credit position doing what Equation 11.1 says it does.

11.2.2 The structured estimator
method = "boudt" fits a statistical factor model by principal components and builds the tensors from Equation 11.4 and its fourth-order counterpart. The pieces are exported and can be called separately.

fit1 <- statistical.factor.model(Re, k = 1)
class(fit1); names(fit1)
#> [1] "stfm"
#> [1] "factor_loadings"     "factor_realizations" "residuals"          
#> [4] "m"                   "k"                   "N"

mom_b <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, mes_spec, method = "boudt")
stopifnot(all.equal(mom_b$sigma, extractCovariance(fit1)),
          all.equal(mom_b$m3,    extractCoskewness(fit1)),
          all.equal(mom_b$m4,    extractCokurtosis(fit1)))

beta <- setNames(as.numeric(fit1$factor_loadings), colnames(Re))
pc_share <- prcomp(zoo::coredata(Re))$sdev^2
stopifnot(all(grepl("_equity$", names(sort(abs(beta), decreasing = TRUE))[1:5])))
round(sort(beta, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 3)
#> EU_equity CH_equity UK_equity US_equity JP_equity 
#>     0.506     0.404     0.400     0.303     0.284

The single factor explains 44% of the total variance and loads most heavily on the equity markets, which is the factor Section 5.2 found; US_credit has a loading of 0.092, and its own residual carries 79% of its variance.






NoteThe number of factors must be a literal



set.portfolio.moments() recovers k from match.call() rather than from its value, so method = "boudt", k = 2 works and k = n_factors with n_factors <- 2 does not: the unevaluated symbol reaches statistical.factor.model(), which fails on k <= 0 with a message about language types.

n_factors <- 2
ok  <- set.portfolio.moments(Re, mes_spec, method = "boudt", k = 2)
bad <- try(set.portfolio.moments(Re, mes_spec, method = "boudt", k = n_factors),
           silent = TRUE)
c(literal = class(ok), variable = class(bad))
#>     literal    variable 
#>      "list" "try-error"

Fit the model with statistical.factor.model(R, k = n_factors), where k is an ordinary argument, and extract the tensors from the fit.


How different the two estimators are is visible in a single element. Take the coskewness of US_equity with US_credit and EU_equity, and the own third moment of US_credit, standardized by the three volatilities so that they read like correlations.

pos   <- function(s) match(s, colnames(Re))
m3_at <- function(M3, i, j, k) M3[i, (j - 1) * N + k]      # element m_ijk of M3
sds   <- apply(zoo::coredata(Re), 2, stats::sd)
std_coskew <- function(M3, a, b, d) {
  i <- pos(a); j <- pos(b); k <- pos(d)
  m3_at(M3, i, j, k) / (sds[i] * sds[j] * sds[k])
}

triple <- tibble::tibble(
  element    = c("US_equity, US_credit, EU_equity", "US_credit, US_credit, US_credit"),
  sample     = c(std_coskew(mom_s$m3, "US_equity", "US_credit", "EU_equity"),
                 std_coskew(mom_s$m3, "US_credit", "US_credit", "US_credit")),
  structured = c(std_coskew(mom_b$m3, "US_equity", "US_credit", "EU_equity"),
                 std_coskew(mom_b$m3, "US_credit", "US_credit", "US_credit"))
)
triple
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   element                         sample structured
#>   <chr>                            <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 US_equity, US_credit, EU_equity -0.432     -0.307
#> 2 US_credit, US_credit, US_credit -1.35      -0.182

frob <- c(M3 = norm(mom_s$m3 - mom_b$m3, "F") / norm(mom_s$m3, "F"),
          M4 = norm(mom_s$m4 - mom_b$m4, "F") / norm(mom_s$m4, "F"))
round(frob, 3)
#>    M3    M4 
#> 0.536 0.468

The structured own third moment of US_credit is 13% of the sample value, and across the whole tensor the two estimates differ by 54% of the sample norm for \(\boldsymbol{M}_3\) and 47% for \(\boldsymbol{M}_4\). Where the difference comes from is the identity \(\mathbb{E}[(\beta f + \varepsilon)^3] = \beta^3\mathbb{E}[f^3] + 3\beta^2\mathbb{E}[f^2\varepsilon] + 3\beta\,\mathbb{E}[f\varepsilon^2] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^3]\), of which Equation 11.4 keeps the first and last terms.

The two cross terms carry 87% of the series’ skewness. US_credit is not skewed because the equity factor is skewed, nor because its residual is; it is skewed because its residual is large and negative in the months when the factor is, which is the joint event Section 4.3 identified and the dependence that Equation 11.7 describes. A factor structure with independent residuals cannot represent it, so the estimator built to reduce the variance of the tensor removes the feature of this asset that the tensor was wanted for. That is the bias half of the trade Martellini and Ziemann (2010) describe, and it decides the allocation in Section 11.3.

11.2.3 The moment interface
optimize.portfolio() obtains its moments from one function, momentFUN, whose default is set.portfolio.moments; Section 7.2 and Section 6.2 replaced it for the first two moments, and the same argument carries the tensors. A moment function of our own also removes the need to pass method through ..., which is fragile for the reason the callout above gives.

four_moments <- function(R, portfolio, ...) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R)
  S <- stats::cov(X)
  list(mu = matrix(colMeans(X), ncol = 1), sigma = S,
       m3 = PerformanceAnalytics::M3.MM(X),
       m4 = PerformanceAnalytics::M4.MM(X),
       mean = colMeans(X), var = S)      # both pairs of names, as chapter 7 requires
}

structured_moments <- function(R, portfolio, ...) {
  fit <- statistical.factor.model(R, k = 1)
  S   <- extractCovariance(fit)
  list(mu = matrix(colMeans(zoo::coredata(R)), ncol = 1), sigma = S,
       m3 = extractCoskewness(fit), m4 = extractCokurtosis(fit),
       mean = colMeans(zoo::coredata(R)), var = S)
}

The contract, read from optimize.portfolio() and constrained_objective(), is this. The function is called once, before the search, with R and portfolio supplied if they are among its formals and any other formal matched by name from the ... of optimize.portfolio(); its own ... is discarded. The list it returns is handed, under DEoptim, random, pso and GenSA, to every objective function by name: each element whose name matches a formal of the objective function is passed as that argument, R and weights are added if the function declares them, and the objective’s arguments list is applied last and overrides anything of the same name. The names mu, sigma, m3 and m4 are therefore not special; they are the formals of StdDev(), VaR() and ES(), and a custom objective can name its inputs as it likes provided the moment function returns them under those names. A missing name fails inside the objective function, ES(method = "modified") with M3 must be a matrix and a function without a default with a missing-argument error; both are reported as a message per evaluation and then surface as a second, unrelated error at the end of the search. The convex solvers read only mu and sigma, the patched behavior recorded in Appendix D.

11.2.4 A custom objective: the CRRA investor
PortfolioAnalytics has no expected-utility objective beyond the quadratic one. It does allow an objective to be any function whose name is passed to add.objective(), so Equation 11.5 is a dozen lines. The function returns the negative of the expansion, because a risk objective is minimized, and takes an order argument so that the same function can be truncated after the second moment for comparison.

crra_utility <- function(R, weights, mu, sigma, m3, m4, gamma = 5, order = 4) {
  w  <- as.numeric(weights)
  Wb <- 1 + sum(w * as.numeric(mu))               # expected terminal wealth, W0 = 1
  m2 <- as.numeric(t(w) %*% sigma %*% w)
  eu <- Wb^(1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma) - gamma / 2 * Wb^(-gamma - 1) * m2
  if (order >= 3)
    eu <- eu + gamma * (gamma + 1) / 6 * Wb^(-gamma - 2) *
      PerformanceAnalytics::portm3(w, m3)
  if (order >= 4)
    eu <- eu - gamma * (gamma + 1) * (gamma + 2) / 24 * Wb^(-gamma - 3) *
      PerformanceAnalytics::portm4(w, m4)
  -eu
}

crra_spec <- function(gamma, order = 4) base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "crra_utility",
                arguments = list(gamma = gamma, order = order))







ImportantAn objective the solver cannot find is skipped, not reported



constrained_objective() resolves the objective’s name with match.fun() from the solver’s own frame, and that lookup reaches the global environment but not the environment the call was made from. A function defined at the console is found; one defined inside a function, a local() block or a private evaluation environment is not. The try() around the lookup prints an error and continues, the objective is skipped, the optimizer minimizes the constraint penalties alone, and optimize.portfolio() returns weights with no objective value attached.

set.seed(1602)
rp <- random_portfolios(mes_spec, permutations = 3000, rp_method = "simplex")

hidden <- local({
  crra_hidden <- crra_utility
  spec <- base_spec |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "crra_hidden", arguments = list(gamma = 5))
  optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "random", rp = rp[1:20, ],
                     momentFUN = four_moments)
})

We therefore put the function where the lookup will find it, and assert after every solve that the objective was evaluated.

assign("crra_utility", crra_utility, envir = globalenv())

solved_for <- function(opt, name) {
  if (is.null(opt$objective_measures[[name]]))
    cli::cli_abort("the objective {.val {name}} was never evaluated")
  invisible(opt)
}

momentFUN is not affected: it is resolved once from the caller’s frame, and a function object can be passed in place of a name, as above.


The package’s route for a non-convex objective is differential evolution (Storn and Price 1997; Ardia et al. 2011). The population size is set from search_size, with a floor of ten times the number of assets, and itermax bounds the generations; the solver prints the raw weight vector on completion, which is why the chunk’s output is hidden.

set.seed(1602)
de5 <- optimize.portfolio(Re, crra_spec(5), optimize_method = "DEoptim",
                          search_size = 2000, itermax = 30, traceDE = 0,
                          momentFUN = four_moments) |>
  solved_for("crra_utility")


w_de5 <- extractWeights(de5)[colnames(Re)]
round(w_de5[w_de5 > 0.005], 3)
#>     CH_credit     CH_equity     EU_credit     EU_equity     UK_equity 
#>         0.134         0.006         0.006         0.238         0.058 
#>     US_credit     US_equity US_government 
#>         0.014         0.534         0.008
unlist(de5$objective_measures)
#> crra_utility.crra_utility 
#>                    0.2454

The other metaheuristic route evaluates the objective on a fixed set of random portfolios and keeps the best. The simplex method of random_portfolios() generates them in a fraction of a second where the default sample method takes seconds and discards most of what it draws, and a set generated once is reused below, so that comparisons across objectives are made on identical candidates.

rn5 <- optimize.portfolio(Re, crra_spec(5), optimize_method = "random", rp = rp,
                          momentFUN = four_moments) |>
  solved_for("crra_utility")
w_rn5 <- extractWeights(rn5)[colnames(Re)]

c(candidates = nrow(rp),
  objective_DEoptim = as.numeric(unlist(de5$objective_measures)),
  objective_random  = as.numeric(unlist(rn5$objective_measures)))
#>        candidates objective_DEoptim  objective_random 
#>         2431.0000            0.2454            0.2454

Both routes work, and neither has converged: the best of 2431 random portfolios reaches a lower objective value than thirty generations of differential evolution. Equation 11.5 is smooth in the weights and the feasible set is a simplex, so a local solver started from either answer finishes the job in a fraction of a second; whether it has found the global optimum is a separate question, and two different starting points reaching the same portfolio is the evidence we ask for.






NoteWorked: polishing the metaheuristic answer





nloptr::slsqp() is a sequential quadratic programming solver that takes bounds and an equality constraint directly. The wrapper below closes over the moments so that the objective is a function of the weights alone.

crra_fn <- function(mom, gamma, order = 4) function(w)
  crra_utility(NULL, w, mom$mu, mom$sigma, mom$m3, mom$m4, gamma, order)

polish <- function(f, w0) {
  w0  <- pmax(as.numeric(w0), 0); w0 <- w0 / sum(w0)
  sol <- nloptr::slsqp(x0 = w0, fn = f, lower = rep(0, N), upper = rep(1, N),
                       heq = function(w) sum(w) - 1,
                       control = list(xtol_rel = 1e-10, maxeval = 2000))
  w <- pmax(sol$par, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(Re))
}
turnover <- function(w1, w2) sum(abs(w1[names(w2)] - w2)) / 2
ce_annual <- function(neg_eu, gamma) 12 * (((1 - gamma) * (-neg_eu))^(1 / (1 - gamma)) - 1)

Two checks before the polished answers are used. Truncated after the second moment, Equation 11.5 is Equation 3.12 up to the wealth factors, so the polished two-moment optimum must land on the quadratic-utility portfolio that ROI solved exactly. And the four-moment optimum reached from the DEoptim answer must coincide with the one reached from the random-portfolio answer.

f2_5 <- crra_fn(mom_s, 5, order = 2)
f4_5 <- crra_fn(mom_s, 5, order = 4)

w_o2_5    <- polish(f2_5, w_qu5)
w_c5_de   <- polish(f4_5, w_de5)
w_c5_rn   <- polish(f4_5, w_rn5)

c(two_moment_vs_ROI = turnover(w_o2_5, w_qu5),
  from_DEoptim_vs_from_random = turnover(w_c5_de, w_c5_rn))
#>           two_moment_vs_ROI from_DEoptim_vs_from_random 
#>               0.02183471235               0.00000004599
stopifnot(turnover(w_o2_5, w_qu5) < 0.05, turnover(w_c5_de, w_c5_rn) < 0.01)
w_c5 <- w_c5_de
# Neither metaheuristic had converged: both stopped well away from the polished answer.
stopifnot(turnover(w_de5, w_c5) > 0.05, turnover(w_rn5, w_c5) > 0.05)

tibble::tibble(
  answer = c("DEoptim, 30 generations", "best of the random portfolios", "polished"),
  objective = c(f4_5(w_de5), f4_5(w_rn5), f4_5(w_c5)),
  ce_annual = ce_annual(objective, 5),
  turnover_to_polished = c(turnover(w_de5, w_c5), turnover(w_rn5, w_c5), 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   answer                        objective ce_annual turnover_to_polished
#>   <chr>                             <dbl>     <dbl>                <dbl>
#> 1 DEoptim, 30 generations           0.245    0.0557                0.263
#> 2 best of the random portfolios     0.245    0.0561                0.276
#> 3 polished                          0.245    0.0601                0

The certainty equivalent of Equation 11.6 puts the solver error in the investor’s units: the DEoptim answer is 44 basis points a year below the polished optimum and 26% of the portfolio away from it. Section 13.1 measures the same shortfall on a problem with a closed form; here the point is that on a flat objective the solver’s error exceeds the effect being studied, which cannot be read off an unpolished answer.




11.2.5 One objective, two estimators of the tensors
The modified expected shortfall of Section 11.1 consumes \(\boldsymbol{M}_3\) and \(\boldsymbol{M}_4\) through Equation 4.6, so its minimum depends on which tensors it is given. We minimize it twice on the same candidate set, once with the sample tensors and once with the structured ones, and polish both.

mes_fn <- function(mom) function(w)
  as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::ES(NULL, p = 0.95, method = "modified",
                                      portfolio_method = "single", weights = w,
                                      mu = mom$mu, sigma = mom$sigma,
                                      m3 = mom$m3, m4 = mom$m4, invert = FALSE))

mes_s <- optimize.portfolio(Re, mes_spec, optimize_method = "random", rp = rp,
                            momentFUN = four_moments) |> solved_for("ES")
mes_b <- optimize.portfolio(Re, mes_spec, optimize_method = "random", rp = rp,
                            momentFUN = structured_moments) |> solved_for("ES")

w_mes_s <- polish(mes_fn(mom_s), extractWeights(mes_s)[colnames(Re)])
w_mes_b <- polish(mes_fn(mom_b), extractWeights(mes_b)[colnames(Re)])

w_gmv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, var_spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_gmv <- pmax(w_gmv[colnames(Re)], 0); w_gmv <- w_gmv / sum(w_gmv)

# The prose: the sample-tensor minimum holds no credit, and the least volatile
# series is among the least skewed.
least_vol <- names(which.min(sds))
stopifnot(w_mes_s[["US_credit"]] < 0.005, least_vol == "US_government",
          rank(abs(shape$skew))[shape$series == least_vol] <= 4)

The two minima are 35% of the portfolio apart. Under the sample tensors the minimum-shortfall portfolio holds 0.0% of US_credit and is 6% away from the minimum-variance portfolio of Equation 9.3: once the tail is priced, credit is out and the answer is close to the one variance gave. Under the structured tensors, which removed 87% of the series’ skewness, it holds 15.1%. The last column is the arbiter: on the realized tail of its own returns the structured answer has the larger shortfall, at 2.85% against 2.40%. On this universe the structured estimator is not a shrinkage toward a safer answer; it is a different estimator, biased in the direction the sample estimator was brought in to correct. The message that both solves print, asking for full_investment to be relaxed to min_sum = 0.99, max_sum = 1.01, concerns how the metaheuristics map candidates onto the constraint set and is Section 13.1’s subject; the answers above sum to one.

11.2.6 Conditional comoments
Everything above is unconditional. CCCgarch.MM() produces conditional moments from a constant-conditional-correlation GARCH fit (Bollerslev 1990): a GARCH(1,1) per series, the correlation matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\) of the standardized residuals and the one-step-ahead volatility forecasts \(\boldsymbol{D}_{t+1}\), assembled as \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{D}_{t+1}\boldsymbol{R}\boldsymbol{D}_{t+1}\), with the tensors taken from the standardized residuals rescaled to the forecast volatilities. Jondeau and Rockinger (2003) show that conditional skewness and kurtosis themselves persist, which the CCC structure holds fixed, and Guidolin and Timmermann (2008) model the same features through regimes, the route Section 19.1 takes. The function requires fGarch, which is not in this book’s library, so the call is shown and not run.

conditional <- CCCgarch.MM(Re)
str(conditional, give.attr = FALSE)     # mu, sigma, m3, m4: the same names

The list has the same four names, so it drops into momentFUN unchanged. One property of it matters: a series whose GARCH alpha1 falls below 0.01 is silently given its unconditional volatility for every date, so a mixed universe receives a conditional matrix for some assets and an unconditional one for the rest, with nothing in the output to say which.

title: 11  Higher Moments
section: 11.3 What the Third and Fourth Moments Buy
text:
11.3 What the Third and Fourth Moments Buy
The application opens with the picture: the sixteen series in the plane that Equation 11.1 cares about and Equation 9.2 does not.







Figure 11.1: The sixteen risky series by skewness and excess kurtosis, total returns over the full sample. The equity markets cluster near the Gaussian origin; US and UK credit are in a region of their own.




The Jarque-Bera test of Equation 4.4 rejected normality for most of these series; Figure 11.1 shows that the rejections are not of one kind. The equity markets sit at a skewness between -0.59 and -0.28 and an excess kurtosis below 4, the region where Samuelson (1970) and Levy and Markowitz (1979) say two moments suffice. US and UK credit sit at an excess kurtosis of about 12, 3.8 times the highest equity value, and that is where the terms of Equation 11.5 have something to do.

11.3.1 Three investors and what they hold
We compare the mean-variance tangency portfolio of Section 9.2, computed as it was there; the quadratic-utility investor of Equation 3.12 at \(\gamma = 5\) and \(\gamma = 10\); the four-moment investor of Equation 11.5 at the same two risk aversions; and the two minimum-shortfall portfolios of Table 11.2.

ef_spec <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")
ef <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, ef_spec, type = "mean-StdDev", n.portfolios = 200)
fr <- as.data.frame(unclass(ef$frontier))
fr$sharpe <- fr$mean / fr$StdDev
wcols <- grep("^w[.]", colnames(fr))
w_tan <- setNames(as.numeric(fr[which.max(fr$sharpe), wcols]),
                  sub("^w[.]", "", colnames(fr)[wcols]))
w_tan <- w_tan[colnames(Re)]

peak <- which.max(fr$w.US_credit)
# The opening said: the tangency portfolio holds less credit than the gamma = 5
# investor, the middle of the frontier more.
stopifnot(w_tan[["US_credit"]] < w_qu5[["US_credit"]],
          fr$w.US_credit[peak] > w_qu5[["US_credit"]])
c(tangency_credit = w_tan[["US_credit"]],
  frontier_peak_credit = fr$w.US_credit[peak],
  at_volatility = fr$StdDev[peak] * sqrt(12))
#>      tangency_credit frontier_peak_credit        at_volatility 
#>             0.004124             0.174900             0.133760

The tangency portfolio holds 0.4% of US_credit, a trace; Figure 9.4 showed the series swelling through the middle of the frontier, and it peaks at 17% at an annualized volatility of 13.4%, which is the region a \(\gamma = 5\) investor occupies.

four_moment_weights <- function(gamma) {
  f <- crra_fn(mom_s, gamma, order = 4)
  starts <- list(qu_weights(gamma), w_gmv, setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re)))
  sols   <- lapply(starts, function(s) polish(f, s))
  sols[[which.min(vapply(sols, f, numeric(1)))]]
}
w_qu10 <- qu_weights(10)
w_c5_ms <- four_moment_weights(5)
w_c10   <- four_moment_weights(10)

# The multi-start answer at gamma = 5 must be the one the metaheuristics were
# polished to; otherwise one of the two searches stopped in a different basin.
stopifnot(turnover(w_c5_ms, w_c5) < 0.01)

ports <- list(
  "tangency"                     = w_tan,
  "quadratic utility, gamma = 5"  = w_qu5,
  "four moments, gamma = 5"       = w_c5,
  "quadratic utility, gamma = 10" = w_qu10,
  "four moments, gamma = 10"      = w_c10,
  "min modified ES, sample"      = w_mes_s,
  "min modified ES, structured"  = w_mes_b
)
stopifnot(all(vapply(ports, function(w) identical(names(w), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))
