title: 14  Risk-Based Allocation
text:
14.1 Allocating Risk Rather Than Capital
Every portfolio so far has been described by how much money sits in each position. That is not the same as how much risk sits in each position, and on this universe the two are far apart: the minimum-variance portfolio of Section 9.1 puts most of its capital in one series and, as this chapter measures, nearly all of its risk there too.
Allocating risk rather than capital is an old idea with a clean definition (Qian 2006; Maillard et al. 2010), a cheap approximation, and an implementation in PortfolioAnalytics that does not work. We set out the decomposition that makes the idea precise, compute the exact answer two ways, and then measure what the package’s own risk-budget objective does with a problem whose optimum it scores correctly and cannot find.

title: 14  Risk-Based Allocation
text:
14.1.1 The decomposition that makes this precise
Portfolio volatility \(\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}) = \sqrt{\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}}\) is homogeneous of degree one in the weights, so by Euler’s theorem it decomposes exactly into additive contributions,
\[
\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{RC}_i,
\qquad
\mathrm{RC}_i = w_i \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial w_i}
= \frac{w_i\,(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w})_i}{\sigma(\boldsymbol{w})} .
\tag{14.1}\]
That exactness is what makes risk budgeting possible at all, and it is the point Qian (2006) makes when he says risk budgets do add up: the shares in 1 are not an approximation or an attribution convention, they sum to the total by construction. Dividing through by \(\sigma\) gives shares summing to one, which is what the code below computes.

risk_contribution <- function(w, S) {
  marginal <- as.numeric(S %*% w)
  (w * marginal) / as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)
}

w_eq <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
round(sort(risk_contribution(w_eq, S), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 4)
#> EU_equity CH_equity UK_equity UK_credit EU_credit 
#>    0.1170    0.0973    0.0942    0.0811    0.0787

Sixteen equally weighted series, and the largest contributes 11.7% of the risk against 6.2% of the capital. Equal capital is not equal risk, and the gap is the entire motivation for what follows.

14.1.2 Equal risk contribution
The equal risk contribution portfolio sets every term of 1 equal,
\[
\mathrm{RC}_i = \frac{\sigma(\boldsymbol{w})}{N}
\quad \text{for every } i,
\qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad
w_i (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w})_i = w_j (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w})_j
\;\; \forall\, i, j .
\tag{14.2}\]
Maillard et al. (2010) give its properties: it always exists and is unique for a long-only portfolio, and its volatility sits between the minimum-variance portfolio’s and the equally weighted portfolio’s, in that order. It has no closed form except in special cases, but it is emphatically not a hard problem. Spinu (2013) shows that Equation 14.2 is the first-order condition of the convex program
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol{w} > 0} \;
  \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
  - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ln w_i ,
\tag{14.3}\]
whose log barrier keeps every weight strictly positive and which any convex solver handles; Bai et al. (2016) give a least-squares formulation with the same property. Keep Equation 14.3 in mind for Section 14.3, because the package solves this problem with a metaheuristic, and the problem is convex.
A simple fixed-point iteration converges in milliseconds.

erc <- function(S, tol = 1e-12, max_iter = 1e5) {
  N <- ncol(S)
  w <- rep(1 / N, N)
  for (i in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    marginal <- as.numeric(S %*% w)
    w_new <- (1 / marginal) / sum(1 / marginal)   # down-weight what contributes most
    if (max(abs(w_new - w)) < tol) break
    w <- w_new
  }
  setNames(w, colnames(S))
}

w_erc <- erc(S)
c(max_deviation_from_equal = max(abs(risk_contribution(w_erc, S) - 1 / N)))
#> max_deviation_from_equal 
#>       0.0000000000003543

Six lines, and the risk contributions are equal to machine precision. That number is worth remembering when Section 14.3 spends twenty thousand function evaluations getting nowhere near it.

round(sort(w_erc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:6], 4)
#>    US_government        US_credit    JP_government GLOBAL_commodity 
#>           0.2210           0.0839           0.0757           0.0607 
#>    UK_government    EU_government 
#>           0.0606           0.0550

US_government still receives the largest allocation, at 22.1%, because it is the least volatile series and equalizing risk means overweighting low-volatility assets. That is a long way from the 82% that minimum variance gives it.

14.1.3 The approximation that is nearly free
Maillard et al. (2010) note a special case worth exploiting. If every pairwise correlation equals a common \(\rho\), then Equation 14.2 is solved exactly by
\[
w_i = \frac{\sigma_i^{-1}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sigma_j^{-1}},
\tag{14.4}\]
inverse-volatility weighting, which needs no matrix inverse and no iteration. Correlations here are not equal, but they are not wild either, so Equation 14.4 should land close.

base <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

# Exported, and rarely used. Note that it wants the portfolio object as well as
# the returns, and returns a full optimize.portfolio object rather than a vector.
w_iv <- inverse.volatility.weight(Re, base)$weights
w_iv <- w_iv[colnames(Re)]

c(l1_distance_from_erc = sum(abs(w_iv - w_erc)) / 2,
  weight_correlation   = stats::cor(w_iv, w_erc),
  max_rc_deviation     = max(abs(risk_contribution(w_iv, S) - 1 / N)))
#> l1_distance_from_erc   weight_correlation     max_rc_deviation 
#>              0.11482              0.90957              0.02699

inverse.volatility.weight() is exported by PortfolioAnalytics and is rarely used. It lands within 0.11 of the exact answer in \(L_1\) terms, with a weight correlation of 0.91, for the cost of one division per asset. The approximation of Equation 14.4 is doing almost all the work that Equation 14.2 does.

title: 14  Risk-Based Allocation
text:
14.2 Implementation
The package has a purpose-built objective for this. It accepts the problem, scores it correctly, and cannot solve it.

rb_spec <- base |>
  add.objective(type = "risk_budget", name = "StdDev", min_concentration = TRUE)


14.2.1 The objective is right
Before blaming a solver it is worth checking what it was asked to minimize. PortfolioAnalytics exposes its own objective function, so we can score two portfolios directly.

score <- function(w) {
  constrained_objective(w = as.numeric(w), R = Re, portfolio = rb_spec,
                        trace = TRUE, normalize = FALSE)$out
}
c(equal_weight = score(w_eq), true_erc = score(w_erc))
#>         equal_weight             true_erc 
#> 1.150416619246363847 0.000000000000002168

1.150 at equal weights and exactly 0.0 at the solution of Equation 14.2. The objective is not misspecified. It knows precisely which portfolio it wants.

14.2.2 The search does not find it

set.seed(1602)

attempt <- function(method, ...) {
  o <- try(suppressWarnings(
    optimize.portfolio(Re, rb_spec, optimize_method = method,
                       trace = FALSE, ...)), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(o, "try-error")) {
    return(tibble::tibble(solver = method, l1_from_erc = NA_real_,
                          max_rc_dev = NA_real_, is_equal_weight = NA))
  }
  w <- extractWeights(o)[colnames(Re)]
  tibble::tibble(solver = method,
                 l1_from_erc = sum(abs(w - w_erc)) / 2,
                 max_rc_dev  = max(abs(risk_contribution(w, S) - 1 / N)),
                 is_equal_weight = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(w), rep(1 / N, N),
                                                    tolerance = 1e-6)))
}

searches <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  attempt("DEoptim", search_size = 20000,  traceDE = 0),
  attempt("DEoptim", search_size = 200000, traceDE = 0),
  attempt("random",  search_size = 20000),
  attempt("pso"),
  attempt("GenSA")
)
#>  [1] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
#> [11] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
#>  [1] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625

14.2.3 What the machinery does do

  Re, base |> add.objective(type = "risk_budget", name = "StdDev", max_prisk = 0.15),

14.2.4 Auditing concentration
HHI() and diversification() are exported and take a weight vector, so any portfolio in this book can be audited for concentration in one line, including one returned by a solver that ignored its constraint (Section 13.2).

  r <- risk_contribution(w, S); r <- r[r > 0]
  exp(-sum(r * log(r)))                      # the entropy of the risk shares
}

title: 14  Risk-Based Allocation
section: 14.3 What Risk Parity Buys and Costs
text:
14.3 What Risk Parity Buys and Costs

14.3.1 The trade, in its own units
Read the last two rows of Table 14.3 together. Minimum variance achieves 4.13% volatility with 2.1 effective bets out of sixteen. Equal risk contribution achieves 6.43% with exactly 16.
That is the trade in its own units: about 55 percent more volatility for 8 times the number of independent bets. Whether it is worth taking depends on how far the covariance matrix behind the minimum-variance answer can be trusted, and Section 9.3 measured that. Resampling the same history moves the minimum-variance portfolio by about five percent of itself, so its concentration is at least stable.
Asness et al. (2012) give the economic argument for taking the trade anyway: if investors are averse to leverage rather than merely to risk, they overpay for high-beta assets, and a portfolio that equalizes risk contributions and then levers up harvests the difference. Clarke et al. (2013) derive the analytic relationships between risk parity, maximum diversification and minimum variance, and show that the three coincide only under conditions this market does not satisfy.

sweep <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", window == 60,
                frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
sr_oos <- function(s) sweep$sharpe[match(s, sweep$strategy)]
to_oos <- function(s) sweep$ann_turnover[match(s, sweep$strategy)]
stopifnot(all(c("inverse_vol", "min_variance", "equal_weight", "max_sharpe")
              %in% sweep$strategy))
# The order the text states, read from the register rather than typed.
stopifnot(sr_oos("min_variance") > sr_oos("equal_weight"),
          sr_oos("equal_weight") > sr_oos("inverse_vol"),
          sr_oos("inverse_vol")  > sr_oos("max_sharpe"),
          to_oos("inverse_vol")  < to_oos("max_sharpe") / 4)

Out of sample, inverse volatility earns a Sharpe ratio of 0.573 against minimum variance’s 0.829, equal weighting’s 0.626 and the tangency portfolio’s 0.546 (Section 25.3), at 20% of the turnover of the mean-variance optimizer, which Section 23.3 converts into the Sharpe ratio each strategy surrenders to its own trading. The risk-based portfolios are not uniformly better: minimum variance leads all four, and inverse volatility sits between equal weighting and the tangency portfolio before costs. They are competitive, cheaper, and easier to explain to whoever has to sign for them.

14.3.2 The covariance is a regime variable
One thing risk parity cannot escape, and it is the same thing that undermines everything else in this book. The number of effective bets is not a property of the portfolio. It is a property of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) moves.

d      <- zoo::index(Re)
in_ep  <- vapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) in_episode(d, e),
                 logical(length(d)))
calm   <- rowSums(in_ep) == 0               # outside all four episodes
crisis <- in_ep[, "credit_crisis"]

spectrum <- function(keep) {
  e <- pmax(eigen(stats::cov(zoo::coredata(Re[keep, ])), symmetric = TRUE,
                  only.values = TRUE)$values, 0)
  c(months = sum(keep), pc1_share = e[1] / sum(e), directions = sum(e)^2 / sum(e^2))
}
regime <- rbind(calm = spectrum(calm), crisis = spectrum(crisis))
stopifnot(regime["crisis", "pc1_share"] > regime["calm", "pc1_share"],
          regime["crisis", "directions"] < regime["calm", "directions"] / 2)
round(regime, 3)
#>        months pc1_share directions
#> calm      320     0.369      4.800
#> crisis      7     0.760      1.664

Section 7.3 measured it on these sixteen series, and the measurement repeats here: outside the four episodes of sim_episodes the first principal component carries 37% of the variance and the matrix behaves like 4.8 independent directions; through the credit crisis it carries 76% and the count falls to 1.7, a figure that the short window exaggerates and that calm windows of the same length still do not reach. A portfolio constructed to hold sixteen equal risk contributions in calm months holds about 2 independent bets when it matters.
Risk parity does not solve that. It measures risk more honestly than capital weighting does, and then allocates against an estimate that halves precisely when the allocation is tested. Roncalli (2013) treats the estimation problem at length, and Section 19.1 is where this book confronts it rather than noting it.

14.3.3 Budgets that are not equal
Equal risk contribution is the special case of a more general idea. A risk budget assigns each asset a share \(b_i\) with \(\sum_i b_i = 1\) and asks for weights satisfying
\[
\mathrm{RC}_i = b_i \,\sigma(\boldsymbol{w})
\quad \text{for every } i ,
\tag{14.5}\]
which reduces to Equation 14.2 when \(b_i = 1/N\). Roncalli (2013) develops the general case, and the convex program of Equation 14.3 generalizes directly by replacing the uniform coefficient on the log barrier with \(b_i\). The fixed point in this chapter generalizes just as easily, dividing the marginal contributions by the budget before renormalizing.
The interest of Equation 14.5 is that it is the natural language of a mandate. A policy statement rarely says hold twenty percent in credit; it says credit may consume no more than a quarter of the risk. Those are different instructions and only the second survives a change in volatility. This is also the form in which the package’s own objective is usable, as the max_prisk result above showed: bounds on Equation 14.5 are checkable by rejection, and a search can satisfy them.

14.3.4 Hierarchical risk parity
The methods in this chapter all require \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) and most require its inverse, which Section 7.1 showed is where the estimate is weakest. López de Prado (2016) proposes an alternative that avoids inversion entirely. Hierarchical risk parity clusters the assets on a distance derived from their correlations, orders them so that similar assets are adjacent, and then allocates by recursive bisection: split the ordered set in two, allocate between the halves in inverse proportion to their variances, and recurse.
Nothing in that procedure inverts a matrix, so it is defined even when \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is singular, which by Equation 7.2 is the normal case at instrument level. The claim is that the resulting portfolios are more stable out of sample than either minimum variance or equal risk contribution, because the quantity being estimated, a clustering, is far coarser than a full inverse.
The method belongs with the sleeve structure of Section 15.1 rather than here, because what it is really doing is imposing a hierarchy on the universe and allocating down it. It is mentioned here because it is the obvious next question once risk contributions are on the table, and because it is the one widely used technique in this area that PortfolioAnalytics does not implement at all.

title: 14  Risk-Based Allocation
text:
Key Takeaways

Portfolio volatility decomposes exactly into additive risk contributions by

The shares are not an attribution convention; they sum to the total by construction (Qian 2006).


Equal capital is not equal risk. Sixteen equally weighted series here put 12% of the risk in one of them, against 6.2% of the capital.
The equal risk contribution portfolio of Equation 14.2 always exists, is unique long-only, and sits between minimum variance and equal weighting in volatility (Maillard et al. 2010).
It is not a hard problem. Equation 14.3 is a convex program with a log barrier, and a six-line fixed point reaches machine precision. The package nonetheless routes it to a metaheuristic.
Of five solvers, 4 hand back the equally weighted portfolio they started from, and a tenfold budget changes nothing. The one-line inverse-volatility approximation of Equation 14.4 is closer to the answer than a twenty-thousand-evaluation search.
Use the risk-budget objective for caps and budgets, which a search can satisfy by rejection, and compute equal risk contribution directly.
Risk parity buys about 8 times the effective bets for about 55 percent more volatility, and out of sample inverse volatility lands between equal weighting and the tangency portfolio at a fraction of the latter’s turnover.
The effective number of bets is a property of the covariance matrix, not of the portfolio, and it falls by more than half going into the credit crisis.

title: 14  Risk-Based Allocation
text:
Exercises

Run the fixed-point erc() on a covariance matrix estimated from the months outside the four episodes of sim_episodes only, then apply the resulting weights to the months of the credit crisis. How equal are the realized risk contributions?

inverse.volatility.weight() ignores correlations entirely. Construct a universe where that is catastrophic — two nearly identical series and one independent one — and report the risk contributions it produces.
Repeat Table 14.1 with a max_prisk objective instead of min_concentration. Do the solvers agree with each other? Does the budget bind?
The effective-bets measure uses entropy. Replace it with 1 / sum(rc^2), the inverse Herfindahl of the risk shares, and recompute Table 14.3. Which portfolios change rank, and which measure would you defend to a client?

Bai, Xi, Katya Scheinberg, and Reha Tutuncu. 2016. “Least-Squares Approach to Risk Parity in Portfolio Selection.” Quantitative Finance 16 (3): 357–76. https://doi.org/10.1080/14697688.2015.1031815.


Clarke, Roger, Harindra de Silva, and Steven Thorley. 2013. “Risk Parity, Maximum Diversification, and Minimum Variance: An Analytic Perspective.” Journal of Portfolio Management 39 (3): 39–53. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2013.39.3.039.


López de Prado, Marcos. 2016. “Building Diversified Portfolios That Outperform Out of Sample.” Journal of Portfolio Management 42 (4): 59–69. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2016.42.4.059.

title: 15  Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation
text:
15.1 The Two-Stage Problem
How should an allocation be organized when nobody can hold the whole problem in one head, and what does the organization cost? Sharpe (1981) posed it as the decentralized investment problem, in which a central office sets budgets for specialist managers who each optimize the sleeve they know and must be told what makes the pieces add up, and Brinson et al. (1986) measured how much of an institution’s return that first, top-level decision explains. The two-layer structure has been the working organization of every large allocator since: classes first, then selection within them.
This is the chapter in which the book’s own structure is made explicit. Parts III to V allocate across the sixteen class series of Section 2.2, and Part VI selects instruments inside a sleeve; the two layers are not a convenience of exposition but a decision with a cost, and the cost can be measured. It is a strategic decision in the sense of Section 3.1: the policy structure is set from unconditional assumptions and revisited rarely. We first state the two-stage problem and read it as a shrinkage of the covariance matrix, then implement it with mult.portfolio.spec() and by hand, then ask whether the hierarchy dominates one-stage optimization out of sample on this universe.

title: 15  Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation
text:
15.1.1 Sleeves, and what is decided at each level
Partition the \(N\) assets into \(K\) sleeves and write the weight vector and the covariance matrix in the same blocks, \(\boldsymbol{w} = (\boldsymbol{w}_1', \ldots, \boldsymbol{w}_K')'\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = [\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{jk}]\). The one-stage, or flat, problem is that of Markowitz (1952) as stated in Section 9.1, over all \(N\) assets at once. The two-stage, or nested, problem solves each sleeve on its own block first,
\[
\boldsymbol{v}_k = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{v}} \; \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{kk}\boldsymbol{v}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,\;
\boldsymbol{v} \geq \boldsymbol{0}, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, K,
\tag{15.1}\]
then treats each sleeve’s portfolio as a single asset with return \(r_{k,t} = \boldsymbol{v}_k'\boldsymbol{r}_{k,t}\) and allocates across the \(K\) sleeve returns,
\[
\boldsymbol{b} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{b}} \; \boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{b}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,\;
\boldsymbol{b} \geq \boldsymbol{0}, \qquad
\Omega_{jk} = \boldsymbol{v}_j'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{jk}\boldsymbol{v}_k .
\tag{15.2}\]
The portfolio that results holds, in every class, the sleeve budget times the within-sleeve weight,
\[
\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{nest}} = (b_1 \boldsymbol{v}_1', \ldots, b_K \boldsymbol{v}_K')' .
\tag{15.3}\]
The objectives in Equation 15.1 and Equation 15.2 need not be the same; a mandate can ask for minimum variance inside the bond sleeves and a tangency portfolio inside equities, and Section 15.3 does exactly that. What matters is the structure: nothing at stage 1 sees any asset outside its own sleeve, and stage 2 sees the sleeves only through \(K\) series.
Equation 15.3 is feasible for the flat problem, so in sample the nested portfolio can never have a lower variance than the flat minimum. The gap is the price of decentralization. Binsbergen et al. (2008) quantify it as a utility loss and show that it is not small when the sleeve managers optimize against their own objectives rather than the office’s; Elton and Gruber (2004) derive the instructions, a benchmark and a risk target for each sleeve, under which the decentralized solution coincides with the centralized one; and Blake et al. (2013) document the practice, in pension funds that split a balanced mandate into specialist sleeves, gained on sleeve performance and paid in coordination. That the top layer nonetheless carries most of the outcome is the finding of Brinson et al. (1986) and Brinson et al. (1991), which Ibbotson and Kaplan (2000) restate carefully: policy explains about ninety percent of a fund’s variation over time, far less of the variation between funds, and essentially all of the average level of return.

sleeve_of <- function(a) dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", a)     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", a) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", a)     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                     ~ "commodity")

# split() returns its groups alphabetically; everything below indexes by name.
sleeves <- split(colnames(Re), sleeve_of(colnames(Re)))
stopifnot(setequal(unlist(sleeves), colnames(Re)))
lengths(sleeves)
#>  commodity     credit     equity government 
#>          1          5          5          5

Four sleeves: commodity, credit, equity, government. Three of them hold five class series and the commodity sleeve holds one, which is a case the implementation has to face rather than assume away.

15.1.2 The shrinkage reading
Stage 1 of the nested problem uses only the diagonal blocks of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). It is therefore the flat problem solved on
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{0} & \cdots \\
\boldsymbol{0} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} & \\
\vdots & & \ddots
\end{pmatrix},
\tag{15.4}\]
the matrix in which every cross-sleeve covariance has been set to zero. In the language of Section 7.1 that is a shrinkage estimator of the form of Equation 7.6 with a target that keeps the blocks and discards the rest, and an intensity of one on the off-block entries and zero elsewhere. The difference from Ledoit and Wolf (2004) is where the intensity comes from. Their \(\lambda\) minimizes expected loss and is estimated from the data; here it is imposed by the mandate, and the justification is economic rather than statistical: the cross-sleeve entries are the ones no sleeve manager is responsible for, and stage 1 declares them unknown. What is known about shrinkage since Stein (1956) transfers directly. Setting parameters to zero helps when their true values are near zero and their estimates are not, because those are the entries the error-maximizer of Michaud (1989) exploits, and hurts when it discards information the portfolio was supposed to use.
Stage 2 restores part of that information, in coarse form. Equation 15.2 uses the \(K \times K\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\), which carries \(K(K-1)/2\) cross-sleeve covariances in place of the \(\sum_{j<k} N_j N_k\) that were dropped, and carries them only for the sleeve compositions already fixed. If stage 2 ignores them as well, taking \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) to be diagonal, the top-level solution is inverse-variance weighting across sleeves and the whole two-stage procedure collapses to the flat minimum-variance portfolio of Equation 9.3 computed on \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}\):
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota} =
\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota},\, \ldots,\,
     \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{KK}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}\big)'
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
w_i = \frac{\sigma_k^{-2}}{\sum_{j} \sigma_j^{-2}}\, v_{k,i}
\;\; \text{for } i \in k,
\qquad \sigma_k^{2} = \frac{1}{\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{kk}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}} ,
\tag{15.5}\]
because the inverse of a block-diagonal matrix is block-diagonal, and \(\sigma_k^2\) is sleeve \(k\)’s own minimum variance. The long-only version separates the same way, given the sleeve budgets, and the worked box below checks it numerically. So the three constructions form a ladder. The flat problem uses every entry of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\); the nested problem uses the diagonal blocks plus \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\); the block-diagonal problem uses the diagonal blocks alone. Where nesting sits on that ladder depends on how much of the cross-block covariance is signal.

S    <- stats::cov(Re)
same <- outer(sleeve_of(colnames(S)), sleeve_of(colnames(S)), "==")
stopifnot(all(dim(same) == dim(S)), isSymmetric(same))
S_block <- S; S_block[!same] <- 0

Cm <- stats::cov2cor(S)
c(cross_block_share = 1 - sum(S_block^2) / sum(S^2),          # of the Frobenius norm
  mean_within_cor   = mean(Cm[same  & upper.tri(Cm)]),
  mean_cross_cor    = mean(Cm[!same & upper.tri(Cm)]))
#> cross_block_share   mean_within_cor    mean_cross_cor 
#>            0.2342            0.5408            0.2686

On the full sample the cross-sleeve entries carry 23% of the squared mass of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), and the average correlation between two series in different sleeves is 0.27 against 0.54 within a sleeve. The blocks are real; the space between them is not empty. Whether the estimate of that space is worth using is the question the out-of-sample race in Section 15.3 answers, and the answer is in keeping with Jagannathan and Ma (2003) rather than with the usual case for shrinkage: a restriction on the weights helps out of sample when it forbids what the estimate gets most wrong, and the cross-sleeve covariances of sixteen classes on sixty months are not that.
Everything in this chapter is the long-only quadratic program of Section 9.2, and the rolling loop of Section 15.3 solves it more than a thousand times, so we call quadprog directly, the solver ROI dispatches to in Section 13.2, and confirm once that the two agree.

gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n   <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}

gmv_spec <- function(assets) {
  portfolio.spec(assets = assets) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
}

w_flat <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, gmv_spec(colnames(Re)),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(max(abs(gmv_qp(S) - w_flat)) < 1e-8)

mu    <- colMeans(Re)
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w) p_ret(w) / p_vol(w)
eff_bets <- function(w) 1 / sum(w^2)              # reciprocal Herfindahl, @sec-09
round(w_flat[w_flat > 0.005], 4)
#>        EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity        JP_equity        UK_equity 
#>           0.0138           0.0507           0.0415           0.0218 
#>        US_equity    US_government 
#>           0.0513           0.8209







NoteWorked: the identity of Equation 15.5, and the ladder in sample





Stage 1, stage 2 with a diagonal \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\), and Equation 15.3:

# A sleeve of one asset is its own portfolio.
within_gmv <- function(S, sleeves) lapply(sleeves, function(a)
  if (length(a) == 1L) setNames(1, a) else gmv_qp(S[a, a]))

unroll <- function(b, v) {
  stopifnot(identical(names(b), names(v)))
  w <- unlist(lapply(names(v), function(k) b[[k]] * v[[k]]))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

v  <- within_gmv(S, sleeves)
s2 <- vapply(names(v), function(k)
  as.numeric(t(v[[k]]) %*% S[sleeves[[k]], sleeves[[k]]] %*% v[[k]]), numeric(1))
b_iv <- (1 / s2) / sum(1 / s2)                # inverse variance across sleeves

w_bd <- gmv_qp(S_block)                       # flat, on the block-diagonal matrix
stopifnot(max(abs(unroll(b_iv, v) - w_bd)) < 1e-10)
round(b_iv, 4)
#>  commodity     credit     equity government 
#>     0.0667     0.2621     0.0686     0.6026

The two-stage construction with inverse-variance budgets and the flat minimum-variance portfolio on \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}\) agree to machine precision, under the long-only constraint. The nested portfolio proper uses the full \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) at the top:

sleeve_returns <- function(Re, v) {
  out <- do.call(cbind, lapply(names(v), function(k) Re[, sleeves[[k]]] %*% v[[k]]))
  colnames(out) <- names(v)
  xts::xts(out, order.by = zoo::index(Re))
}
sl       <- sleeve_returns(Re, v)
Omega    <- stats::cov(sl)
b_nest   <- gmv_qp(Omega)
w_nested <- unroll(b_nest, v)

Oc <- stats::cov2cor(Omega)
stopifnot(Oc["equity", "government"] < 0, sum(Oc[upper.tri(Oc)] < 0) == 1L)
round(Oc, 2)
#>            commodity credit equity government
#> commodity       1.00   0.27   0.16       0.11
#> credit          0.27   1.00   0.27       0.58
#> equity          0.16   0.27   1.00      -0.10
#> government      0.11   0.58  -0.10       1.00

The sleeve correlation matrix is where the discarded information reappears in compressed form. Government and credit move together at 0.58; equity and government at -0.10, the one negative entry, which is the entire reason a balanced portfolio holds both. Stage 2 can act on it. Stage 1 could not, and chose the government sleeve without knowing that the equity sleeve existed.

ladder <- tibble::tibble(
  construction = c("flat", "nested", "block-diagonal"),
  vol    = c(p_vol(w_flat), p_vol(w_nested), p_vol(w_bd)),
  sharpe = c(p_sr(w_flat),  p_sr(w_nested),  p_sr(w_bd)),
  bets   = c(eff_bets(w_flat), eff_bets(w_nested), eff_bets(w_bd)))
stopifnot(diff(ladder$vol) >= -1e-12)          # flat <= nested <= block-diagonal
ladder
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   construction      vol sharpe  bets
#>   <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 flat           0.0413  0.795  1.47
#> 2 nested         0.0423  0.745  1.69
#> 3 block-diagonal 0.0463  0.700  2.81

The ordering is the one Equation 15.3 guarantees, and the sizes are the point: nesting costs 0.10 percentage points of annualized volatility in sample, and dropping the cross-sleeve covariances at both stages costs 0.49.









NoteWorked: hierarchical risk parity is a different hierarchy





López de Prado (2016) uses the word hierarchical for a construction that has no sleeves given to it. It estimates a tree from the correlation matrix, orders the assets along that tree so that similar ones are adjacent, and allocates by recursive bisection: split the ordered list in half, divide the budget between the halves in inverse proportion to their variances, and recurse. Nothing is inverted, which is why it was raised in Section 14.3 as the one popular method the package lacks, and why it is defined even when Equation 7.2 makes \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) singular. Raffinot (2018) examines the linkage and the cut; Mantegna (1999) is the origin of the correlation-distance tree in finance, and Tola et al. (2008) the first use of such a tree to filter a covariance matrix before optimizing on it.

D  <- sqrt(0.5 * (1 - stats::cor(Re)))                  # the correlation distance
hc <- hclust(stats::as.dist(D), method = "single")
ord <- colnames(Re)[hc$order]                            # quasi-diagonalization

hrp <- function(S, ord) {
  iv_var <- function(items) {                            # inverse-variance variance
    s <- S[items, items, drop = FALSE]; iv <- 1 / diag(s); iv <- iv / sum(iv)
    as.numeric(t(iv) %*% s %*% iv)
  }
  w <- setNames(rep(1, length(ord)), ord)
  clusters <- list(ord)
  while (length(clusters)) {
    nxt <- list()
    for (cl in clusters) {
      if (length(cl) < 2L) next
      h <- floor(length(cl) / 2); a <- cl[1:h]; b <- cl[(h + 1):length(cl)]
      alpha <- 1 - iv_var(a) / (iv_var(a) + iv_var(b))
      w[a] <- w[a] * alpha; w[b] <- w[b] * (1 - alpha)
      nxt <- c(nxt, list(a), list(b))
    }
    clusters <- nxt
  }
  w[colnames(S)]
}
w_hrp <- hrp(S, ord)
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_hrp) - 1) < 1e-12)

# Is each country's credit series next to its own government series?
adjacent <- vapply(c("US", "UK", "EU", "CH", "JP"), function(cc)
  abs(match(paste0(cc, "_credit"), ord) - match(paste0(cc, "_government"), ord)) == 1L,
  logical(1))
stopifnot(sum(!adjacent) == 1L,                      # one exception, named below
          all(diff(sort(match(sleeves$equity, ord))) == 1L))   # the equities are contiguous
ord
#>  [1] "GLOBAL_commodity" "JP_equity"        "US_equity"        "CH_equity"       
#>  [5] "EU_equity"        "UK_equity"        "US_government"    "JP_credit"       
#>  [9] "JP_government"    "US_credit"        "CH_credit"        "CH_government"   
#> [13] "EU_credit"        "EU_government"    "UK_credit"        "UK_government"

Read the order. The estimated tree does not find the sleeves. It places the credit series of four of the five countries next to the same country’s government series, with the US pair the one exception, so the fixed-income half of the universe is organized by currency rather than by asset class, which is what Section 4.3 measured: unhedged in dollars, a foreign bond is mostly its currency. The asserted hierarchy of this chapter and the estimated one of López de Prado (2016) disagree about what a sleeve is, and the disagreement is a fact about hedging.

stopifnot(names(which.max(w_hrp)) == names(which.min(diag(S))))   # the prose says so
round(sort(w_hrp, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 4)
#>    US_government        US_credit        JP_credit GLOBAL_commodity 
#>           0.4880           0.0892           0.0880           0.0437 
#>    JP_government 
#>           0.0407
c(volatility = p_vol(w_hrp), effective_bets = eff_bets(w_hrp))
#>     volatility effective_bets 
#>        0.05036        3.79683

The portfolio it produces still puts 49% in US_government, because the bisection allocates by inverse variance and that series has the lowest variance in the universe. The method changes how the hierarchy is found, not what a low-volatility series does to an allocation.




15.1.3 The class series is the sleeve’s benchmark
Each of the sixteen series is an index of the instruments inside it; the equity series are the capitalization-weighted portfolios that Section 21.1 verifies against the instrument level, and US_government stands in for a portfolio of Treasuries. That is what makes the top layer a policy: it is set on investable proxies, in the manner of Sharpe (1992), and the weights it produces are handed down as benchmarks. The sleeve manager then holds instruments and is judged, in Section 24.1, on the return in excess of that benchmark and the tracking error it took. The class series is the sleeve’s benchmark, not its result. Setting the policy on a manager’s realized returns would reward each sleeve for the past alpha it will not repeat, carry that selection into the backtest of Section 25.1, and leave nothing against which the manager could be judged; Roll (1977) is the older statement that the benchmark is a choice with consequences, and Grinold and Kahn (2000) the standard account of what is measured once it has been made.

15.1.4 Hedging is a sleeve decision
The sleeve structure also settles a question that has no answer at the level of the whole portfolio. Section 4.3 found that hedging a Japanese government bond removes most of its volatility and hedging Japanese equity removes almost none, and Campbell et al. (2010) show why the optimal hedge differs systematically between bonds and equities: currencies covary differently with each. A hedge is therefore a property of the sleeve rather than of the country, and it changes what a sleeve holds.

fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedged <- R
for (a in colnames(R)) {
  reg <- sub("_.*$", "", a)
  if (reg %in% unique(fx$region)) {
    f <- fx$fx_return[fx$region == reg][match(zoo::index(R), fx$date[fx$region == reg])]
    stopifnot(!anyNA(f))
    hedged[, a] <- R[, a] - f                  # hedged = unhedged - fx, @sec-04
  }
}
He <- hedged - rf

sleeve_vol <- function(X, a) {
  w <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(X[, a]))
  c(vol = sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% stats::cov(X[, a]) %*% w)) * sqrt(12),
    largest = max(w), bets = eff_bets(w))
}
hedge_tab <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("government", "credit", "equity"), function(k)
  tibble::tibble(sleeve = k,
                 unhedged = sleeve_vol(Re, sleeves[[k]])[["vol"]],
                 hedged   = sleeve_vol(He, sleeves[[k]])[["vol"]],
                 bets_unhedged = sleeve_vol(Re, sleeves[[k]])[["bets"]],
                 bets_hedged   = sleeve_vol(He, sleeves[[k]])[["bets"]])))
gov <- hedge_tab[hedge_tab$sleeve == "government", ]
stopifnot(gov$hedged < gov$unhedged, gov$bets_hedged > gov$bets_unhedged)




Table 15.1: Minimum variance inside each sleeve, unhedged and fully hedged. Volatility annualized; effective bets are the reciprocal Herfindahl of the sleeve weights.











sleeve

Hedging the government sleeve takes its minimum variance from 4.67% to 2.63% and spreads it from 1.2 to 2.1 effective positions, because foreign bonds become holdable once their currency is removed. Hedging the equity sleeve moves its volatility from 13.84% to 13.50%. Perold and Schulman (1988) and Black (1989) are the two classic and opposed general answers; the sleeve view makes the general answer unnecessary, and Section 22.1 takes the bond side of it up where the currency decision and the duration decision turn out not to be separable.

title: 15  Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation
text:
15.2 Implementation
PortfolioAnalytics has a data structure for this problem and almost no documentation of it. mult.portfolio.spec() wraps a top-level specification, add.sub.portfolio() attaches a sleeve specification together with the settings used to optimize it, and optimize.portfolio() recognizes the result. What it then does is not stated anywhere outside the source, so this section reads the source and checks it against a by-hand construction.

15.2.1 A sleeve of one asset

one <- try(optimize.portfolio(Re[, "GLOBAL_commodity", drop = FALSE],
                              gmv_spec("GLOBAL_commodity"), optimize_method = "ROI"),
           silent = TRUE)
stopifnot(inherits(one, "try-error"))
cat(conditionMessage(attr(one, "condition")))
#> all(c(dim_L[1], n_dir) == n_L_constraints) ist nicht TRUE







NoteA single-asset sleeve cannot be a sub-portfolio



With one asset the constraint matrix loses a dimension on its way to ROI::L_constraint(), which rejects it, and every rolling window of that sleeve fails. The commodity sleeve therefore cannot enter mult.portfolio.spec() at all. The package path below runs on the three sleeves that can be optimized; the by-hand construction keeps the commodity as a sleeve whose only asset is its portfolio, which is what Equation 15.1 reduces to when \(N_k = 1\).



15.2.2 mult.portfolio.spec() and add.sub.portfolio()


three <- sleeves[c("equity", "government", "credit")]

top <- gmv_spec(names(three))
mp  <- mult.portfolio.spec(top)
for (k in names(three)) {
  mp <- add.sub.portfolio(mp, gmv_spec(three[[k]]), optimize_method = "ROI",
                          rebalance_on = "months", training_period = 60,
                          trailing_periods = 59)
}

c(class = class(mp), top = class(mp$top.portfolio)[1],
  sub_portfolios = length(mp$sub.portfolios), sub_class = class(mp$sub.portfolios[[1]]))
#>                 class                   top        sub_portfolios 
#> "mult.portfolio.spec"      "portfolio.spec"                   "3" 
#>             sub_class 
#>       "sub.portfolio"
names(mp$sub.portfolios[[1]])
#> [1] "portfolio"        "optimize_method"  "search_size"      "rp"              
#> [5] "rebalance_on"     "training_period"  "trailing_periods"

Three arguments are passed to every sub-portfolio, and none of them is optional in practice. optimize.portfolio() on a mult.portfolio.spec calls the unexported proxy.mult.portfolio(), whose loop is the whole of the method:
for (i in 1:n.sub.portfolios) {
  tmp   <- mult.portfolio$sub.portfolios[[i]]
  R.tmp <- R[, names(tmp$portfolio$assets)]
  opt   <- do.call(optimize.portfolio.rebalancing, <R and the sub-portfolio's settings>)
  w     <- extractWeights(opt)
  ret[[i]] <- Return.portfolio(R.tmp, weights = w)     # named "proxy.i"
}
proxy.ret <- na.omit(do.call(cbind, ret))
after which optimize.portfolio() continues with R <- proxy.ret and portfolio <- portfolio$top.portfolio. Every sleeve is run through optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(), the rolling backtest of Section 25.2, not through a single optimization; the sleeve’s returns are the realized returns of that backtest; and the top level is optimized once, on the full history of those realized sleeve returns.






ImportantThe defaults do not run, and one argument is silently discarded



add.sub.portfolio() defaults rebalance_on to NULL, which optimize.portfolio.rebalancing() passes to xts::endpoints(), which fails with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. A mult.portfolio.spec built with the defaults cannot be optimized. Two further things about the settings. training_period = NULL becomes thirty-six observations. And the length of the window is trailing_periods, the argument add.sub.portfolio() names; passing rolling_window instead, the name the rebalancing function itself uses, looks as if it works and does not, because the sub-portfolio stores trailing_periods = NULL alongside it and the rebalancing function’s compatibility shim overwrites rolling_window with that NULL. The result is an expanding window that nothing reports. Both facts were established by reproducing the proxy series by hand, below.



mp_default <- mult.portfolio.spec(top)
for (k in names(three)) mp_default <- add.sub.portfolio(mp_default, gmv_spec(three[[k]]),
                                                        optimize_method = "ROI")
bad <- try(optimize.portfolio(Re, mp_default, optimize_method = "ROI"), silent = TRUE)
stopifnot(inherits(bad, "try-error"))
cat(strwrap(conditionMessage(attr(bad, "condition")), width = 78), sep = "\n")
#> optimize.portfolio.rebalancing for sub portfolio 1 generated an error or
#> warning: Error in if (on == "secs" || on == "mins") on <- substr(on, 1L, 3L)
#> : Fehlender Wert, wo TRUE/FALSE nötig ist


o_mp <- suppressWarnings(optimize.portfolio(Re, mp, optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE))
round(o_mp$weights, 4)
#> proxy.1 proxy.2 proxy.3 
#>  0.1344  0.8656  0.0000
c(proxy_rows = nrow(o_mp$R), proxy_cols = ncol(o_mp$R),
  first_model_year = model_year(zoo::index(o_mp$R)[1]),
  last_model_year  = model_year(zoo::index(o_mp$R)[nrow(o_mp$R)]))
#>       proxy_rows       proxy_cols first_model_year  last_model_year 
#>              372                3                1               31

Three things in that output need reading. The weights come back named proxy.1 to proxy.3, in the order the sub-portfolios were added, and the names given to the top-level assets are ignored. With trace = TRUE the object stores the proxy returns it optimized in o_mp$R, which is the only way to see them. And they have 372 rows, from January of model year 1, the first month of the sample, although the first sleeve weights are estimated after sixty months. Return.portfolio() back-fills the training period with an equally weighted, buy-and-hold sleeve, the behavior Section 23.2 warns about, and the top level is estimated on that history together with the rolling one.

15.2.3 The same thing by hand

W <- 60L
proxy_by_hand <- function(a) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(Re[, a, drop = FALSE]); n <- nrow(X); out <- numeric(n)
  w <- rep(1 / length(a), length(a))                  # the back-fill: equal, then drifting
  for (t in seq_len(W)) {
    out[t] <- sum(w * X[t, ]); w <- w * (1 + X[t, ]) / (1 + out[t])
  }
  for (t in (W + 1):n)                                # then rolling minimum variance
    out[t] <- sum(gmv_qp(stats::cov(X[(t - W):(t - 1), ])) * X[t, ])
  out
}
by_hand <- sapply(three, proxy_by_hand)
stopifnot(max(abs(zoo::coredata(o_mp$R) - by_hand)) < 1e-10)

b_hand <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(by_hand))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.numeric(o_mp$weights) - as.numeric(b_hand))) < 1e-6)

b_no_backfill <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(by_hand[-(1:W), ]))
round(rbind(package = as.numeric(o_mp$weights), by_hand = b_hand,
            without_backfill = b_no_backfill), 4)
#>                  equity government credit
#> package          0.1344     0.8656      0
#> by_hand          0.1344     0.8656      0
#> without_backfill 0.1178     0.8822      0

The by-hand series reproduce the package’s proxies to machine precision and the top-level weights to the solver’s tolerance, which is the documentation this chapter set out to write. It also shows what the back-fill costs. Dropping the sixty months nobody chose moves the government sleeve’s budget from 86.6% to 88.2%, a difference that is not large here and that the package gives no way to remove.

15.2.4 Holding several optimizations together
The stage-1 problems are ordinary portfolio objects, so their solutions can be collected with combine.optimizations(), and extractWeights() on the result is a matrix rather than a vector. On sleeve problems it is a picture of Equation 15.4.

ol_sleeves <- combine.optimizations(lapply(three, function(a)
  optimize.portfolio(Re[, a], gmv_spec(a), optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE)))

W_sleeves <- extractWeights(ol_sleeves)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W_sleeves), names(three)))
round(W_sleeves[, order(sleeve_of(colnames(W_sleeves)))], 3)
#>            CH_credit EU_credit JP_credit UK_credit US_credit CH_equity
#> equity         0.000         0     0.000         0     0.000     0.167
#> government     0.000         0     0.000         0     0.000     0.000
#> credit         0.004         0     0.153         0     0.843     0.000
#>            EU_equity JP_equity UK_equity US_equity CH_government EU_government
#> equity             0     0.246      0.18     0.407             0             0
#> government         0     0.000      0.00     0.000             0             0
#> credit             0     0.000      0.00     0.000             0             0
#>            JP_government UK_government US_government
#> equity                 0         0.000         0.000
#> government             0         0.097         0.903
#> credit                 0         0.000         0.000


chart.Weights(ol_sleeves, main = "", legend.loc = "topleft", plot.type = "line")






Figure 15.1: The three stage-1 solutions from chart.Weights() on an opt.list. Each line is one sleeve; a line is at zero outside its own block by construction.




The top-level problem takes the sleeve return series as its data, and several candidate policies can be specified at once with combine.portfolios(), which optimize.portfolio() solves in one call.

qu_top <- gmv_spec(names(sleeves)) |> add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean")
qu_top$objectives[[1]]$risk_aversion <- 10        # gamma/2, @sec-91-proofs

policies <- combine.portfolios(list(
  `minimum variance`  = gmv_spec(names(sleeves)),
  `sleeve cap 50%`    = gmv_spec(names(sleeves)) |>
                          add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.5),
  `quadratic utility` = qu_top))

ol_top <- optimize.portfolio(sl, policies, optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE)
names(ol_top) <- names(policies)               # the list's names are not carried over
stopifnot(inherits(ol_top, "opt.list"))

round(extractWeights(ol_top), 4)
#>                   commodity credit equity government
#> minimum variance     0.0423 0.0000 0.1155     0.8422
#> sleeve cap 50%       0.0745 0.3049 0.1205     0.5000
#> quadratic utility    0.0263 0.0000 0.2760     0.6978
round(extractObjectiveMeasures(ol_top), 5)
#>                    StdDev    mean
#> minimum variance  0.01222 0.00263
#> sleeve cap 50%    0.01392 0.00306
#> quadratic utility 0.01400 0.00356







Noteopt.list methods need trace = TRUE



extractObjectiveMeasures() on an opt.list re-evaluates every objective in the list on every portfolio, so that a minimum-variance solution acquires a mean column when a return objective appears anywhere in the list. It reads the returns from each element’s $R, which exists only when the optimization was run with trace = TRUE; without it the call fails with a message about an argument of length zero. chart.RiskReward() goes through the same function and fails the same way.



chart.RiskReward(ol_top, risk.col = "StdDev", return.col = "mean",
                 chart.assets = TRUE, main = "")






Figure 15.2: Three top-level policies on the four sleeve series, from chart.RiskReward() on the opt.list. Circles are the sleeves themselves. Monthly units, not annualized.

title: 15  Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation
text:
15.3 Nested Against Flat

15.3.1 In sample

w_eq <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
insample <- tibble::tibble(
  construction = c("flat minimum variance", "nested minimum variance",
                   "block-diagonal", "hierarchical risk parity", "equal weight"),
  vol    = c(p_vol(w_flat), p_vol(w_nested), p_vol(w_bd), p_vol(w_hrp), p_vol(w_eq)),
  ret    = c(p_ret(w_flat), p_ret(w_nested), p_ret(w_bd), p_ret(w_hrp), p_ret(w_eq)),
  sharpe = c(p_sr(w_flat),  p_sr(w_nested),  p_sr(w_bd),  p_sr(w_hrp),  p_sr(w_eq)),
  bets   = c(eff_bets(w_flat), eff_bets(w_nested), eff_bets(w_bd),
             eff_bets(w_hrp), eff_bets(w_eq)),
  top    = c(max(w_flat), max(w_nested), max(w_bd), max(w_hrp), max(w_eq)))
stopifnot(insample$sharpe[1] > insample$sharpe[2])   # nesting gives up Sharpe ratio in sample




Table 15.2: Five constructions on the full sample. Annualized, in excess of the bill; largest is the biggest single class weight.

In sample the order is fixed by construction and Table 15.2 only measures the gaps. Nesting gives up 0.050 of Sharpe ratio against the flat solution and buys nothing visible in return: the nested portfolio holds 1.69 effective positions against the flat portfolio’s 1.47, with 76% in one series. The sleeve structure did not diversify the answer, because Equation 15.2 is still a minimum-variance problem and still buys the sleeve with the lowest variance; what changes that is a constraint on the budgets, which is Section 12.1’s subject and the sleeve cap 50% row of the opt.list above.

15.3.2 Out of sample
The claim that matters is the one Section 8.1 makes about every method in this book: a restriction that costs variance in sample can buy it back out of sample if what it forbids is mostly estimation error. We run the four constructions on a sixty-month rolling window, monthly, from the same first out-of-sample month as the register of output/tables/oos-sweep.csv, so that the flat line can be checked against it.

FIRST_OOS <- 121L                                # the register's first out-of-sample month
stopifnot(FIRST_OOS == which(model_year(zoo::index(Re)) == 11L)[1])   # first month of model year 11
oos    <- FIRST_OOS:nrow(Re)
rf_oos <- rf[oos]
Xm <- zoo::coredata(Re); Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)

race <- function(W) {
  paths <- lapply(oos, function(t) {
    X  <- Xm[(t - W):(t - 1), ]                    # the W months before t, nothing after
    Sw <- stats::cov(X)
    v  <- within_gmv(Sw, sleeves)
    sr <- sapply(names(v), function(k) X[, sleeves[[k]], drop = FALSE] %*% v[[k]])
    Sb <- Sw; Sb[!same] <- 0
    rbind(flat           = gmv_qp(Sw),
          nested         = unroll(gmv_qp(stats::cov(sr)), v),
          `block-diagonal` = gmv_qp(Sb),
          `equal weight` = rep(1 / N, N))
  })
  strategies <- rownames(paths[[1]])
  ret  <- sapply(strategies, function(s) vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
    sum(paths[[i]][s, ] * Rm[oos[i], ]), numeric(1)))
  # turnover against drifted end-of-period weights, as the register defines it
  turn <- sapply(strategies, function(s) {
    eop <- rep(0, N); out <- numeric(length(oos))
    for (i in seq_along(oos)) {
      w <- paths[[i]][s, ]; r <- Rm[oos[i], ]
      out[i] <- 0.5 * sum(abs(w - eop)); eop <- w * (1 + r) / (1 + sum(w * r))
    }
    mean(out) * 12
  })
  list(ret = ret, turnover = turn,
       sleeve_budget = sapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
         tapply(paths[[i]]["nested", ], sleeve_of(colnames(Re)), sum)))
}

oos_stats <- function(r) {                       # the register's definitions
  n  <- length(r)
  ar <- prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - 1
  af <- prod(1 + rf_oos)^(12 / n) - 1
  v  <- stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12)
  c(ann_return = ar, ann_vol = v, sharpe = (ar - af) / v)
}

race60 <- race(60L)
stats60 <- t(apply(race60$ret, 2, oos_stats))
round(cbind(stats60, turnover = race60$turnover), 4)
#>                ann_return ann_vol sharpe turnover
#> flat               0.0464  0.0413 0.8280   0.3306
#> nested             0.0373  0.0422 0.5931   0.2990
#> block-diagonal     0.0383  0.0485 0.5377   0.2675
#> equal weight       0.0670  0.0875 0.6263   0.1590


sweep <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
sweep_sr <- function(strategy, window) sweep$sharpe[sweep$strategy == strategy &
                                                     sweep$window == window]
stopifnot(abs(stats60["flat", "sharpe"] - sweep_sr("min_variance", 60)) < 0.05,
          abs(stats60["equal weight", "sharpe"] - sweep_sr("equal_weight", 60)) < 0.05)
c(flat_here = stats60["flat", "sharpe"], register = sweep_sr("min_variance", 60))
#> flat_here  register 
#>     0.828     0.829

The flat line lands within 0.001 of the register’s minimum-variance entry, which is the same problem solved by optimize.portfolio.rebalancing() in Section 25.3, and the equal-weight line reproduces it exactly, so the loop is scoring the same months by the same definitions.

windows <- c(36L, 60L, 120L)

  s <- if (W == 60L) stats60 else t(apply(race(W)$ret, 2, oos_stats))
  tibble::tibble(window = W, construction = rownames(s),
                 sharpe = s[, "sharpe"], vol = s[, "ann_vol"])
}))

stopifnot(all(abs(by_window$sharpe[by_window$construction == "flat"] - register_flat) < 0.05))

The hierarchy does not dominate one-stage optimization out of sample on this universe. That is worth pausing on, because the nested rule estimates fewer covariances than the flat one, and the finding of DeMiguel et al. (2009) that the book has met at every turn is that rules which estimate less tend to do better out of sample. At sixty months the nested construction earns a Sharpe ratio of 0.593 against the flat portfolio’s 0.828, a gap of 0.235, and the flat portfolio also has the lower realized volatility, 4.13% against 4.22%. The nested portfolio finishes behind equal weighting as well. Shortening the window to thirty-six months, which makes every estimate worse and should favor the construction that estimates fewer covariances, does not reverse the order, and neither does lengthening it to one hundred and twenty. The block-diagonal construction trails the nested one at every window, which places the two on the ladder of Section 15.1: what stage 2 recovers through \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is worth 0.055 of Sharpe ratio at sixty months, and what stage 1 discards is worth more.
That is the shrinkage reading confirmed from the other side. Ledoit and Wolf (2004) shrink because the sample matrix is badly conditioned, and on sixteen series and sixty months it is not: Section 7.1 found no rank-deficient window in thirty-one model years at class level. The cross-sleeve covariances are 23% of the matrix and, at this dimension, mostly information. The case for a hierarchy that discards them is the case Section 7.2 made for holding fewer things, and it arrives when the flat matrix cannot be estimated at all, which is the situation of Section 21.1 and not of this chapter. Here the structure is a governance decision, and the table prices it.

budget <- t(race60$sleeve_budget)
round(colMeans(budget), 3)
#>  commodity     credit     equity government 
#>      0.022      0.016      0.125      0.837

Figure 15.3 shows the gap opening steadily rather than in any one episode: the largest share any named episode of sim_episodes contributes to it is 12%, in the rates shock. The sleeve budgets show why it does not close. Averaged over the out-of-sample period the nested construction gives the government sleeve 84% of the portfolio and the equity sleeve 13%. Inside the government sleeve, stage 1 chose the composition on government covariances alone; the flat problem chose its government holdings for how they sit against equities, and that is the part of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) stage 1 never sees. Turnover, which Section 23.3 prices, is 30% a year for the nested construction against 33% for the flat one, so costs do not change the ranking.

15.3.3 The policy view
A policy is not usually minimum variance everywhere. The structure of Equation 15.1 and Equation 15.2 lets each level carry its own objective, and the combination a mandate most often asks for is a tangency portfolio where returns are believed to be forecastable and minimum variance where they are not. The long-only tangency portfolio is one quadratic program, minimum variance at unit expected return, rescaled to a full budget; it is the point Equation 9.5 picks out, and rather than scanning a frontier for it as Section 9.2 does we solve it directly and check it against a scan of forty frontier points on the sleeve series.

tan_qp <- function(S, mu) {
  stopifnot(any(mu > 0))
  n   <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}

# the check: no long-only frontier portfolio has a higher Sharpe ratio
S_sl <- stats::cov(sl); mu_sl <- colMeans(sl); n_sl <- ncol(sl)
sr_of <- function(w) sum(mu_sl * w) / sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S_sl %*% w))
scan <- vapply(seq(min(mu_sl), max(mu_sl), length.out = 42)[2:41], function(target) {
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S_sl, dvec = rep(0, n_sl),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n_sl), mu_sl, diag(n_sl)),
                            bvec = c(1, target, rep(0, n_sl)), meq = 2)
  sr_of(sol$solution)
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(sr_of(tan_qp(S_sl, mu_sl)) >= max(scan) - 1e-8)
c(tangency = sr_of(tan_qp(S_sl, mu_sl)) * sqrt(12), best_of_scan = max(scan) * sqrt(12))
#>     tangency best_of_scan 
#>       0.8827       0.8824

w_policy  <- unroll(b_policy, v_policy)

Table 15.4 is what a strategic asset allocation looks like as a document, the policy portfolio that Ang (2014) places at the center of institutional practice: 68% to the government sleeve, 29% to equity, and inside each a regional split the sleeve manager inherits. The equity manager of Section 21.1 receives the five regional weights in the equity rows as a benchmark and selects instruments against it; the fixed-income manager of Section 22.1 receives the government rows and a hedging instruction with them. The policy earns an in-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.954 against 0.991 for the flat tangency portfolio, and after Section 9.3 neither number should be read as a forecast. The anchored variant of this problem, in which the sleeve manager optimizes around the benchmark under a tracking-error budget rather than from scratch, is a different formulation and belongs to Section 24.2.

title: 15  Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation
text:
Key Takeaways

The nested problem of Equation 15.1 and Equation 15.2 is the structure every large allocator uses, and Sharpe (1981) posed the question it raises: what the top level must tell the sleeves so that the parts add up. In sample it can never dominate the flat problem, because Equation 15.3 is feasible for it.
Stage 1 is the flat problem on the block-diagonal matrix of Equation 15.4: a shrinkage estimator whose intensity is set by the mandate rather than estimated. With inverse-variance budgets at the top, the two constructions coincide exactly, by Equation 15.5.

mult.portfolio.spec() runs each sleeve through the rolling backtest of optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(), back-fills the training period with a drifting equal-weight sleeve, and optimizes the top level once on the result. Its defaults do not run, rolling_window is silently discarded in favor of trailing_periods, a one-asset sleeve cannot be optimized, and the proxy series are visible only with trace = TRUE.
On sixteen classes and a sixty-month window the hierarchy loses out of sample, at every window length tried, and the block-diagonal construction loses by more. At this dimension the cross-sleeve covariances are information rather than noise; the case for discarding them arrives at instrument level, where the flat matrix cannot be estimated.
The estimated hierarchy of hierarchical risk parity groups fixed income by currency rather than by class, which is the hedging decision of Campbell et al. (2010) seen from the data: a hedge is a property of the sleeve, and it changes what the bond sleeves hold while leaving the equity sleeve alone.
The class series is the sleeve’s benchmark. The policy is set on investable proxies and handed down; the sleeve manager is judged against it.

title: 15  Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation
text:
Exercises

The tree in the hierarchical-risk-parity box grouped the bond series by currency. Build the sleeves that way instead, one sleeve per currency with the commodity on its own, and rerun race(60L). Does the currency hierarchy dominate the class hierarchy out of sample, and does either dominate the flat construction?
Replace the top-level minimum-variance step in race() with the inverse-variance rule of Equation 15.5 and confirm, window by window, that the result coincides with the block-diagonal line to machine precision. Then say in one sentence what the difference between the nested and block-diagonal rows of Table 15.3 measures.
Repeat the hierarchical-risk-parity construction with complete linkage in place of single linkage and cut the tree at four clusters. Does the estimated hierarchy recover the four sleeves? Report the cross-tabulation of clusters against sleeves.
The package back-fills the first training_period months of every proxy with a buy-and-hold equal-weight sleeve. Using proxy_by_hand(), vary the training period over 36, 60 and 120 months and report how far the top-level weights move when the back-filled months are dropped. At which window does the back-fill matter most, and why?
