title: 16  Signals and Return Forecasts
text:
16.1 Predictability, In Sample and Out
Can the excess return on an asset class be forecast, and does a forecast that fits the past help an investor who must act on it before the future arrives? Welch and Goyal (2008) put the first question to every predictor the literature had proposed for the equity premium and found that hardly any of them would have helped an investor in real time: the regressions fit in sample and failed out of sample. Campbell and Thompson (2008) replied that the same predictors do help, by a small but economically meaningful margin, once the forecast is constrained by what theory says its sign must be, and between them the two papers fixed the terms on which every later claim of predictability is judged: an out-of-sample \(R^2\) against the historical mean, and the certainty-equivalent gain of an investor who uses the forecast.
This is the first tactical chapter of the book in the sense of Section 3.1: the inputs are conditioned on information available at the time rather than estimated unconditionally, and the question is whether the conditioning is worth anything. We first set out the predictive regression and its two \(R^2\) statistics, the test of one forecast against another, and the economic-value criterion; then say which signals this universe can carry and build them from the shipped data, momentum from the return histories and the term spread, the credit spread and a turbulence index from the bond curve factors and the cross-section; then test each signal in sample and out of sample, one at a time and combined through an elastic net; and finally scale the forecasts into a monthly tilt around the equal-weight policy and price it after costs.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill for the reasons of Section 3.1, and the assertion that the bill’s dates are the return dates is the first of several in this chapter that exist because a signal one month out of place produces a plausible table.

title: 16  Signals and Return Forecasts
text:
16.1.1 The predictive regression
Write \(r^e_{t+1}\) for the excess return on one series over month \(t+1\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) for a vector of \(K\) signals observed by the end of month \(t\). The predictive regression is
\[
r^e_{t+1} = a + \boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{x}_t + \varepsilon_{t+1},
\tag{16.1}\]
and its in-sample \(R^2\) is the share of the variance of \(r^e\) that the fitted values account for over the whole sample,
\[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{t}\hat{\varepsilon}_{t+1}^2}
               {\sum_{t}\left(r^e_{t+1} - \bar{r}^e\right)^2},
\tag{16.2}\]
with \(\bar{r}^e\) the full-sample mean. Three things about Equation 16.1 are settled before any signal is chosen. The dating is the whole of the discipline: \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) must be known when the position for \(t+1\) is taken, and Section 16.2 asserts that alignment in code rather than trusting it. The \(R^2\) will be small, because Section 4.1 showed, following Merton (1980), that a mean is known only to within \(\sigma/\sqrt{\tau}\) over \(\tau\) years, and a conditional mean that moves with \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) is a fraction of a number that is itself barely visible: one percent a month is a strong result in this literature. And the slope is biased when the signal is persistent and its innovations are correlated with the return’s, as for every valuation ratio and most yields; Stambaugh (1999) derived the bias and Cochrane (2008) showed that the same persistence constrains what the joint system of return and signal can say. Inference uses the Newey and West (1987) standard errors of Equation 5.5, and with sixteen series and four signals the sixty-four regressions below are a multiple-testing problem of the kind Harvey et al. (2016) describe, so a \(t\)-statistic of two begins a case rather than ending one.

16.1.2 The out-of-sample \(R^2\)

An in-sample fit estimates \(a\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) on the whole history and scores the fitted values on the same history. An investor cannot do that. At the end of each month \(t\) she has the data through \(t\), estimates Equation 16.1 on them, and forecasts \(\hat{r}^e_{t+1}\); the alternative that uses no signal is the historical mean through \(t\), \(\bar{r}^e_t\), the strategic input of Section 6.1 re-estimated each month. Campbell and Thompson (2008) score the two sequences of forecasts against each other over the out-of-sample months \(t = T_0, \dots, T-1\) by
\[
R^2_{\text{OS}} = 1 -
  \frac{\sum_{t=T_0}^{T-1}\left(r^e_{t+1} - \hat{r}^e_{t+1}\right)^2}
       {\sum_{t=T_0}^{T-1}\left(r^e_{t+1} - \bar{r}^e_t\right)^2},
\tag{16.3}\]
which is positive when the signal’s forecast errors are smaller than the mean’s and negative when they are larger. Unlike Equation 16.2 it has no floor at zero, and a negative value is the common case: Welch and Goyal (2008) report it for most predictors over most periods, Goyal et al. (2024) find on data through 2021 that almost nothing proposed since fares better, and McLean and Pontiff (2016) show that the cross-sectional predictors which did work decay after publication. The burn-in \(T_0\) is a choice, and the window can roll or expand; an expanding window uses everything the investor knows, and it is what we use. Campbell and Thompson (2008) also restricted the forecast by theory, setting a negative forecast of the equity premium to zero, and found that the restriction turns most of their negative \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) positive; exercise 2 applies it here.

16.1.3 Testing one forecast against another
Two forecasts of the same series are compared on their squared errors. Write \(e^0_{t+1} = r^e_{t+1} - \bar{r}^e_t\) for the mean’s error, \(e^1_{t+1}\) for the model’s, and \(d_{t+1} = (e^0_{t+1})^2 - (e^1_{t+1})^2\) for the loss differential. Diebold and Mariano (1995) observed that under the null of equal accuracy \(d\) has mean zero, so the test is a \(t\)-test on its mean with a standard error that allows the losses to be serially correlated and heteroskedastic,
\[
\text{DM} = \frac{\bar{d}}{\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar{d})}},
\tag{16.4}\]
with the variance estimated as in Equation 5.5, asymptotically standard normal. When the two models are nested, as a predictive regression and the historical mean are, the larger model estimates parameters whose true value is zero under the null and pays for them in forecast variance, so its squared errors exceed the mean’s even when the signal is useless and Equation 16.4 is biased against it. Clark and West (2007) correct this by adding back the term the estimation noise contributes,
\[
\text{CW} = \frac{\overline{d_{t+1} + \left(\bar{r}^e_t - \hat{r}^e_{t+1}\right)^2}}
                 {\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\cdot)}},
\tag{16.5}\]
read against the normal distribution as a one-sided test. It is the statistic reported below whenever a signal is set against the mean, with Equation 16.4 beside it to show what the correction changes.

16.1.4 Why a small \(R^2\) can matter
An \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) of half a percent looks like nothing, and it is not. Kandel and Stambaugh (1996) showed that the decision of a mean-variance investor responds to a predictive relation far weaker than any statistical test would accept, because what the investor cares about is not the fit but the position the forecast changes. The link is short. Under Equation 3.12 an investor with risk aversion \(\gamma\) facing one risky asset with conditional mean \(\mu_t\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) holds \(w_t = \mu_t / (\gamma\sigma^2)\) and earns an expected excess return of \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_t^2]/(\gamma\sigma^2)\). Using the unconditional mean \(\mu\) instead earns \(\mu^2/(\gamma\sigma^2) = S^2/\gamma\), with \(S = \mu/\sigma\) the Sharpe ratio; the difference is \(\operatorname{Var}(\mu_t)/(\gamma\sigma^2)\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\mu_t)/\sigma^2\) is the \(R^2\) of the forecast. So, as Campbell and Thompson (2008) write it,
\[
\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[r^e] \approx \frac{R^2_{\text{OS}}}{\gamma},
\qquad
\frac{\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[r^e]}{S^2/\gamma} \approx \frac{R^2_{\text{OS}}}{S^2}.
\tag{16.6}\]
The proportional gain is the \(R^2\) relative to the squared Sharpe ratio, and monthly Sharpe ratios are small numbers. Take \(R^2_{\text{OS}} = 0.5\%\) a month, an annual Sharpe ratio of \(0.5\) so that \(S = 0.5/\sqrt{12} = 0.144\) and \(S^2 = 0.0208\), and \(\gamma = 5\): the proportional gain is \(0.005 / 0.0208
= 24%\) of the unconditional expected excess return, and in return units \(0.005 / 5 = 10\) basis points a month, 1.2 percentage points a year. That is what a predictive \(R^2\) no referee would find impressive is worth to an investor who acts on it without constraint, and it is why in-sample significance and out-of-sample profit are different questions: the first asks whether \(\boldsymbol{b}\) is distinguishable from zero, the second whether acting on \(\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\), estimated with error and passed through a position rule and a cost model, beats not acting. Pesaran and Timmermann (1995) made the same point with switching rules run in real time.
The criterion that answers the second question is the certainty equivalent of Section 3.1. For a strategy whose realized excess returns have mean \(\hat{\mu}_p\) and variance \(\hat{\sigma}^2_p\) over the out-of-sample months,
\[
\text{CE}_p = \hat{\mu}_p - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\hat{\sigma}^2_p,
\qquad
\Delta = \text{CE}_{\text{forecast}} - \text{CE}_{\text{mean}},
\tag{16.7}\]
is the riskless excess return the investor would accept in place of each, and \(\Delta\) is the fee she would pay to switch from the strategy built on the mean to the one built on the forecast. It is computed from realized returns, gross or net of costs, and it decides Section 16.3. What it does not do is score the forecast itself, independently of a position rule. That measure, the risk-adjusted forecast error that Section 8.3 introduced and Section 26.1 derives, expresses a forecast’s error as the Sharpe ratio it costs (Salcher et al. 2026); whether a forecaster should be trained on that loss rather than on squared error is the question of Section 27.1.

16.1.5 Which signals this universe can carry
The literature’s signals fall into three families, and the shipped data support two of them.
Momentum needs nothing but the return history. Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) documented that stocks which rose over the past three to twelve months continue to rise over the next, and the construction that became standard skips the most recent month to avoid short-term reversal: the signal at \(t\) is the return over months \(t-11\) to \(t-1\),
\[
\text{mom}_{i,t} = \prod_{k=1}^{11}\left(1 + R_{i,t-k}\right) - 1 .
\tag{16.8}\]
Moskowitz et al. (2012) showed that the sign of an asset’s own past twelve-month excess return forecasts its next month across fifty-eight futures on equity indices, bonds, currencies and commodities, the asset-class level of this book rather than the stock level, and Asness et al. (2013) found value and momentum premia in every class and region they examined, negatively correlated with each other. Value is the family this universe cannot support: it needs a fundamental, a book value or an earnings stream, that the market does not carry, so the chapter builds momentum without its partner and the value side waits for Section 21.1.
Macro state signals are the family Welch and Goyal (2008) tested: the dividend yield, the term spread, the default spread, the short rate, inflation. Fama and French (1989) showed that the term spread and the default spread forecast the excess returns on stocks and bonds together, tracking business conditions, and both are in the shipped data. sim_curve_weekly, described in Section 2.2, carries the level, slope and curvature of a Nelson and Siegel (1987) curve per region in the dynamic form of Diebold and Li (2006), plus an investment-grade and a high-yield credit spread per region. In that parametrization the slope factor is the short end minus the long end, so the term spread of Fama and French (1989) is minus the slope, and the IG spread is their default spread. These are the same predictors, built inside the universe: the bond block was simulated from them, so a signal that forecasts the bond and credit series here is forecasting the state that generated them, the state Section 22.1 decomposes the bond returns on. Whether it forecasts the equity series is the open question.
Cross-sectional dispersion is the third family, and it is the one Section 5.3 already built. The turbulence index of Chow et al. (1999) and Kritzman and Li (2010), the Mahalanobis distance of a month’s return vector from its trailing mean in Equation 5.6, measures how unusual the pattern across the sixteen series is; Stöckl (2022b) show that dispersion measured within a cross-section forecasts the premia earned on it, and Stöckl (2022a) link the same construction to parameter uncertainty and to the aggregate premium. It is a signal about the whole market rather than about one series, so it enters every regression with the same value and a series-specific slope.
The real-world versions of the macro signals are one call away for a reader with a network connection: tidyfinance serves the Welch and Goyal (2008) predictor file, whose tms and dfy columns are the term and default spreads built below; the dates are any range of the predictor file’s own, real calendar.

gw <- tidyfinance::download_data_macro_predictors(
  dataset = "macro_predictors_monthly",
  start_date = "2000-01-01", end_date = "2020-12-31")   # an illustrative range
gw[, c("date", "tms", "dfy", "dp")]

Nothing below depends on it; every signal is built from the shipped data so that the chapter reproduces offline.

title: 16  Signals and Return Forecasts
text:
16.2 Building and Testing the Signals

16.2.1 Signals at month end, lagged once
Momentum first. Equation 16.8 is a ratio of two lagged values of the total-return index, and the assertion checks it against the product it is meant to be.

P   <- cumprod(1 + R)                                   # total-return index
mom <- xts::lag.xts(P, 1) / xts::lag.xts(P, 12) - 1     # months t-11 .. t-1; month t skipped
k <- 100L
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(mom[k, ]),
                    unname(apply(1 + zoo::coredata(R)[(k - 11):(k - 1), ], 2, prod) - 1)))

The curve is weekly and the returns are monthly, so each month end takes the last weekly observation on or before it, never after. The sign convention is then checked against the data rather than assumed: the short rate in the Diebold and Li (2006) parametrization is level plus slope, so level minus term spread must track the bill.

cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(series %in% c("US_Level", "US_Slope", "US_IG_Spread", "US_HY_Spread")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)          # last weekly row on or before each month end
# Weekly dates are six to eight days apart, so the matched week is at most
# seven days before the month end and never after it.
stopifnot(all(cv$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[i_last] < 8))

curve <- xts::xts(cbind(level = cv$US_Level[i_last],
                        term  = -cv$US_Slope[i_last],           # long minus short, in pp
                        ig    = 100 * cv$US_IG_Spread[i_last],  # pp
                        hy    = 100 * cv$US_HY_Spread[i_last]),
                  order.by = dates)

cor_short <- stats::cor(as.numeric(curve$level - curve$term),
                        100 * sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual)
stopifnot(cor_short > 0.9)
round(cor_short, 3)
#> [1] 0.975

The correlation between the curve’s implied short rate and the bill is 0.975, and the assertion would have failed the render at a sign error. The turbulence index is Section 5.3’s call, unchanged: a sixty-month trailing window, so the index for month \(t\) is computed from the moments of months \(t-60\) to \(t-1\) and the return vector of \(t\) itself.

turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
colnames(turb) <- "turb"
common <- merge(curve, turb)
stopifnot(identical(zoo::index(common), dates))

Every signal now sits at the month end it was observed. Shifting the whole block forward by one month puts the signal observed at \(t\) on the row of the return it predicts, \(t+1\), and the assertion states that the shift did what it was meant to do.

common_lag <- xts::lag.xts(common, 1)
mom_lag    <- xts::lag.xts(mom, 1)
rev_lag    <- xts::lag.xts(Re, 1)                       # last month's own excess return
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(common_lag[k + 1, ]), as.numeric(common[k, ])),
          all.equal(as.numeric(mom_lag[k + 1, ]),    as.numeric(mom[k, ])),
          is.na(common_lag[1, "term"]))

# For one series: the excess return in month m beside every signal as it stood
# at the end of m - 1. This is the frame @eq-16-predictive is estimated on.
pairs_of <- function(s) {
  data.frame(date = dates, y = as.numeric(Re[, s]),
             mom = as.numeric(mom_lag[, s]), rev = as.numeric(rev_lag[, s]),
             zoo::coredata(common_lag))
}
first_row <- function(v) min(which(!is.na(pairs_of("US_equity")[[v]])))
c(momentum = first_row("mom"), curve = first_row("term"), turbulence = first_row("turb"))
#>   momentum      curve turbulence 
#>         14          2         61

The first row carries no signal, the momentum column begins in month 14 and turbulence, which needs sixty months of history, in month 61.







Figure 16.1: The four signals as they stood at each month end. The term spread and the IG spread are read off the US curve in percentage points; turbulence is the sixty-month out-of-sample Mahalanobis distance of chapter 5; momentum is the 12-1 return of US_equity, one of sixteen such series.





16.2.2 In sample: sixty-four regressions
Each series is regressed on each of the four signals over the whole sample, one signal at a time, with the standard errors of Equation 5.5 at six lags as in Section 5.2.

sig4 <- c(mom = "12-1 momentum", term = "term spread", ig = "IG spread", turb = "turbulence")

nw_t <- function(m, j = 2L) {
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  unname(stats::coef(m)[j] / sqrt(nw[j, j]))
}

ins <- lapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s)
  lapply(names(sig4), function(v) {
    dd <- d[!is.na(d[[v]]), ]
    m  <- stats::lm(y ~ x, data = data.frame(y = dd$y, x = dd[[v]]))
    tibble::tibble(series = s, signal = v, slope = unname(stats::coef(m)[2]),
                   t = nw_t(m), r2 = summary(m)$r.squared, n = nrow(dd))
  }) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

ins_sum <- ins |>
  dplyr::group_by(signal) |>
  dplyr::summarise(positive = sum(slope > 0), t_above_2 = sum(abs(t) > 2),
                   t_above_3 = sum(abs(t) > 3), median_r2 = median(r2), max_r2 = max(r2))
ins_sum

Read Table 16.1 by column. The term spread is the strongest signal in the table: its slope is positive for 12 of the sixteen series, among them every one of the 10 bond and credit series, 7 of its \(t\)-statistics exceed two and none exceeds three, the largest being CH_government at 2.93. That is Fama and French (1989) on modeled data: a steep curve forecasts high excess returns on bonds. The IG spread is second, with 5 above two, again on the credit and bond series where the state was built in. Turbulence clears two on 1 series and its median \(R^2\) is 0.30%. Momentum clears two nowhere: its slope is negative for 3 of the five equity series, positive for the government series, and its largest \(R^2\) is 0.47%. The premium Moskowitz et al. (2012) document in futures is not in these class indices at a monthly horizon; they found it across fifty-eight instruments with a sign rule, not one series at a time with a slope. The largest \(R^2\) anywhere in the table is 5.2%, which by Equation 16.6 is not a small number. The question is whether any of it is available in real time.

16.2.3 Out of sample: an expanding window from model year 11
The out-of-sample scheme is an expanding window with a burn-in, and rsample::rolling_origin() describes the same sequence of splits in the vocabulary of tidymodels, so the count of splits is asserted to match.

burn <- 120L
oos  <- seq.int(burn + 1L, nrow(Re))       # forecast months 121 .. 372
stopifnot(model_year(dates[oos[1]]) == 11L)   # the register's out-of-sample start

ols_fc <- function(d, v, m) {
  tr <- which(!is.na(d[[v]]) & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)          # strictly before m
  b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d[[v]][tr]), d$y[tr])$coefficients
  unname(b[1] + b[2] * d[[v]][m])
}

splits <- rsample::rolling_origin(data.frame(m = seq_len(nrow(Re))),
                                  initial = burn, assess = 1, cumulative = TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(splits) == length(oos))
c(forecast_months = length(oos), first = fmt_model(dates[oos[1]]))
#>            forecast_months                      first 
#>                      "252" "January of model year 11"

The burn-in is the first 120 months; forecasts begin in January of model year 11 and run to the end of the sample, 252 months, which are the months the register of Section 25.3 scores. At each month \(m\) in that range the regression is fit on every pair dated before \(m\) where the signal exists, the forecast is made for \(m\), and the historical mean of the excess return through \(m-1\) is recorded beside it.
One signal at a time is what Welch and Goyal (2008) tested and what a practitioner rarely does. With seven predictors per series, the four above plus last month’s return, the high-yield spread and the level of the curve, least squares on sixty to three hundred months fits noise, and the remedy is to shrink. The elastic net of Zou and Hastie (2005) minimizes the squared error plus a penalty \(\lambda\left[\alpha\|\boldsymbol{b}\|_1 + (1-\alpha)\|\boldsymbol{b}\|_2^2/2\right]\), which at \(\alpha = 1/2\) both shrinks coefficients toward zero and sets some exactly to zero; Gu et al. (2020) use it as the first of their machine-learning forecasters for the cross-section of stock returns, and Coqueret and Guida (2020) give the algorithm and its glmnet implementation, which we do not reproduce. What matters here is the tuning, because it is where the future leaks in: \(\lambda\) is chosen by five-fold cross-validation on contiguous blocks of the training window, in time order rather than shuffled, re-tuned once a year, and the coefficients are refit every month on the data through \(m-1\). Two values of \(\lambda\) are kept, the one that minimizes cross-validated error and the most penalized one within a standard error of it, because the choice turns out to matter.

en_vars <- c("mom", "rev", "term", "ig", "hy", "level", "turb")

enet_fc <- function(d) {
  ok  <- stats::complete.cases(d[, en_vars])
  lam <- c(NA_real_, NA_real_)
  t(vapply(oos, function(m) {
    tr <- which(ok & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)
    X  <- as.matrix(d[tr, en_vars]); y <- d$y[tr]
    if ((m - oos[1]) %% 12L == 0L) {                      # re-tune once a year
      fold <- ceiling(seq_along(tr) / (length(tr) / 5))   # five contiguous blocks
      cvf  <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5, foldid = fold)
      lam <<- c(cvf$lambda.min, cvf$lambda.1se)
    }
    fit <- glmnet::glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5)
    as.numeric(stats::predict(fit, newx = as.matrix(d[m, en_vars]), s = lam))
  }, numeric(2)))
}

The loop below produces, for every series and every out-of-sample month, the historical mean, the four single-signal forecasts, their equal-weighted combination, which Rapach et al. (2010) showed is more stable than any of its parts, and the two elastic-net forecasts.

fc <- lapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s)
  out <- data.frame(date = dates[oos], series = s, y = d$y[oos],
                    mean = vapply(oos, function(m) mean(d$y[seq_len(m - 1L)]), numeric(1)))
  for (v in names(sig4)) out[[v]] <- vapply(oos, function(m) ols_fc(d, v, m), numeric(1))
  out$comb <- rowMeans(out[, names(sig4)])
  en <- enet_fc(d); out$enet_min <- en[, 1]; out$enet_1se <- en[, 2]
  out
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
stopifnot(nrow(fc) == N * length(oos), !anyNA(fc))

Equation 16.3, Equation 16.5 and Equation 16.4 are then three short functions.

models <- c(names(sig4), "comb", "enet_min", "enet_1se")
model_label <- c(sig4, comb = "combination",
                 enet_min = "elastic net, lambda.min", enet_1se = "elastic net, lambda.1se")

r2_os <- function(y, f, f0) 1 - sum((y - f)^2) / sum((y - f0)^2)
cw_t  <- function(y, f, f0) nw_t(stats::lm(I((y - f0)^2 - (y - f)^2 + (f0 - f)^2) ~ 1), 1L)
dm_t  <- function(y, f, f0) nw_t(stats::lm(I((y - f0)^2 - (y - f)^2) ~ 1), 1L)

oos_tbl <- fc |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(models), names_to = "model", values_to = "f") |>
  dplyr::group_by(series, model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(r2os = r2_os(y, f, mean), cw = cw_t(y, f, mean), dm = dm_t(y, f, mean),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = factor(model, levels = models))

oos_sum <- oos_tbl |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(positive = sum(r2os > 0), median_r2os = median(r2os), best = max(r2os),
                   cw_above = sum(cw > 1.645), dm_above = sum(dm > 1.645))

Figure 16.2: Out-of-sample R² by series and forecast, from one data frame. Series are ordered by the term spread’s value. Anything left of the vertical line lost to the historical mean over the same months.




Three findings, in decreasing order of comfort.
The term spread survives. Its \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) is positive on 10 of the sixteen series, its median is +0.52%, and it beats the mean by the Clark-West test on 6 of them, with CH_credit at +2.5%. The uncorrected statistic of Equation 16.4 finds 0, which is the nesting bias of Clark and West (2007) in one column: the regression carries two estimated parameters whose noise the mean does not pay for, and without the correction that noise is scored against the signal. The IG spread, second in sample, keeps a positive \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) on 3 series and turbulence on 1; the in-sample fit of the first was concentrated in credit and of the second in a few crisis months, and an expanding window estimated before those months cannot see either. Turbulence’s worst case is JP_equity at -8.1%.
The combination helps and does not rescue. Averaging the four forecasts, the rule of Rapach et al. (2010), is positive on 7 series with a median of -0.11%, between its best and its worst constituent, which is what an average does.
The elastic net loses. At the cross-validated minimum it beats the mean on 1 series with a median \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) of -1.95%; at the more penalized lambda.1se the median rises to -0.57% and the count to 5, still short of the single term spread. This is what Gu et al. (2020) report for the same model on the cross-section of stocks, where the elastic net is the weakest of their forecasters and its gains come from thousands of stocks and hundreds of signals, not from seven signals on sixteen series. The more the model is allowed to fit, the more it fits the burn-in’s noise, and the rule that shrinks hardest is the one that comes closest to the mean it is trying to beat. The lesson of Section 8.1, that the cost of an input is set by how well it can be estimated, applies to a conditional mean as it applied to an unconditional one.

title: 16  Signals and Return Forecasts
section: 16.3 The Economic Value of a Tilt
text:
16.3 The Economic Value of a Tilt

16.3.1 A tilt around the policy
The strategic policy is the equal-weight portfolio of Equation 8.3, built through the package’s own equal.weight() as in Section 8.2. It is the anchor because it estimates nothing, so that every difference between it and the tilted portfolio is attributable to the forecast, and because the constrained minimum-variance portfolio of Section 9.2 holds most of its weight in one series and leaves no room to tilt.

base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
w_policy <- extractWeights(equal.weight(Re, base_spec))[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(w_policy), rep(1 / N, N)))

The tilt converts a forecast into a weight in three steps. The forecast for month \(t+1\) is divided by the series’ trailing sixty-month volatility, both known at \(t\), so that a forecast of one percent means something different on a government bond than on an equity market; the cross-sectional mean is removed, because under full investment only a relative view can be expressed; and the result is scaled by \(\kappa\) and clipped to a band of \(\pm\delta\) around the policy weight,
\[
s_{i,t} = \frac{\hat{r}^e_{i,t+1}}{\hat{\sigma}_{i,t}}
        - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\hat{r}^e_{j,t+1}}{\hat{\sigma}_{j,t}},
\qquad
w_{i,t} = w^{\text{policy}}_i + \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\kappa\,s_{i,t},\,-\delta,\,\delta\right),
\tag{16.9}\]
re-centered so that the weights sum to one. With \(\delta = 1/(2N)\) no weight can fall below zero or above three halves of the policy weight, and \(\kappa\) is set so that a forecast Sharpe ratio of one half a year fills the band. The weights for month \(t+1\) are set at the end of month \(t\) from forecasts made at \(t\), which is the dating Equation 16.1 was built on.

vol60 <- zoo::rollapply(Re, 60, stats::sd, align = "right", fill = NA)
band  <- 0.5 / N
kappa <- band / (0.5 / sqrt(12))              # a forecast Sharpe ratio of 0.5 a year fills the band

tilt_weights <- function(model) {
  F <- fc |> dplyr::select(date, series, f = dplyr::all_of(model)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = f)
  Fm <- as.matrix(F[, colnames(Re)])
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(Fm), colnames(Re)), nrow(Fm) == length(oos))
  W <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(Fm)), function(i) {
    m  <- oos[i]
    s  <- Fm[i, ] / as.numeric(vol60[m - 1L, ])       # forecast in volatility units, known at m - 1
    s  <- s - mean(s)                                  # relative view
    tl <- pmin(pmax(kappa * s, -band), band)
    w  <- w_policy + tl - mean(tl)
    w  <- pmax(w, 0); w / sum(w)
  }, numeric(N)))
  dimnames(W) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re))
  stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W) - 1) < 1e-12), all(W >= 0))
  W
}

W_policy <- matrix(1 / N, length(oos), N, dimnames = list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re)))
W_term   <- tilt_weights("term")
c(mean_abs_tilt = mean(abs(W_term - 1 / N)),
  share_at_band = mean(abs(abs(W_term - 1 / N) - band) < 1e-9))
#> mean_abs_tilt share_at_band 
#>       0.01526       0.00000

The term-spread tilt moves the average weight by 1.5 percentage points against a band of 3.1, and the band binds on none of the weights. The forecasts are modest and so is the tilt.






NoteapplyFUN() and trailingFUN() do not roll anything



The two exported utilities whose names suggest they were written for this chapter were not. applyFUN(R, weights, FUN) evaluates one risk or return function, by name, for a weight vector or for every row of a weight matrix on the whole of R; it is the helper behind chart.Scatter(), which uses it to place random portfolios on the risk-return plane. trailingFUN(R, weights, n, FUN, FUNargs) evaluates FUN once on the last n + 1 rows of R, not the last n, and returns one number. Neither produces a time series. Rolling estimation in this book is zoo::rollapply(), as in Section 5.3 and the vol60 line above, or the explicit loop of enet_fc(). Both are run here so that the behavior is measured rather than described.



# applyFUN: one metric, many static weight vectors, the full return history.
applyFUN(Re, weights = rbind(policy = w_policy, average_tilt = colMeans(W_term)),
         FUN = "StdDev")
#> [1] 0.02326 0.02322

# trailingFUN: FUN once, on the last n + 1 rows. n = 11 gives twelve months.
x  <- Re[, "US_equity"]
tf <- trailingFUN(x, weights = NULL, n = 11, FUN = "mean", FUNargs = list())
stopifnot(all.equal(tf, mean(utils::tail(as.numeric(x), 12))))
c(trailingFUN_n11 = tf,
  mean_last_12 = mean(utils::tail(as.numeric(x), 12)),
  mean_last_11 = mean(utils::tail(as.numeric(x), 11)))
#> trailingFUN_n11    mean_last_12    mean_last_11 
#>       -0.012380       -0.012380       -0.009272


16.3.2 Rebalancing, turnover and costs
The portfolio is rebalanced monthly. Its accounting is written out rather than handed to Return.portfolio(), because that function back-fills equal weights before the first supplied weight vector, the trap Section 23.2 documents, and because the drifted weights are needed for the cost. By the end of month \(t+1\) each weight has drifted to \(w^{-}_{i,t+1} = w_{i,t}(1 + R_{i,t+1}) / (1 + r_{p,t+1})\); the trade back to the target has the turnover of Equation 23.1 and costs what Equation 23.2 charges, at the per-class one-way rates of pm_costs_default() that Section 23.3 uses on the register, mapped to each series by its class suffix.

cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(Re)

run_path <- function(W) {
  Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(Re)), nrow(W) == nrow(Rm))
  r       <- rowSums(W * Rm)                                  # month t+1, weights set at t
  drifted <- W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + r)                            # weights before the trade
  trade   <- abs(W[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(W), , drop = FALSE])
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[oos], gross = r,
                 turnover = c(rowSums(trade) / 2, 0),
                 cost     = c(as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate), 0)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(net = gross - cost)
}

# Sharpe ratio as the register computes it: compounded, in excess of the bill.
sharpe_realized <- function(r, rf) {
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
gamma <- 5
summarise_path <- function(p, label) {
  rf_o <- rf[oos]
  ce <- function(r) { e <- r - rf_o; 12 * mean(e) - gamma / 2 * 12 * stats::var(e) }
  tibble::tibble(
    portfolio    = label,
    ret          = prod(1 + p$gross)^(12 / nrow(p)) - 1,
    vol          = stats::sd(p$gross) * sqrt(12),
    sharpe_gross = sharpe_realized(p$gross, rf_o),
    turnover     = 12 * mean(p$turnover),
    cost_drag    = 12 * mean(p$cost),
    sharpe_net   = sharpe_realized(p$net, rf_o),
    max_dd       = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(xts::xts(p$net, order.by = p$date))),
    ce_net       = ce(p$net))
}

tilts <- c(mom = "momentum", term = "term spread", comb = "combination",
           enet_min = "elastic net, lambda.min", enet_1se = "elastic net, lambda.1se")
paths <- c(list(policy = run_path(W_policy)),
           lapply(names(tilts), function(k) run_path(tilt_weights(k))) |> setNames(names(tilts)))
res <- dplyr::bind_rows(Map(summarise_path, paths, c("equal weight (policy)", unname(tilts)))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(ce_gain = ce_net - ce_net[1])

16.3.3 Reading the result
Of the five forecasts, 2 leave the investor better off after costs, and only one of them by more than a few basis points: the term spread, the one signal that survived Table 16.2. Its tilt earns a net Sharpe ratio of 0.650 against the policy’s 0.622, a certainty-equivalent gain of 25 basis points a year at \(\gamma = 5\), with a slightly shallower drawdown and turnover of 21% against 14%, which the per-class rates price at 5 basis points a year. The combination is a wash at +5 basis points. Momentum loses 21 basis points, and the least-penalized elastic net turns the portfolio over 67% a year, almost 5 times the policy’s, to lose 20 net. A model that fits noise trades on it, and Section 23.3 shows the same monotone relation between how much a strategy estimates and how much it pays to trade.
The gain that exists is small against its own uncertainty. The standard error of an annualized Sharpe ratio estimated over 252 months is, by the formula of Lo (2002) under independence, about 0.22; the term tilt’s advantage of 0.028 is well inside it, and the paired test of Section 25.3, which exploits the correlation of the two series, would be sharper but not by enough to turn this into evidence. The honest reading is the one Campbell and Thompson (2008) gave for the equity premium: the signal that theory motivates, the term structure that Fama and French (1989) tied to business conditions, is worth a little to an investor who uses it with restraint, and the signals that data alone motivate are worth nothing after costs. Sharpe (1987) described tactical allocation as the strategic policy re-solved with current information; on this universe the re-solving is worth a few tens of basis points where the information is real and costs about as much where it is not.
Two things this chapter did not do are done elsewhere. It built the forecasts from data; a view that comes from an opinion and must become a return vector before an optimizer can use it is the subject of Section 17.1. And it scaled each forecast into a weight by a rule chosen by hand, Equation 16.9; Section 18.1 skips the forecast and estimates the map from signal to weight on the investor’s objective directly, in the manner of Brandt et al. (2009), while Section 19.1 lets the whole policy switch with a detected state rather than tilt with a continuous signal. Whether any of the three should be judged on squared forecast error at all is the question Section 26.1 takes up.

title: 16  Signals and Return Forecasts
text:
Key Takeaways

A predictive regression is judged out of sample, against the historical mean, by the \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) of Equation 16.3, and against that nested benchmark by the Clark-West correction of Equation 16.5 to the Diebold-Mariano test, because the mean does not pay the estimation noise a regression does (Welch and Goyal 2008; Campbell and Thompson 2008; Diebold and Mariano 1995; Clark and West 2007).
A small \(R^2\) is not a small effect. By Equation 16.6 the proportional gain to a mean-variance investor is \(R^2_{\text{OS}} / S^2\), so half a percent a month against an annual Sharpe ratio of one half is a quarter of the expected excess return (Kandel and Stambaugh 1996).
This universe supports momentum from returns, the term and credit spreads from sim_curve_weekly, and turbulence from the cross-section; it does not support value, which needs fundamentals it does not carry.
Of four signals on sixteen series, the term spread is the only one with out-of-sample evidence, positive on 10 series and significant on 6; momentum, the IG spread and turbulence lose to the mean out of sample, and a regularized seven-signal model loses on 11 to 15 of the sixteen, the more of them the less it shrinks (Gu et al. 2020).
A tilt of at most half the policy weight pays after costs on the term spread, by 25 basis points a year of certainty equivalent, inside the sampling error of the Sharpe ratio; the combination earns a few basis points, and momentum and the elastic net trade more and lose.

applyFUN() scores static weight vectors on the full history and trailingFUN() evaluates a function once on the last n + 1 rows. Neither rolls; rolling estimation is zoo::rollapply() or an explicit loop.

title: 16  Signals and Return Forecasts
text:
Exercises

The curve signals above are the US term spread and the US IG spread for every series. Replace them, for each non-US series, with the term spread and IG spread of the series’ own region, keeping the US ones for GLOBAL_commodity, and recompute the term-spread points of Figure 16.2. Does a local curve forecast a local bond better than the US curve does?

Campbell and Thompson (2008) set a forecast of the equity premium to zero whenever the regression produces a negative one. Apply the restriction to the term-spread forecasts of the five equity series and recompute their \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) and Clark-West statistics. Which series does the restriction help, and what does the answer say about the sign of the estimated slope in those months?
The tilt of Equation 16.9 fills its band at a forecast Sharpe ratio of one half a year. Double \(\kappa\) and halve it, and recompute Table 16.3 for the term-spread and momentum tilts. Does the certainty-equivalent gain scale with \(\kappa\), and which tilt is hurt more by a larger \(\kappa\)?
The tilt expresses only a relative view. For US_equity alone, implement the timing rule of Campbell and Thompson (2008), \(w_t = \hat{r}^e_{t+1} / (\gamma\hat{\sigma}^2_t)\) with the balance in the bill and the weight confined to \([0, 1.5]\), using the term-spread forecast and \(\gamma = 5\), and compare its certainty equivalent with a constant weight of one. Does the absolute view earn what Equation 16.6 predicts from the series’ \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\)?

title: 17  Expressing Views
text:
17.1 A View as a Bayesian Update
An allocator has an opinion: European credit will lag, commodities will pay, Japanese equity is cheap. How does that opinion become a weight? Black and Litterman (1992) answered that it should not become one directly, because an optimizer handed a hand-written return vector produces the extreme, unstable portfolios that Michaud (1989) called error maximization; the opinion should instead be blended with an equilibrium prior in proportion to how confidently it is held, and the optimizer given the blend. That construction, the Black-Litterman model, is the standard answer, and this chapter sets it beside two others that ask less of the allocator: views on the probabilities of historical scenarios (Meucci 2008), and views that are only a ranking (Almgren and Chriss 2006).
This chapter is tactical in the sense of Section 3.1: a view is conditioning information, and every portfolio below is a deviation from the strategic policy that Section 6.1 anchored on the equilibrium vector. We first state the three formulations as mathematics, then implement each on the sixteen risky class series, and finally express one opinion three ways and compare what each formulation committed to.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill for the reasons of Section 3.1.

title: 17  Expressing Views
text:
17.1.1 The Black-Litterman posterior
Write \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) for the vector of expected excess returns and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) for their covariance, as in Section 9.1. Black and Litterman (1991) treat \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) as unknown and center its prior on the equilibrium vector of Equation 6.6, read from market weights by the reverse optimization of Sharpe (1974),
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu} \sim N\!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}},\, \tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}} = \delta\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}},
\tag{17.1}\]
where \(\tau\) scales the prior’s uncertainty relative to the returns. A view is a statement about \(K\) linear combinations of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), collected in a \(K \times N\) pick matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\), with a stated value \(\boldsymbol{q}\) and an error whose covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) says how sure the allocator is:
\[
\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{q} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim N(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{\Omega}).
\tag{17.2}\]
A row of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) with a single one is an absolute view on one asset; a row with \(+1\) and \(-1\) is a relative view on a spread. Prior and likelihood are normal, so the posterior is normal, with mean and covariance
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{BL}}
= \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}
+ \tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'
  \left(\boldsymbol{P}\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}' + \boldsymbol{\Omega}\right)^{-1}
  \left(\boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\right),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
= \tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
- \tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'
  \left(\boldsymbol{P}\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}' + \boldsymbol{\Omega}\right)^{-1}
  \boldsymbol{P}\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.
\tag{17.3}\]
Satchell and Scowcroft (2000) give the Bayesian derivation, Kolm and Ritter (2017) the cleanest statement of what is conditioned on what, and Cheung (2010) and Walters (2014) the bookkeeping the original paper left out. Two features of Equation 17.3 decide everything below. The posterior mean moves away from the prior only in the directions \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\), so a view on one asset moves every asset that covaries with it. And \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) is the covariance of the mean, not of returns, and is never to be handed to a risk objective, the fourth point of the callout in Section 6.2.
Two parameters have no data behind them. \(\tau\) is the more discussed and the less important: He and Litterman (1999) set it at 0.05, Idzorek (2007) at 0.025, Walters (2014) surveys a range from \(1/T\) upward, and Meucci (2010) observes that if \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is proportional to \(\tau\) then \(\tau\) cancels from the posterior mean, which is the convention here. \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is the parameter that matters. He and Litterman (1999) take it diagonal with \(\omega_k = \boldsymbol{p}_k'\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{p}_k\), so a view on a volatile spread is held less tightly; Idzorek (2007) asks for a confidence between zero and one and solves for the \(\omega_k\) that delivers that fraction of the full-confidence tilt; Meucci (2010) gives the closed form of the same idea, used throughout this chapter:
\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \frac{1-c}{c}\;\boldsymbol{P}\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}',
\qquad c \in (0, 1).
\tag{17.4}\]
Substituting Equation 17.4 into Equation 17.3, the bracketed matrix becomes \(\boldsymbol{P}\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'/c\), \(\tau\) cancels, and the posterior value of each view portfolio is a weighted average of prior and view:
\[
\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{BL}}
= (1-c)\,\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}} + c\,\boldsymbol{q}.
\tag{17.5}\]
At \(c = \tfrac12\) allocator and market are weighted equally; as \(c \to 1\) the view is imposed and as \(c \to 0\) ignored. The confidence is therefore the size of the position rather than a nuisance parameter, and Section 17.2 traces it.
What the optimizer does with \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{BL}}\) is the result He and Litterman (1999) wrote the model to obtain. An investor with the market’s risk aversion holds \(\boldsymbol{w} = (\delta\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}\), and substituting Equation 17.3 with Equation 17.4 gives
\[
\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{BL}}
= (\delta\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{BL}}
= \boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mkt}} + \boldsymbol{P}'\boldsymbol{\Lambda},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \frac{c}{\delta}
  \left(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\right)^{-1}
  \left(\boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{eq}}\right).
\tag{17.6}\]
The posterior portfolio is the market plus a position in each view portfolio, and nothing else: an asset in no view keeps its market weight, however strongly it covaries with the assets that are. This is what distinguishes Black-Litterman from writing a number into \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) by hand: the update through \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\) moves the means of correlated assets by exactly enough that the optimizer sees no spread to exploit between them. Bertsimas et al. (2012) reach the same construction from inverse optimization, and Section 17.3 shows what happens without it. Under a long-only constraint Equation 17.6 holds until a weight reaches zero, after which the portfolio is the quadratic program of Section 12.1.

17.1.2 Views on scenarios: entropy pooling
Black-Litterman is a view on the mean under normality, and Meucci (2008) removes both restrictions. Take as the prior not a distribution but \(J\) scenarios \(\boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{r}_J\) with probabilities \(p_1, \dots, p_J\), here the 372 months of the sample with uniform weight. A view is any constraint on expectations under new probabilities \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{p}}\): a mean, a variance, a probability of loss, a ranking. Among all probability vectors that satisfy it, the posterior is the one closest to the prior in relative entropy,
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol{p}}
= \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{x}} \sum_{j=1}^{J} x_j \left(\ln x_j - \ln p_j\right)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\sum_j x_j = 1,
\quad \boldsymbol{H}\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{h},
\quad \boldsymbol{F}\boldsymbol{x} \le \boldsymbol{f},
\tag{17.7}\]
where each row of \(\boldsymbol{H}\) or \(\boldsymbol{F}\) holds the scenario values of one view function. The objective is the divergence of Kullback and Leibler (1951); choosing the least-divergent distribution consistent with stated moments is the maximum-entropy principle of Jaynes (1957); Csiszár (1975) proved the solution exists and is unique; and Robertson et al. (2005) brought the same device to macroeconomic forecasting. The solution is an exponential tilt,
\[
\tilde{p}_j \propto p_j \exp\!\left(-\boldsymbol{\theta}'\boldsymbol{H}_{\cdot j}
- \boldsymbol{\lambda}'\boldsymbol{F}_{\cdot j}\right),
\qquad \boldsymbol{\lambda} \ge \boldsymbol{0},
\tag{17.8}\]
with one multiplier per view, so the optimization runs over \(K\) numbers rather than \(J\) probabilities. Equation 17.8 is also why entropy pooling reproduces Black-Litterman when the scenarios are normal and the views are on means (Meucci 2006, 2008): a tilt in the direction of a view portfolio shifts every other asset by its covariance with that portfolio. Where the scenarios are not normal the two part, and Section 17.3 measures by how much.
A posterior that concentrates on a few months has thrown the rest of the history away, and the diagnostic is the effective number of scenarios,
\[
N_{\text{eff}} = \exp\!\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{J} \tilde{p}_j \ln \tilde{p}_j\right),
\tag{17.9}\]
the construction Meucci (2009) uses for the effective number of bets in Section 9.3: \(J\) under the uniform prior, falling toward one as the mass concentrates. For a view that moves one mean by \(k\) standard errors, the divergence of the tilt is \(k^2/2T\) to second order, so
\[
N_{\text{eff}} \approx T \exp\!\left(-\frac{k^2}{2T}\right),
\tag{17.10}\]
which says where the entropy step bites: a view within a few standard errors costs almost nothing, and one tens of standard errors away leaves a fraction of the history. Confidence enters by opinion pooling, \(\boldsymbol{p}_c = (1-c)\,\boldsymbol{p} + c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{p}}\) (Meucci 2008), which gives the posterior mean the form of Equation 17.5.

17.1.3 Views as an ordering: the centroid
Both formulations ask for a number, and Salcher et al. (2026) argue that a number is often more than an allocator honestly has: what survives estimation error in a cross-section of means is their ordering, and a rule that commits to the ranking alone loses less out of sample than one that commits to magnitudes. Almgren and Chriss (2006) formalize the ranking as a view. If the allocator believes \(\mu_{\pi(1)} \ge \dots \ge \mu_{\pi(N)}\) for a permutation \(\pi\), the mean vectors consistent with that belief form a cone \(Q\), and for any convex feasible set the portfolio that maximizes expected return over \(Q\) maximizes \(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{c}\), where
\[
\boldsymbol{c} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\boldsymbol{\mu} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu} \in Q\right],
\qquad
c_{\pi(j)} \approx \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{N + 1 - j - \alpha}{N - 2\alpha + 1}\right),
\quad \alpha = 0.4424 - 0.1185\,N^{-0.21},
\tag{17.11}\]
is the centroid of the cone under a spherically symmetric distribution, with the closed-form approximation of the same paper. It is the vector of expected order statistics of \(N\) standard normals: symmetric about zero, wider-spaced at the ends, carrying no level and no scale. Herold (2003) works the same problem with qualitative forecasts, and Grinold (1989) supplies the reason a ranking can be worth money: the value of a signal is its correlation with realized returns, which a correct ordering delivers without any magnitude. What a centroid does not say is how large the position should be.

title: 17  Expressing Views
section: 17.2 Three Ways to Make a Weight
text:
17.2 Three Ways to Make a Weight
The prior is the class-level equilibrium of Section 6.2, rebuilt verbatim so that the two chapters cannot disagree; the market weights of the eleven non-equity classes are the stated proxy of that chapter’s worked box.






NoteThe prior of Section 6.2, rebuilt






eq_ids     <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
region_of  <- setNames(sim_assets$region, sim_assets$asset_id)
eq_classes <- grep("_equity$", colnames(Re), value = TRUE)

cap_region <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% eq_ids) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = paste0(region_of[asset], "_equity")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(cap = sum(market_cap), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = class, values_from = cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
cap_mat <- as.matrix(cap_region[, eq_classes])
d <- zoo::index(Re)
W_eq <- t(vapply(seq_along(d), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) d[1] - 31 else d[i - 1]
  j <- max(which(cap_region$date <= cutoff))
  cap_mat[j, ] / sum(cap_mat[j, ])
}, numeric(length(eq_classes))))
colnames(W_eq) <- eq_classes

# ASSUMPTION, not data: the split of world wealth across the four blocks.
block <- c(equity = 0.40, government = 0.40, credit = 0.15, commodity = 0.05)
W16 <- matrix(0, nrow(Re), N, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Re)))
for (r in sub("_equity$", "", eq_classes)) {
  s <- W_eq[, paste0(r, "_equity")]
  W16[, paste0(r, "_equity")]     <- block[["equity"]]     * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_government")] <- block[["government"]] * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_credit")]     <- block[["credit"]]     * s
}
W16[, "GLOBAL_commodity"] <- block[["commodity"]]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W16) - 1) < 1e-10), identical(colnames(W16), colnames(Re)))

mkt16_e <- rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re))
delta16 <- mean(mkt16_e) / stats::var(mkt16_e)                        # @eq-06-delta
w_mkt   <- colMeans(W16)
mu_eq   <- setNames(delta16 * as.numeric(S %*% w_mkt), colnames(Re))  # @eq-06-equilibrium

# The equity-only equilibrium of the same chapter, for the five-class examples.
mkt_e  <- rowSums(W_eq * zoo::coredata(Re[, eq_classes]))
delta  <- mean(mkt_e) / stats::var(mkt_e)
w_mkt5 <- colMeans(W_eq)
S5     <- S[eq_classes, eq_classes]
mu_eq5 <- setNames(delta * as.numeric(S5 %*% w_mkt5), eq_classes)

c(delta = delta16, delta_equity = delta)
#>        delta delta_equity 
#>       10.887        4.789




Two functions from Section 6.3 are reused unchanged: tangency_lo() solves the long-only tangency problem as one quadratic program, and make_moments() hands a mean vector the package did not compute to optimize.portfolio().

tangency_lo <- function(mu, S) {
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(mu)), names(mu)))
  N <- length(mu)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, N),
                            Amat = cbind(mu, diag(N)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, N)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), names(mu))
}
make_moments <- function(mu, S) {
  force(mu); force(S)
  function(R, portfolio, ...) list(mu = mu, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = mu, var = S)
}
spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

w_prior <- tangency_lo(mu_eq, S)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(w_prior, w_mkt, tolerance = 1e-6)))   # the prior buys the market


17.2.1 Black-Litterman with two views
Two views, one relative and one absolute: United States credit will outperform European credit by two percentage points a year, and commodities will earn four percent a year above the bill. Each is a row of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) and an entry of \(\boldsymbol{q}\), in the monthly units of the data.

P <- matrix(0, 2, N, dimnames = list(c("credit_spread", "commodity"), colnames(Re)))
P["credit_spread", "US_credit"]     <-  1
P["credit_spread", "EU_credit"]     <- -1
P["commodity",     "GLOBAL_commodity"] <- 1
q <- c(credit_spread = 0.02, commodity = 0.04) / 12
stopifnot(identical(colnames(P), colnames(Re)), identical(names(q), rownames(P)))

prior_views <- as.numeric(P %*% mu_eq)
stopifnot(prior_views[1] < 0)      # the prior puts US_credit below EU_credit, as the text explains




Table 17.1: The two views as rows of the pick matrix, with what the equilibrium prior says about the same portfolios. Only the nonzero columns of P are shown; annualized.





view portfolio
prior says
view says



credit_spread
-1 EU_credit +1 US_credit
-3.36%
2.00%


commodity
+1 GLOBAL_commodity
3.87%
4.00%








The prior disagrees with the first view by 5.4 percentage points, because under the proxy weights European credit covaries more with the market than United States credit; the second view is 0.1 points from the prior. Equation 17.3 with Equation 17.4 is a few lines, and writing them is the only way to have a confidence parameter, because black.litterman() has none.

bl_post <- function(mu, S, P, q, conf, tau = 1) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(P), names(mu)), nrow(P) == length(q))
  Omega   <- (1 - conf) / conf * P %*% (tau * S) %*% t(P)          # @eq-17-omega
  M       <- solve(P %*% (tau * S) %*% t(P) + Omega)
  mu_post <- mu + as.numeric((tau * S) %*% t(P) %*% M %*% (q - P %*% mu))   # @eq-17-posterior
  S_mu    <- tau * S - (tau * S) %*% t(P) %*% M %*% P %*% (tau * S)
  list(mu = setNames(mu_post, names(mu)), S_mu = S_mu, Omega = Omega)
}

post <- bl_post(mu_eq, S, P, q, conf = 0.5)
bl   <- black.litterman(Re, P = P, Mu = mu_eq, Views = q)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(post$mu), as.numeric(bl$BLMu))),          # the package at c = 1/2
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(post$S_mu), unname(bl$BLSigma))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(bl_post(mu_eq, S, P, q, 0.5, tau = 0.05)$mu, post$mu)),  # tau cancels
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(P %*% post$mu), 0.5 * prior_views + 0.5 * unname(q))))  # @eq-17-pooling
round(cbind(prior = prior_views, view = q, posterior = as.numeric(P %*% post$mu)) * 12, 4)
#>                 prior view posterior
#> credit_spread -0.0336 0.02   -0.0068
#> commodity      0.0387 0.04    0.0394

The four assertions carry the theory: black.litterman() is Equation 17.3 at \(c = \tfrac12\), since its fixed \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\) is Equation 17.4 at that confidence; changing \(\tau\) leaves the posterior mean untouched; and each view portfolio lands at the midpoint of prior and view.






Noteblack.litterman() with views: three things to check before believing it



The function takes the full matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\) as \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\), off-diagonals included, so covarying view portfolios are treated as correlated errors, which is Equation 17.4 and not the diagonal convention of He and Litterman (1999); a textbook example with independent views will not match it. P must be a matrix even for one view, since a plain vector fails inside tcrossprod(). And Views is not checked against nrow(P): a shorter vector is recycled without a message, so one number silently becomes every view.

one_number <- black.litterman(Re, P = P, Mu = mu_eq, Views = q[1])
both_same  <- black.litterman(Re, P = P, Mu = mu_eq, Views = c(q[1], q[1]))
c(recycled_silently = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(one_number$BLMu), as.numeric(both_same$BLMu))),
  vector_P_fails    = inherits(try(black.litterman(Re, P = P[2, ], Mu = mu_eq, Views = q[2]),
                                   silent = TRUE), "try-error"))
#> recycled_silently    vector_P_fails 
#>              TRUE              TRUE

The stopifnot() at the top of bl_post() is the guard the package lacks.


What the two views do to the sixteen means comes first, from one frame with one row per asset and estimate.

mu_long <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = rep(colnames(Re), 2),
  kind  = rep(c("prior", "posterior, c = 0.5"), each = N),
  value = c(mu_eq, post$mu) * 12
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(asset = factor(asset, levels = names(sort(mu_eq))))
stopifnot(nrow(mu_long) == 2 * N, !anyNA(mu_long$value))

shift <- (post$mu - mu_eq) * 1200
stopifnot(all(shift[grep("^(EU|CH|UK)_", names(shift))] < 0))   # the caption of @fig-17-bl-means
round(sort(shift), 2)
#>        EU_credit        EU_equity    EU_government        CH_credit 
#>            -2.87            -2.67            -2.48            -2.17 
#>        UK_credit    CH_government        CH_equity    UK_government 
#>            -1.95            -1.94            -1.68            -1.50 
#>        UK_equity        JP_credit    JP_government        US_equity 
#>            -1.47            -0.82            -0.60            -0.47 
#>        JP_equity        US_credit GLOBAL_commodity    US_government 
#>            -0.33            -0.19             0.06             0.11








Figure 17.1: Equilibrium and Black-Litterman means for the sixteen series at a confidence of one half, annualized. Each segment joins an asset’s prior to its posterior. The view on European credit pulls down everything that covaries with it, which on this market is every European, Swiss and British series; the view on commodities moves almost nothing else.




A view on two credit series moved 11 of the sixteen means by more than half a percentage point: EU_credit falls by 2.9 points and EU_equity, in no view, by 2.7, because it covaries with European credit. That is Equation 17.3 at work, and Equation 17.6 says what it buys.

w_post <- tangency_lo(post$mu, S)
w_pkg  <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                                            momentFUN = make_moments(post$mu, S)))
stopifnot(max(abs(w_pkg[colnames(Re)] - w_post)) < 1e-6)

# @eq-17-weights, unconstrained: the tilt lives only on the assets a view names.
tilt    <- solve(delta16 * S, post$mu) - w_mkt
in_view <- colSums(P != 0) > 0
stopifnot(max(abs(tilt[!in_view])) < 1e-8)
round(tilt[in_view], 4)
#>        EU_credit GLOBAL_commodity        US_credit 
#>          -0.3381           0.0768           0.3381

moved <- (w_post - w_prior)[abs(w_post - w_prior) > 0.005]
round(sort(moved), 3)
#>    EU_government        EU_equity    UK_government    CH_government 
#>           -0.070           -0.051           -0.034           -0.030 
#>        EU_credit    JP_government        JP_credit        UK_credit 
#>           -0.026           -0.020           -0.014           -0.013 
#>        CH_credit        JP_equity        US_equity        US_credit 
#>           -0.011            0.009            0.021            0.040 
#> GLOBAL_commodity    US_government 
#>            0.054            0.144

Unconstrained, Equation 17.6 holds to machine precision: the thirteen assets in no view keep their market weight, US_credit and EU_credit move by +33.8 and -33.8 points, and commodities by +7.7. The long-only tangency portfolio cannot short EU_credit, so it sells what it has and the constraint redistributes the rest: 14 weights move by more than half a point, US_government by 14.4, because it is the least volatile home for money the constraint would otherwise have shorted, as Section 12.1 explains.
The confidence is the size of all of this, and tracing it shows the weights sliding from the market portfolio to the portfolio the views alone would buy.

confs <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.99)
trace <- lapply(confs, function(cc) {
  w <- tangency_lo(bl_post(mu_eq, S, P, q, cc)$mu, S)
  tibble::tibble(conf = cc, asset = names(w), weight = w)
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
stopifnot(nrow(trace) == length(confs) * N, !anyNA(trace$weight))
shown <- c("US_government", "US_credit", "GLOBAL_commodity", "EU_equity", "EU_credit")
us_c  <- trace$weight[trace$asset == "US_credit"]
stopifnot(any(diff(us_c) > 0), any(diff(us_c) < 0))   # the path of a named asset is not monotone








Figure 17.2: Long-only tangency weights of five series as the confidence in the two views rises from 0.01 to 0.99. At the left every series holds its market weight; at the right the views are imposed exactly. The path between is not monotone even for the assets a view names, because the long-only constraint decides where the money shorted from European credit goes.




At \(c = 0.01\) the portfolio is the market to within 0.7 points in any weight; at \(c = 0.99\) US_government holds 43% and commodities 13%. Nothing in the data chose any point on that path; the confidence is a statement about the allocator, and Section 28.1 treats the same number as the size of an uncertainty set rather than a probability.

17.2.2 Through set.portfolio.moments()

The route that needs no custom function is method = "black_litterman", which set.portfolio.moments() passes on to black.litterman(). The arguments must travel through optimize.portfolio(), because a direct call recovers them with match.call() and sees symbols rather than values, as Section 6.2 showed; with views the route works and carries one more trap.

opt_spm <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                              momentFUN = "set.portfolio.moments", method = "black_litterman",
                              Mu = mu_eq, P = P, Views = q)
opt_fix <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                              momentFUN = "set.portfolio.moments", method = "black_litterman",
                              Mu = mu_eq, P = P, Views = q, momentargs = list(sigma = S))
c(mu_is_posterior      = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(opt_spm$moment_values$mu), as.numeric(bl$BLMu))),
  sigma_is_BLSigma     = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(opt_spm$moment_values$sigma), unname(bl$BLSigma))),
  max_weight_gap_pp    = 100 * max(abs(extractWeights(opt_spm)[colnames(Re)] - w_post)),
  fixed_max_gap_pp     = 100 * max(abs(extractWeights(opt_fix)[colnames(Re)] - w_post)))
#>   mu_is_posterior  sigma_is_BLSigma max_weight_gap_pp  fixed_max_gap_pp 
#>       1.000000000       1.000000000      12.986621033       0.000001196







WarningWith views, BLSigma is no longer a rescaled \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)



With the prior alone, set.portfolio.moments(method = "black_litterman") hands the optimizer \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/2\), which a tangency portfolio does not notice. With views it hands \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) of Equation 17.3, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) minus a rank-\(K\) correction in the directions of the view portfolios, and the tangency portfolio is solved on the wrong risk: the commodity weight comes out at 23% against 10% on \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), a gap of 13 points in one weight, and nothing warns. The remedy is momentargs: set.portfolio.moments() fills only the moments it is not given, so momentargs = list(sigma = S) keeps the posterior mean, restores the return covariance, and agrees with the hand computation to 1e-08.



17.2.3 Entropy pooling on the 372 months
The prior is uniform over the 372 months; the series is US_equity; the views are that its mean will be two percentage points a year above the sample mean and that its volatility will be twenty percent below the sample volatility. A view on a mean is a row of \(\boldsymbol{H}\) holding the series; a view on a volatility is a row holding its square, with \(\boldsymbol{h}\) set to the second moment the view implies.

p0    <- rep(1 / T, T)                          # the uniform prior
Aeq0  <- matrix(1, 1, T)                        # probabilities sum to one
V     <- as.numeric(zoo::coredata(Re[, "US_equity"]))
m0    <- mean(V); s0 <- stats::sd(V)
m_v   <- m0 + 0.02 / 12                         # the mean view
s_v   <- 0.8 * s0                               # the volatility view

eff_n <- function(p) exp(-sum(p[p > 0] * log(p[p > 0])))     # @eq-17-effective

ep_mean <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, Aeq = rbind(Aeq0, V),      beq = c(1, m_v)))
ep_vol  <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, Aeq = rbind(Aeq0, V, V^2), beq = c(1, m0, s_v^2 + m0^2)))
ep_both <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, Aeq = rbind(Aeq0, V, V^2), beq = c(1, m_v, s_v^2 + m_v^2)))

posterior <- list(`mean view` = ep_mean$p_, `volatility view` = ep_vol$p_, `both views` = ep_both$p_)
stopifnot(all(vapply(posterior, function(p) abs(sum(p) - 1) < 1e-6, logical(1))),
          abs(sum(ep_both$p_ * V) - m_v) < 1e-8,
          abs(sqrt(sum(ep_both$p_ * V^2) - sum(ep_both$p_ * V)^2) - s_v) < 1e-8)
vapply(posterior, eff_n, numeric(1))
#>       mean view volatility view      both views 
#>           371.7           362.8           363.1







NoteEntropyProg(): what the signature does not say



Aeq and beq have no default, so a view expressed only as inequalities still needs Aeq = matrix(1, 1, J), beq = 1 for the probabilities to sum to one; leave them out and the error names a missing argument, not the constraint. The prior must sum to one within \(10^{-5}\). Every call runs nloptr’s derivative checker and reports as an R message, hence the suppressMessages() above; on a squared series the checker sometimes reports one error from its finite-difference tolerance while the optimization converges and hits the constraint, which the stopifnot() confirms. The result p_ is a \(J \times 1\) matrix, not a vector. And a view the scenarios cannot satisfy, a mean beyond the range of the data or a volatility near zero, does not fail as infeasible: the multipliers diverge and the function stops with Sum of revised probabilities is greater than 1!, the symptom rather than the cause.


The mean view leaves 371.7 effective months of 372, the volatility view 362.8. The probabilities themselves are the object to look at, from one frame.

p_long <- lapply(names(posterior), function(k) {
  tibble::tibble(date = zoo::index(Re), kind = k,
                 p_rel = as.numeric(posterior[[k]]) * T)          # relative to the prior 1/T
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = sprintf("%s: %.0f effective months",
                               kind, vapply(kind, function(k) eff_n(posterior[[k]]), numeric(1))))
stopifnot(nrow(p_long) == 3 * T, !anyNA(p_long$p_rel))

worst <- p_long |> dplyr::filter(grepl("^volatility", kind)) |> dplyr::slice_min(p_rel, n = 3)
stopifnot(all(in_episode(worst$date, "liquidity_shock") | in_episode(worst$date, "credit_crisis")),
          in_episode(worst$date[1], "liquidity_shock"))
worst
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   date       kind                                   p_rel
#>   <date>     <chr>                                  <dbl>
#> 1 2129-03-31 volatility view: 363 effective months 0.0299
#> 2 2129-04-30 volatility view: 363 effective months 0.0564
#> 3 2117-10-31 volatility view: 363 effective months 0.219








Figure 17.3: Posterior scenario probabilities relative to the uniform prior, month by month, for a view on the mean, a view on the volatility, and both. The mean view tilts every month by a little; the volatility view removes the months of the liquidity shock and the credit crisis almost entirely and spreads their mass over the calm ones.




The mean view is an exponential tilt in US_equity’s own return, Equation 17.8, so good months are weighted up and bad months down by a few percent each. The volatility view is a tilt in the squared return and falls hardest on the months furthest from the mean in either direction: March of model year 29, in the liquidity shock, keeps 3.0% of its prior probability. meucci.moments() turns the probabilities into probability-weighted first and second moments.

mm <- meucci.moments(Re, ep_both$p_)
mu_ep <- setNames(as.numeric(mm$mu), colnames(Re)); S_ep <- mm$sigma
stopifnot(identical(rownames(mm$mu), colnames(Re)),
          abs(mu_ep[["US_equity"]] - m_v) < 1e-8,
          abs(sqrt(S_ep["US_equity", "US_equity"]) - s_v) < 1e-8)

moved_mu  <- (mu_ep - mu_s) * 1200
moved_vol <- sqrt(diag(S_ep)) / sqrt(diag(S)) - 1
round(rbind(mean_shift_pp = moved_mu, vol_change = 100 * moved_vol)[, order(-abs(moved_mu))][, 1:6], 2)
#>               EU_equity CH_equity UK_equity US_equity JP_equity EU_credit
#> mean_shift_pp      3.74      2.68      2.28         2      1.87      1.04
#> vol_change       -11.65    -10.39    -11.55       -20     -6.43     -9.32

The view named one series and moved sixteen: EU_equity’s mean rises by 3.7 points and UK_equity’s volatility falls by 12%, because the months the volatility view discarded were their bad months too. With the uniform prior meucci.moments() returns \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\,(T-1)/T\), which differs from stats::cov() by 0.27% and is invisible to a tangency portfolio. The portfolio follows by the package route, method = "meucci" with the posterior probabilities, which unlike the Black-Litterman branch reads its argument by value and so also works on a direct call.

opt_ep <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                             method = "meucci", posterior_p = ep_both$p_)
w_ep   <- extractWeights(opt_ep)[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(opt_ep$moment_values$mu), as.numeric(mm$mu))),
          max(abs(w_ep - tangency_lo(mu_ep, S_ep))) < 1e-6)
w_smp  <- tangency_lo(mu_s, S)

cmp <- cbind(sample = w_smp, entropy = w_ep)
round(cmp[rowSums(cmp > 0.005) > 0, ], 3)
#>                  sample entropy
#> EU_equity         0.094   0.124
#> GLOBAL_commodity  0.031   0.012
#> JP_equity         0.000   0.010
#> US_credit         0.004   0.221
#> US_equity         0.186   0.277
#> US_government     0.684   0.352

The sample tangency portfolio holds 68% in US_government and 0.4% in US_credit; under a view about US_equity’s volatility the second becomes 22%. Nothing was said about credit, but US_credit has the skewness of -1.45 that Section 4.1 measured and its worst months are the equity market’s worst months, so a view that discounts those months re-rates it. The view is on one number and the posterior is on the whole history.
Where the step bites is a matter of distance, and Equation 17.10 says how to measure it.

se_m <- s0 / sqrt(T)
ks   <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 40)
rs   <- c(0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.25)
cost <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(ks, function(k) {
    e <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, Aeq = rbind(Aeq0, V), beq = c(1, m0 + k * se_m)))
    tibble::tibble(view = sprintf("mean %+d standard errors (%.0f pp a year)", k, k * se_m * 1200),
                   n_eff = eff_n(e$p_), max_p = max(e$p_) * T, approx = T * exp(-k^2 / (2 * T)))
  }),
  lapply(rs, function(r) {
    e <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, Aeq = rbind(Aeq0, V, V^2), beq = c(1, m0, (r * s0)^2 + m0^2)))
    tibble::tibble(view = sprintf("volatility at %.0f%% of sample", 100 * r),
                   n_eff = eff_n(e$p_), max_p = max(e$p_) * T,
                   approx = T * exp(-0.5 * (r^2 - 1 - log(r^2))))
  }))
