A mean view five standard errors from the sample, already 14 percentage points a year, keeps 359 of 372 months; forty keep 60 and put 111 times the prior mass on the single best month. Equation 17.10 tracks the measured number until the tilt reaches the skewed tail, where the normal approximation understates what the data can still supply. In the units an allocator states them in, the volatility view is the expensive one: a twenty percent cut costs 9 months where two points on the mean cost 0.3, because Equation 4.3 made the variance the input a sample knows well and Equation 6.1 the mean the one it does not. In standard errors of the respective estimate, two points on the mean are 0.7 standard errors away and the twenty percent cut 5.5, and Equation 17.10 prices a view by that distance alone.

17.2.4 Ordinal views on the five equity classes
The last formulation asks for no number. The view is that Japanese equity will lead and that the other four keep the order the sample gave them; order lists the classes from lowest expected return to highest, by column index, built here by name.

Req      <- Re[, eq_classes]
asc_smp  <- names(sort(mu_s[eq_classes]))                      # sample order, ascending
view_asc <- c(setdiff(asc_smp, "JP_equity"), "JP_equity")      # Japan promoted to the top
ord      <- match(view_asc, colnames(Req))
stopifnot(!anyNA(ord), length(ord) == 5L)
view_asc
#> [1] "CH_equity" "UK_equity" "US_equity" "EU_equity" "JP_equity"

meucci.ranking() writes each adjacent pair of the ranking as an inequality row of Equation 17.7, \(\mathbb{E}[r_{\pi(j)}] - \mathbb{E}[r_{\pi(j+1)}] \le 0\), and returns the posterior moments. It discards the probabilities, so the same constraints go to EntropyProg() beside it to recover them.

mr  <- suppressMessages(meucci.ranking(Req, p0, ord))
Vk  <- zoo::coredata(Req)[, ord[1:4]] - zoo::coredata(Req)[, ord[2:5]]   # the rows meucci.ranking() builds
epr <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, A = t(Vk), b = rep(0, 4), Aeq = Aeq0, beq = 1))
mu_rank <- setNames(as.numeric(mr$mu), eq_classes)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(t(zoo::coredata(Req)) %*% epr$p_), unname(mu_rank))),
          all(diff(mu_rank[view_asc]) > -1e-6))                            # the ranking holds, to solver tolerance
tied <- names(which(abs(mu_rank - mu_rank[["JP_equity"]]) < 1e-6))
stopifnot(names(which.min(mu_s[eq_classes])) == "JP_equity",               # the text: Japan's sample mean is the lowest
          setequal(tied, c("JP_equity", tail(setdiff(asc_smp, "JP_equity"), 2))))   # tied with the two highest

round(rbind(sample = mu_s[eq_classes], ranked = mu_rank)[, view_asc] * 12, 4)
#>        CH_equity UK_equity US_equity EU_equity JP_equity
#> sample    0.0970    0.0991    0.1130    0.1341    0.0563
#> ranked    0.0765    0.0765    0.0975    0.0975    0.0975
c(effective_months = eff_n(epr$p_))
#> effective_months 
#>              370

The ranking holds in the posterior, but not as a ranking. The constraint is weak, and the least-divergent way to put JP_equity, whose sample mean is the lowest of the five by up to 7.8 points, at the top is to tie it with the two highest at 9.7% and pull the other two below; 3 of the four inequalities hold as ties. That costs 2.0 effective months, almost nothing, and hands the optimizer three assets it cannot tell apart by mean. The centroid of Equation 17.11 commits to more, a definite spacing, and ac.ranking() returns it for a complete sort.

set.seed(1602)
c_ac <- setNames(ac.ranking(Req, ord), colnames(Req))
c_mc <- setNames(centroid.complete.mc(ord, simulations = 1000), colnames(Req))

# @eq-17-centroid by hand, assigned so that the top of the ranking gets the largest value.
centroid_ac <- function(n) {
  alpha <- 0.4424 - 0.1185 * n^(-0.21)
  qnorm((n + 1 - seq_len(n) - alpha) / (n - 2 * alpha + 1))
}
c_an <- setNames(numeric(5), colnames(Req)); c_an[rev(ord)] <- centroid_ac(5)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c_ac / max(c_ac), c_an / max(c_an))),   # ac.ranking() is the formula, rescaled
          max(abs(c_mc - c_an)) < 0.05)                              # Monte Carlo agrees

round(rbind(ac_ranking = c_ac, formula = c_an, monte_carlo = c_mc)[, view_asc], 4)
#>             CH_equity UK_equity US_equity EU_equity JP_equity
#> ac_ranking     -0.050   -0.0211    0.0000    0.0211     0.050
#> formula        -1.167   -0.4937    0.0000    0.4937     1.167
#> monte_carlo    -1.151   -0.4882    0.0181    0.5250     1.189







Warningac.ranking() ignores its scale argument



The documentation says the centroid is scaled to the median of the asset means, and the function reads a max.value argument to that end. The scaling helper then discards it and maps the centroid onto \([-0.05, 0.05]\) whatever the data: the top-ranked asset is assigned five percent per period, 60 percent a year on monthly data, and passing max.value changes nothing. The vector carries no names. Treat the output as a direction, name it yourself, and set the scale yourself.


The three other centroid functions encode views that are less than a complete sort, each returning an unnamed vector in asset-index order.

set.seed(1602)
tibble::tibble(
  fn = c("centroid.complete.mc(order)", "centroid.buckets(list)",
         "centroid.sign(positive, negative)", "centroid.sectors(list)"),
  view = c("a complete ordering of all assets",
           "groups ordered against each other, no order inside a group",
           "positive and negative expected returns, each side ordered",
           "an ordering inside each sector, no view across sectors"),
  example = c(paste(round(centroid.complete.mc(c(2, 1, 3, 5, 4)), 2), collapse = " "),
              paste(round(centroid.buckets(list(c(1, 5), c(2, 4), 3)), 2), collapse = " "),
              paste(round(centroid.sign(positive = c(2, 3), negative = c(5, 4)), 2), collapse = " "),
              paste(round(centroid.sectors(list(c(2, 1, 3), c(5, 4))), 2), collapse = " "))
) |>
  kable(align = "lll", col.names = c("function", "the view it encodes", "five-asset example"))

Every one is a Monte Carlo average of sorted normal draws, so the result depends on the seed and on simulations; the sector variant centers each sector at zero and says nothing about one sector against another; the bucket variant gives every member of a bucket the same value, the right encoding of “these are in the middle” and the wrong one if the allocator has any opinion inside the bucket.
A centroid is a direction. Handed to a tangency solver alone it selects the top of the ranking and nothing else, because the Sharpe ratio is invariant to the scale of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and a zero-mean vector on five correlated assets offers no diversification.

kappa5 <- diff(range(mu_eq5)) / diff(range(c_an))    # the ranking given the prior's dispersion
mu_c5  <- mu_eq5 + kappa5 * c_an

W5 <- cbind(`equilibrium`      = tangency_lo(mu_eq5, S5),
            `sample mean`      = tangency_lo(mu_s[eq_classes], S5),
            `entropy ranking`  = tangency_lo(mu_rank, mr$sigma),
            `centroid alone`   = tangency_lo(c_an, S5),
            `prior + centroid` = tangency_lo(mu_c5, S5))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W5), eq_classes),
          isTRUE(all.equal(W5[, "equilibrium"], w_mkt5, tolerance = 1e-6)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(tangency_lo(c_an, S5), tangency_lo(10 * c_an, S5))))
zeroed <- names(which(W5[, "prior + centroid"] < 0.005))
stopifnot(view_asc[4] == "EU_equity", setequal(zeroed, view_asc[1:2]),       # the text names them
          W5["JP_equity", "prior + centroid"] > w_mkt5[["JP_equity"]],
          W5["EU_equity", "prior + centroid"] > w_mkt5[["EU_equity"]])

The entropy ranking, which tied three classes, holds 64% US_equity and 30% JP_equity: with equal means the optimizer sorts by variance and covariance, which is Equation 9.3 at work inside a tangency problem. The centroid alone holds 100% JP_equity. The level came from the prior and the size from a choice; the ranking supplied only the direction, which is all a ranking is.

title: 17  Expressing Views
text:
17.3 One Opinion, Three Formulations
The opinion is that United States credit is expensive and Japanese equity is cheap: as a portfolio, long JP_equity and short US_credit. Each formulation receives it in its own language: a relative view three percentage points a year above the equilibrium spread at a confidence of one half; the same spread as an entropy view on the historical scenarios, pooled at the same confidence; and a bucket ranking with US_credit at the bottom, JP_equity at the top, and no opinion about the fourteen between.

P_a <- matrix(0, 1, N, dimnames = list("JP_vs_UScredit", colnames(Re)))
P_a[1, "JP_equity"] <- 1; P_a[1, "US_credit"] <- -1
spread_eq <- as.numeric(P_a %*% mu_eq)
q_a <- spread_eq + 0.03 / 12
c_a <- 0.5

# A: Black-Litterman.
mu_A <- bl_post(mu_eq, S, P_a, q_a, c_a)$mu

# B: entropy pooling. The scenarios are the sample months shifted so that
# their mean is the equilibrium vector: the three formulations share a prior,
# and the covariance and every higher moment of the history are untouched.
Rc <- sweep(zoo::coredata(Re), 2, mu_s - mu_eq)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(colMeans(Rc)), unname(mu_eq))))
V_a  <- as.numeric(Rc %*% t(P_a))
stopifnot(0.03 < stats::sd(V_a) * sqrt(12) / sqrt(T / 12))   # the view is within one standard error of the mean
ep_a <- suppressMessages(EntropyProg(p0, Aeq = rbind(Aeq0, V_a), beq = c(1, q_a)))
p_a  <- (1 - c_a) * p0 + c_a * as.numeric(ep_a$p_)                     # opinion pooling
mm_a <- meucci.moments(Rc, p_a)
mu_B <- setNames(as.numeric(mm_a$mu), colnames(Re)); S_B <- mm_a$sigma

# C: a bucket centroid, given the size the other two used.
set.seed(1602)
i_top <- match("JP_equity", colnames(Re)); i_bot <- match("US_credit", colnames(Re))
cb    <- setNames(centroid.buckets(list(i_bot, setdiff(seq_len(N), c(i_bot, i_top)), i_top)),
                  colnames(Re))
kappa <- c_a * (q_a - spread_eq) / (cb[["JP_equity"]] - cb[["US_credit"]])
mu_C  <- mu_eq + kappa * cb

spreads <- c(prior = spread_eq, BL = P_a %*% mu_A, entropy = P_a %*% mu_B, centroid = P_a %*% mu_C)
stopifnot(all(abs(spreads[-1] - ((1 - c_a) * spread_eq + c_a * q_a)) < 1e-10))
round(spreads * 12, 4)
#>    prior       BL  entropy centroid 
#>   0.0419   0.0569   0.0569   0.0569

All three posteriors put the spread at 5.69% a year, halfway from the equilibrium’s 4.19% to the view’s 7.19%, so the strength of the opinion about its own subject is identical. Everything else differs.

W3 <- cbind(market = w_mkt, `Black-Litterman` = tangency_lo(mu_A, S),
            `entropy pooling` = tangency_lo(mu_B, S_B), `centroid` = tangency_lo(mu_C, S))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W3), colnames(Re)), !anyNA(W3))

p_te <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w - w_mkt) %*% S %*% (w - w_mkt))) * sqrt(12)
p_sr <- function(w, m, SS = S) sum(m * w) * 12 / (sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% SS %*% w)) * sqrt(12))
turnover <- function(w) sum(abs(w - w_mkt)) / 2

summ <- tibble::tibble(
  formulation = colnames(W3),
  specified   = c("market weights", "a number and a confidence",
                  "a number and a confidence", "an order"),
  te          = apply(W3, 2, p_te),
  turnover    = apply(W3, 2, turnover),
  held        = colSums(W3 > 0.005),
  sr_prior    = apply(W3, 2, p_sr, m = mu_eq),
  jp          = W3["JP_equity", ],
  usc         = W3["US_credit", ]
)
stopifnot(identical(summ$formulation, colnames(W3)))

named <- c("JP_equity", "US_credit")
d_ep  <- (W3[, "entropy pooling"] - w_mkt)[setdiff(colnames(Re), named)]
stopifnot(sum(abs(W3[, "Black-Litterman"] - w_mkt) > 1e-6) == 2L,   # @eq-17-weights: only the named assets move
          summ$formulation[which.max(summ$turnover)] == "centroid",
          W3["US_credit", "centroid"] < 0.005)

Figure 17.4: Long-only tangency weights under the three formulations of one opinion, against the market portfolio, from one data frame. Black-Litterman and entropy pooling move the two assets the opinion named and little else; the centroid, written into the mean vector asset by asset, is turned by the optimizer into a hedged position across the credit and government series.




Read 2 across. Black-Litterman and entropy pooling put the tracking error within 0.01 points of each other, at 0.69% and 0.70%, and both move JP_equity from 3.8% to about 7.2%. The first touches nothing else, which is Equation 17.6: the unconstrained tilt is \(\boldsymbol{P}'\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), and the long-only constraint does not bind. The second moves 9 other weights by more than half a point, CH_government the most at 3.0 points, the difference between an exponential tilt on 372 skewed months and a normal update; it is small here because the spread series has a skewness of -0.19, and on the volatility view above it was not.
The centroid committed to the least and moved the portfolio the most: a turnover of 20% against 3%, US_credit sold to zero, and 10 other weights changed by more than half a point. The reason is not the ranking but the way it entered \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\). Adding \(\kappa\boldsymbol{c}\) to the prior lowered US_credit’s mean and left US_government’s where it was, and the optimizer read that as an opinion about the spread between two series that move together: the unconstrained tilt \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\kappa\boldsymbol{c}\) is a large short in credit hedged with a large long in government bonds, which the long-only constraint clips into what Figure 17.4 shows. Black-Litterman moved US_government’s mean by -0.12 points along with credit’s, so no such spread appeared. A view is coherent with the covariance matrix only when the shift in \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) times a portfolio, and the centroid’s shift is not; the remedy is to pass the ranking through Equation 17.3 as absolute views on the two named assets, which exercise 3 asks for. The lesson of He and Litterman (1999) is that the point of Black-Litterman is less the Bayesian update than the guarantee that the answer is the market plus the views.
Two readings from Section 8.1 close the comparison. A view is an estimate: the spread has an annualized volatility of 20.0%, so the standard error of its mean over 31 model years is, by Equation 6.1, 3.6 percentage points, and the three-point deviation the opinion asserted is less than one standard error of what the entire sample could say about it; the entropy program priced it at 0.4 effective months of 372. And a ranking commits to less: it is invariant to the magnitude errors that Chopra and Ziemba (1993) found an order of magnitude more costly than errors in variances, which is the case Salcher et al. (2026) make for it, and on these numbers the formulation that asked for a rank matched the two that asked for a number until the rank was written into \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) without the covariance. Whether the ranking is right is a separate question from whether it was expressed well, and only the second is settled here.
None of this is out of sample, and it cannot be. A view is dated, held at a moment about a horizon, and a backtest of views needs a record of what the allocator believed month by month, which no dataset supplies and this book does not invent. The chapter therefore stops at in-sample comparisons of what each formulation buys. Where the view is generated from data, a momentum ranking or a signal of Section 16.1, a history of views exists by construction, and Section 16.3 is where such a view is run through the rolling machinery of Section 25.3. Section 18.1 takes the alternative route of skipping \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) altogether, and Section 19.1 reads a regime as a view on which scenarios apply, Equation 17.7 with the probabilities set by a state rather than an opinion.

title: 17  Expressing Views
text:
Key Takeaways

Black-Litterman is Equation 17.3: a normal prior on \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) centered on the equilibrium of Equation 6.6, views as linear statements with error, and a posterior that moves every asset by its covariance with the view portfolios (Black and Litterman 1992; Satchell and Scowcroft 2000).
With \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \tfrac{1-c}{c}\boldsymbol{P}\tau\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{P}'\) the scale \(\tau\) cancels and each view lands at \((1-c)\) times the prior plus \(c\) times the view (Meucci 2010). The confidence is the size of the position; black.litterman() fixes it at one half.
The posterior tangency portfolio is the market plus a position in each view portfolio, Equation 17.6, and assets in no view keep their weight (He and Litterman 1999). A view written into \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) by hand lacks that property and becomes a hedged spread trade.
Entropy pooling replaces the distribution with 372 scenarios and the view with a constraint on their probabilities (Meucci 2008). A mean view within a few standard errors costs nothing; a volatility view discards the months of the liquidity shock and the credit crisis and re-rates everything with a left tail.
A ranking is a direction, and the centroid of Equation 17.11 is its expected value (Almgren and Chriss 2006). It has no level and no scale, ac.ranking() assigns it a wrong one, and the size of the position is a choice the allocator has to make explicitly.

text:

title: 18  Parametric Portfolio Policies
text:
18.1 Weights as a Function of Characteristics
What if an investor skipped the forecast altogether and wrote the weight of each asset directly as a function of what can be observed about it? Brandt et al. (2009) proposed exactly that: a portfolio policy with a handful of coefficients on asset characteristics, estimated by maximizing the utility the policy would have delivered, with no expected return and no covariance matrix computed along the way. The appeal is arithmetic. A mean-variance problem on \(N\) assets consumes \(N\) means and \(N(N+1)/2\) variances and covariances, whose estimation error Section 8.1 priced; a policy on \(K\) characteristics has \(K\) parameters however large \(N\) is.
We first set out the policy, its estimator and the standard errors that say whether a tilt is real, with the long-only and transaction-cost variants and the version that times a few asset classes on state variables; then write the policy in about forty lines of R and estimate it twice, across the 123 equities of the modeled market on size and momentum and across the sixteen classes on momentum, the term spread and the credit spread; and finally re-estimate both on an expanding window and hold them out of sample against their benchmarks, gross and net of costs. On the horizon axis of Section 3.1 the chapter is tactical in its positions, which move every month with characteristics observed at the time, and strategic in its rule: the coefficients are estimated from the unconditional history and then held fixed, so that conditioning information enters through the characteristics and never through re-estimated moments.
The data are the two panels of Section 2.2, the sixteen risky class series and the 123 equities of the instrument table. They enter as total returns rather than in excess of the bill: both policies are fully invested in risky assets, and the utility function below is defined on gross wealth.

title: 18  Parametric Portfolio Policies
text:
18.1.1 The policy and its estimator
Let \(\bar{w}_{i,t}\) be the weight of asset \(i\) in a benchmark portfolio at the end of month \(t\), and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i,t}\) a vector of \(K\) characteristics of the asset observed at that date, standardized across the \(N_t\) assets then available to mean zero and unit standard deviation. The policy of Brandt et al. (2009) is linear in them:
\[
w_{i,t} = \bar{w}_{i,t} + \frac{1}{N_t}\,\boldsymbol{\theta}'\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i,t},
\qquad i = 1, \dots, N_t .
\tag{18.1}\]
Three features carry the method. The coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are the same for every asset and every month, so the policy knows characteristics, not assets. Because the standardized characteristics sum to zero across assets, so do the tilts, and the weights sum to one whenever the benchmark’s do. And the division by \(N_t\) keeps the active position from growing with the number of assets. The benchmark is the capitalization-weighted or the equal-weighted portfolio, and \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \boldsymbol{0}\) returns it.
The coefficients maximize the average utility the policy would have earned over the sample,
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} u\big(r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\big),
\qquad
r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_t} w_{i,t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,r_{i,t+1},
\qquad
u(r) = \frac{(1+r)^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma},
\tag{18.2}\]
with \(r_{i,t+1}\) the simple return of Equation 2.1 and \(u\) the power utility of Section 3.1 with relative risk aversion \(\gamma\). The whole distribution of the portfolio return enters, not only the two moments of Section 9.1. Nothing is forecast: Equation 18.2 never computes \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) or \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\). Estimating the decision rule from the investor’s optimality condition, bypassing the return distribution, goes back to Brandt (1999), who did it nonparametrically for one risky asset; Aït-Sahalia and Brandt (2001) used the idea to ask which predictors matter for the portfolio as opposed to the return, and Brandt (2010) surveys the line of work.
The dimension is what the method buys. For the 123 equities the plug-in rule of Equation 8.2 needs 123 means and 7626 variances and covariances from 372 months; the policy needs two coefficients. Michaud (1989) named what the first route does with estimation error, Kan and Zhou (2007) priced it, DeMiguel et al. (2009) showed that it loses to equal weighting out of sample, and Jagannathan and Ma (2003) that constraining the weights acts as shrinkage. A parametric policy is the far end of that road: weights may differ across assets only as far as characteristics do.
Equation 18.1 is linear in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), and so therefore is the portfolio return:
\[
r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = r_{b,t+1} + \boldsymbol{\theta}'\boldsymbol{a}_{t+1},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{a}_{t+1} = \frac{1}{N_t}\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i,t}\,r_{i,t+1},
\tag{18.3}\]
where \(r_{b,t+1}\) is the benchmark’s return and \(a_{k,t+1}\) the return of a zero-investment portfolio that is long the assets with a high value of characteristic \(k\) and short those with a low one. The policy is a position in \(K + 1\) portfolios, the benchmark and one long-short portfolio per characteristic, and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is the weight vector over the last \(K\). Hjalmarsson and Manchev (2012) solve the mean-variance version of that problem in closed form, and Brandt and Santa-Clara (2006) had made the same move in the time series, taken up below.

18.1.2 Standard errors
Because \(u\) is concave and \(r_p\) linear in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), the objective is concave and the estimate solves the first-order condition
\[
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\boldsymbol{h}_{t+1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = \boldsymbol{0},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{h}_{t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = u'\big(r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\big)\,\boldsymbol{a}_{t+1},
\tag{18.4}\]
\(K\) moment conditions in \(K\) unknowns: at the optimum the marginal-utility-weighted return of every characteristic portfolio is zero. That makes \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) an exactly identified method-of-moments estimator in the sense of Hansen (1982), with asymptotic covariance matrix
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
= \frac{1}{T}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{V}}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{-1},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{G}} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}_{t+1}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}'},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{V}} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\boldsymbol{h}_{t+1}\boldsymbol{h}_{t+1}' .
\tag{18.5}\]
The middle matrix takes the scores to be serially uncorrelated; when they are not, the estimator of Newey and West (1987) in Equation 5.5 replaces it. A bootstrap that resamples whole months, in blocks to preserve serial dependence (Künsch 1989), is the check that does not lean on the asymptotics. The \(t\)-statistic of \(\hat{\theta}_k\) tests whether characteristic \(k\) belongs in the portfolio, which is not the question of whether it forecasts returns: by Equation 18.4 a characteristic whose portfolio earns nothing on average still enters if it pays in the months in which marginal utility is high.

18.1.3 Long-only weights, and costs
Equation 18.1 shorts freely. A long-only mandate can be imposed as Brandt et al. (2009) do, by truncating the weights at zero and renormalizing,
\[
w^{+}_{i,t} = \frac{\max(0, w_{i,t})}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_t}\max(0, w_{j,t})} ,
\tag{18.6}\]
and it costs two things. The weights are no longer linear in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), so Equation 18.3 is lost; and \(\max(0, \cdot)\) has a kink, so the objective is not differentiable wherever a weight crosses zero. The gradient that a quasi-Newton optimizer and Equation 18.5 rely on does not exist there, and estimation falls back on a derivative-free search and the bootstrap. The alternative, which we use at class level, keeps the smooth objective and restricts the parameters instead: \(w_{i,t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \ge 0\) for every asset and month of the estimation sample is a set of linear inequalities in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). Ammann et al. (2016) treat leverage constraints on the policy in the same spirit.
Trading costs enter the objective rather than being subtracted afterwards. With one-way rates \(c_i\), the net return of Equation 23.2 is
\[
r^{\text{net}}_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
- \sum_{i=1}^{N_t} c_i\,\big|w_{i,t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - w^{h}_{i,t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\big|,
\qquad
w^{h}_{i,t} = w_{i,t-1}\,\frac{1 + r_{i,t}}{1 + r_{p,t}},
\tag{18.7}\]
where \(w^{h}\) is the weight the previous position has drifted to, and maximizing the utility of \(r^{\text{net}}\) shrinks most the coefficients on the characteristics that change fastest. Section 23.1 showed that under proportional costs the optimal policy is a no-trade region around the target (Constantinides 1986), or a partial adjustment toward it when the target moves (Gârleanu and Pedersen 2013). Brandt et al. (2009) put that region into the policy as one more parameter: the portfolio stays where it has drifted while it is close to the target and trades to the edge of the region otherwise. DeMiguel et al. (2020) show that costs also change which characteristics matter, because trades in different characteristics net against each other and more of them are worth holding jointly than one at a time.

18.1.4 Timing across a few asset classes
With sixteen assets there is little cross-section to learn from, and the information is in the time series. Brandt and Santa-Clara (2006) write the weight of each asset as a linear function of state variables \(\boldsymbol{z}_t\) and observe that the dynamic problem becomes a static one on an augmented set of assets, the managed portfolios \(z_{k,t}\,r_{i,t+1}\): Equation 18.3 with a signal in place of the characteristic. Their unrestricted version has \(N \times K\) coefficients. We keep the parsimony of Equation 18.1 by giving each signal one coefficient and a fixed pattern of loadings \(g_{k,i}\) across classes that sums to zero,
\[
w_{i,t} = \bar{w}_{i} + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\theta_k\,z_{k,t}\,g_{k,i},
\tag{18.8}\]
so that a positive \(\theta_k\) moves weight toward the classes loading on signal \(k\) when the signal is high. The signals are those Section 16.1 built and tested: the term spread, loading on the government series, and the credit spread, loading on the credit series, the two state variables of Fama and French (1989); and each class’s own 12-1 momentum, a characteristic in the ordinary sense, which Asness et al. (2013) document across asset classes.
What separates all of this from Section 16.3 is the loss function. There the forecasts were chosen by squared error and turned into weights by a rule set by hand, Equation 16.9; here the map from signal to weight is estimated on the investor’s own objective, costs and constraints included. It is the cleanest case in this book of an estimator trained on the decision it serves, and Section 27.1 generalizes it to forecasters with many more parameters, where the linear index \(\boldsymbol{\theta}'\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\) gives way to the nonlinear ones of Gu et al. (2020).
Brandt et al. (2009) use the three characteristics of the cross-sectional literature, size and book-to-market (Fama and French 1992) and momentum (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993). The modeled market supports two of them: size comes from sim_marketcap_weekly and momentum from the returns, while value needs a book value the market does not carry and waits for Section 21.1.

title: 18  Parametric Portfolio Policies
text:
18.2 Estimation of Two Policies

18.2.1 The equity panel
The benchmark is the capitalization-weighted portfolio of 1: the weight held over a month is the last capitalization observed on or before the end of the month before, a weight an investor could have held. Size is the logarithm of the same number and momentum the 12-1 return of Equation 16.8. Both are standardized each month within region rather than across all 123 names. 1 showed that a global size sort in this market sorts on region and that the region-neutral construction carries the more reliable premium; standardizing within region makes every tilt sum to zero region by region, so the policy selects stocks and leaves the regional allocation to the benchmark.

held  <- 14:Tn          # the months whose return the policy earns
known <- held - 1L      # the month end at which their weights are set

lag_rows <- function(M, k) rbind(matrix(NA_real_, k, ncol(M)),
                                 M[seq_len(nrow(M) - k), , drop = FALSE])
zscore   <- function(M) (M - rowMeans(M)) / apply(M, 1, stats::sd)
mom_12_1 <- function(Rm) {                 # @eq-16-mom: months t-11 .. t-1, month t skipped
  P <- apply(1 + Rm, 2, cumprod)
  lag_rows(P, 1) / lag_rows(P, 12) - 1
}

cap <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% eq) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = asset, values_from = market_cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cap$date)    # last weekly row on or before each month end
stopifnot(all(cap$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cap$date[i_last] < 8))
ME <- as.matrix(cap[i_last, colnames(Ra)])

region <- sim_assets$region[match(colnames(Ra), sim_assets$asset_id)]
within_region <- function(M) {
  for (g in unique(region)) M[, region == g] <- zscore(M[, region == g])
  M
}

Everything a policy needs is stored as one array, months by assets by characteristics, with names on every dimension, and each row holds what was known at the end of the month before the return in the same row. The assertions check that alignment against the raw tables for one month rather than trust it.

panel <- function(chars, Rm) {
  X <- array(unlist(lapply(chars, function(M) M[known, ])),
             dim = c(length(held), ncol(Rm), length(chars)),
             dimnames = list(as.character(dates[held]), colnames(Rm), names(chars)))
  Rn <- Rm[held, ]; rownames(Rn) <- dimnames(X)[[1]]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(X), max(abs(apply(X, c(1, 3), sum))) < 1e-10)   # every tilt sums to zero
  list(X = X, Rn = Rn)
}

Rm_eq  <- zoo::coredata(Ra)
mom_eq <- mom_12_1(Rm_eq)
p_eq   <- panel(list(size = within_region(log(ME)), momentum = within_region(mom_eq)), Rm_eq)
X_eq <- p_eq$X; Rn_eq <- p_eq$Rn
wbar_eq <- (ME / rowSums(ME))[known, ]; dimnames(wbar_eq) <- dimnames(Rn_eq)

# One arbitrary month m against the raw tables: the weight is the last
# capitalization on or before the end of m - 1, momentum the product of the
# returns of m - 12 .. m - 2, and the return that of m.
m   <- 200L
row <- as.character(dates[m])
wk  <- max(cap$date[cap$date <= dates[m - 1L]])
raw <- dplyr::filter(sim_marketcap_weekly, date == wk, asset %in% eq)
stopifnot(
  all.equal(unname(wbar_eq[row, raw$asset]), raw$market_cap / sum(raw$market_cap)),
  all.equal(unname(mom_eq[m - 1L, ]), unname(apply(1 + Rm_eq[(m - 12):(m - 2), ], 2, prod) - 1)),
  all.equal(unname(Rn_eq[row, ]), as.numeric(Ra[dates[m], colnames(Rn_eq)])),
  identical(dimnames(X_eq)[1:2], dimnames(wbar_eq)), identical(dimnames(wbar_eq), dimnames(Rn_eq)))
dim(X_eq)
#> [1] 359 123   2

The panel has 359 months, beginning in February of model year 2 because momentum needs twelve months of history and is lagged once, and all 123 equities are present in every one of them, so \(N_t = 123\) throughout.

18.2.2 The policy in forty lines

ppp_weights <- function(theta, X, wbar, long_only = FALSE) {
  stopifnot(length(theta) == dim(X)[3], identical(dimnames(X)[1:2], dimnames(wbar)))
  tilt <- 0
  for (k in seq_along(theta)) tilt <- tilt + theta[k] * X[, , k]
  w <- wbar + tilt / ncol(wbar)                                # @eq-18-policy
  if (long_only) { w <- pmax(w, 0); w <- w / rowSums(w) }      # @eq-18-longonly
  w
}

crra <- function(r, gamma) (1 + r)^(1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma)

# Row t of W is held over month t. The trade into it is measured from where
# last month's weights drifted to, is charged to month t, and the portfolio
# starts flat: the accounting of the register.
path_returns <- function(W, Rn, cost) {
  gross <- rowSums(W * Rn)
  hold  <- W * (1 + Rn) / (1 + gross)
  trade <- abs(W - rbind(0, hold[-nrow(W), , drop = FALSE]))
  cbind(gross = gross, net = gross - as.numeric(trade %*% cost),   # @eq-18-cost
        turnover = rowSums(trade) / 2)                             # @eq-23-turnover
}

ppp_utility <- function(theta, X, wbar, Rn, cost = NULL, gamma = 5) {
  W <- ppp_weights(theta, X, wbar)
  r <- if (is.null(cost)) rowSums(W * Rn) else path_returns(W, Rn, cost)[, "net"]
  mean(crra(r, gamma))                                         # @eq-18-estimator
}

# simplex = TRUE restricts theta to the set on which no weight of the
# estimation sample is negative: linear inequalities, one per month and asset.
ppp_estimate <- function(X, wbar, Rn, cost = NULL, simplex = FALSE,
                         start = rep(0, dim(X)[3])) {
  f   <- function(th) -ppp_utility(th, X, wbar, Rn, cost, gamma)
  ctl <- list(reltol = 1e-12)
  par <- if (!simplex) {
    stats::optim(start, f, method = "BFGS", control = ctl)$par
  } else {
    stats::constrOptim(start, f, function(th) numDeriv::grad(f, th, method = "simple"),
                       ui = matrix(X, ncol = dim(X)[3]) / ncol(wbar), ci = -as.numeric(wbar),
                       mu = 1e-6, outer.eps = 1e-12, control = ctl)$par
  }
  setNames(par, dimnames(X)[[3]])
}

path_returns() follows the accounting of the register in Section 25.3; ppp_estimate() maximizes Equation 18.2 with the BFGS method of optim(), or with constrOptim() under the restriction that keeps the weights in the simplex.

theta_eq <- ppp_estimate(X_eq, wbar_eq, Rn_eq)
theta_nl <- stats::nlminb(c(2, 2), function(th) -ppp_utility(th, X_eq, wbar_eq, Rn_eq,
                                                             gamma = gamma))$par
stopifnot(max(abs(theta_eq - theta_nl)) < 0.01)
rbind(optim_from_zero = theta_eq, nlminb_from_2_2 = theta_nl)
#>                   size momentum
#> optim_from_zero -4.047    1.954
#> nlminb_from_2_2 -4.048    1.954

A second optimizer from a distant start reaches the same coefficients, as it must on a concave objective.

18.2.3 Standard errors two ways
Equation 18.5 needs the scores month by month and the Hessian of the objective, and numDeriv supplies both from ppp_weights() without any algebra. The bootstrap resamples months in blocks of twelve, as in Section 9.3, and uses Equation 18.3: each draw is a two-parameter problem on three return series, so the panel is never rebuilt.

u_t <- function(th) crra(rowSums(ppp_weights(th, X_eq, wbar_eq) * Rn_eq), gamma)
H   <- numDeriv::jacobian(u_t, theta_eq)                       # T x K scores, @eq-18-foc
G   <- numDeriv::hessian(function(th) mean(u_t(th)), theta_eq)
V_theta     <- solve(G) %*% (crossprod(H) / nrow(H)) %*% solve(G) / nrow(H)   # @eq-18-avar
se_sandwich <- setNames(sqrt(diag(V_theta)), names(theta_eq))

r_b <- rowSums(wbar_eq * Rn_eq)                                # benchmark return
A   <- vapply(names(theta_eq), function(k) rowSums(X_eq[, , k] * Rn_eq),
              numeric(nrow(Rn_eq))) / ncol(Rn_eq)              # characteristic portfolios
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(r_b + A %*% theta_eq),
                    unname(rowSums(ppp_weights(theta_eq, X_eq, wbar_eq) * Rn_eq))))

set.seed(1602)
block_index <- function(n, block = 12L) {
  starts <- sample.int(n - block + 1L, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE)
  as.vector(outer(0:(block - 1L), starts, "+"))[seq_len(n)]
}
boot <- t(vapply(seq_len(400L), function(b) {
  i <- block_index(length(r_b))
  stats::optim(theta_eq, function(q) -mean(crra(r_b[i] + A[i, ] %*% q, gamma)),
               method = "BFGS")$par
}, numeric(2)))
se_boot <- setNames(apply(boot, 2, stats::sd), names(theta_eq))

The two standard errors agree to within 0.07. The size coefficient is -4.05 with a \(t\)-statistic of -3.10: the policy moves weight from the large names of each region to the small ones, and the size portfolio of Equation 18.3, long large and short small, loses 1.8% a year. The momentum coefficient is positive at 1.95, 2.0 standard errors from zero, and it is the instructive one, because the momentum portfolio earns 0.5% a year with a \(t\)-statistic of 0.63: nothing. A return forecaster would drop the characteristic. The policy keeps it because Equation 18.4 weighs returns by marginal utility: the momentum portfolio has a correlation of -0.23 with the benchmark, pays in the months in which the size-tilted portfolio loses, and its marginal-utility-weighted mean at \(\theta_{\text{mom}} = 0\) is 1.6% a year. That momentum has no premium of its own is a property of this market and not of the method: the idiosyncratic components of the equities were drawn independently over time (Section 2.2), so a stock’s past return says nothing about its future one beyond what the replayed factors carry. In sample the policy lifts the certainty equivalent from 7.2% to 12.5% a year, a number Section 18.3 will not repeat. It does so with leverage: 46% of all weights are negative and the short side averages 103% of wealth.

18.2.4 The timing policy across sixteen classes
At class level the benchmark is the equal-weight policy portfolio of Section 16.3, for the reason given there: it estimates nothing, so every difference from it is attributable to the policy. The two curve signals are standardized with what was known at the time, the mean and standard deviation of their own history through \(t\), and clipped at two so that one crisis month does not set the scale of the tilt. Each is multiplied by a standardized indicator of the classes it loads on, which is Equation 18.8.

grp <- sub(".*_", "", colnames(R))               # government, credit, equity, commodity
cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(series %in% c("US_Slope", "US_IG_Spread")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
j_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)
stopifnot(all(cv$date[j_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[j_last] < 8))

expanding_z <- function(x, first = 12L, clip = 2) {
  z <- vapply(seq_along(x), function(t)
    if (t < first) NA_real_ else (x[t] - mean(x[1:t])) / stats::sd(x[1:t]), numeric(1))
  pmax(pmin(z, clip), -clip)
}
term   <- -cv$US_Slope[j_last]                   # long minus short, as in chapter 16
z_term <- expanding_z(term)
z_cred <- expanding_z(cv$US_IG_Spread[j_last])
stopifnot(all.equal(expanding_z(term[1:200])[200], z_term[200]))   # no later month enters
loading <- function(g) { x <- as.numeric(grp == g); (x - mean(x)) / stats::sd(x) }

Rm_cl <- zoo::coredata(R)
p_cl  <- panel(list(momentum = zscore(mom_12_1(Rm_cl)),
                    term     = outer(z_term, loading("government")),
                    credit   = outer(z_cred, loading("credit"))), Rm_cl)
X_cl <- p_cl$X; Rn_cl <- p_cl$Rn
wbar_cl <- Rn_cl; wbar_cl[] <- 1 / ncol(R)
cost_cl <- setNames(pm_costs_default()[grp], colnames(R))   # per-class rates of chapter 23
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_cl))

The first estimate uses the first 120 months, the burn-in of the register, and is made twice: freely, and under the restriction that no weight of those months is negative.

burn <- 120L
ins  <- held <= burn
theta_free <- ppp_estimate(X_cl[ins, , ], wbar_cl[ins, ], Rn_cl[ins, ])
theta_cl   <- ppp_estimate(X_cl[ins, , ], wbar_cl[ins, ], Rn_cl[ins, ], simplex = TRUE)
theta_cl2  <- ppp_estimate(X_cl[ins, , ], wbar_cl[ins, ], Rn_cl[ins, ], simplex = TRUE,
                           start = c(0.05, -0.05, 0.05))
stopifnot(max(abs(theta_cl - theta_cl2)) < 0.001)

W_free <- ppp_weights(theta_free, X_cl[ins, , ], wbar_cl[ins, ])
W_ins  <- ppp_weights(theta_cl,   X_cl[ins, , ], wbar_cl[ins, ])
bind   <- which(W_ins < 1e-7, arr.ind = TRUE)            # the weights held at zero
stopifnot(all(theta_cl > 0), names(which.max(theta_cl)) == "momentum",
          min(W_ins) > -1e-8, nrow(bind) == length(theta_cl))
round(rbind(free    = c(theta_free, lowest_weight = min(W_free)),
            simplex = c(theta_cl,   lowest_weight = min(W_ins))), 3)
#>         momentum  term credit lowest_weight
#> free       0.858 2.385 -0.662          -0.5
#> simplex    0.287 0.199  0.205           0.0

Left free, the policy puts 2.39 on the term spread and takes one class to a weight of -50%. Restricted to the simplex, all three coefficients are positive and small, the largest on momentum at 0.29, and the estimate sits at a vertex of the feasible set: 3 weights are exactly zero, as many as there are coefficients (CH_government in June of model year 9, JP_equity in June of model year 10, US_government in March of model year 4). A long-only mandate is set by its most extreme months. The average weight moves 2.3 percentage points from the benchmark’s 6.25. Out of sample a signal can exceed anything in the estimation sample, so there the truncation of Equation 18.6 stands behind the restriction.






NoteThe policy itself is outside PortfolioAnalytics



optimize.portfolio() searches over weight vectors; a parametric policy searches over the coefficients of a function that returns weight vectors, and the package has no objective, constraint or solver interface for that. Nor do its rolling utilities help: Section 16.3 showed that applyFUN() and trailingFUN() roll nothing. Three things can be reused once the weights exist. Return.portfolio() turns a weight path into returns, with the back-fill trap of Section 23.2 waiting for any path that starts after the data do. turnover() measures a trade, on a different scale from Equation 23.1: it divides the summed absolute changes by \(N\), not by two. And the optimizers remain the comparison: the register of Section 25.3 is constrained re-optimization on the same months, and Section 18.3 reads it.



acc_ins <- path_returns(W_ins, Rn_cl[ins, ], cost_cl)
W_xts   <- xts::xts(W_ins, order.by = dates[known[ins]])       # dated when they are set

rp <- Return.portfolio(R[dates[held[ins]], ], weights = W_xts)
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(rp), unname(acc_ins[, "gross"])))

# Handed the whole burn-in instead, the call warns and prepends equal weights
# for the months before the first weight vector.
rp_all <- suppressWarnings(Return.portfolio(R[seq_len(burn), ], weights = W_xts))

hold_1 <- W_ins[1, ] * (1 + Rn_cl[ins, ][1, ]) / (1 + acc_ins[1, "gross"])
to_pa  <- turnover(W_ins[2, ], wts.init = hold_1)
stopifnot(all.equal(to_pa * ncol(W_ins) / 2, unname(acc_ins[2, "turnover"])))
c(months_with_weights = nrow(rp), months_returned = nrow(rp_all),
  turnover_package = to_pa, turnover_eq_23 = unname(acc_ins[2, "turnover"]))
#> months_with_weights     months_returned    turnover_package      turnover_eq_23 
#>           107.00000           120.00000             0.00722             0.05776

title: 18  Parametric Portfolio Policies
text:
18.3 The Policies Out of Sample

18.3.1 The coefficients through time
Both policies are now run as an investor would have run them. The first estimate uses the months through December of model year 10; the coefficients are re-estimated at the end of every model year on all data to that date; and the weights of each month are set from the latest estimate and the characteristics of the month end before, so the out-of-sample period is that of the register, from observation 121 on. Each policy is estimated twice, on the utility of gross returns and on that of net returns, at 10 basis points one way for every equity and at the per-class rates of pm_costs_default() for the classes.

refit <- seq(burn, Tn - 1L, by = 12L)      # month ends at which theta is re-estimated
oos   <- held > burn
stopifnot(held[oos][1] == burn + 1L, all(model_year(dates[refit + 1L]) == 11:31))

theta_path <- function(X, wbar, Rn, cost = NULL, simplex = FALSE) {
  TH <- matrix(0, length(refit), dim(X)[3],
               dimnames = list(as.character(dates[refit]), dimnames(X)[[3]]))
  for (j in seq_along(refit)) {
    k <- held <= refit[j]                  # nothing after the estimation date
    TH[j, ] <- ppp_estimate(X[k, , ], wbar[k, ], Rn[k, ], cost, simplex,
                            start = if (j > 1 && !simplex) TH[j - 1, ] else rep(0, dim(X)[3]))
  }
  TH
}

cost_eq <- setNames(rep(pm_costs_default()[["equity"]], ncol(Ra)), colnames(Ra))
TH <- list(
  `equity sleeve.gross returns` = theta_path(X_eq, wbar_eq, Rn_eq),
  `equity sleeve.net returns`   = theta_path(X_eq, wbar_eq, Rn_eq, cost_eq),
  `sixteen classes.gross returns` = theta_path(X_cl, wbar_cl, Rn_cl, simplex = TRUE),
  `sixteen classes.net returns`   = theta_path(X_cl, wbar_cl, Rn_cl, cost_cl, simplex = TRUE))








Figure 18.1: The estimated coefficients of both policies at each annual re-estimation, from one data frame. Solid lines maximize the utility of gross returns, dashed lines that of returns net of trading costs.




Figure 18.1 answers the question of stability differently for the two characteristics of the equity policy. The size coefficient is negative at every one of the 21 estimation dates, between -5.9 and -2.1. The momentum coefficient is not stable: it starts at -1.4, is negative at the first 4 dates and ends at 1.8. Putting costs into the objective shrinks momentum to 71% of its size on average and size to 97%: the faster-moving characteristic pays more to be held, as Equation 18.7 says it should. The class coefficients keep their signs throughout and move within narrow bands, but that stability is the restriction’s as much as the data’s, since the simplex caps them.

18.3.2 Performance against the benchmarks

policy_path <- function(TH, X, wbar, long_only = FALSE) {
  j <- findInterval(held[oos] - 1L, refit)          # the latest estimate before each month
  W <- wbar[oos, ]
  for (e in unique(j))
    W[j == e, ] <- ppp_weights(TH[e, ], X[oos, , ][j == e, , ], wbar[oos, ][j == e, ], long_only)
  W
}
breach <- sum(rowSums(policy_path(TH[[cl_g]], X_cl, wbar_cl) < 0) > 0)   # months needing the truncation

W_oos <- list(
  eq_bench = wbar_eq[oos, ],
  eq_gross = policy_path(TH[["equity sleeve.gross returns"]], X_eq, wbar_eq),
  eq_net   = policy_path(TH[["equity sleeve.net returns"]],   X_eq, wbar_eq),
  cl_bench = wbar_cl[oos, ],
  cl_gross = policy_path(TH[["sixteen classes.gross returns"]], X_cl, wbar_cl, long_only = TRUE),
  cl_net   = policy_path(TH[["sixteen classes.net returns"]],   X_cl, wbar_cl, long_only = TRUE))
acc <- lapply(names(W_oos), function(nm) {
  if (grepl("^eq", nm)) path_returns(W_oos[[nm]], Rn_eq[oos, ], cost_eq)
  else                  path_returns(W_oos[[nm]], Rn_cl[oos, ], cost_cl)
}) |> setNames(names(W_oos))

rf_o <- rf[held[oos]]
sharpe_reg <- function(r) {                # as the register computes it
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf_o)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
perf <- function(a, label) {
  tibble::tibble(portfolio = label,
                 sharpe_gross = sharpe_reg(a[, "gross"]), sharpe_net = sharpe_reg(a[, "net"]),
                 ce_gross = ce_crra(a[, "gross"]), ce_net = ce_crra(a[, "net"]),
                 turnover = 12 * mean(a[, "turnover"]),
                 max_dd = as.numeric(maxDrawdown(xts::xts(a[, "net"], order.by = dates[held[oos]]))))
}
labels <- c(eq_bench = "Equities: capitalization weight", eq_gross = "Equities: policy",
            eq_net = "Equities: policy, costs in the objective",
            cl_bench = "Classes: equal weight", cl_gross = "Classes: policy",
            cl_net = "Classes: policy, costs in the objective")
res <- dplyr::bind_rows(Map(perf, acc, labels[names(acc)]))

# The register's rows for the same months, read and not retyped. Our

reg <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", window == burn, frequency == "months")
reg_of <- function(s, b, col) reg[[col]][reg$strategy == s & reg$basis == b]
ew <- res[res$portfolio == labels[["cl_bench"]], ]
stopifnot(all.equal(ew$sharpe_gross, reg_of("equal_weight", "gross", "sharpe"), tolerance = 1e-6),

Both policies finish ahead of their benchmarks out of sample, and neither does so by a margin that the sample can certify. Inside the equity sleeve the policy earns a net Sharpe ratio of 0.92 against the capitalization-weighted benchmark’s 0.61 and a certainty equivalent of 9.0% a year against 4.8%, after paying for a turnover of 333% a year. The gap of 0.32 is large as these things go. It is also 1.4 times the standard error of a single Sharpe ratio over 252 months, which Equation 25.2 puts at 0.22, and the paired test that Section 25.3 names for two strategies on the same months (Jobson and Korkie 1981; Memmel 2003) gives a \(z\)-statistic of 1.78: suggestive, not significant at five percent. The policy is also not the benchmark’s kind of portfolio. It is short 121% of wealth on average, and its drawdown of 52% is deeper than the benchmark’s 47%. What it earns is the size tilt, the one characteristic whose coefficient was stable in Figure 18.1.
Costs in the objective do what Equation 18.7 promises and no more. Turnover falls from 333% to 274%, and the net Sharpe ratio is 0.920 against 0.923 for the policy that ignored costs when it was estimated: at 10 basis points the trades the cost-aware policy avoids were worth about what they cost.
Across the sixteen classes the timing policy raises the net Sharpe ratio from 0.62 to 0.73 and the certainty equivalent by 95 basis points a year, with a shallower drawdown and 3.3 times the turnover; the truncation was needed in 6 of 252 months. The gap of 0.11 is 0.5 standard errors by Equation 25.2, and the paired \(z\)-statistic is 1.87, higher than the raw gap suggests because the policy’s returns have a correlation of 0.97 with the benchmark’s. Set beside the register, 1 of its 5 strategies has a higher net Sharpe ratio than these three coefficients re-estimated once a year, among them minimum variance at 0.90, which estimates a covariance matrix and no mean.
The class-level gain is larger than the few tens of basis points that Section 16.3 found for the term-spread tilt, and it comes from the same information plus momentum. What the policy adds is that nobody chose the scale of the tilt: it was estimated, on the objective, with the mandate as a constraint. Whether the next step, a policy with many signals and a flexible functional form, earns more than it overfits is the subject of Section 27.1, and Section 21.1 returns to the equity policy with the long-only mandate that a sleeve usually carries.

title: 18  Parametric Portfolio Policies
text:
Key Takeaways

A parametric policy writes each weight as the benchmark weight plus a linear function of standardized characteristics, Equation 18.1, and estimates the coefficients by maximizing realized utility: 2 parameters for 123 equities in place of 7749 moments (Brandt et al. 2009).
The estimate solves a moment condition, so it has a sandwich covariance matrix (Hansen 1982), and a block bootstrap over months agrees with it. The test is whether a characteristic belongs in the portfolio, not whether it forecasts returns: momentum earns nothing here and still enters, as a hedge.
Truncating at zero imposes a long-only mandate at the price of differentiability; restricting \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) so that no in-sample weight is negative keeps the objective smooth, and the restriction is set by the most extreme months.
Out of sample the equity policy earns a net Sharpe ratio of 0.92 against 0.61 and the class policy 0.73 against 0.62; the paired \(z\)-statistics are 1.8 and 1.9, short of significance.
The size coefficient keeps its sign at every re-estimation and the momentum coefficient does not; costs in the objective shrink the faster-moving characteristic more and cut the equity policy’s turnover while leaving its net Sharpe ratio where it was.

PortfolioAnalytics has no parametric policy. Return.portfolio() reproduces the returns of a weight path that starts where the data do, and turnover() divides by \(N\) rather than by two.

title: 18  Parametric Portfolio Policies
text:
Exercises

Standardize size and momentum across all 123 equities instead of within region and re-estimate the policy on the full sample. How do the coefficients change, and how far does the policy’s average weight in US names now differ from the benchmark’s? Relate the answer to




Re-estimate the equity policy at \(\gamma = 2\) and \(\gamma = 10\). Do the coefficients scale with \(1/\gamma\), as the invested fraction of Equation 3.15 does, and what happens to the short side?
Estimate the equity policy on the full sample with costs of 10 and of 50 basis points in the objective. Which coefficient shrinks more, and how does the turnover of each characteristic portfolio explain it?
Replace the simplex restriction of the class policy by the truncation of Equation 18.6: maximize the utility of the truncated policy over the first 120 months with a derivative-free search from two starting points. What happens to the scale of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\), and why?

title: 19  Regime-Dependent Allocation
text:
19.1 Regimes, Filters, and Mixtures
What if the right portfolio depends on the state of the world? Hamilton (1989) gave that question its statistical form, a series whose parameters switch with an unobserved Markov chain, and Ang and Bekaert (2002) carried the form into portfolio choice, with an international investor who faces a normal regime and a bear regime of lower means, higher volatilities and higher correlations. The descriptive chapters supplied the reason to ask. In Section 4.3 the tails of this market arrived as a handful of episodes in which correlations rose, and in Section 14.3 the effective number of bets fell in the same months.
This is a tactical chapter in the sense of Section 3.1: the allocation is conditioned on a state inferred at the time, and deviates from a policy estimated without one. We first state the regime-switching model, the filter that infers its state and the mixture moments an investor faces one month ahead; then date the regimes of the modeled market with hindsight, detect them without it in two ways, a turbulence threshold and a two-state hidden Markov model, and show what PortfolioAnalytics offers for switching between portfolio specifications; and finally ask whether a regime-switching allocation is ahead of a static one out of sample once the regime has to be detected rather than dated.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill for the reasons of Section 3.1.

title: 19  Regime-Dependent Allocation
text:
19.1.1 The regime-switching model
Let \(s_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) be an unobserved state and \(\boldsymbol{r}_t\) the vector of excess returns. In the model of Hamilton (1989), applied to returns,
\[
\boldsymbol{r}_t \mid s_t = s \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_s, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s),
\qquad
\Pr(s_{t+1} = j \mid s_t = i) = p_{ij},
\tag{19.1}\]
with the \(p_{ij}\) collected in a transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) whose rows sum to one. A regime lasts \(1/(1 - p_{ss})\) periods on average, and the chain spends a long-run share \(\bar{\pi}_s\) of its time in state \(s\), where \(\bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}}'\boldsymbol{P} = \bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}}'\). Turner et al. (1989) fitted a two-state version to excess stock returns, with a mean and a variance that both switch, and Ang and Timmermann (2012) survey what the model has been used for since.

19.1.2 The Hamilton filter
The state is never observed, so everything rests on the probability of each state given the returns seen so far. Write \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|\tau}\) for the vector with elements \(\Pr(s_t = j \mid \boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{r}_\tau)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_t\) for the vector of regime densities \(f(\boldsymbol{r}_t \mid s_t = j)\). The filter of Hamilton (1989) alternates two steps. The prediction step moves the probabilities one period through the chain,
\[
\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|t} = \boldsymbol{P}'\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t},
\tag{19.2}\]
and the update step reweights them by how well each regime explains the new observation,
\[
\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t}
= \frac{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t-1} \odot \boldsymbol{\eta}_t}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t-1} \odot \boldsymbol{\eta}_t\right)},
\tag{19.3}\]
where \(\odot\) is the elementwise product. The denominator is the density of \(\boldsymbol{r}_t\) given the past, so the sum of its logarithms is the log-likelihood. It is maximized by the EM algorithm of Dempster et al. (1977), which for a hidden Markov chain is the procedure of Baum et al. (1970) and was adapted to regime-switching models by Hamilton (1990): given state probabilities, the means, variances and transition frequencies are weighted sample moments; given those, the probabilities are recomputed.
The probabilities EM needs use the whole sample. They are the smoothed probabilities \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|T}\), obtained from the filtered ones by the backward recursion of Kim (1994),
\[
\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|T}
= \boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t} \odot
  \left[\boldsymbol{P}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|T} \oslash \boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|t}\right)\right],
\tag{19.4}\]
with \(\oslash\) elementwise division. The difference between \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|T}\) is the subject of this chapter.

19.1.3 One-step-ahead moments as a mixture
An investor standing at \(t\) does not know \(s_{t+1}\). With \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|t}\), next month’s return is a mixture of the regime distributions, with mean and covariance
\[
\bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \sum_{s} \pi_s \boldsymbol{\mu}_s,
\qquad
\bar{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \sum_{s} \pi_s \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s
  + \sum_{s} \pi_s \left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_s - \bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right)
                   \left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_s - \bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right)'.
\tag{19.5}\]
The covariance is not the average of the regime covariances. The second sum, the between-regime term, is the risk of not knowing which regime next month belongs to, and it is largest for the assets whose means differ most across regimes. A mixture of normals is also not normal. For a single series whose regimes share a mean, the variance is \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \sum_s \pi_s \sigma_s^2\) and the excess kurtosis is
\[
\bar{K} = 3\left(\frac{\sum_s \pi_s \sigma_s^4}{\left(\sum_s \pi_s \sigma_s^2\right)^2} - 1\right) \;\geq\; 0,
\tag{19.6}\]
strictly positive whenever the regime variances differ, and skewness appears as soon as the low-mean regime is also the high-variance one (Timmermann 2000). Regimes therefore produce the fat tails and the asymmetry of Section 4.3 from Gaussian ingredients, which Rydén et al. (1998) found sufficient for most stylized facts of daily returns. They produce them jointly, because all assets change regime together: the co-moments that Section 11.1 carries as tensors are here the by-product of two covariance matrices, and Ang and Chen (2002) find that a regime-switching model reproduces the higher correlations of falling markets documented by Longin and Solnik (2001) better than the alternatives they test.

19.1.4 Two ways to use the state
Given \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) there are two rules. The first treats Equation 19.5 as the inputs of Section 9.1 and holds the tangency portfolio of Equation 9.5 computed from \(\bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and \(\bar{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\); its weights move continuously with the probabilities. The second holds one of \(K\) portfolios, each built for one regime, and switches when the most probable regime changes,
\[
\boldsymbol{w}_t = \boldsymbol{w}^{(\hat{s}_{t+1})},
\qquad
\hat{s}_{t+1} = \arg\max_s \, \pi_s .
\tag{19.7}\]
The two agree when one probability is one and differ in between, where the mixture rule holds a compromise and the switching rule a bet. Clarke and Silva (1998) showed for two states how a state-dependent mix enlarges the opportunity set of a static one. Ang and Bekaert (2002) solve the dynamic problem of an investor with constant relative risk aversion and find the cost of ignoring regimes small for an all-equity investor and substantial once a risk-free asset can be held, because the bear regime is then a reason to leave the market; Ang and Bekaert (2004) turn that into a mean-variance rule and report that it outperforms static allocations out of sample. Guidolin and Timmermann (2007) need four regimes to describe stocks and bonds jointly, Guidolin and Timmermann (2008) add preferences over skewness and kurtosis, and Tu (2010) finds that a Bayesian investor who ignores regimes gives up more than two percent a year in certainty-equivalent terms. The out-of-sample evidence on simple switching rules in Bulla et al. (2011) and Nystrup et al. (2015), both of which leave equities for safer assets on a filtered state, is favorable.
All of these condition on a state estimated from the data, and the estimate is where the difficulty lies.

19.1.5 Dating and detecting
A regime can be established in two ways that are easily confused. Dating assigns each month to a regime with the whole sample in view: by a rule that locates peaks and troughs, as in Pagan and Sossounov (2003), by naming episodes after the fact, or by the smoothed probabilities of Equation 19.4. Detecting assigns month \(t\) using only what was known at \(t\): the filtered probabilities of Equation 19.3, computed with parameters that were themselves estimated on data through \(t\). A turning point needs observations on both sides to be recognized, so detection lags dating, and Chauvet and Piger (2008) measure that lag for business-cycle turning points in months.
A backtest of a regime strategy has three places to leak. Smoothed probabilities at \(t\) contain returns after \(t\). Filtered probabilities computed with full-sample parameters contain them less visibly, because the parameters that describe the stress regime were learned from the very months the filter then appears to recognize. And the regime definition itself, the number of states and the series they are fitted to, is usually settled after looking at the sample. The first two are coding errors of the kind Section 16.2 guards against by lagging and asserting, and we assert them away below. The third is the design problem of Section 25.3 and cannot be asserted away.

19.1.6 Turbulence as a model-free detector
A regime model has parameters to estimate before it says anything. The turbulence index of Equation 5.6 has none beyond a trailing mean and covariance matrix: it measures how unusual this month’s return vector is by the standards of the recent past. Chow et al. (1999) used it to separate a calm from a turbulent subsample and blended the two covariance matrices according to the probability of, and the aversion to, each regime, which is the first sum of Equation 19.5 with \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) chosen by the investor. Kritzman and Li (2010) documented that turbulence is persistent and that risk is poorly rewarded while it lasts, the two properties a detector needs, and Kritzman et al. (2012) fitted hidden Markov models to turbulence and to macroeconomic series and reported out-of-sample gains from tilting on the filtered state. A threshold on the index is the simplest detector there is: stress when \(d_t\) exceeds a quantile of its own past.

19.2.2 A detected regime: the turbulence threshold
The index is the one of Section 5.3, from the same call. Before thresholding it we check what a value is made of: the package returns a monotone transform of Equation 5.6, \(\sqrt{d_t}/N\), computed from month \(t\) and the sixty months before it.

turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
tb   <- as.numeric(turb)
stopifnot(length(tb) == nrow(R), all(zoo::index(turb) == dates))

first_oos <- 121L                                    # the register's first out-of-sample month
past <- zoo::coredata(R)[(first_oos - 60L):(first_oos - 1L), ]
d    <- stats::mahalanobis(zoo::coredata(R)[first_oos, ], colMeans(past), stats::cov(past))
stopifnot(all.equal(tb[first_oos], sqrt(d) / N))

A month is flagged when the index exceeds the 75th percentile of its own history, the convention of Kritzman and Li (2010), with the percentile computed on an expanding window that ends the month before. The flag for month \(t\) is known at the end of month \(t\) and decides the portfolio held in \(t + 1\).

turb_flag <- function(tb, q = 0.75, burn = 24L) {
  threshold <- vapply(seq_along(tb), function(t) {
    past <- tb[seq_len(t - 1L)]; past <- past[!is.na(past)]
    if (length(past) < burn) NA_real_ else stats::quantile(past, q, names = FALSE)
  }, numeric(1))
  tb > threshold
}
flag_turb <- turb_flag(tb)

# No look-ahead: reverse everything after `cut`, and the flags through `cut` must not move.
cut    <- first_oos + 119L
tb_alt <- replace(tb, (cut + 1L):length(tb), rev(tb[(cut + 1L):length(tb)]))
stopifnot(identical(turb_flag(tb_alt)[seq_len(cut)], flag_turb[seq_len(cut)]),
          !identical(turb_flag(tb_alt), flag_turb))


19.2.3 A detected regime: a two-state hidden Markov model
Equation 19.1 on all sixteen classes with two states has 306 parameters, two mean vectors, two covariance matrices and two transition probabilities, against 372 months. We fit it instead to one summary series, the equal-weighted excess return of the sixteen, where the same model has six. No hidden-Markov package is needed: the filter of Equation 19.2 and Equation 19.3 is a loop, the smoother of Equation 19.4 another, and EM alternates them with weighted moments.

hamilton <- function(y, th) {
  n <- length(y); filt <- pred <- matrix(NA_real_, n, 2); loglik <- 0
  dens <- cbind(stats::dnorm(y, th$mu[1], th$sigma[1]), stats::dnorm(y, th$mu[2], th$sigma[2]))
  xi <- c(0.5, 0.5)                                  # prior for the first month
  for (t in seq_len(n)) {
    pred[t, ] <- xi                                  # xi_{t|t-1}
    joint     <- xi * dens[t, ]
    loglik    <- loglik + log(sum(joint))
    filt[t, ] <- joint / sum(joint)                  # the update step
    xi        <- as.numeric(filt[t, ] %*% th$P)      # the prediction step
  }
  list(filtered = filt, predicted = pred, loglik = loglik)
}

kim <- function(h, P) {                              # smoothed probabilities
  sm <- h$filtered
  for (t in (nrow(sm) - 1L):1L)
    sm[t, ] <- h$filtered[t, ] * as.numeric(P %*% (sm[t + 1L, ] / h$predicted[t + 1L, ]))
  sm
}

fit_hmm <- function(y, max_iter = 200L, tol = 1e-6) {
  far <- abs(y - stats::median(y)); hi <- far > stats::quantile(far, 0.8)
  th  <- list(mu = c(mean(y[!hi]), mean(y[hi])), sigma = c(stats::sd(y[!hi]), stats::sd(y[hi])),
              P = rbind(c(0.95, 0.05), c(0.10, 0.90)))
  floor_sd <- stats::sd(y) / 4; ll_old <- -Inf; n <- length(y)
  for (iter in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    h  <- hamilton(y, th); sm <- kim(h, th$P)                                # E-step
    J  <- (t(h$filtered[-n, ]) %*% (sm[-1L, ] / h$predicted[-1L, ])) * th$P  # expected transitions
    th$P     <- J / rowSums(J)                                               # M-step
    th$mu    <- colSums(sm * y) / colSums(sm)
    th$sigma <- pmax(sqrt(colSums(sm * outer(y, th$mu, "-")^2) / colSums(sm)), floor_sd)
    if (h$loglik - ll_old < tol) break
    ll_old <- h$loglik
  }
  o <- order(th$sigma)                               # state 2 is the high-volatility state
  list(mu = th$mu[o], sigma = th$sigma[o], P = th$P[o, o], loglik = h$loglik, iter = iter)
}

y        <- rowMeans(X)                              # equal-weighted excess return
fit_full <- fit_hmm(y)
smoothed <- kim(hamilton(y, fit_full), fit_full$P)[, 2]
round(c(mu = 12 * fit_full$mu, sigma = sqrt(12) * fit_full$sigma, stay = diag(fit_full$P)), 3)
#>    mu1    mu2 sigma1 sigma2  stay1  stay2 
#>  0.049  0.053  0.061  0.142  0.984  0.931

The volatility floor is there because the likelihood of a Gaussian mixture is unbounded when one state collapses onto a single observation. On the full sample the two states differ in volatility, 6.1% against 14.2% a year, and hardly in mean; the high-volatility state lasts 15 months on average and the other 63.






NoteWorked: the mixture moments of the summary series






P_hat   <- fit_full$P
pi_bar  <- c(P_hat[2, 1], P_hat[1, 2]) / (P_hat[1, 2] + P_hat[2, 1])     # long-run state shares
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(pi_bar %*% P_hat), pi_bar))
sg      <- 100 * fit_full$sigma                                          # percent a month
within  <- sum(pi_bar * sg^2)
between <- sum(pi_bar * (100 * fit_full$mu - sum(pi_bar * 100 * fit_full$mu))^2)
kurt    <- 3 * (sum(pi_bar * sg^4) / within^2 - 1)
sample  <- c(kurtosis = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::kurtosis(y, method = "excess")),
             skewness = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::skewness(y)))
c(mixture_vol = sqrt(within + between), sample_vol = 100 * stats::sd(y),
  mixture_kurtosis = kurt, sample)
#>      mixture_vol       sample_vol mixture_kurtosis         kurtosis 
#>           2.3837           2.3256           2.6319           5.3462 
#>         skewness 
#>          -0.8958

With long-run shares \(\bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = (0.81,
0.19)\) and regime volatilities of \(\sigma_1 = 1.77\) and \(\sigma_2 = 4.10\) percent a month, the scalar version of Equation 19.5 gives
\[
\bar{\sigma}^2
= \underbrace{0.81 \times 1.77^2
  + 0.19 \times 4.10^2}_{\text{within}}
  + \underbrace{0.0002}_{\text{between}}
= 5.68 ,
\]
a volatility of 2.38 percent a month against 2.33 in the sample, and Equation 19.6 gives
\[
\bar{K} = 3\left(\frac{0.81 \times 1.77^4
                       + 0.19 \times 4.10^4}
                      {5.68^2} - 1\right)
        = 2.63 .
\]
Two Gaussian regimes account for an excess kurtosis of 2.6 of the 5.3 in the sample. They account for none of its skewness of -0.90: the fitted regime means are almost equal, so the between-regime term is 0.003% of the variance. What this model has found is a volatility regime rather than a bear market.



Those estimates used every month. In real time the parameters are re-estimated each December on an expanding window, the filter is run with them through each month of the following year, and nothing after month \(t\) enters the probability for \(t\).

hmm_realtime <- function(y, start) {
  refit <- seq(start, length(y), by = 12L)
  fits  <- lapply(refit, function(e) fit_hmm(y[seq_len(e)]))
  prob  <- t(vapply(start:length(y), function(t) {
    th <- fits[[max(which(refit <= t))]]             # the latest fit, on data through its own date
    xi <- hamilton(y[seq_len(t)], th)$filtered[t, ]
    c(filtered = xi[2], predicted = as.numeric(xi %*% th$P)[2])
  }, numeric(2)))
  list(refit = refit, fits = fits, month = start:length(y), prob = prob)
}
rt <- hmm_realtime(y, start = first_oos - 1L)

# No look-ahead: the same procedure on a truncated sample returns the same probabilities.
cut_h <- first_oos + 23L
stopifnot(all.equal(hmm_realtime(y[seq_len(cut_h)], first_oos - 1L)$prob,
                    rt$prob[rt$month <= cut_h, ]))


live     <- rt$month                                 # months in which both detectors exist
flag_hmm <- rep(NA, length(y)); flag_hmm[live] <- rt$prob[, "filtered"] > 0.5
detect <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(ep)), function(i) {
  m   <- intersect(which(in_episode(dates, ep$episode[i])), live)
  lag <- function(f) if (any(f[m])) which(f[m])[1] - 1L else NA_integer_
  tibble::tibble(episode = ep$label[i], months = length(m),
                 turb_lag = lag(flag_turb), turb_share = mean(flag_turb[m]),
                 hmm_lag  = lag(flag_hmm),  hmm_share  = mean(flag_hmm[m]),
                 smoothed_share = mean(smoothed[m] > 0.5))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
calm_live <- setdiff(live, which(in_any))
false_alarm <- c(turbulence = mean(flag_turb[calm_live]), hmm = mean(flag_hmm[calm_live]),
                 smoothed = mean(smoothed[calm_live] > 0.5))
