Figure 19.1 and Table 19.2 are the chapter’s argument in small. With hindsight the model is clean: the smoothed probability is above one half in 100% of the credit-crisis months and in 16% of the months outside any episode. In real time it is not. Before the credit crisis the sample contains no high-volatility regime to learn from, so the second state is fitted to whatever divides a calm sample: EM stops at its iteration limit in 6 of the 22 refits, and the filtered probability is above one half in 26% of the months before that crisis against 1% for the smoothed one. A regime cannot be detected by a model that has not yet seen it. Once it has, the filter recognizes the liquidity shock 1 month after it begins and the rates shock after 5; the turbulence threshold, which needs no stress history, flags the credit crisis in its first month and the other two after 1 and 2. Neither sees the equity bear market as a whole, a slow decline with bonds rising that is unusual in direction and not in size. Outside the episodes the threshold flags 15% of months and the filter 35%.

19.2.4 Regime portfolios in PortfolioAnalytics

PortfolioAnalytics ships the machinery for the switching rule. combine.portfolios() turns a list of specifications into one portfolio.list object; regime.portfolios() attaches a regime series to such a list; and optimize.portfolio.rebalancing() then solves, at each rebalancing date, the specification the regime selects. Our two specifications are a calm portfolio, the long-only tangency of Equation 9.5, and a stress portfolio, long-only minimum variance.

win <- 60L
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
calm_spec   <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")
stress_spec <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")

both <- combine.portfolios(list(calm_spec, stress_spec))
opt_both <- optimize.portfolio(Re[(first_oos - win):(first_oos - 1L), ], both,
                               optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE)
w_both <- extractWeights(opt_both)
class(opt_both)
#> [1] "opt.list"
round(w_both[, colSums(w_both) > 0.02], 3)
#>       CH_equity EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity JP_equity UK_equity US_equity
#> opt 1     0.000     0.079            0.000     0.000     0.000     0.180
#> opt 2     0.023     0.004            0.099     0.046     0.073     0.013
#>       US_government
#> opt 1         0.741
#> opt 2         0.711

Handed to optimize.portfolio() directly, a portfolio.list is solved specification by specification and extractWeights() returns a matrix with a row for each. The backtest needs both portfolios at every month. The stress portfolio comes from optimize.portfolio.rebalancing() on a sixty-month window, set up as in Section 25.2. The calm one is computed as the single quadratic program of Section 8.2, because maxSR = TRUE under ROI is a one-dimensional search that solves a quadratic program at every step, and the package run below confirms that the two routes agree.

reb <- (first_oos - 1L):(nrow(Re) - 1L)     # weights are set at the end of these months
oos <- reb + 1L                             # and earn the returns of these

# Long-only tangency: min y'Sy subject to y'mu = 1, y >= 0, then w = y / sum(y).
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(setNames(rep(NA_real_, n), names(mu)))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu))
}
W_calm <- t(vapply(reb, function(t) {
  Z <- X[(t - win + 1L):t, ]; tan_qp(colMeans(Z), stats::cov(Z))
}, numeric(N)))

bt_stress <- optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re[(first_oos - win):nrow(Re), ], stress_spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = win, rolling_window = win - 1L)
W_stress <- extractWeights(bt_stress)
W_stress <- zoo::coredata(W_stress)[match(dates[reb], zoo::index(W_stress)), colnames(Re)]

dimnames(W_calm) <- list(as.character(dates[reb]), colnames(Re))
rownames(W_stress) <- rownames(W_calm)
stopifnot(!anyNA(W_calm), !anyNA(W_stress))

The regime object is built from the turbulence flags, coded 1 for calm and 2 for stress, and run over a short stretch that begins with the credit crisis.

regime_turb <- xts::xts(ifelse(flag_turb, 2L, 1L), order.by = dates)[!is.na(flag_turb)]
reg_spec    <- regime.portfolios(regime_turb, both)

demo <- min(which(in_episode(dates, "credit_crisis"))) + 0:17
bt_demo <- optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re[(demo[1] - win + 1L):max(demo), ], reg_spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = win, rolling_window = win - 1L, maxSR = TRUE)
W_demo <- extractWeights(bt_demo)
used   <- vapply(bt_demo$opt_rebalancing, function(o) o$regime, numeric(1))

by_hand <- W_calm[as.character(dates[demo]), ]
by_hand[used == 2, ] <- W_stress[as.character(dates[demo]), ][used == 2, ]
stopifnot(all(zoo::index(W_demo) == dates[demo]),
          all(used == as.numeric(regime_turb[dates[demo]])),   # the regime of the rebalancing date itself
          used[1] == 2,
          max(abs(zoo::coredata(W_demo) - by_hand)) < 1e-6)
table(specification = used)
#> specification
#>  1  2 
#>  7 11

The assertions say what the package did: at every date it read the regime of that date, solved the matching specification on the trailing window, and returned the weights we obtain by picking rows from the two separate runs. Switching in the package is row selection. What it does around that is worth measuring before it is trusted.

pick <- function(regime, t, specs = both) {     # the specification a regime series selects at month t
  o <- try(optimize.portfolio(Re[(t - win + 1L):t, ], regime.portfolios(regime, specs),
                              optimize_method = "ROI"), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(o, "try-error")) NULL else o
}
t_stress <- demo[1]; t_calm <- max(which(!flag_turb[seq_len(demo[1])]))
shifted  <- xts::xts(zoo::coredata(regime_turb), order.by = zoo::index(regime_turb) + 1)
half     <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0.5, max_sum = 0.5) |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.2) |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")

quirk <- list(
  coded_01_stress = pick(regime_turb - 1L, t_stress)$regime,     # 1: the calm specification
  coded_01_calm   = is.null(pick(regime_turb - 1L, t_calm)),     # TRUE: index zero, the solve fails
  dates_shifted   = pick(shifted, t_stress)$regime,              # 1, with a warning
  third_value     = inherits(try(regime.portfolios(replace(regime_turb, 1, 3L), both),
                                 silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
  half_invested   = sum(extractWeights(pick(regime_turb, t_stress,
                                            combine.portfolios(list(calm_spec, half))))),
  stats_labels    = lengths(extractStats(bt_demo)),
  measure_labels  = vapply(extractObjectiveMeasures(bt_demo), nrow, integer(1)))
stopifnot(identical(quirk$coded_01_stress, 1), quirk$coded_01_calm,
          identical(quirk$dates_shifted, 1), as.numeric(regime_turb[dates[t_stress]]) == 2,
          quirk$third_value, abs(quirk$half_invested - 0.5) < 1e-8,
          quirk$stats_labels[["regime.1"]] == sum(used == 2),
          quirk$measure_labels[["regime.1"]] == sum(used == 1))
str(quirk, give.attr = FALSE)
#> List of 7
#>  $ coded_01_stress: num 1
#>  $ coded_01_calm  : logi TRUE
#>  $ dates_shifted  : num 1
#>  $ third_value    : logi TRUE
#>  $ half_invested  : num 0.5
#>  $ stats_labels   : Named int [1:2] 11 7
#>  $ measure_labels : Named int [1:2] 7 11







NoteWhat regime.portfolios() does with the regime series



Each line is one of the measurements above.


The regime is a list index. optimize.portfolio() selects portfolio.list[[regime]], so the series must be coded 1, 2, … in the order of the list. A series coded 0 and 1 passes the constructor. A stress month, coded 1, then receives the calm specification without a message, and a calm month, coded 0, fails and leaves a row of NA in the weights.

The lookup is contemporaneous. The regime is read at the last date of the estimation window, the rebalancing date. The series must hold at each date what was known on that date; a hand-dated series is used unlagged, and a regime dated with hindsight enters the backtest with nothing to mark it.

Dates must match exactly. When the rebalancing date is missing from the regime index, here because the index is a day off, the first specification is used and the only trace is a warning.

Every value needs a specification and every specification a value. The constructor counts distinct values and refuses a series with a third value, with an NA, or one that never visits a regime.

Only the assets must agree. Constraints and objectives may differ: a stress specification confined to half the budget, with the rest in the bill, returns weights that sum to 0.5.

Arguments in ... reach every specification. maxSR = TRUE is passed to the stress specification too, which has no return objective; its weights are unaffected and a warning is raised at each stress date.

extractWeights() returns one xts, a row per rebalancing date, whichever specification produced it, and the regime used is in $opt_rebalancing[[i]]$regime. extractObjectiveMeasures() and extractStats() return lists by regime and label them differently: the first sorts the regimes, the second numbers them in order of first appearance, so that here its regime.1 holds the 11 stress dates.

title: 19  Regime-Dependent Allocation
section: 19.3 Detected Against Dated Regimes, Out of Sample
text:
19.3 Detected Against Dated Regimes, Out of Sample

19.3.1 The strategies and their accounting
From observation 121, the first month of model year 11 and the start of the register of Section 25.3, we run the static policy, which holds the calm portfolio throughout, and four alternatives; the stress portfolio held throughout is reported beside them as a second static row. Three switch to the stress portfolio by Equation 19.7: on the dated episodes, using the label of the month the return is earned in, which no investor had and which is the infeasible upper bound; on the turbulence flag of the rebalancing month; and on the predicted probability of Equation 19.2 from the real-time filter. The fourth holds the tangency portfolio of the mixture moments of Equation 19.5. For it the regime moments of the sixteen classes are sample moments weighted by the smoothed probabilities of each December’s fit, on the expanding sample because a sixty-month window need not contain a stress month at all.

p_stress <- rep(NA_real_, length(y)); p_stress[rt$month] <- rt$prob[, "predicted"]
stress_by <- list(dated      = in_any[oos],          # the month ahead: hindsight
                  turbulence = flag_turb[reb],       # known at the rebalancing date
                  hmm        = p_stress[reb] > 0.5)
stopifnot(!anyNA(unlist(stress_by)))
switch_W <- function(s) { W <- W_calm; W[s, ] <- W_stress[s, ]; W }

regime_moments <- function(k) {                      # weighted moments of the sixteen at refit k
  e  <- rt$refit[k]; th <- rt$fits[[k]]
  sm <- kim(hamilton(y[seq_len(e)], th), th$P)
  list(m = lapply(1:2, function(s) stats::cov.wt(X[seq_len(e), ], wt = sm[, s] / sum(sm[, s]),
                                                 method = "ML")),
       share = colMeans(sm), n_eff = colSums(sm),
       all = stats::cov.wt(X[seq_len(e), ], method = "ML"))
}
mixture <- function(m, p) {                          # the mixture moments
  mu <- p[1] * m[[1]]$center + p[2] * m[[2]]$center
  S  <- p[1] * (m[[1]]$cov + tcrossprod(m[[1]]$center - mu)) +
        p[2] * (m[[2]]$cov + tcrossprod(m[[2]]$center - mu))
  list(mu = mu, S = S)
}
rm_k <- lapply(seq_along(rt$refit), regime_moments)

# At the sample's own state shares the mixture is the sample: the law of total covariance.
chk <- mixture(rm_k[[1]]$m, rm_k[[1]]$share)
stopifnot(all.equal(chk$mu, rm_k[[1]]$all$center), all.equal(chk$S, rm_k[[1]]$all$cov))

mix_at <- function(t) mixture(rm_k[[max(which(rt$refit <= t))]]$m, c(1 - p_stress[t], p_stress[t]))
W_mix  <- t(vapply(reb, function(t) { m <- mix_at(t); tan_qp(m$mu, m$S) }, numeric(N)))
dimnames(W_mix) <- dimnames(W_calm)
stopifnot(!anyNA(W_mix))

# The same portfolio from the package, with the mixture moments supplied through momentFUN.
make_moments <- function(mu, S) {
  force(mu); force(S)
  function(R, portfolio, ...) list(mu = mu, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = mu, var = S)
}
m1    <- mix_at(reb[1])
w_pkg <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, calm_spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                                           momentFUN = make_moments(m1$mu, m1$S)))
stopifnot(max(abs(w_pkg[colnames(Re)] - W_mix[1, ])) < 1e-4)

The accounting is that of the register: weights set at the end of month \(t\) earn the returns of \(t + 1\), drift, and are traded back at the turnover of Equation 23.1 and the cost of Equation 23.2, at the per-class rates of pm_costs_default() from Section 23.3. A switch is a trade like any other, so its cost is in the same column.

cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(R))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(R)

run_path <- function(W) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(R)), nrow(W) == length(oos))
  Rm    <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, ]
  gross <- rowSums(W * Rm)                                       # month t+1, weights set at t
  held  <- rbind(0, (W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + gross))[-nrow(W), ])    # drifted weights; flat before the first trade
  trade <- abs(W - held)
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[oos], gross = gross, turnover = rowSums(trade) / 2,
                 cost = as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(net = gross - cost)
}
sharpe_of <- function(r) {                                       # as the register: compounded, over the bill
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf[oos])^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
performance <- function(path) {
  x <- xts::xts(path$gross, order.by = path$date)
  tibble::tibble(vol = stats::sd(path$gross) * sqrt(12), sharpe = sharpe_of(path$gross),
                 es = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "historical",
                                                          invert = FALSE)),
                 drawdown = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(x)),
                 turnover = 12 * mean(path$turnover), cost = 12 * mean(path$cost),
                 sharpe_net = sharpe_of(path$net))
}
# Difference of two Sharpe ratios in standard errors (Jobson-Korkie, as corrected by Memmel).
z_against <- function(p, q) {
  a <- p$gross - rf[oos]; b <- q$gross - rf[oos]
  s <- c(mean(a) / stats::sd(a), mean(b) / stats::sd(b)); rho <- stats::cor(a, b)
  (s[1] - s[2]) / sqrt((2 - 2 * rho + (s[1]^2 + s[2]^2 - 2 * s[1] * s[2] * rho^2) / 2) / length(a))
}

label <- c(static = "static: calm portfolio", stress = "static: stress portfolio",
           dated = "switching, dated (infeasible)", turbulence = "switching, turbulence",
           hmm = "switching, filtered HMM", mixture = "mixture mean-variance")
weights <- c(list(static = W_calm, stress = W_stress), lapply(stress_by, switch_W),
             list(mixture = W_mix))
stopifnot(identical(names(weights), names(label)))
paths <- lapply(weights, run_path)
share <- c(static = 0, stress = 1, vapply(stress_by, mean, numeric(1)), mixture = NA)

perf <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(paths, performance), .id = "key") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    z = vapply(paths, z_against, numeric(1), q = paths$static),
    stress_share = share[key],
    same_mix = vapply(stress_share, function(s) {    # the constant mix with the same time in stress
      if (is.na(s)) NA_real_ else sharpe_of(run_path(s * W_stress + (1 - s) * W_calm)$gross)
    }, numeric(1)))

19.3.2 Reading the result
The two static rows are checks before they are results. The static policy’s Sharpe ratio of 0.546 is the register’s 0.546 for the maximum-Sharpe strategy at this window, and the stress portfolio’s 0.828 is its 0.829 for minimum variance, both read from output/tables/oos-sweep.csv; the accounting here is the register’s.
With the regimes dated, switching works. The infeasible strategy raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.546 to 0.811 and cuts the maximum drawdown from 20.1% to 12.6% while spending 12% of the months in the stress portfolio. The constant mix with the same share earns 0.582, so 0.23 of the gain is timing and the rest is holding some of a portfolio that the register already ranks above the calm one.
That last column is what the detected strategies have to be read against. The turbulence switch reaches 0.582, which keeps 14% of the dated strategy’s advantage over the static policy, and it is -0.02 against its own constant mix: the flag chooses its months no better than a fixed blend would, at 142% turnover and 24 basis points a year in costs against 15 for the static policy. The filtered model reaches 0.525, below the static policy, and it is in the stress portfolio in 37% of all months against 12% for the dated regimes: in 29% of the months before the credit crisis, where the smoothed probability of Figure 19.1 marks almost nothing, and in 41% of the months from the crisis on, most of them the model years of elevated volatility that follow it. The constant mix with its share earns 0.659, so its timing is worth -0.13, against +0.23 for the dated regimes. The mixture rule, at 0.524, is below the static policy: its regime covariance matrices are estimated from as few as 4 effective months, and Equation 19.5 passes that error to the optimizer.
None of this is distinguishable from sampling error. By Equation 25.2 the standard error of the static policy’s Sharpe ratio over 252 months is 0.22; the paired statistic in the z column, which uses the correlation between the two return series (Memmel 2003), is +0.30 for the turbulence switch and -0.30 for the filtered model, and +2.78 for the strategy that knew the dates. And one row needs no detector at all: the stress portfolio held throughout has a Sharpe ratio of 0.828, above both detected strategies. On this market the question of when to hold the minimum-variance portfolio matters less than the question of whether to.

Table 19.4 shows where each number comes from. In the credit crisis the static policy loses 10.8% and the stress portfolio 1.6%. The turbulence switch, flagged in the first month, captures most of the difference at -2.8%. The filtered model, at -10.7%, captures almost none of it: it flags the crisis one month after it begins, the switch takes effect the month after that, and by then the static policy had already lost 13.5%, against 10.8% for the episode as a whole. That is the episode a two-state model is built for, and a lag of two months was enough to miss it. In the rates shock there is nothing to capture: the stress portfolio is mostly government bonds, it loses 10.1%, and the investor who knew every date loses the same. The detected strategies lose more, 12.4% and 13.8%, because they enter and leave during it. A stress portfolio is a hedge against the stress that resembles the past, and Table 19.1 had already said that the fourth episode does not.
Three limits on that conclusion. One path of 252 months contains 4 episodes, and the ranking of the detectors rests on them. The threshold, the summary series, the number of states and the two portfolios were each chosen once and not searched over, which is why the exercises vary them rather than the chapter. And the stress portfolio is a model too: what to do when the regime model itself may be wrong, rather than only its state, is the question of Section 28.1.

title: 19  Regime-Dependent Allocation
text:
Key Takeaways

A regime-switching model is Equation 19.1 plus a filter. The prediction and update steps of Equation 19.2 and Equation 19.3 give the probability of each state from data through \(t\); the smoother of Equation 19.4 gives it from the whole sample, and only the first is available to an investor (Hamilton 1989; Kim 1994).
One month ahead the investor faces the mixture moments of Equation 19.5. The covariance contains a between-regime term, and a mixture of Gaussian regimes has fat tails by Equation 19.6; the two-state model of the equal-weighted return accounts for about half of its excess kurtosis and none of its skewness.
Dating and detecting are different operations. Smoothed probabilities and full-sample parameters both carry the future into a backtest, and before the first stress regime has occurred a two-state model has nothing to detect it with.

regime.portfolios() switches between specifications by a regime series and is equivalent to selecting rows from separate rebalancing runs. It reads the regime of the rebalancing date itself, uses the regime value as a list index, and checks neither the coding nor the timing of the series.
On this market the infeasible dated switch is well ahead of the static policy; the turbulence switch keeps a small part of that by point estimate, the filtered model none, neither is distinguishable from the static policy by a paired test, and holding the stress portfolio throughout has a higher Sharpe ratio than either detector. In the rates shock no version of the switch helps, because the stress portfolio was built for a different stress.

title: 19  Regime-Dependent Allocation
text:
Exercises

The turbulence flag uses the 75th percentile. Recompute the switching strategy with the 50th and the 90th, and report for each the share of months in the stress portfolio, the Sharpe ratio, and the Sharpe ratio of the constant mix with the same share. Which threshold, if any, times its months?

regime.portfolios() reads the regime of the rebalancing date. Feed the dated episodes to the switch in that way, so that the portfolio for month \(t + 1\) is chosen by the label of month \(t\), and compare with the infeasible row of Table 19.3. How much of the dated advantage is lost to a delay of one month, and in which episode?
Simulate 100,000 months from a two-state chain with annual regime volatilities of 6% and 14%, equal means, and probabilities of staying of 0.98 and 0.93. Compare the sample excess kurtosis with Equation 19.6, and compute the first-order autocorrelation of the squared returns. Which property of Section 4.3 does the persistence of the chain add to the fat tails?
Replace the stress portfolio by one that puts half the budget in the bill: half of the minimum-variance weights, which in PortfolioAnalytics is a weight_sum constraint of 0.5. Recompute the dated switch and its return inside each episode. Does leaving the market help in the rates shock where moving to bonds did not?

title: 20  Sustainable Investing Constraints
text:
20.1 Tastes, Floors, and Exclusions
An investor who excludes a set of names, or who requires the portfolio’s average sustainability rating to clear a floor, has added a line to the mandate: what does the line cost, and who pays? Pedersen et al. (2021) answered the first question by drawing the ESG-efficient frontier, the highest Sharpe ratio attainable at each level of a portfolio’s rating, so that the cost of a floor is a distance along a curve rather than an opinion; Pástor et al. (2021) answered the second in equilibrium, where a taste for green assets lowers their expected return, so that the investor who holds them pays in expectation and the firm that issues them is paid in a lower cost of capital. The two results together fix what this chapter can and cannot claim: a constraint that does not bind costs nothing, a constraint that binds costs tracking error and expected return at a rate the Lagrange multiplier of Section 12.1 prices, and neither is an alpha.
We first set out the investor’s problem with a taste for a rating and with a floor on it, the exclusion as a restriction of the universe, the tilt as a factor-exposure constraint on a score, and the two facts that complicate all three, that a rating is an estimate and that tastes are priced; then construct rating levels for the 123 equities from the rating changes the modeled market ships, and implement an exclusion, a floor and a best-in-class floor on the equity sleeve of Section 21.2, auditing each with the functions of Section 12.2; then measure what the three cost out of sample inside the policy of Section 15.3, and how much of an exclusion list survives a second rater. On the horizon axis of Section 3.1 a sustainability constraint is strategic: it is a permanent line of the policy, set once, and it conditions on nothing but the ratings in force.

title: 20  Sustainable Investing Constraints
text:
20.1.1 The investor’s problem with a taste for a rating
Let \(\boldsymbol{s}\) be a vector of ratings over the \(N\) names, one number per name on a fixed scale, and \(\bar{s}_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{s}'\boldsymbol{w}\) the portfolio’s rating. Pedersen et al. (2021) give the investor of Section 3.1 a third term,
\[
\max_{\boldsymbol{w}} \;
\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu}
- \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
+ \theta\,\boldsymbol{s}'\boldsymbol{w},
\tag{20.1}\]
a taste \(\theta \geq 0\) for the rating, and show that every solution lies on the ESG-efficient frontier: for each attainable \(\bar{s}\), the portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio among those with \(\boldsymbol{s}'\boldsymbol{w} = \bar{s}\). An investor with \(\theta = 0\) sits at the frontier’s peak, the tangency portfolio of Equation 9.5; an investor with a taste moves along it, giving up Sharpe ratio for rating at the rate the curve’s slope sets. The same frontier is traced by a mandate written as a floor,
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol{w}} \; \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w} = 1, \;\; \boldsymbol{w} \geq \boldsymbol{0}, \;\;
\boldsymbol{s}'\boldsymbol{w} \geq \bar{s},
\tag{20.2}\]
because the floor’s multiplier \(\lambda_s\) in the Lagrangian of Equation 12.2 is the taste that would have produced the same portfolio: \(\theta = \lambda_s\) at the optimum. Complementary slackness then says what the floor costs. When the unconstrained portfolio already clears \(\bar{s}\), \(\lambda_s = 0\) and the line could have been left out; when it binds, \(\lambda_s > 0\) is the shadow price of Equation 12.3, the rate at which variance, or tracking error when the objective is active risk, falls per notch of floor given up. A floor is a constraint of the linear-exposure family of Table 12.1, so the feasible set stays convex and Equation 20.2 is one quadratic program (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004). Jagannathan and Ma (2003) and Frost and Savarino (1988) read a binding constraint as information about the estimates; a sustainability floor is not that. It is a preference, and its cost is a cost, which is why Pedersen et al. (2021) draw it as a frontier rather than argue it away.

20.1.2 Exclusion as a restriction of the universe
The oldest form of the constraint is a list of names that may not be held, \(w_i = 0\) for \(i \in E\): a box constraint with both bounds at zero, or equivalently a smaller universe. For a capitalization-weighted sleeve with benchmark \(\boldsymbol{b}\), reweighting the survivors pro rata gives active weights
\[
x_i =
\begin{cases}
-\,b_i & i \in E, \\[2pt]
\;\; b_i \dfrac{b_E}{1 - b_E} & i \notin E,
\end{cases}
\qquad
b_E = \sum_{i \in E} b_i,
\qquad
\text{active share} = b_E ,
\tag{20.3}\]
so the active share of Cremers and Petajisto (2009) is the benchmark weight of the excluded set, and the tracking error of Equation 24.2 is \(\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{x}}\) with that \(\boldsymbol{x}\): an exclusion costs active risk in proportion to how much of the index it removes and how differently the removed names move. For an optimized sleeve the cost has a sharper reading. In the first-order condition \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} = \lambda_0\boldsymbol{\iota} + \boldsymbol{\delta}\) of Equation 12.4, the multiplier of an excluded name is unrestricted in sign, and the Jagannathan–Ma identity still holds: the constrained portfolio is the unconstrained minimum-variance portfolio on \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} - (\boldsymbol{\delta}\boldsymbol{\iota}' + \boldsymbol{\iota}\boldsymbol{\delta}')\). A name the optimizer would not have held anyway has \(\delta_i \geq 0\) and its exclusion is slack. A name it wanted has \(\delta_i < 0\), and excluding it is the same as raising every covariance involving it by \(-\delta_i\) until the optimizer drops it on its own. An exclusion that binds is therefore an implicit risk view about the excluded name, and \(-\delta_i\) is its price. Hong and Kacperczyk (2009) found the equilibrium counterpart: names shunned by norm-constrained institutions are held by fewer investors, trade at lower valuations and earn higher expected returns, which is the premium the excluding investor forgoes; Heinkel et al. (2001) had derived the mechanism, a higher cost of capital for the excluded firm when enough capital excludes it.

20.1.3 Tilts as a factor-exposure constraint on a score
A floor on the portfolio’s rating is Equation 20.2, and in the vocabulary of Section 12.2 it is factor_exposure_constraint() with the score vector in place of a column of betas. A best-in-class mandate imposes the floor within each group \(g\) rather than across the universe, and because
\[
\frac{\sum_{i \in g} w_i s_i}{\sum_{i \in g} w_i} \;\geq\; \bar{s}
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
\sum_{i \in g} w_i \,(s_i - \bar{s}) \;\geq\; 0 ,
\tag{20.4}\]
it is linear too: one row per group of a factor-exposure matrix whose entries are the centered scores, bounded below at zero. The difference between the two forms is where the rating is bought. An across-the-universe floor lets the solver meet it in whichever region has the cheapest rating in tracking-error terms, which, when the regions’ budgets are fixed by the policy above the sleeve, means concentrating the tilt where it costs least; a best-in-class floor spreads the tilt and costs more, which Equation 20.4 makes measurable.

20.1.4 A rating is an estimate
The score in Equation 20.2 is treated as data, and it is not. Berg et al. (2022) document that the ratings of six major providers for the same firm correlate at 0.54 on average, with pairwise correlations from 0.38 to 0.71, and decompose the divergence into what is measured, how it is measured and how the pieces are weighted. For a constraint the consequence is direct: the floor is imposed on \(\hat{\boldsymbol{s}} = \boldsymbol{s} + \boldsymbol{e}\), and with a different rater the same mandate excludes different names and tilts toward different ones. Avramov et al. (2022) put the error into Equation 20.1 and find that rating uncertainty lowers the demand for green assets and weakens their expected-return effect, as estimation error in \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) did in Section 8.1; Gibson Brandon et al. (2021) find that the disagreement itself is priced in the cross-section. The one dimension on which the measurement problem is smaller is carbon, where emissions are a quantity rather than an opinion, and Bolton and Kacperczyk (2021) find a premium on it. The modeled market carries no emissions data, so a carbon budget is the one construction this chapter cannot run; its mechanics are Equation 20.2 with emissions in place of a rating and an upper bound in place of a floor.

20.1.5 Tastes are priced
Finally, the equilibrium of Pástor et al. (2021): when investors have a taste for green assets, those assets’ expected returns are lower in equilibrium by the amount of the taste, so that the frontier of Pedersen et al. (2021) slopes down for the reason the demand curve slopes down. The realized returns of a green tilt can nevertheless be high for a long time, and Pástor et al. (2022) show that the green outperformance of their sample is what an unexpected strengthening of tastes produces, not what the equilibrium promises. A constraint and an alpha are different objects: the first is a cost paid for a property of the portfolio, the second a claim about expected returns that Section 24.1 would ask for an error bar on. The evidence on the alpha is mixed on purpose: Friede et al. (2015) aggregate some two thousand studies and find a non-negative relation in most of them, Serafeim and Yoon (2022) find that only financially material rating news moves prices, and Zerbib (2019) measures the green premium in bonds at a few basis points. None of that is needed to price the constraint, which is what the rest of the chapter does.

title: 20  Sustainable Investing Constraints
text:
20.2 Implementation

20.2.1 A level from a path of changes






ImportantThe market ships rating changes, not ratings



sim_esg_changes_quarterly holds 1113 integer rating changes on 122 of the 123 equities, dated at quarter ends from model year 11 on, and no starting level, as Section 2.2 records. Cumulating the changes gives each name’s rating up to its own unknown constant, and a screen or a floor needs the constant. The chapter therefore constructs the levels under a stated assumption, and the assumption is an argument of a function so that a reader can change it.


The assumption is this. Each name has a latent score on a seven-point scale, the number of grades the common letter scales use; its starting value is drawn once, with the book’s seed, from a normal distribution centered on the scale’s midpoint with a standard deviation of 1.2 grades, so that the middle three grades hold 79% of the names in expectation and the extremes are rare, the bell shape a vendor’s grade distribution has; the shipped changes then move the score by whole grades from the quarter in which they are dated, and the score is clipped to the scale. A different distribution is a different rater, which Berg et al. (2022) say is the realistic case, and the application redraws it.

esg_start <- function(assets, dist = function(n) stats::rnorm(n, mean = 4, sd = 1.2),
                      seed = 1602, scale = c(1, 7)) {
  set.seed(seed)
  setNames(pmin(pmax(dist(length(assets)), scale[1]), scale[2]), assets)
}
esg_levels <- function(start, changes = sim_esg_changes_quarterly, dates = d, scale = c(1, 7)) {
  stopifnot(all(changes$asset %in% names(start)))
  L <- matrix(start, length(dates), length(start), byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(NULL, names(start)))
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(changes))) {
    from <- match(TRUE, dates > changes$date[k])   # in force from the first month that starts after the change
    if (is.na(from)) next
    L[from:nrow(L), changes$asset[k]] <- L[from:nrow(L), changes$asset[k]] + changes$esg_change[k]
  }
  pmin(pmax(L, scale[1]), scale[2])
}
grade <- function(s) pmin(pmax(round(s), 1), 7)

s0 <- esg_start(eq$asset_id)
L  <- esg_levels(s0)
t1 <- 121L                                           # the register's first out-of-sample month
stopifnot(identical(colnames(L), colnames(X)), all(L[t1, ] == s0))   # no change is in force yet at t1
esg <- sim_esg_changes_quarterly
net <- tapply(esg$esg_change, esg$asset, sum)
c(share_upgrades = mean(esg$esg_change > 0), mean_net_change = mean(net),
  mean_score_t1 = mean(L[t1, ]), mean_score_end = mean(L[nrow(L), ]),
  share_top_grade_end = mean(grade(L[nrow(L), ]) == 7))
#>      share_upgrades     mean_net_change       mean_score_t1      mean_score_end 
#>              0.6469              4.1885              4.0364              6.5154 
#> share_top_grade_end 
#>              0.7642

The changes are not symmetric: 65% of them are upgrades, and a rated name ends the sample 4.2 grades above where it started. On a bounded scale that drift is a compression toward the ceiling, and Table 20.1 shows it: a cross-section that began bell-shaped around grade 4 ends with 76% of the names at the top grade. Figure 20.1 draws the path.







Figure 20.1: The constructed ratings over the sample: the cross-sectional mean score, and the share of names at the top grade. Flat until the first shipped change, then drifting upward because the shipped changes are mostly upgrades.




One sentence settles what the ratings can and cannot do to the returns. Appendix A records that the changes have no effect on the returns, so any performance difference below is a universe and constraint effect, measured on a market in which no rating premium exists, and not a priced rating factor; what it can still be, an exposure the rating carries to characteristics that are priced, is what the application finds.

20.2.2 The sleeve, its benchmark, and its covariance
The sleeve is the one Section 21.2 built: all 123 names, capitalization weighted within region on the last capitalization before the month began, with the regional budgets fixed above the sleeve. Here the five regions receive one fifth each, the simplest multi-region policy; the application uses the policy’s own split. Moments are estimated on the 120 months before the register’s first out-of-sample month with the shrinkage of Section 7.2, because the sample matrix of 123 names on that window is singular by Equation 7.2.

W <- 120L
shrunk <- function(X) {
  S <- corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE)
  matrix(as.numeric(S), ncol(X), ncol(X), dimnames = list(colnames(X), colnames(X)))
}
bench_of <- function(t, budget) {                   # regional budgets, cap weighted within region, by name
  b <- setNames(numeric(N), colnames(X))
  for (g in names(budget)) { j <- names(region)[region == g]; b[j] <- budget[[g]] * cap_w_of(t, j) }
  b
}
budget <- setNames(rep(0.2, length(regions)), regions)
b <- bench_of(t1, budget)
S <- shrunk(X[(t1 - W):(t1 - 1L), ])
s <- L[t1, ]
stopifnot(abs(sum(b) - 1) < 1e-12, identical(names(b), names(s)), identical(rownames(S), names(b)))

te_of    <- function(w, b, S) sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(w - b) %*% S %*% (w - b)))
p_vol    <- function(w, S)    sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w))
score_of <- function(w, s)    sum(w * s) / sum(w)
c(benchmark_score = score_of(b, s), benchmark_vol = p_vol(b, S))
#> benchmark_score   benchmark_vol 
#>          4.1287          0.1104


20.2.3 Exclusion
The screen removes the bottom fifth of each region by score, ties broken by position so that the count is fixed, and reweights the survivors within their region so that the policy’s regional budgets are untouched.

bottom_of <- function(s, q = 0.2)                    # the names in the bottom fifth of their region
  unlist(lapply(split(names(s), region[names(s)]), function(j)
    j[rank(s[j], ties.method = "first") <= ceiling(q * length(j))]), use.names = FALSE)
screen_w <- function(b, excl) {                      # drop the names, reweight within region
  w <- b; w[excl] <- 0
  for (g in unique(region[names(b)])) {
    j <- names(b)[region[names(b)] == g]
    if (sum(w[j]) > 0) w[j] <- w[j] * sum(b[j]) / sum(w[j])
  }
  w
}
excl <- bottom_of(s)
w_ex <- screen_w(b, excl)
b_E  <- sum(b[excl])
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_ex) - 1) < 1e-12, abs(sum(abs(w_ex - b)) / 2 - b_E) < 1e-12)   # eq-20-exclusion
c(excluded = length(excl), benchmark_weight_removed = b_E,
  active_share = sum(abs(w_ex - b)) / 2, tracking_error = te_of(w_ex, b, S),
  score_benchmark = score_of(b, s), score_screened = score_of(w_ex, s))
#>                 excluded benchmark_weight_removed             active_share 
#>                 27.00000                  0.18653                  0.18653 
#>           tracking_error          score_benchmark           score_screened 
#>                  0.01853                  4.12869                  4.43719

The screen removes 27 names carrying 18.7% of the benchmark, which by Equation 20.3 is the active share exactly, at a tracking error of 1.85% a year; it lifts the sleeve’s score from 4.13 to 4.44. For the optimized sleeve the price of each excluded name follows from the multipliers, and the identity of Equation 12.4 is checked with the excluded names’ multipliers in it.

gmv_lo <- function(S) {                              # long-only minimum variance, eq-09-gmv under w >= 0
  n <- ncol(S)
  w <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, rep(0, n), cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)), c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)$solution
  w <- pmax(w, 0); setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
w_mv  <- gmv_lo(S)
keep  <- setdiff(colnames(X), excl)
w_mvx <- setNames(numeric(N), colnames(X)); w_mvx[keep] <- gmv_lo(S[keep, keep])
lambda0 <- as.numeric(t(w_mvx) %*% S %*% w_mvx)
delta   <- setNames(as.numeric(S %*% w_mvx) - lambda0, colnames(X))
free0   <- setdiff(names(which(w_mvx <= 1e-6)), excl)           # at zero by choice, not by exclusion
stopifnot(all(abs(delta[w_mvx > 1e-6]) < 1e-7), all(delta[free0] > -1e-7))   # complementary slackness
S_tilde <- S - (outer(delta, rep(1, N)) + outer(rep(1, N), delta))
w_jm    <- as.numeric(solve(S_tilde, rep(1, N))); w_jm <- w_jm / sum(w_jm)
stopifnot(max(abs(w_jm - w_mvx)) < 1e-6)                        # eq-12-jm with the exclusions in it
wanted  <- excl[delta[excl] < -1e-7]                            # excluded names the optimizer would have held
c(reproduced_to = max(abs(w_jm - w_mvx)), excluded = length(excl), binding = length(wanted),
  held_unconstrained = sum(w_mv[excl] > 1e-6),
  vol_unconstrained = p_vol(w_mv, S), vol_screened = p_vol(w_mvx, S))
#>          reproduced_to               excluded                binding 
#>  0.0000000000000002042 27.0000000000000000000 12.0000000000000000000 
#>     held_unconstrained      vol_unconstrained           vol_screened 
#> 10.0000000000000000000  0.0786390938852850191  0.0818493596425207276
round(sort(-delta[wanted] * 12 * 1e4, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 2)   # the dearest exclusions, annualized variance x 1e4
#> EU_EQU_26 JP_EQU_11 CH_EQU_11 
#>     33.50     31.66     20.65

Of the 27 exclusions, 12 bind on the minimum-variance sleeve and the rest are slack, names the optimizer would not have held given the others; for comparison, the unconstrained portfolio holds 10 of them. The identity reproduces the screened solution to 2e-16, and the multiplier of each binding exclusion is the amount by which its covariances would have to rise for the optimizer to drop it unasked. The screen costs the minimum-variance sleeve 0.32 percentage points of volatility, from 7.86% to 8.18%.

20.2.4 A floor on the sleeve’s rating
The floor enters as factor_exposure_constraint() with the score vector as \(\boldsymbol{B}\), bound by name and asserted, on a minimum-variance sleeve under a ten percent cap per name and the regional budgets as a group constraint with equal bounds, the construction of Section 12.2. The best-in-class form is Equation 20.4, one column per region of centered scores.

shrinkage_moments <- function(R, portfolio) {
  S <- shrunk(zoo::coredata(R))
  list(mu = colMeans(R), sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL)
}
grp  <- split(seq_len(N), region[colnames(X)])
gbud <- budget[names(grp)]
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(gbud)))
base_sleeve <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(X)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.10) |>
  add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp, group_min = unname(gbud), group_max = unname(gbud))

floor_spec <- function(spec, s, floor) {             # s'w >= floor, across the universe
  stopifnot(identical(names(s), names(spec$assets)))
  spec |> add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = s, lower = floor, upper = max(s))
}
bic_B <- function(s, floor, groups = unique(region[names(s)])) {   # eq-20-bic: one column per region
  B <- sapply(groups, function(g) (s - floor) * (region[names(s)] == g))
  rownames(B) <- names(s); B
}
bic_spec <- function(spec, s, floor) {
  B <- bic_B(s, floor); stopifnot(identical(rownames(B), names(spec$assets)))
  spec |> add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = B, lower = rep(0, ncol(B)), upper = rep(max(s), ncol(B)))
}
pa_minvar <- function(spec) {
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(A[(t1 - W):(t1 - 1L), ],
                                         spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                                         optimize_method = "ROI", momentFUN = shrinkage_moments))
  stopifnot(!is.null(w), !anyNA(w), setequal(names(w), colnames(X)))
  w[colnames(X)]
}
# the highest rating the cap and the budgets allow: two names at ten percent per region
top2 <- vapply(names(grp), function(g) mean(sort(s[grp[[g]]], decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]), numeric(1))
s_max <- c(across = sum(gbud * top2), within = min(top2))
floors <- seq(4, 6, by = 0.5); floors <- floors[floors < min(s_max)]
w_mv0 <- pa_minvar(base_sleeve)
round(c(s_max, unconstrained_score = score_of(w_mv0, s)), 3)
#>              across              within unconstrained_score 
#>               6.078               5.598               4.094







NoteThe package has no tracking-error objective, so the second frontier is solved by hand



Section 24.2 established that PortfolioAnalytics cannot write a tracking-error budget, and the same is true of tracking error as an objective: the covariance of active returns is singular along the benchmark, which its quadratic path refuses. The minimum-tracking-error sleeve under the same floor is therefore \(\min_{\boldsymbol{w}} (\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{b})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{b})\) written directly in quadprog, which also returns the multipliers; the two routes are checked against each other on the problem both can solve.



min_te <- function(S, b, cap = pmax(0.10, b), B = NULL, lower = NULL, budget, mu = NULL) {
  # min (w-b)'S(w-b)  s.t. regional budgets, 0 <= w <= cap, B'w >= lower; with mu: min w'Sw instead
  n <- length(b); G <- sapply(names(budget), function(g) as.numeric(region[names(b)] == g))
  Amat <- cbind(G, diag(n), -diag(n)); bvec <- c(unname(budget), rep(0, n), -cap)
  k <- if (is.null(B)) 0L else NCOL(B)
  if (k > 0) { Amat <- cbind(Amat, B); bvec <- c(bvec, lower) }
  dvec <- if (is.null(mu)) 2 * as.numeric(S %*% b) else rep(0, n)
  sol  <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, dvec, Amat, bvec, meq = length(budget))
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0); w <- setNames(w / sum(w), names(b))
  attr(w, "lambda") <- if (k > 0) sol$Lagrangian[ncol(Amat) - k + seq_len(k)] else numeric(0)
  w
}
# the quadratic program and the package agree on the minimum-variance problem with a floor
w_pa <- pa_minvar(floor_spec(base_sleeve, s, 5))
w_qp <- min_te(S, b, cap = rep(0.10, N), B = s, lower = 5, budget = gbud, mu = TRUE)
stopifnot(max(abs(w_pa - w_qp)) < 1e-5)

w_te0 <- min_te(S, b, budget = gbud)                                   # no floor: the benchmark itself
stopifnot(te_of(w_te0, b, S) < 1e-6)
frontier <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(floors, function(f) {
  B_f  <- bic_B(s, f)
  w_a  <- pa_minvar(floor_spec(base_sleeve, s, f)); w_b <- pa_minvar(bic_spec(base_sleeve, s, f))
  t_a  <- min_te(S, b, B = s,   lower = f,               budget = gbud)
  t_b  <- min_te(S, b, B = B_f, lower = rep(0, ncol(B_f)), budget = gbud)
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    tibble::tibble(floor = f, form = "across the universe", objective = "minimum variance: volatility",
                   score = score_of(w_a, s), cost = p_vol(w_a, S), lambda = NA_real_),
    tibble::tibble(floor = f, form = "best in class",       objective = "minimum variance: volatility",
                   score = score_of(w_b, s), cost = p_vol(w_b, S), lambda = NA_real_),
    tibble::tibble(floor = f, form = "across the universe", objective = "minimum tracking error: tracking error",
                   score = score_of(t_a, s), cost = te_of(t_a, b, S), lambda = attr(t_a, "lambda")[1]),
    tibble::tibble(floor = f, form = "best in class",       objective = "minimum tracking error: tracking error",
                   score = score_of(t_b, s), cost = te_of(t_b, b, S), lambda = max(attr(t_b, "lambda"))))
}))








Figure 20.2: The ESG-efficient frontier of the sleeve at the register’s first out-of-sample month: the cost of a rating floor against the rating it buys, for a minimum-variance sleeve (volatility) and a minimum-tracking-error sleeve (tracking error against the capitalization-weighted benchmark), with the floor imposed across the universe or within each region. A flat segment is a floor that does not bind.




Read Figure 20.2 from the left. A floor across the universe at or below the benchmark’s own rating of 4.13 costs the minimum-tracking-error sleeve nothing, which the hidden check asserts: the solution is the benchmark and the multiplier is zero. Above it the cost rises at an increasing rate, as a convex frontier must, reaching 3.76% of tracking error at a floor of 5.5. The best-in-class form costs more at every floor, 4.99% at the top, and it already binds at a floor of 4, because the US benchmark’s own rating is 3.81 and a floor every region must clear cannot buy the rating where it is cheapest. The minimum-variance panel tells the same story in volatility from a different starting point: the unconstrained sleeve’s rating is 4.09, so floors below that are slack for it too.

20.2.5 The multiplier, checked by perturbation

f_chk <- top_f
w_f   <- min_te(S, b, B = s, lower = f_chk, budget = gbud)
w_fh  <- min_te(S, b, B = s, lower = f_chk + 0.01, budget = gbud)
te2   <- function(w) as.numeric(t(w - b) %*% S %*% (w - b))          # monthly variance of active return
fd    <- (te2(w_fh) - te2(w_f)) / 0.01
lam   <- attr(w_f, "lambda")[1]
stopifnot(lam > 0, abs(fd / lam - 1) < 0.05)
c(multiplier = lam, finite_difference = fd, ratio = fd / lam)
#>        multiplier finite_difference             ratio 
#>         0.0002965         0.0003001         1.0122324

The multiplier quadprog returns and the finite difference of Equation 12.3 agree to 1.2%: at a floor of 5.5 the sleeve pays 2.96e-04 of monthly active variance per grade of floor at the margin, which, up to the scale of the objective, is the taste \(\theta\) in Equation 20.1 an investor would have to hold for this to be their unconstrained choice.

20.2.6 The audit
Every solution above is checked against the specification it came from with the audit_spec() of Section 12.2, restricted to the constraint types this chapter writes, and the slack of each floor is read off directly.

audit_spec <- function(w, spec, tol = 1e-6) {
  w <- w[names(spec$assets)]
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(spec$constraints, function(cn) {
    if (!isTRUE(cn$enabled)) return(NULL)
    ok <- switch(cn$type,
      full_investment = , weight_sum = sum(w) >= cn$min_sum - tol && sum(w) <= cn$max_sum + tol,
      box = , long_only = all(w >= cn$min - tol) && all(w <= cn$max + tol),
      group = { g <- vapply(cn$groups, function(i) sum(w[i]), numeric(1))
                all(g >= cn$cLO - tol & g <= cn$cUP + tol) },
      factor_exposure = { e <- as.numeric(t(cn$B) %*% w)
                          all(e >= cn$lower - tol & e <= cn$upper + tol) },
      NA)
    tibble::tibble(constraint = cn$type, satisfied = ok)
  }))
}
spec_a <- floor_spec(base_sleeve, s, 5); spec_b <- bic_spec(base_sleeve, s, 5)
w_a5 <- pa_minvar(spec_a); w_b5 <- pa_minvar(spec_b)
audit <- dplyr::bind_rows(audit_spec(w_a5, spec_a) |> dplyr::mutate(form = "across the universe"),
                          audit_spec(w_b5, spec_b) |> dplyr::mutate(form = "best in class"))
stopifnot(all(audit$satisfied))
slack <- tibble::tibble(
  form  = c("across the universe", rep("best in class", length(grp))),
  where = c("universe", names(grp)),
  slack = c(score_of(w_a5, s) - 5,
            vapply(names(grp), function(g) score_of(w_b5[grp[[g]]], s[grp[[g]]]) - 5, numeric(1))))
slack |> dplyr::mutate(binds = abs(slack) < 1e-6)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   form                where        slack binds
#>   <chr>               <chr>        <dbl> <lgl>
#> 1 across the universe universe -8.88e-16 TRUE 
#> 2 best in class       CH        1.78e-15 TRUE 
#> 3 best in class       EU        0        TRUE 
#> 4 best in class       JP        0        TRUE 
#> 5 best in class       UK        2.08e- 1 FALSE
#> 6 best in class       US        8.88e-16 TRUE

Both solutions pass every line. The across-the-universe floor binds once, at the universe level, and the regions’ own ratings sit wherever the solver found the rating cheapest; the best-in-class floor binds in 4 of the 5 regions, which is where its extra cost in Figure 20.2 comes from.






NoteThe same constructions on real data



The modeled market has no industries to exclude and no emissions to cap; the real-data universes of Section 2.3 have the first. tidypm::pm_screen() returns the column names of the Kenneth French forty-nine industries that a sin, fossil-fuel or weapons screen removes, and an exclusion is then the universe restriction of Equation 20.3:

ind      <- pm_universe("industries49", from = "1990-07-01")       # downloads, then caches
screened <- ind[, setdiff(names(ind), pm_screen(c("sin", "fossil")))]
c(before = ncol(ind), after = ncol(screened))

The screens are conventions, and the point of the chapter is to price the line, not to argue about where it is drawn.

title: 20  Sustainable Investing Constraints
section: 20.3 What the Constraints Cost Out of Sample
text:
20.3 What the Constraints Cost Out of Sample
The sleeve now sits inside the policy of Section 15.3, recomputed as Section 21.3 recomputed it, so that the equity budget \(\omega\) and its regional split are computed rather than quoted.

Re <- R - rf; S16 <- stats::cov(Re); mu16 <- colMeans(Re)
qp <- function(S, a) {       # min w'Sw s.t. a'w = 1, w >= 0, rescaled: a = 1 gives GMV, a = mu the tangency
  n <- ncol(S)
  w <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, rep(0, n), cbind(a, diag(n)), c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)$solution
  w <- pmax(w, 0); setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
kind <- sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re)); sl <- split(colnames(Re), kind)
v <- lapply(names(sl), function(k) {
  a <- sl[[k]]; if (length(a) == 1L) return(setNames(1, a))
  qp(S16[a, a], if (k == "equity") mu16[a] else rep(1, length(a)))
}); names(v) <- names(sl)
sr      <- sapply(v, function(x) as.numeric(Re[, names(x)] %*% x))
budget16 <- qp(stats::cov(sr), colMeans(sr))
policy  <- unlist(lapply(names(v), function(k) budget16[[k]] * v[[k]]))[colnames(R)]
omega   <- budget16[["equity"]]
eq_split <- v$equity[v$equity > 1e-6]; eq_split <- eq_split / sum(eq_split)
stopifnot(!anyNA(policy), abs(sum(policy) - 1) < 1e-10)
budget_app <- setNames(as.numeric(eq_split), sub("_equity$", "", names(eq_split)))
js <- names(region)[region %in% names(budget_app)]        # the sleeve's names
round(c(equity_budget = omega, budget_app), 4)
#> equity_budget            EU            US 
#>        0.2909        0.2951        0.7049

The sleeve holds the 72 names of the EU and US regions at the policy’s split. Three constructions fill it, re-estimated monthly on the trailing 120 months from the register’s first out-of-sample month, with the ratings in force at each month’s start: the screen, which removes the bottom fifth of each region and reweights the survivors; the floor, a minimum-tracking-error sleeve whose rating must reach 5, one grade above the drawn cross-section’s center; and the best-in-class floor, 5 in each region. The floor is fixed for the whole period because the constraint is strategic, and the drift of Figure 20.1 will test what a fixed floor means on a rising scale. The benchmark, the capitalization-weighted sleeve at the same split and the same monthly machinery, is the unconstrained sleeve every cost is measured against.

oos <- seq.int(t1, nrow(X)); floor_app <- 5
bench_app <- function(t) {
  b <- setNames(numeric(length(js)), js)
  for (g in names(budget_app)) { j <- js[region[js] == g]; b[j] <- budget_app[[g]] * cap_w_of(t, j) }
  b
}
runs <- lapply(oos, function(t) {
  b_t <- bench_app(t); s_t <- L[t, js]; S_t <- shrunk(X[(t - W):(t - 1L), js])
  B_t <- bic_B(s_t, floor_app, groups = names(budget_app))
  ex  <- bottom_of(s_t)
  list(benchmark = b_t,
       screen    = screen_w(b_t, ex),
       floor     = min_te(S_t, b_t, B = s_t, lower = floor_app, budget = budget_app),
       `best in class` = min_te(S_t, b_t, B = B_t, lower = rep(0, ncol(B_t)), budget = budget_app),
       excluded = ex, bench_score = score_of(b_t, s_t))
})
fillers <- c("benchmark", "screen", "floor", "best in class")
Wm <- lapply(fillers, function(f) t(vapply(runs, function(r) as.numeric(r[[f]]), numeric(length(js)))))
names(Wm) <- fillers
stopifnot(all(vapply(Wm, function(M) max(abs(rowSums(M) - 1)) < 1e-8, logical(1))))

rate <- pm_costs_default()[["equity"]]
path <- function(Wm, Xj) {                          # weights set at each month start, as in chapter 21
  gross   <- rowSums(Wm * Xj)
  drifted <- Wm * (1 + Xj) / (1 + gross)
  trade   <- rbind(0, abs(Wm[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(Wm), , drop = FALSE]))
  tibble::tibble(gross = gross, cost = rate * rowSums(trade), turnover = rowSums(trade) / 2)
}
paths <- lapply(Wm, path, Xj = X[oos, js])


register_score <- function(r, rf_oos) {             # the register's definitions
  n <- length(r)
  c(ann_return = prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - 1, ann_vol = stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12),
    sharpe = (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf_oos)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12)))
}
te <- function(a) stats::sd(a) * sqrt(12)
ir <- function(a) mean(a) / stats::sd(a) * sqrt(12)
Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, ]; rest <- setdiff(colnames(R), names(eq_split))
r_rest  <- as.numeric(Rm[, rest] %*% policy[rest])
r_bench <- paths$benchmark$gross
scores <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(fillers, function(f) {
  s_ <- paths[[f]]$gross; tot <- r_rest + omega * s_; tot_b <- r_rest + omega * r_bench
  tibble::tibble(sleeve = f, !!!as.list(register_score(s_, rf[oos])),
                 te = te(s_ - r_bench), ir = ir(s_ - r_bench),
                 turnover = mean(paths[[f]]$turnover) * 12,
                 total_sharpe = register_score(tot, rf[oos])[["sharpe"]],
                 total_sharpe_net = register_score(tot - omega * paths[[f]]$cost, rf[oos])[["sharpe"]],
                 total_te = te(tot - tot_b))
}))

Three things are in Table 20.2. First, the costs in active risk. The screen tracks the unconstrained sleeve at 3.03% a year, the floor at 1.44% and the best-in-class floor at 1.39%, each arriving at the policy multiplied by \(\omega\) as Equation 21.1 says. Second, the turnover. The unconstrained sleeve trades 36% a year to follow its own capitalization weights; the screen trades 43%, the excess being the 33 months in which a rating change moved a name across the quintile boundary and forced a sale or a repurchase, which is the trading Section 23.3 prices and which the net column charges at 10 basis points. Third, the returns, and here the table does not say what the construction led us to expect. The two floors earn information ratios of -0.30 and -0.06 against the unconstrained sleeve, within two standard errors of zero by Equation 24.10, and cost the policy 0.028 and 0.006 of Sharpe ratio. The screen earns -0.57, which is 2.6 standard errors from zero, and costs the policy 0.122 of Sharpe ratio, from 0.879 to 0.756. On a market whose returns do not respond to the ratings, a screen that costs two percentage points of return a year needs an explanation, and the first question is whether it is the draw.

z0 <- (s0 - 4) / 1.2                                  # the first rater's standardized draw
second_rater <- function(rho, seed)
  esg_start(eq$asset_id, seed = seed,
            dist = function(n) 4 + 1.2 * (rho * z0 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * stats::rnorm(n)))
screen_ir <- function(L2) {                           # the screen's record under another rater's levels
  W2 <- t(vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
    as.numeric(screen_w(runs[[i]]$benchmark, bottom_of(L2[oos[i], js]))), numeric(length(js))))
  ir(rowSums(W2 * X[oos, js]) - r_bench)
}
seeds  <- 1:20
ir_ens <- vapply(seeds, function(sd) screen_ir(esg_levels(second_rater(0, sd))), numeric(1))
stopifnot(mean(ir_ens) < 0, sum(ir_ens < 0) > length(seeds) / 2)
c(mean_ir = mean(ir_ens), negative = sum(ir_ens < 0), of = length(seeds), base_rater = g_("screen", "ir"))
#>    mean_ir   negative         of base_rater 
#>    -0.2540    17.0000    20.0000    -0.5742

It is not the draw. Under 20 raters whose starting cross-sections share nothing with ours, the screen’s information ratio is negative 17 times out of 20 and averages -0.25. What the raters share is the shipped change path, and the change path is not independent of the names’ other characteristics.

net_all <- setNames(numeric(N), colnames(X)); net_all[names(net)] <- net
sector  <- setNames(eq$sector, eq$asset_id)
by_sector <- tibble::tibble(asset = colnames(X), sector = sector[colnames(X)],
                            net_change = net_all, oos_return = colMeans(X[oos, ]) * 12) |>
  dplyr::group_by(sector) |>
  dplyr::summarise(names = dplyr::n(), net_change = mean(net_change), oos_return = mean(oos_return)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(net_change))
rho_sector <- stats::cor(by_sector$net_change, by_sector$oos_return, method = "spearman")
stopifnot(rho_sector < 0)

Table 20.3 is the explanation. The shipped upgrades cluster by sector: Healthcare names gained 5.1 grades on average over the sample and Basic Materials names 3.2, and the sectors upgraded most are the sectors whose names earned least in this sample, with a rank correlation of -0.71 across the 8 sectors. A rating is therefore partly a sector label, and a screen that removes the lowest-rated fifth of each region removes names from the sectors that happened to pay, under any rater who sees the same changes. The returns do not respond to the ratings; the ratings respond to something the returns also respond to. That is the general case rather than a quirk of this market: real ratings load on industry, size and region (Berg et al. 2022), and Pedersen et al. (2021) price a rating constraint through exactly those exposures. The cost of a constraint on an unpriced characteristic is the cost of the priced characteristics it is correlated with, which is what Section 5.2 would recover by regressing the screen’s active return on the sector series.







Figure 20.3: The unconstrained sleeve’s own rating over the out-of-sample period against the floor of 5, and the ex-ante tracking error the floor costs each month. The floor binds while the benchmark’s rating is below it and is slack, at zero cost, once the drift of the shipped changes carries the benchmark past it.




Figure 20.3 is complementary slackness on a calendar. The floor binds from the register’s first month until July of model year 14, when the unconstrained sleeve’s own rating reaches 5 on the strength of the shipped upgrades; from then on the floor sleeve is the benchmark, its ex-ante tracking error is zero, and the line in the mandate costs nothing. Everything the floor cost in Table 20.2 was paid in the first 3.5 model years. A strategic constraint written as an absolute level on a scale that drifts is a constraint that expires; one written relative to the benchmark, a grade above it, would bind throughout and cost throughout, and the exercises ask for it.

20.3.1 A second rater
The last question is how much of the exclusion list is the rater’s. A second rater draws a different starting cross-section, correlated with the first at \(\rho\), sees the same shipped changes, and runs the same screen; the share of the first rater’s exclusions that the second does not exclude is the disagreement Berg et al. (2022) measured, in the units a mandate feels it. Their average correlation across providers is 0.54; a correlation of zero is a rater who shares nothing but the changes, and 0.8 a close one.

flip_share <- function(rho, seed, t) {
  L2 <- esg_levels(second_rater(rho, seed))
  e1 <- bottom_of(L[t, js]); e2 <- bottom_of(L2[t, js])
  1 - length(intersect(e1, e2)) / length(e1)
}
t_end <- nrow(X)
disagree <- tidyr::expand_grid(rho = c(0, 0.54, 0.8), when = c("register start", "end of sample")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(flipped = purrr::map2_dbl(rho, when, function(r, w)
    mean(vapply(seeds, function(sd) flip_share(r, sd, if (w == "register start") t1 else t_end), numeric(1)))))
stopifnot(all(diff(disagree$flipped[disagree$when == "register start"]) < 0),   # closer raters disagree less
          all(disagree$flipped[disagree$when == "end of sample"] <
              disagree$flipped[disagree$when == "register start"]))              # the shared changes pull the lists together
disagree |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = when, values_from = flipped)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>     rho `register start` `end of sample`
#>   <dbl>            <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1  0               0.807           0.407
#> 2  0.54            0.54            0.283
#> 3  0.8             0.337           0.187

At the correlation Berg et al. (2022) report, 54% of the first rater’s exclusion list is not on the second rater’s at the register’s start, and 28% at the end of the sample, when twenty model years of shared changes have pulled the two cross-sections together. With uncorrelated raters the lists share almost nothing at the start, 81% flipped, which is what two independent draws of a bottom fifth must give; with closely agreeing raters the list still turns over by 34%. The content of the mandate, which names are out, is therefore largely the rater’s choice, while its cost in Table 20.2 and the sector exposure behind that cost are not, because every rater sees the same changes. That is the state of the data, and it is the reason the chapter has priced the constraint rather than the names: the price survives a change of rater, the list does not. What a screen does to a backtest’s error bar is a question for Section 25.3, and whether the tilt’s realized cost is stable across re-estimation windows is the kind of question Section 28.3 asks of every construction in the book.

title: 20  Sustainable Investing Constraints
text:
Key Takeaways

A taste for a rating and a floor on it trace the same ESG-efficient frontier (Pedersen et al. 2021): the floor’s multiplier is the taste, a floor the unconstrained portfolio already clears costs nothing, and one that binds costs variance or tracking error at the rate of Equation 12.3. In equilibrium the taste is priced (Pástor et al. 2021), so the constraint is a cost and not an alpha.
An exclusion is a box constraint at zero. For a capitalization-weighted sleeve its active share is the benchmark weight removed, Equation 20.3; for an optimized sleeve the Jagannathan–Ma identity holds with the excluded names’ multipliers in it, and a binding exclusion is the same as raising the excluded name’s covariances until the optimizer drops it (Jagannathan and Ma 2003; Hong and Kacperczyk 2009).
A rating floor is factor_exposure_constraint() with the score as \(\boldsymbol{B}\); a best-in-class floor is Equation 20.4, linear in centered scores, and costs more because it cannot buy the rating where it is cheapest. The package cannot write tracking error as an objective, so the minimum-tracking-error sleeve is solved by hand and checked against the package on the problem both can solve.
The modeled market ships rating changes and no levels, so the levels here are a construction, stated and seeded, and the returns do not respond to them. The shipped changes are mostly upgrades, so a fixed floor expires as the scale drifts and costs nothing once it is slack. The screen nevertheless costs return out of sample under every rater, because the changes cluster by sector and the sectors upgraded most earned least: a constraint on an unpriced characteristic costs what the priced characteristics it is correlated with cost.
A rating is an estimate (Berg et al. 2022; Avramov et al. 2022): at the correlation between real raters, roughly half of an exclusion list is the rater’s choice. Price the constraint, not the names.

title: 20  Sustainable Investing Constraints
text:
Exercises

Replace the absolute floor of 5 in Section 20.3 with a relative one, the unconstrained sleeve’s own rating plus half a grade, capped at the attainable maximum. Recompute Table 20.2 for the floor sleeve. Does the constraint bind throughout, and what does it cost in tracking error and turnover against the absolute version?
Redraw the starting cross-section with a standard deviation of 0.6 grades instead of 1.2 and rebuild Figure 20.2. Explain, using Equation 20.2 and the multiplier, why a narrower cross-section makes every floor more expensive.
Impose the screen of Section 20.2 as a box constraint with max = 0 on the excluded names, by name, in PortfolioAnalytics, and verify with audit_spec() that the minimum-variance solution agrees with the universe restriction w_mvx. Then exclude the bottom tenth instead and report how many exclusions bind.
Repeat the second-rater exercise for the floor sleeve rather than the screen: at \(\rho = 0.54\), how far apart are the two raters’ floor portfolios in active share and in tracking error against each other at the register’s start? Relate the answer to Gibson Brandon et al. (2021).
