title: 21  The Equity Sleeve
text:
21.1 Selection Inside a Budget
An equity sleeve arrives with two things fixed from above: a budget, and a benchmark it will be measured against. Which stocks should fill it, and is whatever the selection earns still visible once the sleeve is one line of the allocation that set the budget? Fama and French (1992) and Fama and French (1993) showed that the cross-section of stock returns lines up with a few observable characteristics, which is what makes selection by sorting a method rather than a habit, and Treynor and Black (1973) showed how a portfolio selected for its alpha is to be combined with the passive portfolio it departs from, so the two questions have been one question since. This is the first chapter of the book to work inside a class rather than across classes: the granularity axis of Section 3.1 made concrete, on the 123 equities behind the five equity series that Parts III to V allocated as single numbers.
We first set out the sleeve’s benchmark and mandate, the arithmetic that carries its active return into the total portfolio, the sorts this market can run, and the estimation problem that so many names create; then we rebuild the benchmark from its instruments, measure equal against capitalization weighting, sort on size and momentum, race a factor covariance against shrinkage, and build a minimum-variance sleeve under a tracking-error budget, directly and as a sub-portfolio; then we fill the equity budget of the policy of Section 15.3 three ways and ask what the total portfolio noticed. On the horizon axis a permanent tilt toward a characteristic is strategic and a signal re-read every month, such as momentum, is tactical. The sleeve built here is strategic: it conditions on nothing but a rolling covariance estimate and the benchmark’s weights.

title: 21  The Equity Sleeve
text:
21.1.1 The benchmark, the mandate, and the arithmetic of a sleeve
The sleeve’s benchmark is the class series it sits inside: the capitalization-weighted regional equity index of Section 2.2, which Section 15.1 handed down as the policy’s investable proxy. Write \(\boldsymbol{b}\) for the benchmark’s weights over the \(N\) names of the region, \(\boldsymbol{v}\) for the sleeve’s, and \(\boldsymbol{x} =
\boldsymbol{v} - \boldsymbol{b}\) for the active weights of Equation 24.1. The mandate is the one Section 24.1 wrote down: as much active return as a tracking-error budget \(\tau\) buys, \(\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{x}} \leq \tau\), scored by the information ratio of Equation 24.3.
The sleeve holds a share \(\omega\) of the total portfolio and the policy holds the same share in the benchmark. With every other line of the policy held as it is,
\[
r^{P}_t - r^{B}_t = \omega\,(r^{S}_t - r^{b}_t),
\qquad
\alpha_P = \omega\,\alpha_S,
\qquad
\text{TE}_P = \omega\,\text{TE}_S,
\qquad
\text{IR}_P = \text{IR}_S ,
\tag{21.1}\]
where \(r^{S}\) and \(r^{b}\) are the sleeve’s return and its benchmark’s. The budget scales active return and tracking error alike and leaves the information ratio alone: selection skill is not diluted by the allocation above it, only its weight in the outcome is. How much the total portfolio’s Sharpe ratio can gain is the result of Treynor and Black (1973). With the sleeve’s excess return regressed on the benchmark’s, \(\alpha\) the intercept and \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) the residual volatility, the optimal combination of active sleeve and passive portfolio reaches
\[
\text{SR}^2_{P} = \text{SR}^2_{B} + \left(\frac{\alpha}{\sigma_\varepsilon}\right)^2 ,
\tag{21.2}\]
the second term being the appraisal ratio of Section 24.1. An appraisal ratio of one quarter added to a policy Sharpe ratio of three quarters gives \(\sqrt{0.75^2 + 0.25^2} = 0.791\), a ceiling reached only if \(\omega\) is chosen for it rather than set by the policy. The application checks both: whether the sleeve earned an information ratio at all, and how much of it a fixed budget let through.

21.1.2 Selection by characteristic
A sort ranks the names on a characteristic known at the start of the month and holds the favored group. Size was the first (Banz 1981; Fama and French 1992), momentum the most durable (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993), value the one that completes the standard set (Fama and French 1993; Asness et al. 2013). Building the factors as tradable portfolios is the subject of Scheuch et al. (2023) and is not reproduced here. Size and momentum need capitalizations and past returns, which ship; value needs a fundamental, and the modeled market carries none, so no value sort can be built on it, and Asness et al. (2013) is the account of what it would add, a premium negatively correlated with momentum in every market they study. Fama and French (2012) find the premia local rather than global, and Section 5.2 found why on this market: a global size sort in a five-region universe sorts on region. Every sort below is therefore run within a region and averaged across the five, as Griffin (2002) recommends; Section 18.2 estimates the same two characteristics as a parametric policy with standard errors.
What a sleeve buys with many names is breadth. The fundamental law of Grinold (1989), Equation 24.4, puts the attainable information ratio at \(\text{IC}\sqrt{\text{BR}}\cdot\text{TC}\): a monthly sort over one region’s names takes several hundred independent decisions a year where the sixteen-class allocator of Section 24.1 takes sixteen, so the same information ratio needs a far smaller information coefficient (Grinold and Kahn 2000), less what the long-only constraint takes back (Clarke et al. 2002).

21.1.3 Equal weighting is an active bet
The simplest alternative to the benchmark holds every name at \(1/N\). Its active weights are \(1/N - b_i\), long every name smaller than average and short every larger one, rebalanced against drift every month: a size tilt and a contrarian rule at once, and Plyakha et al. (2021) find both parts matter. DeMiguel et al. (2009) is the reason the rule is taken seriously; Section 24.3 showed that as a benchmark it embeds a permanent bet against the largest market. Inside a sleeve it is a bet against the largest names, and the question is whether it pays.

21.1.4 The covariance matrix of a sleeve
Everything the sleeve optimizes needs \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) over its names, and Equation 7.2 settles what the sample estimate can deliver: with \(N = 123\), any window shorter than 124 months gives a singular matrix, and Section 7.1 showed that a minimizer handed one finds the portfolios it believes are riskless and holds them. A sleeve over the full universe therefore needs one of the repairs of Section 7.2 before it can be optimized at all. Shrinkage (Ledoit and Wolf 2003, 2004) pulls the sample matrix toward a well-conditioned target; the alternative is to assert a structure. With \(k\) statistical factors extracted from the returns themselves,
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_k = \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}' + \boldsymbol{D},
\tag{21.3}\]
where \(\boldsymbol{B}\) is \(N \times k\), the first \(k\) principal components scaled by their volatilities, and \(\boldsymbol{D}\) the diagonal matrix of residual variances: \(N(k+1)\) parameters in place of \(N(N+1)/2\), and full rank whatever \(T\) is because \(\boldsymbol{D}\) is positive. Connor and Korajczyk (1993) justify principal components as the factors and give a test for \(k\); Bai and Ng (2002) give the criteria for choosing \(k\) that are now standard. Which repair is better is settled out of sample, as Section 7.3 settled it.
Within one region, with \(N\) between 17 and 37, the matrix is estimable but a ten-year window gives about three observations per parameter, and shrinkage still keeps the weights from reading noise. The practical form of a concentrated sleeve is a cardinality limit, at most \(K\) names, which Section 12.2 showed to be a mixed-integer program (Bienstock 1996) that the package honors only on its linear paths; the convex substitute is a cap per name, itself a shrinkage of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) by Jagannathan and Ma (2003). The tracking-error budget has a closed-form reading for a minimum-variance sleeve: the Lagrangian of variance subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{x} \leq \tau^2\) is, up to a constant and a positive scale, the one-parameter family
\[
\boldsymbol{v}(\theta) = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{v}}\;
  \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{v}
  - 2\theta\,\boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{v},
\qquad \theta = \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda} \in [0, 1),
\tag{21.4}\]
so that without further constraints \(\boldsymbol{v}(\theta) = \theta\boldsymbol{b}
+ (1-\theta)\boldsymbol{v}_{\text{mv}}\): the budget picks a blend of the benchmark and the minimum-variance portfolio. Under a box the blend is no longer linear, but Equation 21.4 is still one quadratic program per \(\theta\), and a root search finds the \(\theta\) that spends the budget exactly, which spares the rolling loop a cone solver several hundred times. Roll (1992) is the standing warning: the family does not ask whether the benchmark is efficient.

title: 21  The Equity Sleeve
text:
21.2 Implementation

21.2.1 The benchmark, rebuilt from its instruments
The class series are capitalization weighted on the previous week’s capitalization, weekly, and compounded to months, the one-period lag Section 5.2 imposed on its market proxy. Rebuilding them from the instruments is the check that the benchmark is one the sleeve could have held.

cap_w <- sim_marketcap_weekly[sim_marketcap_weekly$asset %in% eq$asset_id, ] |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = asset, values_from = market_cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
Aw <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_weekly[sim_asset_returns_weekly$asset %in% eq$asset_id, ],
                date, asset, return)[, eq$asset_id]
wk   <- zoo::index(Aw)
prev <- match(wk, cap_w$date) - 1L                 # the week before each return week
stopifnot(!anyNA(prev), all(prev >= 1L))
cap_prev <- as.matrix(cap_w[prev, eq$asset_id])
stopifnot(!anyNA(cap_prev))
month_of <- findInterval(wk, d, left.open = TRUE) + 1L   # every week lies in the month it compounds into
stopifnot(all(month_of %in% seq_along(d)))

rebuilt <- sapply(regions, function(g) {
  j <- names(region)[region == g]
  w <- cap_prev[, j] / rowSums(cap_prev[, j])
  tapply(rowSums(w * zoo::coredata(Aw[, j])), month_of, function(x) prod(1 + x) - 1)
})
shipped <- zoo::coredata(R[, paste0(regions, "_equity")])
gap <- max(abs(rebuilt - shipped))
stopifnot(gap < 1e-12)
c(months = nrow(rebuilt), weeks = length(wk), largest_gap = gap)
#>                   months                    weeks              largest_gap 
#>  372.0000000000000000000 1618.0000000000000000000    0.0000000000000006384

The five series reproduce to 6e-16. For the monthly work that follows, the benchmark weight for month \(t\) is the last capitalization observed before \(t\) began, indexed by name.

Cap <- as.matrix(cap_w[findInterval(c(wk[1] - 1, d[-length(d)]), cap_w$date), eq$asset_id])
stopifnot(!anyNA(Cap), nrow(Cap) == nrow(X), identical(colnames(Cap), colnames(X)))
bench_w <- function(t, j) Cap[t, j] / sum(Cap[t, j])      # the benchmark's weights for month t

conc <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(regions, function(g) {
  j  <- names(region)[region == g]
  Wb <- Cap[, j] / rowSums(Cap[, j])
  tibble::tibble(region = g, names = length(j),
    ratio = mean(apply(Cap[, j], 1, max) / apply(Cap[, j], 1, min)),
    top5  = mean(apply(Wb, 1, function(w) sum(sort(w, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]))),
    eff   = mean(1 / rowSums(Wb^2)),
    largest = max(Wb))
}))

21.2.2 Equal against capitalization weighting

ew_cw <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(regions, function(g) {
  j  <- names(region)[region == g]
  cw <- as.numeric(R[, paste0(g, "_equity")])        # the shipped benchmark
  ew <- rowMeans(X[, j])                              # one over N, rebalanced monthly
  tibble::tibble(region = g, cw_ret = ann_ret(cw), ew_ret = ann_ret(ew),
                 cw_vol = ann_vol(cw), ew_vol = ann_vol(ew),

}))

Equal weighting earns more than its benchmark in every region, by 1.3 to 4.1 percentage points a year, at a tracking error of 3.9% to 7.3%, larger than most mandates allow. The information ratios run from 0.24 to 0.49; by Equation 24.10 their standard error over 372 months is about 0.18, so the smaller ones are not distinguishable from zero and the larger ones barely are. Whether the gap is a size premium or the rebalancing of Plyakha et al. (2021) is what the sorts separate.

21.2.3 Sorting on size and momentum
Size is the benchmark weight itself; momentum is the return over months \(t-12\) to \(t-2\), skipping the most recent month as Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) do. Both are sorted into terciles within each region and the five spreads are averaged. The long-short spread is the favored tercile minus the opposite one; the long-only spread, which a sleeve can hold, is the favored tercile minus the equally weighted region. Standard errors are those of Newey and West (1987) at six lags, the call Section 5.2 uses.

mom <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(X), ncol(X), dimnames = dimnames(X))
for (t in 13:nrow(X)) mom[t, ] <- apply(1 + X[(t - 12):(t - 2), ], 2, prod) - 1

sort_spread <- function(signal, favored) {        # favored tercile: 1 lowest, 3 highest
  t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(t) {
    if (anyNA(signal[t, ])) return(c(long_short = NA_real_, long_only = NA_real_))
    legs <- vapply(regions, function(g) {
      j <- names(region)[region == g]; q <- dplyr::ntile(signal[t, j], 3)
      c(fav = mean(X[t, j][q == favored]), opp = mean(X[t, j][q == 4 - favored]),
        all = mean(X[t, j]))
    }, numeric(3))
    m <- rowMeans(legs)                             # each region counts once
    c(long_short = m[["fav"]] - m[["opp"]], long_only = m[["fav"]] - m[["all"]])
  }, numeric(2)))
}
nw <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]; m <- stats::lm(x ~ 1)
  c(mean = 12 * mean(x), t = unname(stats::coef(m)) /
      sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)[1, 1]), months = length(x))
}
size_s <- sort_spread(Cap, favored = 1)             # small minus big
mom_s  <- sort_spread(mom, favored = 3)             # winners minus losers
sorts  <- tibble::tibble(
  sort = rep(c("size, small minus big", "momentum, winners minus losers"), each = 2),
  leg  = rep(c("long-short", "long-only"), 2)) |>
  dplyr::bind_cols(dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(list(size_s[, 1], size_s[, 2], mom_s[, 1], mom_s[, 2]),
                                           function(x) as.list(nw(x)))))

Size is there and momentum is not. Small names earn 4.9 percentage points a year more than large ones within their region, at \(t = 3.7\), and the long-only version a sleeve could hold keeps 2.5 points of it at \(t = 3.1\); this is the gap of Table 21.2 seen from the characteristic’s side, and Section 18.2 recovers the same sign with a standard error on the coefficient. The momentum spread is +1.6 points at \(t = 0.96\). The absence is a property of the modeled data rather than of the strategy: each instrument’s idiosyncratic component is drawn independently period by period, as Section 2.2 describes, so a name’s own past return carries no information about its own future return, and cross-sectional momentum, which lives in exactly that autocorrelation, cannot exist here by construction. A real market has it (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993; Fama and French 2012); this one tests the machinery, and a reader who wants the premium should run the same code on the real-data sleeves of Section 2.3.

21.2.4 A covariance matrix for one hundred and twenty-three names
statistical.factor.model() fits Equation 21.3 by principal components and extractCovariance() assembles the matrix. On the full sample it runs; on the ten-year window it is needed for, it does not.

fm  <- lapply(1:3, function(k) statistical.factor.model(A, k = k))
S_k <- lapply(fm, extractCovariance)
share <- stats::prcomp(X)$sdev^2; share <- share / sum(share)      # variance by component

factor_covs <- function(X, ks = 1:3) {             # eq-21-factor-cov for several k at once
  pc <- stats::prcomp(X)
  lapply(ks, function(k) {
    B <- pc$rotation[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE]; f <- X %*% B
    e <- X - f %*% t(B); e <- sweep(e, 2, colMeans(e))
    B %*% stats::cov(f) %*% t(B) + diag(colSums(e^2) / (nrow(X) - k - 1L))
  })
}
stopifnot(all(mapply(function(a, b) max(abs(a - b)) < 1e-12, factor_covs(X), S_k)))
refused <- tryCatch(statistical.factor.model(A[1:120, ], k = 3), error = conditionMessage)
c(first_component = share[1], next_two = sum(share[2:3]), refused = refused)
#>                  first_component                         next_two 
#>              "0.272666293574177"             "0.0797665088248939" 
#>                          refused 
#> "fewer observations than assets"







Importantstatistical.factor.model() refuses the case it exists for



The function stops whenever \(T < N\), which Section 7.2 recorded and which is exactly the window on which Equation 21.3 is needed: principal components need enough components, not enough columns. factor_covs() is the body of the function without the check, and the assertion above shows that it returns the package’s matrix wherever the package returns one.


The first component carries 27% of the variance and the next two 8% together. The race is the one R/ch05-estimator-race.R ran for Section 7.3: minimum variance, long only, on a rolling window of one hundred and twenty months, held one month, from the register’s first out-of-sample month. The sample matrix is singular on every window by Equation 7.2, and quadprog refuses it rather than inverting noise.

min_var <- function(S) {                           # long only, fully invested
  n <- ncol(S)
  sol <- try(quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, rep(0, n), cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
                                c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(sol, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0); w / sum(w)
}
shrunk <- function(X) {                            # corpcor's matrix, stripped to a plain one
  S <- corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE)
  matrix(as.numeric(S), ncol(X), ncol(X), dimnames = list(colnames(X), colnames(X)))
}
N   <- ncol(X)
W   <- 120L
oos <- seq.int(W + 1L, nrow(X))                     # the register's out-of-sample months
stopifnot(oos[1] == 121L)
sample_refused <- is.null(min_var(stats::cov(X[seq_len(W), ])))

paths <- lapply(oos, function(t) {
  Xw <- X[(t - W):(t - 1L), ]
  c(list(shrunk = min_var(shrunk(Xw))),
    setNames(lapply(factor_covs(Xw), min_var), paste("factor, k =", 1:3)))
})
score <- function(r, rf_oos) {                      # the register's definitions
  n <- length(r)
  c(ann_return = prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - 1, ann_vol = stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12),
    sharpe = (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf_oos)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12)))
}
race <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(paths[[1]]), function(nm) {
  Wm <- t(vapply(paths, function(p) p[[nm]], numeric(N)))
  r  <- rowSums(Wm * X[oos, ])
  tibble::tibble(estimator = nm, !!!as.list(score(r, rf[oos])),
                 eff_names = mean(1 / rowSums(Wm^2)), held = mean(rowSums(Wm > 1e-6)))
}))
race <- dplyr::bind_rows(race, tibble::tibble(estimator = "equal weight",
                                              !!!as.list(score(rowMeans(X[oos, ]), rf[oos])),
                                              eff_names = N, held = N))

Scored on the months the register’s race covers, the shrinkage row reproduces Section 7.3’s to six decimals, which the hidden chunk asserts. The factor matrices give the lowest realized volatility, 11.1% for factor, k = 3 against 11.8% for shrinkage and 17.0% for equal weighting; the shrinkage matrix gives the highest Sharpe ratio, 0.82 against 0.67. Which repair is better depends on which number the mandate scores.

21.2.5 The selected sleeve
The sleeve is built for the United States as of the first out-of-sample month, with the shrinkage moments of Section 7.2 passed through momentFUN.

us   <- names(region)[region == "US"]
t1   <- oos[1]
A_us <- A[(t1 - W):(t1 - 1L), us]                   # the window before t1
S_us <- shrunk(zoo::coredata(A_us)); b_us <- bench_w(t1, us)
shrinkage_moments <- function(R, portfolio) {
  S <- shrunk(zoo::coredata(R))
  list(mu = colMeans(R), sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = colMeans(R), var = S)
}
base_us <- portfolio.spec(us) |>
  add.constraint("full_investment") |> add.constraint("long_only")
w_mv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(A_us, base_us |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                                          optimize_method = "ROI", momentFUN = shrinkage_moments))
p_vol <- function(w, S = S_us) sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w))
c(held = sum(w_mv > 1e-6), largest = max(w_mv), vol = p_vol(w_mv), benchmark_vol = p_vol(b_us))
#>          held       largest           vol benchmark_vol 
#>       19.0000        0.1504        0.1145        0.1470

Unconstrained, minimum variance holds 19 of the 35 names and puts 15% in one of them. A mandate limits that, and the two ways of writing the limit behave differently in the package.






ImportantA position limit is honored on the ES path and dropped on the variance path




K <- 10L
spec_K <- base_us |> add.constraint(type = "position_limit", max_pos = K)
w_K_var <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(A_us, spec_K |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                                             optimize_method = "ROI", momentFUN = shrinkage_moments))
w_K_es  <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(A_us, spec_K |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES"),
                                             optimize_method = "ROI"))
stopifnot(sum(w_K_es > 1e-6) <= K, isTRUE(all.equal(w_K_var, w_mv)))
c(limit = K, held_variance = sum(w_K_var > 1e-6), held_ES = sum(w_K_es > 1e-6))
#>         limit held_variance       held_ES 
#>            10            19            10

Under a variance objective ROI has no integer formulation, so the limit of 10 names is read and discarded: 19 names come back, identical to the unconstrained solution, as Section 12.2 measured on the sixteen classes. Under a minimum-ES objective the same constraint goes to Rglpk as a mixed-integer linear program and is honored. A concentrated minimum-variance sleeve has no exact solver in the package; Chang et al. (2000)’s screening heuristic is the practical route, and the convex substitute used below is a cap per name.


The cap is ten percent, or the benchmark’s own weight where that is larger, since the largest American name reaches 24% of its index and a flat ten percent would force an underweight of that size whatever the budget said. The budget is four percent a year, the figure Section 24.2 spent, and it enters through Equation 21.4, because the package cannot express it, for the reasons that chapter’s callout gives; the cone solver built there solves the same problem once, and the family solves it several hundred times.

te_of <- function(w, b, S) sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(w - b) %*% S %*% (w - b)))
sleeve_family <- function(S, b, cap) {               # eq-21-family under a box
  n <- length(b); Sb <- as.numeric(S %*% b)
  Amat <- cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n), -diag(n)); bvec <- c(1, rep(0, n), -cap)
  function(theta) {
    w <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, 2 * theta * Sb, Amat, bvec, meq = 1)$solution
    w <- pmax(w, 0); setNames(w / sum(w), names(b))
  }
}
select_sleeve <- function(S, b, tau, cap = pmax(0.10, b)) {
  f  <- sleeve_family(S, b, cap)
  w0 <- f(0)
  if (te_of(w0, b, S) <= tau) return(w0)             # the budget is slack
  theta <- stats::uniroot(function(th) te_of(f(th), b, S) - tau, c(0, 1), tol = 1e-9)$root
  f(theta)
}
tau   <- 0.04
w_sel <- select_sleeve(S_us, b_us, tau)
stopifnot(abs(te_of(w_sel, b_us, S_us) - tau) < 1e-6, all(w_sel <= pmax(0.10, b_us) + 1e-8))
c(held = sum(w_sel > 1e-6), largest = max(w_sel), tracking_error = te_of(w_sel, b_us, S_us),
  vol = p_vol(w_sel), active_share = sum(abs(w_sel - b_us)) / 2)
#>           held        largest tracking_error            vol   active_share 
#>       29.00000        0.09989        0.04000        0.12408        0.34957

The sleeve holds 29 names, spends the budget exactly, and has an estimated volatility of 12.4% against the benchmark’s 14.7% and the unconstrained minimum’s 11.5%: the budget bought 71% of the distance between the two, which is Equation 21.4 read as a blend.

21.2.6 The sleeve as a sub-portfolio
mult.portfolio.spec() is the package’s structure for a sleeve the allocation layer can consume, and Section 15.2 established what it does and which arguments have to be set for it to run. Each regional sleeve becomes a sub-portfolio, minimum variance under the cap, re-estimated yearly on the trailing window; the top level allocates across the five proxies.

sleeve_spec <- function(a) portfolio.spec(a) |>
  add.constraint("full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.10) |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
top <- portfolio.spec(regions) |>
  add.constraint("full_investment") |> add.constraint("long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

mp <- mult.portfolio.spec(top)
for (g in regions)
  mp <- add.sub.portfolio(mp, sleeve_spec(names(region)[region == g]), optimize_method = "ROI",
                          rebalance_on = "years", training_period = W, trailing_periods = W - 1L,
                          momentFUN = shrinkage_moments)      # passed through to the rolling solver
o_mp <- optimize.portfolio(A, mp, optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE)
top_w <- setNames(as.numeric(o_mp$weights), regions)   # returned as proxy.1 .. proxy.5, in order added
stopifnot(length(top_w) == length(regions), abs(sum(top_w) - 1) < 1e-8, nrow(o_mp$R) == nrow(A))
round(top_w, 4)
#>     US     EU     UK     CH     JP 
#> 0.4269 0.1021 0.1456 0.1410 0.1843

Three things carry over from Section 15.2: trailing_periods is the window less one, because the rolling solver counts the end point; the proxies in o_mp$R have 372 rows, the first 120 back-filled with a drifting equal-weight sleeve nobody chose; the weights come back as proxy.1 to proxy.5 in the order added. One is new: momentFUN passes through the dots of add.sub.portfolio(), so a sleeve can carry its own covariance estimator into the structure. It cannot carry the tracking-error budget, so the two stages of the application are run by hand.

title: 21  The Equity Sleeve
section: 21.3 Selection Under the Allocation Above It
text:
21.3 Selection Under the Allocation Above It
The allocation above the sleeve is the policy of Section 15.3: a tangency portfolio inside the equity sleeve, minimum variance inside the bond sleeves, a tangency portfolio across the sleeves, all on the full sample. It is recomputed here so that the number it hands down is computed rather than quoted.

Re <- R - rf; S16 <- stats::cov(Re); mu16 <- colMeans(Re)
qp <- function(S, a) {       # min w'Sw s.t. a'w = 1, w >= 0, rescaled: a = 1 gives GMV, a = mu the tangency
  n <- ncol(S)
  w <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, rep(0, n), cbind(a, diag(n)), c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)$solution
  w <- pmax(w, 0); setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
kind <- sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re)); sl <- split(colnames(Re), kind)
v <- lapply(names(sl), function(k) {
  a <- sl[[k]]; if (length(a) == 1L) return(setNames(1, a))
  qp(S16[a, a], if (k == "equity") mu16[a] else rep(1, length(a)))
}); names(v) <- names(sl)
sr     <- sapply(v, function(x) as.numeric(Re[, names(x)] %*% x))
budget <- qp(stats::cov(sr), colMeans(sr))
policy <- unlist(lapply(names(v), function(k) budget[[k]] * v[[k]]))[colnames(R)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(policy), abs(sum(policy) - 1) < 1e-10)

omega    <- budget[["equity"]]
eq_split <- v$equity[v$equity > 1e-6]; eq_split <- eq_split / sum(eq_split)
stopifnot(max(abs(policy[names(eq_split)] - omega * eq_split)) < 1e-10)
round(c(equity_budget = omega, eq_split), 4)
#> equity_budget     EU_equity     US_equity 
#>        0.2909        0.2951        0.7049

The equity budget is \(\omega = 29.1%\), split 70% United States and 30% Europe; the other three equity series receive nothing. We fill it three ways, holding every other line of the policy at its weight: with the benchmark itself, with the equally weighted sleeve, and with the selected sleeve, re-estimated monthly on the trailing 120 months in each region. Costs are the 10 basis points per unit traded of pm_costs_default(), charged on each sleeve’s monthly trades against its drifted weights as Equation 23.2 charges them; the benchmark pays for tracking its own capitalization weights, which on this market move by more than returns explain. Rebalancing the policy’s class weights costs the same under all three and is not charged.

rate <- pm_costs_default()[["equity"]]
path <- function(Wm, Xj, gross = rowSums(Wm * Xj)) {   # weights set at each month start
  drifted <- Wm * (1 + Xj) / (1 + rowSums(Wm * Xj))
  trade   <- rbind(0, abs(Wm[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(Wm), , drop = FALSE]))
  tibble::tibble(gross = gross, cost = rate * rowSums(trade), turnover = rowSums(trade) / 2)
}
fill <- lapply(names(eq_split), function(cls) {
  j  <- names(region)[region == sub("_equity$", "", cls)]
  Xj <- X[oos, j]
  W_b   <- t(vapply(oos, function(t) bench_w(t, j), numeric(length(j))))
  W_ew  <- matrix(1 / length(j), length(oos), length(j))
  W_sel <- t(vapply(oos, function(t)
    select_sleeve(shrunk(X[(t - W):(t - 1L), j]), bench_w(t, j), tau), numeric(length(j))))
  list(benchmark      = path(W_b, Xj, gross = as.numeric(R[oos, cls])),  # the shipped series
       `equal weight` = path(W_ew, Xj),
       selected       = path(W_sel, Xj))
})
names(fill) <- names(eq_split)
fillers <- names(fill[[1]])

sleeve_of <- function(f, what)                    # the equity sleeve: both regions at the policy's split
  rowSums(vapply(names(fill), function(cls) eq_split[[cls]] * fill[[cls]][[f]][[what]],
                 numeric(length(oos))))
Rm       <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, ]
rest     <- setdiff(colnames(R), names(eq_split))
r_rest   <- as.numeric(Rm[, rest] %*% policy[rest])
r_policy <- as.numeric(Rm %*% policy)
r_bench  <- as.numeric(Rm[, names(eq_split)] %*% eq_split)      # the sleeve's benchmark
totals <- lapply(fillers, function(f) {
  s <- sleeve_of(f, "gross"); k <- sleeve_of(f, "cost")
  list(sleeve = s, total = r_rest + omega * s, total_net = r_rest + omega * (s - k),
       turnover = mean(sleeve_of(f, "turnover")) * 12)
})
names(totals) <- fillers
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(totals$benchmark$total, r_policy)))


# eq-21-omega in the numbers: the total's active return is omega times the sleeve's, month by month
for (f in fillers)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(totals[[f]]$total - r_policy, omega * (totals[[f]]$sleeve - r_bench))))
ir <- function(a) mean(a) / stats::sd(a) * sqrt(12)
te <- function(a) stats::sd(a) * sqrt(12)
round(c(sleeve_TE = te(totals$selected$sleeve - r_bench), total_TE = te(totals$selected$total - r_policy),
        ratio = te(totals$selected$total - r_policy) / te(totals$selected$sleeve - r_bench), omega = omega,
        sleeve_IR = ir(totals$selected$sleeve - r_bench), total_IR = ir(totals$selected$total - r_policy)), 4)
#> sleeve_TE  total_TE     ratio     omega sleeve_IR  total_IR 
#>    0.0363    0.0106    0.2909    0.2909   -0.0526   -0.0526

The ratio of the two tracking errors is \(\omega\) to four decimals and the two information ratios coincide: Equation 21.1 in the data rather than on the page.

mdd <- function(r) PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(xts::xts(r, order.by = d[oos]))
row_of <- function(level, basis, f, r, ref) tibble::tibble(
  level = level, basis = basis, filler = f, !!!as.list(score(r, rf[oos])),
  te = te(r - ref), ir = ir(r - ref), mdd = mdd(r))
scores <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(fillers, function(f) dplyr::bind_rows(
  row_of("sleeve", "gross", f, totals[[f]]$sleeve, r_bench),
  row_of("total",  "gross", f, totals[[f]]$total, r_policy),
  row_of("total",  "net",   f, totals[[f]]$total_net, r_policy))))
se_ir <- function(a) sqrt((1 + (mean(a) / stats::sd(a))^2 / 2) / length(a)) * sqrt(12)   # eq-24-se

Read the sleeve rows first. Equal weighting earns an information ratio of +0.26 against the benchmark over 252 months, with a standard error by Equation 24.10 of 0.22; the selected sleeve earns -0.05 with a standard error of 0.22. Neither is two standard errors from zero, which Section 24.3 said in advance about any ratio of this size at this length. What the selected sleeve did deliver is what it was built for: a volatility of 14.2% against the benchmark’s 16.5%, a realized tracking error of 3.6% against the four percent budgeted, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.72 against 0.61.
Now the total rows. With the benchmark in the sleeve the total portfolio is the policy, at a Sharpe ratio of 0.876; with the equally weighted sleeve it reaches 0.934, with the selected sleeve 0.951, and the net rows sit within a hundredth of the gross ones because the sleeves turn over 43% and 34% a year at ten basis points, against the 35% the benchmark itself needs to track its weights. The two sleeves get there by different routes. Equal weighting adds return, 6.36% against 6.01%, at the policy’s volatility; the selected sleeve adds nothing to return and takes the total’s volatility from 5.47% to 5.00%, because \(\omega\) times a sleeve 2.3 points less volatile than its benchmark is a policy about half a point less volatile. Its departures reach the policy at a tracking error of 1.1%, against 1.3% for the equally weighted sleeve.
Against sampling error, none of this is established. The two totals are correlated with the policy at 0.973 or more, and the test for a difference between two Sharpe ratios of Jobson and Korkie (1981) with the correction of Memmel (2003) uses that correlation; even so it gives \(z = 1.07\) for the equally weighted total and \(z = 1.75\) for the selected one, nearer the conventional threshold than the information ratios but on the same side of it. Selection survived the allocation in the sense Equation 21.1 allows: the information ratio is intact, active return and tracking error arrive scaled by \(\omega\), and what the total portfolio registers most clearly is the sleeve’s variance rather than its alpha, which 252 months cannot distinguish from zero. The policy’s largest drawdown bottoms in September of model year 31, inside the rates shock, and the maximum drawdowns of the three totals lie within 1.7 percentage points of one another.







Figure 21.1: Cumulative active return of the equally weighted and the selected sleeve, at the sleeve level against the benchmark and at the total level against the policy, out of sample. One frame, two panels; the lower panel is the upper one multiplied by the equity budget, which is eq-21-omega drawn.




Figure 21.1 is the chapter in one picture: two panels of the same shape and different scales, because the total’s active return is the sleeve’s times \(\omega\) month by month. The sleeve manager’s record is the upper panel; the investor who owns the policy lives in the lower one, where the breadth Equation 24.4 promised has been divided by the budget Section 15.3 set. That is the arithmetic a sleeve is hired under, and Section 22.1 meets it with a duration in place of a characteristic. Whether a sleeve’s information ratio is real is a question for Equation 24.10 and the register of Section 25.3; what reaches the total is a question for \(\omega\), and Section 23.3 prices the trading it costs.

title: 21  The Equity Sleeve
text:
Key Takeaways

A sleeve’s benchmark is the class series it sits inside, which reproduces from the instruments to machine precision with a one-week lag on the capitalization weights, and the sleeve is judged against it under a tracking-error budget (Grinold and Kahn 2000; Roll 1992).
Inside an allocation a sleeve’s active return and tracking error scale by its budget \(\omega\) and its information ratio does not, by Equation 21.1; Equation 21.2 bounds what the total Sharpe ratio can gain (Treynor and Black 1973).
On this market the size sort is present and momentum is absent by construction, because each name’s idiosyncratic component is drawn independently; value cannot be built for want of fundamentals. Equal weighting is a size tilt and a contrarian rule at once (Plyakha et al. 2021).
One hundred and twenty-three names make the sample covariance singular on any window shorter than one hundred and twenty-four months; the sleeve needs shrinkage or the factor structure of Equation 21.3. Out of sample the factor matrices give the lowest volatility and the shrinkage matrix the highest Sharpe ratio (Ledoit and Wolf 2004; Bai and Ng 2002).
A cardinality limit is dropped silently on the variance path and honored on the ES path; a cap per name is the convex substitute. The tracking-error budget is the one-parameter family Equation 21.4, and a sub-portfolio in mult.portfolio.spec() can carry its own covariance estimator but not the budget.

title: 21  The Equity Sleeve
text:
Exercises

Repeat the United States sleeve of Section 21.2 with tracking-error budgets of two, four and eight percent, re-estimated monthly as in the application. Report realized tracking error, information ratio and volatility for each, and say whether the realized tracking error stays inside the budget and why it might not.
Change the momentum signal to the return over months \(t-6\) to \(t-2\), sort into quintiles, and recompute Table 21.3. Does momentum appear at any horizon or granularity on this market, and what would its appearance have to mean given how the instruments are modeled?
The equally weighted sleeve rebalances monthly. Rebalance it annually instead, compute its turnover and net Sharpe ratio against the monthly version, and attribute the difference between the two to the size tilt and to the rebalancing, in the manner of Plyakha et al. (2021).
Estimate the appraisal ratio of the equally weighted United States sleeve against its benchmark and the sleeve weight \(\omega^{*}\) that Equation 21.2 would assign it. Compare \(\omega^{*}\) with the policy’s equity budget and explain what the comparison does and does not say.

title: 22  The Fixed Income Sleeve
text:
22.1 Bonds as Exposures to the Curve
What changes in portfolio construction when the asset has a duration? Litterman and Scheinkman (1991) answered that three common factors, the level, the slope and the curvature of the yield curve, explain nearly all of the variation in government bond returns, so that a bond portfolio is described better by its exposures to those factors than by the list of bonds it holds. The curve itself has the three-parameter form of Nelson and Siegel (1987), which Diebold and Li (2006) turned into a dynamic model whose factors carry the same three names. This chapter is about the fixed income sleeve, the bond part of the allocation one level below the class series on which Section 15.1 allocates, and its claim is that duration targeting and portfolio optimization are the same problem in different clothes.
We first derive why a bond is a set of exposures rather than a return series, and what credit and currency add; then measure the exposures of the government and credit instruments of the modeled market on the curve factors that ship with it, build a sleeve whose duration is a constraint, and fit a duration overlay as a parametric policy; then run the sleeves out of sample against the class series the allocation sees. On the horizon axis of Section 3.1 the duration decision is strategic, a level of exposure held for the long run, and the positioning along the curve that the overlay varies with the term spread is tactical.
The data are the weekly curve factors of sim_curve_weekly and the bond instruments of sim_asset_returns_weekly, both described in Section 2.2 and Appendix A; monthly instrument and class series enter in the application. Everything is in dollars, unhedged, and the hedged return of a foreign bond is its unhedged return less the matching fx_return, Equation 2.4.
The curve table has one week more than the return table: it starts a week earlier, so that a change in the curve exists for the first return.

title: 22  The Fixed Income Sleeve
text:
22.1.1 Price, duration and the return decomposition
A zero-coupon bond paying one unit at maturity \(\tau\) has, at a continuously compounded yield \(y_t(\tau)\), the price
\[
P_t(\tau) = e^{-\tau\, y_t(\tau)} .
\tag{22.1}\]
Hold it for a period \(\Delta\). It ages to maturity \(\tau-\Delta\) and is priced at the new yield for that maturity, so the log return is exactly
\[
\log\frac{P_{t+\Delta}(\tau-\Delta)}{P_t(\tau)}
= \underbrace{\Delta\, y_t(\tau)}_{\text{carry}}
+ \underbrace{(\tau-\Delta)\big[y_t(\tau) - y_t(\tau-\Delta)\big]}_{\text{rolldown}}
- \underbrace{(\tau-\Delta)\big[y_{t+\Delta}(\tau-\Delta) - y_t(\tau-\Delta)\big]}_{\text{duration}\times\text{yield change}} ,
\tag{22.2}\]
an identity obtained by adding and subtracting \((\tau-\Delta)\,y_t(\tau-\Delta)\). The first term is the yield earned by standing still, the second what the bond gains by sliding down an upward-sloping curve that does not move, and the third the loss from a rise in the yield at the bond’s new maturity, scaled by that maturity. Ilmanen (2011) treats the first two as the expected return of a bond on an unchanged curve, and Koijen et al. (2018) show that the same carry logic prices assets well beyond bonds. The scale factor on the yield change is the duration of Macaulay (1938), the maturity for a zero-coupon bond; the simple return \(e^{r}-1\) adds the second-order convexity term \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\tau-\Delta)^2(\Delta y)^2\), positive whichever way yields move. In the modeled market every government bond is a zero-coupon bond held at a constant maturity of two, five or ten years (Section A.2), so its duration is known rather than estimated, a gift for teaching and a limitation for realism.
The third term of Equation 22.2 is why a bond portfolio is a set of exposures. Suppose the yield changes at all maturities are driven by \(K\) factors, \(\Delta y(\tau) = \sum_k b_k(\tau)\,\Delta f_k\). A portfolio with weights \(w_i\) in bonds of maturities \(\tau_i\) then earns, up to carry and rolldown,
\[
r_p \approx -\sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k\, \Delta f_k,
\qquad
\beta_k = \sum_{i} w_i\, \tau_i\, b_k(\tau_i),
\tag{22.3}\]
and the weights matter only through the \(K\) numbers \(\beta_k\). Two portfolios with the same exposures have the same risk, whatever bonds they hold. With \(K=3\) this is the finding of Litterman and Scheinkman (1991), and it is the reason the sleeve below is specified as a set of exposures rather than as a set of weights.

22.1.2 Three factors of the curve
Nelson and Siegel (1987) write the whole curve at a date as
\[
y_t(\tau) = L_t
+ S_t\,\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda\tau}
+ C_t\left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda\tau} - e^{-\lambda\tau}\right),
\tag{22.4}\]
with loadings that Diebold and Li (2006) read as level, slope and curvature: the loading on \(L_t\) is one at every maturity, the loading on \(S_t\) falls from one at the short end to zero at the long end, so that \(S_t\) is the short rate minus the long rate, and the loading on \(C_t\) is a hump that peaks in the middle. Diebold and Li (2006) fix the decay \(\lambda\) at \(0.0609\) per month, which puts the hump at thirty months, estimate the factors by least squares at each date, and show that they track three observable quantities almost perfectly: the long yield, the short minus the long yield, and twice a middle yield minus the two ends. Litterman and Scheinkman (1991) reached the same three factors without a functional form, as the first three principal components of yield changes, the first explaining about ninety percent of the variance. With three maturities and three factors, as here, any three-factor description is an exact rotation of the three yields; which rotation the data ship, Section 22.2 measures. The rank deficiency of the bond block in Section 7.1 is the same fact seen from the covariance matrix: five curves of three factors span the fifteen government bonds, and one credit factor per region spans the credit bonds with them.

22.1.3 Credit as a separate exposure
A corporate bond of maturity \(\tau\) yields the government rate plus a spread \(s_t(\tau)\), so its price is \(e^{-\tau(y_t + s_t)}\) and Equation 22.2 acquires a fourth term, \(-(\tau-\Delta)\,\Delta s\): the spread duration, which for a zero-coupon bond equals its duration. Merton (1974) explains the spread as the value of the default option the bondholder has written; Elton et al. (2001) show that the expected loss from default explains only a small part of it, with taxes and a premium for systematic risk making up the rest; and Collin-Dufresne et al. (2001) find that spread changes across issuers are driven mostly by one common factor, which is also how this market is built: the two grades of a region share one credit factor. Two features matter for the sleeve. The spread is persistent: the weekly first-order autocorrelation of the US investment-grade spread is 0.990, a half-life of 67 weeks, so a spread that widens in a crisis stays wide for as long as the credit cycle does. And the volatility of a spread is roughly proportional to its level, which is why Ben Dor et al. (2007) measure credit exposure as duration times spread rather than as duration alone: in this market the weekly changes of the US high-yield spread have 3.4 times the standard deviation of the investment-grade changes.

22.1.4 Duration targeting as a constrained optimization
The classical use of duration is immunization: Fisher and Weil (1971) showed that a bond portfolio whose duration equals the investor’s horizon is protected, to first order, against a parallel shift of the curve. A duration target is therefore a linear constraint on the weights, \(\sum_i w_i D_i = \bar D\), and minimizing variance subject to it is still a quadratic program of the kind Section 12.1 and Section 13.1 solve. In PortfolioAnalytics such a constraint is a factor_exposure constraint with the durations as the exposure vector \(\boldsymbol{B}\): the package has no notion of a bond, and does not need one, because by Equation 22.3 a duration target is a bound on the portfolio’s loading on the level factor, and a second column bounds the loading on the slope, which decides whether the duration is delivered by a bullet at the middle of the curve or a barbell of its ends. The level \(\bar D\) is strategic: for a long-horizon investor Campbell and Viceira (2002) argue that the long bond, not the bill, is the riskless asset, and how much duration the policy portfolio carries is a decision of that kind. The deviation from \(\bar D\) conditioned on the curve is tactical, and Section 22.2 writes it as the parametric policy of Section 18.1.

22.1.5 Currency, and why the two decisions are not separable abroad
Every series is in dollars, so a foreign bond carries its local return and its currency’s move together, and Section 4.3 showed that how much of a foreign holding is currency depends on the asset. For a bond it is most of it:

fx_share <- function(series, region) {
  f <- sim_fx_monthly[sim_fx_monthly$region == region, ]
  stopifnot(all(f$date == dates))
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  1 - stats::var(u - f$fx_return) / stats::var(u)          # @eq-04-fx: share removed by hedging
}
round(c(JP_government = fx_share("JP_government", "JP"),
        EU_government = fx_share("EU_government", "EU")), 3)
#> JP_government EU_government 
#>         0.916         0.842

Hedging removes 92% of the variance of JP_government: a dollar investor who buys a Japanese bond for its duration takes a currency position several times the size of the interest-rate position. That is the case for fully hedging bonds that Campbell et al. (2010) make and the “free lunch” of Perold and Schulman (1988); Black (1989) argues for a universal partial hedge, and Karnosky and Singer (1994) attribute the result to the two decisions separately. For the sleeve the consequence is that the duration and currency decisions cannot be taken one at a time: an unhedged foreign bond is a currency position with a small duration attached, and Section 22.2 measures what that does to the fit of the curve factors.

22.1.6 Predictability from the curve
The tactical case rests on the finding that the shape of the curve forecasts bond returns. Fama and Bliss (1987) showed that forward spreads forecast the excess return of long bonds over short ones; Campbell and Shiller (1991) showed that the yield spread forecasts long-bond returns in the direction opposite to the expectations hypothesis; Cochrane and Piazzesi (2005) found that a single combination of forward rates forecasts the excess returns on bonds of every maturity with \(R^2\) up to about forty percent; and Fama and French (1989) placed the term spread among the business-cycle predictors of both stock and bond returns. Section 16.3 tested the term spread on this market and found it the one signal whose out-of-sample \(R^2\) survives, which is the signal the duration overlay below conditions on.

title: 22  The Fixed Income Sleeve
text:
22.2 Measuring and Targeting the Exposures

22.2.1 The factor series and their units
Nothing in a column of numbers says whether a level of four is four percent or four hundred, so the units are read from the magnitudes before anything is computed from them.

units <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = sub("^[A-Z]+_", "", series)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(kind) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_abs = median(abs(value)), max_abs = max(abs(value)))
units
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   kind      median_abs max_abs
#>   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Curvature    0.193    1.58  
#> 2 HY_Spread    0.0191   0.156 
#> 3 IG_Spread    0.00468  0.0580
#> 4 Level        2.74    10     
#> 5 Slope        0.873    3.05
lsc <- grep("_(Level|Slope|Curvature)$", names(cv), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(units$max_abs[units$kind == "Level"] > 1,              # a level of 8 is 8 percent
          all(units$max_abs[grepl("Spread", units$kind)] < 1))   # a spread of 0.14 is 14 percent
cv[lsc] <- cv[lsc] / 100                                          # decimals from here on

The level reaches 10.0, which can only be percentage points, and the spreads peak at 0.16, which can only be a decimal, as Section 16.2 also found; the chunk puts everything in decimals so that a loading is a duration in years.







Figure 22.1: Level, slope and curvature of the US curve, weekly, in percentage points. The slope is the short end minus the long end, so an inverted curve shows as a positive slope. The shaded bands are the four episodes of sim_episodes.





22.2.2 Factor exposures, and which bond is which
The exposures of Equation 22.3 are regression coefficients: each instrument’s weekly return on the weekly changes of its region’s level, slope and curvature, and for credit also of its grade’s spread. Each regression is run twice, on the return as shipped and on the hedged return, which subtracts the region’s fx_return.

dcv <- as.data.frame(lapply(cv[-1], diff))                 # factor changes, aligned with the returns
exposure <- function(id) {
  rg <- bonds$region[bonds$asset_id == id]; gr <- bonds$credit_grade[bonds$asset_id == id]
  X  <- data.frame(level = dcv[[paste0(rg, "_Level")]], slope = dcv[[paste0(rg, "_Slope")]],
                   curvature = dcv[[paste0(rg, "_Curvature")]],
                   spread = if (is.na(gr)) 0 else dcv[[paste0(rg, "_", gr, "_Spread")]])
  f   <- if (rg == "US") 0 else fx[[rg]]
  fml <- if (is.na(gr)) y ~ level + slope + curvature else y ~ level + slope + curvature + spread
  mh  <- stats::lm(fml, data = cbind(y = as.numeric(A[, id]) - f, X))   # hedged
  mu  <- stats::lm(fml, data = cbind(y = as.numeric(A[, id]),     X))   # unhedged, as shipped
  b   <- stats::coef(mh)
  tibble::tibble(asset = id, region = rg, class = bonds$asset_class[bonds$asset_id == id],
                 grade = ifelse(is.na(gr), "", gr),
                 level = b[["level"]], slope = b[["slope"]], curvature = b[["curvature"]],
                 spread = if (is.na(gr)) NA_real_ else b[["spread"]],
                 r2_hedged = summary(mh)$r.squared, r2_unhedged = summary(mu)$r.squared)
}
expo <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(colnames(A), exposure))

sim_assets carries no maturity, so which instrument is the two-, five- or ten-year has to be inferred, and Equation 22.2 says how: the loading on the level is minus the duration, and the ten-year is the most rate-sensitive bond of its region and grade. The inference is asserted rather than assumed, by requiring every implied duration to lie within ten percent of the maturity it has been assigned.

expo <- expo |>
  dplyr::group_by(region, class, grade) |>
  dplyr::mutate(maturity = c(10, 5, 2)[rank(level)]) |>      # most negative loading: the ten-year
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(all(abs(-expo$level / expo$maturity - 1) < 0.10),
          all(table(expo$region, expo$maturity) == 3L))      # three bonds per maturity and region
mat <- setNames(expo$maturity, expo$asset)
id_of <- function(rg, tau, cls = "government", gr = "")
  expo$asset[expo$region == rg & expo$class == cls & expo$grade == gr & expo$maturity == tau]

The level loadings of the government bonds in Table 22.1 are -1.92, -4.80, -9.58, minus the maturity divided by one plus the yield: the modified duration under annual compounding, so the bonds are repriced in full rather than through the first-order term of Equation 22.2. The credit bonds have the same durations and a spread duration of the same size, as the theory says, and every \(R^2\) is 0.970 or better: a US bond is spanned by the factors up to the time variation of its carry, the rank deficiency of Section 7.1 seen one instrument at a time.
The slope and curvature columns reveal which rotation of the three yields the factors are: the ten-year loads on the level alone, the two-year equally on level and slope, the five-year on the level and half of the slope and half of the curvature.

B_hat <- expo |>
  dplyr::filter(class == "government") |>
  dplyr::group_by(maturity) |>
  dplyr::summarise(slope = mean(slope / level), curvature = mean(curvature / level)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(level = 1, .after = maturity)                # loadings relative to the level loading
B_hat
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   maturity level    slope curvature
#>      <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1        2     1  1.00     0.000242
#> 2        5     1  0.498    0.498   
#> 3       10     1 -0.00348  0.00137
B_emp <- rbind(`2` = c(1, 1, 0), `5` = c(1, 0.5, 0.5), `10` = c(1, 0, 0))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.matrix(B_hat[, -1]) - B_emp)) < 0.05)

So the shipped factors are the observable level, slope and curvature that Diebold and Li (2006) use to interpret their latent ones: the ten-year yield, the two-year minus the ten-year, and twice the five-year minus the two- and ten-year. The latent loadings of Equation 22.4 at the Diebold–Li decay, three lines of code, are a different rotation of the same three yields, and the exposures of Equation 22.3 transform with the rotation while the risk they describe does not.

lam <- 0.0609 * 12                                            # Diebold-Li decay, per year
ns_load <- function(tau) cbind(level = 1, slope = (1 - exp(-lam * tau)) / (lam * tau),
                               curvature = (1 - exp(-lam * tau)) / (lam * tau) - exp(-lam * tau))
yields <- function(rg) {                                       # the three yields, from B_emp
  F <- as.matrix(cv[, paste0(rg, c("_Level", "_Slope", "_Curvature"))])
  Y <- F %*% t(B_emp); colnames(Y) <- c("y2", "y5", "y10"); Y
}
Y_us <- yields("US")
round(ns_load(c(2, 5, 10)), 3)                                 # latent loadings at 2, 5 and 10 years
#>      level slope curvature
#> [1,]     1 0.526     0.294
#> [2,]     1 0.267     0.241
#> [3,]     1 0.137     0.136

The principal components of Litterman and Scheinkman (1991) are the third description, and the one that needs no functional form at all.

pc <- stats::prcomp(diff(Y_us))
share <- summary(pc)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ]
round(share, 3)
#>   PC1   PC2   PC3 
#> 0.913 0.073 0.014
round(pc$rotation, 2)
#>      PC1   PC2   PC3
#> y2  0.52 -0.77  0.38
#> y5  0.63  0.04 -0.78
#> y10 0.58  0.64  0.50
stopifnot(length(unique(sign(pc$rotation[, 1]))) == 1L,            # a level: all one sign
          sign(pc$rotation["y2", 2]) != sign(pc$rotation["y10", 2]), # a slope: ends opposed
          sign(pc$rotation["y5", 3]) != sign(pc$rotation["y2", 3]))  # a curvature: middle opposed

The first component moves all three yields the same way and carries 91.3% of the variance of weekly yield changes; the second opposes the two ends and carries 7.3%; the third opposes the middle to the ends and carries the remaining 1.4%, within a few points of the proportions Litterman and Scheinkman (1991) report.






NoteWorked: the week the ten-year moved most





Equation 22.2 is checked on the week in which the US ten-year yield moved most, with \(y^{c} = \log(1+y)\) the continuously compounded yield.

yc  <- log(1 + Y_us[, "y10"])                                  # continuously compounded
i   <- which.max(abs(diff(yc)))                                # the week of the largest move
dy  <- diff(yc)[i]; y0 <- yc[i]; tau <- 10; d <- 1 / 52
r_actual <- as.numeric(A[i, id_of("US", 10)])
carry    <- d * y0
duration <- -(tau - d) * dy
convexity <- 0.5 * (tau - d)^2 * dy^2
round(c(yield_change_bp = 1e4 * dy, carry = carry, duration = duration,
        convexity = convexity, first_order = carry + duration,
        second_order = carry + duration + convexity, actual = r_actual), 5)
#> yield_change_bp           carry        duration       convexity     first_order 
#>        53.15923         0.00060        -0.05306         0.00141        -0.05245 
#>    second_order          actual 
#>        -0.05105        -0.05084

In May of model year 18 the ten-year yield rose by 53 basis points. Substituting into Equation 22.2,
\[
r \approx \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{52}\times 0.0314}_{\text{carry}}
\;-\; \underbrace{9.981 \times 0.00532}_{\text{duration}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\times 99.62 \times 0.00532^{\,2}}_{\text{convexity}}
= -0.0510,
\]
against an actual return of -0.0508. The duration term is the whole of the move, the convexity gives back 14 basis points of the loss, and the 2 basis points that remain are that week’s rolldown and the error of the expansion.




22.2.3 What the currency does to the fit
Outside the US the same regressions tell two stories.

Hedged, the foreign government bonds are explained by their own curves as well as the US bonds are, a mean \(R^2\) of 0.959 across the four regions, the lowest JP_GOV_01 at 0.696. Unhedged, the mean is 0.144: the same local return sits inside a currency move that explains most of the variance, the share computed in Section 22.1, so a duration target set on an unhedged foreign sleeve controls a minority of its risk.

22.2.4 The sleeve as a set of exposures
The sleeve is the fifteen government bonds, weekly and unhedged, and the duration is a factor_exposure constraint whose \(\boldsymbol{B}\) holds the duration of each bond from the level loadings above. The matrix is bound to the asset names and the binding asserted, for the reason the callout below gives; every bound is widened by a millionth of a year, for the reason the callout in Section 22.3 gives.

gov <- expo$asset[expo$class == "government"]
G   <- A[, gov]
B   <- cbind(duration = -expo$level, slope = -expo$slope)[match(gov, expo$asset), ]
rownames(B) <- gov
stopifnot(identical(rownames(B), colnames(G)))
sleeve <- function(assets, B, lower, upper = lower, band = 1e-6) {
  stopifnot(identical(if (is.matrix(B)) rownames(B) else names(B), assets))
  portfolio.spec(assets) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = B,            # band: the application says why
                   lower = lower - band, upper = upper + band) |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
}
exposures <- function(w) setNames(as.numeric(t(w[rownames(B)]) %*% B), colnames(B))
ann_vol   <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% stats::cov(G) %*% w) * 52)

w_free <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B[, "duration"], 0, 20),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_five <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B[, "duration"], 5),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))
round(w_free[w_free > 0.005], 3)
#> UK_GOV_01 US_GOV_01 
#>     0.005     0.995
round(w_five[w_five > 0.005], 3)
#> CH_GOV_03 EU_GOV_03 JP_GOV_03 UK_GOV_03 US_GOV_01 US_GOV_03 
#>     0.008     0.018     0.106     0.057     0.600     0.212
rbind(unconstrained = c(exposures(w_free), vol = ann_vol(w_free)),
      duration_5    = c(exposures(w_five), vol = ann_vol(w_five))) |> round(3)
#>               duration slope   vol
#> unconstrained    1.922 1.919 0.016
#> duration_5       5.000 1.133 0.038

Left to itself, minimum variance holds the US two-year and almost nothing else, at a duration of 1.92: the least volatile bond is the shortest one in the home currency, and the argument of Section 9.3 applies unchanged. Told to carry a duration of five, the optimizer delivers it as a barbell: the US two-year and ten-year carry 81% of the portfolio between them, with 19% in foreign ten-year bonds whose currency moves diversify the dollar curve, and the five-year is not held at all. The duration is met exactly, and the slope exposure that comes with it is 1.13.






Warningfactor_exposure_constraint() binds B by position, not by name



The constructor checks that B has as many rows as there are assets and nothing else: row names are stored, never compared with the asset names. A B whose rows are in a different order than colnames(R) is accepted and the constraint is applied to the wrong bonds.

B_rev  <- B[rev(rownames(B)), "duration"]                    # same numbers, reversed order
w_rev  <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(rev(gov), B_rev, 5),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))
c(what_the_solver_believed = 5, true_duration = sum(w_rev * B[names(w_rev), "duration"]))
#> what_the_solver_believed            true_duration 
#>                    5.000                    4.903

The solver reports a duration of five and the portfolio has one of 4.90. sleeve() refuses a B whose names are not identical to the assets in the order of the return matrix, the rule of Section 9.2 applied to a constraint; random_portfolios() ignores factor-exposure bounds altogether, which Section 28.2 returns to.


A second column of \(\boldsymbol{B}\) bounds the slope exposure. With the duration fixed, the slope decides where on the curve the duration sits.

w_bullet <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B, lower = c(5, 2), upper = c(5, 2.5)),
                                              optimize_method = "ROI"))
round(w_bullet[w_bullet > 0.005], 3)
#> CH_GOV_03 JP_GOV_03 UK_GOV_02 UK_GOV_03 US_GOV_01 US_GOV_02 
#>     0.007     0.085     0.016     0.036     0.147     0.709
rbind(barbell = c(exposures(w_five), vol = ann_vol(w_five)),
      bullet  = c(exposures(w_bullet), vol = ann_vol(w_bullet))) |> round(3)
#>         duration slope   vol
#> barbell        5 1.133 0.038
#> bullet         5 2.000 0.042

Requiring a slope exposure of at least two pushes the sleeve into the five-year, a bullet, at the same duration and a volatility of 4.15% against 3.83% for the barbell: the same exposure to a parallel shift, different exposures to a twist, and on this sample the ends of the curve hedged each other better than the middle hedged itself.
A bound the bonds cannot meet is the last case. No long-only combination of two-, five- and ten-year bonds has a duration of twelve:

o_bad <- optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B[, "duration"], 12), optimize_method = "ROI")
c(class = class(o_bad)[1], weights_are_na = anyNA(o_bad$weights), status = o_bad$solver_status)
#>                                        class 
#>                     "optimize.portfolio.ROI" 
#>                               weights_are_na 
#>                                       "TRUE" 
#>                                       status 
#> "Constraints are inconsistent, no solution."

No error and no warning: the object has the usual class, weights of NA and the solver’s message stored inside it. In a rebalancing loop this is a period of NA, the failure Section 25.2 is built to catch, and the application uses pm_backtest() for that reason.

22.2.5 The duration overlay as a parametric policy
The tactical layer is written as the policy of Equation 18.1 with one characteristic. Let \(z_t\) be the US term spread, the ten-year less the two-year yield, standardized, and let the long end of the sleeve be the US ten-year and the short end the US two-year. The weight on the long end is
\[
w_t = \bar w + \theta\, z_t,
\qquad
\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t} u\!\big(w_t\, r^{10}_{t+1} + (1-w_t)\, r^{2}_{t+1}\big),
\tag{22.5}\]
with \(u\) the power utility of Equation 18.2 at \(\gamma = 5\). The anchor \(\bar w\) is the strategic decision, set so that the policy at \(z_t = 0\) has the duration of the equal-weighted two-, five- and ten-year ladder, which is the class series the allocation sees; \(\theta\) is the tactical one. The data are monthly, with the curve read at each month end from the last weekly observation of that month, as Section 16.2 does.

i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)                      # last weekly curve point in each month
stopifnot(all(format(cv$date[i_last], "%Y-%m") == format(dates, "%Y-%m")))
term    <- -cv$US_Slope[i_last]                             # ten-year less two-year, decimal
r_long  <- as.numeric(Am[, id_of("US", 10)])
r_short <- as.numeric(Am[, id_of("US", 2)])
gamma   <- 5
D_bar   <- mean(c(2, 5, 10))                                # the ladder's duration, in years
w_bar   <- (D_bar - 2) / (10 - 2)                           # long-end weight that delivers it


crra <- function(r) (1 + r)^(1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma)
policy_utility <- function(theta, z, rl, rs) {
  w <- w_bar + theta * z
  mean(crra(w * rl + (1 - w) * rs))                         # @eq-22-overlay
}
z <- (term - mean(term)) / stats::sd(term)
# the signal at t sits beside the return of t + 1: z[-Tn] against r[-1]
fit_theta <- function(i) stats::optimize(policy_utility, c(-3, 3), z = z[-Tn][i],
                                         rl = r_long[-1][i], rs = r_short[-1][i],
                                         maximum = TRUE)$maximum
theta_hat <- fit_theta(seq_len(Tn - 1L))

set.seed(1602)
block_index <- function(n, block = 12L) {                   # the block bootstrap of chapter 9
  starts <- sample.int(n - block + 1L, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE)
  as.vector(outer(0:(block - 1L), starts, "+"))[seq_len(n)]
}
boot  <- vapply(seq_len(500L), function(b) fit_theta(block_index(Tn - 1L)), numeric(1))
ce    <- function(theta)                                    # monthly certainty equivalent
  ((1 - gamma) * policy_utility(theta, z[-Tn], r_long[-1], r_short[-1]))^(1 / (1 - gamma)) - 1
round(c(theta = theta_hat, se_block_bootstrap = stats::sd(boot), t = theta_hat / stats::sd(boot),
        ce_gain_annual = 12 * (ce(theta_hat) - ce(0))), 3)
#>              theta se_block_bootstrap                  t     ce_gain_annual 
#>              0.715              0.461              1.553              0.007

The fitted \(\hat\theta\) is 0.72: one standard deviation of term spread moves the long-end weight by 72 percentage points, or the duration by 5.7 years, in the direction Cochrane and Piazzesi (2005) predicts. Its block-bootstrap standard error (Künsch 1989) is 0.46, a \(t\)-statistic of 1.55, and the in-sample certainty-equivalent gain over the constant policy is 0.74 percentage points a year: the sign the literature predicts without the precision to be sure of it, the usual state of a tactical signal (Welch and Goyal 2008).

title: 22  The Fixed Income Sleeve
text:
22.3 The Sleeve Out of Sample
The application runs from observation 121, the first out-of-sample month of the register of Section 25.3, with a sixty-month window and monthly rebalancing. One plain limitation first: the five government class series are each the equal-weighted ladder of the same three maturities, so they share one duration and a duration target cannot be set on them. The sleeves therefore run on the fifteen government instruments behind those classes and are judged against the class series. The equal-weighted sleeve holds the five government class series equally, the benchmark the allocation sees, with a duration of 5.67. The constant-duration sleeve is minimum variance on the fifteen instruments with the duration bound to that same 5.67, the durations being the maturities, which need no estimation. The duration overlay is the same optimization with the target moved by the policy of Equation 22.5, re-estimated every month on the data available then. And credit enters as a separate exposure: the five credit class series join the universe with a second column of \(\boldsymbol{B}\), the spread duration, bound so that the sleeve carries the duration and the spread duration of an equal-weighted portfolio of all ten bond classes, its benchmark.

tilt <- vapply(120:Tn, function(t) {                           # everything indexed <= t
  zt <- (term[1:t] - mean(term[1:t])) / stats::sd(term[1:t])
  th <- stats::optimize(policy_utility, c(-3, 3), z = zt[-t],
                        rl = r_long[2:t], rs = r_short[2:t], maximum = TRUE)$maximum
  th * zt[t]
}, numeric(1))
w_long <- pmin(pmax(w_bar + tilt, 0), 1)                     # long only: clipped at the ends
D_path <- setNames(2 + 8 * w_long, as.character(dates[120:Tn]))   # one target per rebalancing date
round(c(min = min(D_path), mean = mean(D_path), max = max(D_path),
        share_at_a_bound = mean(w_long %in% c(0, 1))), 2)
#>              min             mean              max share_at_a_bound 
#>             2.00             5.59            10.00             0.21








Figure 22.2: The duration target of the overlay at each rebalancing date, set from the term spread with the policy re-estimated on the data available at that date. The dashed line is the constant target; the shaded bands are the episodes.





oos  <- 61:Tn                      # a 60-month window ending at 120 puts the first OOS month at 121
cost_of <- setNames(unname(pm_costs_default()[sim_assets$asset_class]), sim_assets$asset_id)
gov_cl <- grep("_government$", colnames(R), value = TRUE)
cre_cl <- grep("_credit$",     colnames(R), value = TRUE)
ew_spec <- function(assets) portfolio.spec(assets) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |> add.constraint(type = "long_only")

equal_weight <- pm_strategy("equal_weight", spec = ew_spec, weight_fun = equal.weight,
                            metric = "sharpe", label = "Equal weight")
constant_duration <- pm_strategy("constant_duration", optimize_method = "ROI",
  spec  = function(assets) sleeve(assets, mat[assets], D_bar),
  label = "Constant duration")
overlay <- pm_strategy("overlay", label = "Duration overlay",
  spec  = function(assets) sleeve(assets, mat[assets], D_bar),
  weight_fun = function(R, portfolio, ...) {                 # R is the window ending at the rebalance
    D <- D_path[[as.character(zoo::index(R)[nrow(R)])]]
    optimize.portfolio(R, sleeve(colnames(R), mat[colnames(R)], D), optimize_method = "ROI")
  })
U_cre <- cbind(Am[oos, gov], R[oos, cre_cl])
B_cre <- cbind(duration = c(mat[gov], setNames(rep(D_bar, 5), cre_cl)),
               spread   = c(setNames(rep(0, 15), gov), setNames(rep(D_bar, 5), cre_cl)))
with_credit <- pm_strategy("with_credit", optimize_method = "ROI",
  spec  = function(assets) sleeve(assets, B_cre[assets, ], c(D_bar, D_bar / 2)),
  label = "Constant duration plus credit")

run <- function(X, ..., costs = pm_costs_default())
  pm_backtest(X, pm_register(...), riskfree = sim_riskfree_monthly, estimation_window = 60L,
              costs = costs, verbose = FALSE)
bt <- list(
  ew_gov = run(R[oos, gov_cl], equal_weight),
  sleeve = run(Am[oos, gov], constant_duration, overlay, costs = cost_of[gov]),
  ew_all = run(R[oos, c(gov_cl, cre_cl)], equal_weight),
  credit = run(U_cre, with_credit, costs = c(cost_of[gov], credit = pm_costs_default()[["credit"]]))
)
labels <- c(ew_gov = "Equal weight, five government classes", ew_all = "Equal weight, ten bond classes")
mets <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(bt), function(k) {
  m <- bt[[k]]$metrics
  if (k %in% names(labels)) m$label <- labels[[k]]
  dplyr::mutate(m, key = k, .before = 1)                     # two strategies share a name
}))
stopifnot(all(mets$n_failed == 0L), all(vapply(bt, function(b) b$meta$oos_start, Sys.Date()) == dates[121]))


G_oos  <- Am[oos, gov]
ends   <- 60:nrow(G_oos)                                     # the rebalancing dates of the backtest
failed <- vapply(ends, function(e) {                         # the same windows, lower == upper
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G_oos[(e - 59):e, ],
                                         sleeve(gov, mat[gov], D_bar, band = 0),
                                         optimize_method = "ROI"))
  anyNA(w)
}, logical(1))
stopifnot(length(ends) == bt$sleeve$metrics$n_periods[1])

The class series the allocation of Section 15.1 sees, US_government and its four siblings, is the equal-weighted ladder, and that is the sleeve’s benchmark: the allocation decides how much of the portfolio is government bonds, and the sleeve’s job is a set of exposures relative to the ladder, a duration, a position on the curve, a spread duration, each written here as a bound on a factor loading. The package can nest the sleeve under the allocation itself, through mult.portfolio.spec() and add.sub.portfolio(), which optimize each sleeve on its own rebalancing calendar and allocate across the proxy return series; exercise 4 runs it and finds the proxies back-filled with equal weights before the first rebalance, the trap of Section 23.2. The same loadings are what a scenario needs: Appendix H shocks the level, the slope and the spreads directly and reads off, through Equation 22.3, what every sleeve and every class does. What the exposures cost to maintain is the subject of Section 23.1, and whether the overlay’s single sample is evidence is the subject of Section 25.1.

title: 22  The Fixed Income Sleeve
text:
Key Takeaways

A bond’s return is carry plus rolldown minus duration times the yield change, Equation 22.2, so a bond portfolio is a set of exposures to the factors that move yields, and two portfolios with the same exposures have the same interest-rate risk whatever bonds they hold (Litterman and Scheinkman 1991).
Three factors describe the curve. The modeled market ships the observable level, slope and curvature of Diebold and Li (2006), a rotation of the two-, five- and ten-year yields; the principal components of yield changes recover the same three shapes.
A duration target is a factor_exposure constraint on the level loading, a second column decides between barbell and bullet, and minimum variance subject to both is still a quadratic program. B is bound by position, an exact target can be reported infeasible, and an infeasible one returns NA weights without a warning.
For a dollar investor a foreign government bond is mostly currency: hedged, the curve factors explain it as well as a US bond; unhedged, a fraction of it. The duration and currency decisions are taken together or not at all (Campbell et al. 2010).
The duration overlay is the parametric policy of chapter 18 with one characteristic: the sign the literature predicts, a \(t\)-statistic below two, and out of sample the smallest loss in the rates shock because the curve had flattened first, which is one episode.

title: 22  The Fixed Income Sleeve
text:
Exercises

Repeat the duration-five sleeve of Section 22.2 on hedged returns, subtracting each region’s fx_return before optimizing. Which bonds does the sleeve hold now, what is its volatility against the unhedged one, and what does the difference say about where the lowest-cost duration is bought?
Refit the overlay of Equation 22.5 at \(\gamma = 2\) and \(\gamma = 10\). How does \(\hat\theta\) move, and does the bootstrap \(t\)-statistic move with it? What does that imply about who should run a duration overlay?
Solve a dozen of the windows that failed with band = 0 above with optimize_method = c("CVXR", "OSQP"). Does that backend meet an exact exposure target, and what does pm_backtest() do with a window that fails?
Nest the constant-duration sleeve and an equal-weighted credit sleeve under a minimum-variance top level with mult.portfolio.spec() and add.sub.portfolio(), quarterly rebalancing, sixty months of training. Read the proxy returns with PortfolioAnalytics:::proxy.mult.portfolio(): how many months precede the first rebalance, and what weights produced them?
