Read the table from the bottom. The strategy estimating most, a full mean vector followed by a maximization over it, is last at this window, with 5 times the turnover of equal weighting and a drawdown 1.6 times as deep as minimum variance’s. Every rule that estimates no mean finishes ahead of it: the order is Minimum CVaR, Minimum variance, Equal weight, Inverse volatility, Maximum Sharpe. Minimum CVaR and minimum variance, which estimate a covariance matrix and no mean, lead; equal weighting, which estimates nothing, ranks 3 of 5. The window matters. At 36 months the tangency portfolio is also last, 0.41 of Sharpe ratio behind the best rule that estimates no mean; at 120 months it ranks 3 of 5 and the gap is 0.20.
The claim the book carries out of this table is the one that holds at every window: the rules that estimate no mean are ahead of the rule that estimates one, and the gap closes as the estimation window lengthens, which is what a sampling error in the mean that shrinks with \(W\) predicts. Neither part is a surprise to the literature: DeMiguel et al. (2009) find, across fourteen rules and seven datasets, that no mean-based rule consistently outperforms equal weighting, and Jagannathan and Ma (2003) report the strength of minimum variance. What this table adds is that it happens on a market whose covariance structure can be inspected and with a solver whose failures have been counted.

25.3.2 A backtest is a measurement, and it has an error bar
The Sharpe ratios above are point estimates from 252 monthly observations of Equation 25.1. Under independent and identically distributed returns, Lo (2002) gives the asymptotic standard error
\[
\operatorname{se}(\widehat{SR}) \approx
\sqrt{\frac{1 + \tfrac{1}{2}SR^2}{T}} ,
\tag{25.2}\]
which, applied to the monthly Sharpe ratio over 252 months and annualized, works out as follows.

sr <- reg |>
  dplyr::select(strategy, sharpe) |>
  dplyr::mutate(se = sqrt((1 + (sharpe / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / Tn) * sqrt(12),
                lower = sharpe - 1.96 * se,
                upper = sharpe + 1.96 * se)
sr
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   strategy     sharpe    se lower upper
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 min_cvar      0.893 0.222 0.458 1.33 
#> 2 min_variance  0.829 0.221 0.395 1.26 
#> 3 equal_weight  0.626 0.220 0.195 1.06 
#> 4 inverse_vol   0.573 0.220 0.143 1.00 
#> 5 max_sharpe    0.546 0.220 0.115 0.976
stopifnot(all(outer(sr$lower, sr$upper, `<=`)))   # every interval overlaps every other

Every interval overlaps every other. On this sample none of the differences between these five strategies is statistically distinguishable from zero, including the gap between the best and the worst.
Two caveats point in opposite directions. Equation 25.2 assumes independent and identically distributed returns, which Section 4.3 showed this market violates, so the true intervals are if anything wider; Ledoit and Wolf (2008) give a bootstrap procedure that does not need the assumption, and Jobson and Korkie (1981) with the correction of Memmel (2003) give the test for a difference between two Sharpe ratios rather than for each separately. Against that, these five strategies were not selected from a large search, so the multiple-testing correction of White (2000) and Sullivan et al. (1999), and the deflated Sharpe ratio of Bailey and López de Prado (2014), would not widen them much further. A study that had tried a hundred specifications would need all of that machinery.
The honest reading does not undo the chapter, because two things survive it. The turnover and cost differences are not estimates but arithmetic on observed trades, and they are large. The failure count is not an estimate either: a strategy infeasible in 6 months of one year has a property no confidence interval averages away.
The conclusions worth keeping are the ones that do not depend on the third decimal of a Sharpe ratio. Most of the useful ones do not.
Two later chapters take this further rather than repeating it. Section 26.1 asks what forecast error costs in Sharpe ratio directly, instead of inferring it from a table of outcomes, and Section 28.1 asks what to do when the model itself is in doubt rather than only its parameters.

25.3.3 Attribution: where the return came from
A backtest says what a strategy earned. Attribution says which decisions earned it, and the standard decomposition is Brinson et al. (1986) and Brinson et al. (1991). Writing \(w_i\) and \(b_i\) for the portfolio and benchmark weights in segment \(i\), and \(r_i\) and \(\beta_i\) for the segment returns,
\[
\underbrace{\sum_i (w_i - b_i)\beta_i}_{\text{allocation}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_i b_i (r_i - \beta_i)}_{\text{selection}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_i (w_i - b_i)(r_i - \beta_i)}_{\text{interaction}}
= \sum_i w_i r_i - \sum_i b_i \beta_i .
\tag{25.3}\]
The three terms separate the decision to overweight a segment from the decision of what to hold inside it. For this book that split is the one the part structure is built on: allocation is Parts IV and V, selection is Part VI, and Equation 25.3 is what tells an investor afterwards which of the two was worth paying for.
The raw material is already available. Return.portfolio(verbose = TRUE) returns per-asset contributions for every period, as Section 23.2 showed, and those contributions are the \(w_i r_i\) terms of Equation 25.3. Section 24.1 does the work.
One caution about the famous result. Brinson et al. (1986) is routinely cited for the claim that asset allocation explains about ninety percent of performance, and Ibbotson and Kaplan (2000) show that the number answers a different question from the one it is usually quoted for: it is the share of the variance of returns over time for a single fund, not the share of the difference between funds, which is far smaller. Both are worth knowing, and conflating them is the most common misuse of an attribution result in the industry.

25.3.4 A taxonomy of look-ahead
Equation 25.1 is defined so that \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t\) sees only data before \(t\). Violations of that rule are the most common defect in a backtest and they are rarely as obvious as using next month’s return. Four kinds recur.
The estimation window can be misaligned, using data through \(t\) rather than \(t-1\). The one-period lag in the market proxy of Section 5.2 exists for exactly this reason.
The universe can be chosen with hindsight. Every asset in this book’s modeled market survives to the end of the sample, which is a survivorship bias by construction and one the real data sleeves of Section 2.3 do not share.
Parameters can be tuned on the same sample they are scored on. An estimation window length, a shrinkage intensity, a rebalancing frequency: each is a choice, and choosing it by looking at the out-of-sample result makes that result in-sample (Harvey and Liu 2015). The sweep behind Table 25.2 reports all nine configurations rather than the best one for this reason.
Vendor data can be revised after the fact. Macroeconomic series in particular are restated for years, so a backtest using the current vintage uses numbers nobody had at the time.
Only the first is a coding error. The other three are design decisions, and Lo (2004) makes the broader point that a rule fitted to one regime and tested on the same history is measuring the regime rather than the rule.

title: 25  Backtesting and Diagnostics
text:
Key Takeaways

A backtest is Equation 25.1: an estimate produced by a rule that may see only the past. Every statistic computed from it carries a standard error (Harvey and Liu 2015).

rolling_window is inclusive at both ends, so asking for 60 gives 61 observations. Almost no published result says which convention it used.

optimize.portfolio.rebalancing() stores a failed period in the result list, as a portfolio of NA weights when ROI reports no solution and as a condition object when a solver throws, and completes normally. The object has the right class, the right length and the right names.
The failures are not random. All 6 here fall within one year, at the end of the equity bear market and just after it, which is precisely the stretch in which the mandate was impossible. Dropping them reports the average of the easy months.
Always diagnose every period and always carry the failure count into the result table. A backtest with 6 failures is a different object from one with none.
The rebalancing loop contains %dopar% but registers no backend, so it runs on one core and says so in a warning that reads like noise. Registering eight workers cut 273 seconds to 61 with identical results.
Applying Equation 25.2 to the register, every confidence interval overlaps every other. The differences in turnover, in cost, and in feasibility are not estimates and do not overlap.

title: 25  Backtesting and Diagnostics
text:
Exercises

Rerun the mandate backtest with return_target at 0.002 and 0.005 monthly. Report the number of failed periods in each and when they occur. At which target does the strategy stop being a strategy?
Replace rolling_window = win - 1L with rolling_window = win and confirm that the windows now hold sixty-one observations. How much does the Sharpe ratio of the minimum-variance strategy move?
Run the same backtest with an expanding window (rolling_window = NULL). Does it do better or worse, and is the difference larger than the error bar computed above?
Take the failed periods and ask what a manager would actually have done. Implement one answer, rerun, and say plainly how your version differs from the strategy that was specified.

title: 26  The Cost of Forecast Error
text:
26.1 The Loss in Risk Units
What does an error in a return forecast cost, and in which units should the cost be written? Salcher et al. (2026b) answer that the natural unit is the investor’s own: the forecast error measured in the risk metric of the optimizer that consumes it, of which the root mean squared error is a special case under assumptions that are rarely true. Chopra and Ziemba (1993) had put a number on the cost two decades earlier, finding errors in means roughly ten times as costly as errors in variances, and the number has been quoted ever since without the formula behind it. The formula exists: for a mean-variance investor the loss from acting on a wrong mean vector is an identity, a squared distance in which the covariance matrix is the metric (Salcher et al. 2026a). Every statistical score that ignores that metric, the RMSE of Welch and Goyal (2008) and Goyal et al. (2024), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of Campbell and Thompson (2008), the predictive-accuracy test of Diebold and Mariano (1995), throws part of the cost away; Granger and Pesaran (2000) and Elliott and Timmermann (2016) are the forecasting literature’s own statement that an evaluation belongs in the units of the decision.
This chapter sits on neither side of the horizon axis of Section 3.1: it is about measurement, and the measure applies to a strategic estimate and a tactical forecast alike. We first derive the loss identity and read the risk-adjusted forecast error, the Sharpe-ratio shortfall, the RMSE and the covariance channel off it, then implement the measures and score three forecasts of the mean on rolling windows, check the covariance channel against the expectation of Kan and Zhou (2007) by simulation, and bound what the term-spread forecast of Section 16.2 could ever have earned; finally we ask which channel costs more on this market, where the cost is largest, and whether the register of Section 25.3 ranks its strategies by how much they estimate.
The data are the sixteen risky class series of Section 2.2, in excess of the Treasury bill as in Section 9.1. The full-sample moments serve as the truth wherever a truth is needed, as they did in Section 8.3.

title: 26  The Cost of Forecast Error
text:
26.1.1 The certainty equivalent and the plug-in loss
A mean-variance investor with risk aversion \(\gamma\) values a position \(\boldsymbol{w}\) by its certainty equivalent, the objective of Section 3.1,
\[
CE(\boldsymbol{w}) = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{w}^* = \frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\gamma},
\qquad
CE^* = \frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}{2\gamma} = \frac{\theta^2}{2\gamma},
\tag{26.1}\]
with \(\theta\) the maximum Sharpe ratio of Equation 9.5. Write positions and means in risk units, with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) the symmetric square root,
\[
\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{w},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{a},
\quad
\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} = \|\boldsymbol{v}\|^2,
\quad
\|\boldsymbol{a}\| = \theta .
\tag{26.2}\]
The vector \(\boldsymbol{a}\) lists the Sharpe ratios of \(N\) orthogonal directions, and the optimum is \(\boldsymbol{v}^* = \boldsymbol{a}/\gamma\). For any position the loss is then a squared distance:
\[
\begin{aligned}
CE^* - CE(\boldsymbol{w})
&= \frac{1}{2\gamma}\|\boldsymbol{a}\|^2 - \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{a} + \frac{\gamma}{2}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|^2
= \frac{1}{2\gamma}\left(\|\boldsymbol{a}\|^2 - 2\gamma\,\boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{a} + \gamma^2\|\boldsymbol{v}\|^2\right)
= \frac{1}{2\gamma}\,\|\gamma\boldsymbol{v} - \boldsymbol{a}\|^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.3}\]
This is the loss function of Klein and Bawa (1976) and Kan and Zhou (2007) written in risk units, and it holds for every position, not only the plug-in. Now let the investor hold a forecast \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), from any source, and know \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). The plug-in position \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\gamma\) has \(\gamma\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\), and Equation 26.3 becomes
\[
CE^* - CE(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}) = \frac{1}{2\gamma}\,\|\hat{\boldsymbol{a}} - \boldsymbol{a}\|^2
= \frac{1}{2\gamma}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})
= \frac{\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^2}{2\gamma} ,
\tag{26.4}\]
where the risk-adjusted forecast error \(\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}) = \|\hat{\boldsymbol{a}} - \boldsymbol{a}\|\) is the Mahalanobis distance between forecast and truth under \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), the distance Stöckl and Hanke (2014) proposed as a multivariate forecast score and Salcher et al. (2026b) named. Equation 26.4 says three things at once. Welfare is lost only through forecast error; the error matters only in risk units; and the loss is exact, with no bound and no approximation. The metric is the one the optimizer uses: an error in a direction of low risk is multiplied by a large entry of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), which is the same multiplication that turns the error into a position, the mechanism Michaud (1989) called error maximization and Best and Grauer (1991) wrote down. For the sample mean on \(T\) independent months, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}} \sim N(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{I}_N/T)\) and the expected squared error is \(\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{I}_N/T) = N/T\): each of the \(N\) dimensions of the forecast costs \(1/T\), the variance of an estimated Sharpe ratio, whatever signal it carries (Salcher et al. 2026a). That is Equation 8.6 with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) known, and it is why the precision result of Merton (1980) in Section 4.1 is the price of everything in this chapter.

26.1.2 From the certainty equivalent to the Sharpe ratio
A Sharpe-ratio investor sees the direction of a position and not its length, so the identity turns into a bound. With \(\varphi\) the angle between \(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{a}\),
\[
SR(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})
= \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}
       {\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}}
= \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}'\boldsymbol{a}}{\|\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\|}
= \theta\cos\varphi ,
\qquad
\Delta = \theta - SR(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}) = \theta\,(1 - \cos\varphi) ,
\tag{26.5}\]
so the Sharpe-ratio shortfall \(\Delta\) depends on the forecast only through its angle with the truth. The distance from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to the ray through \(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\) is \(\theta\sin\varphi\) when \(\varphi \le \pi/2\) and \(\theta\) otherwise, and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\) lies on that ray, so \(\text{RAFE} \ge \theta\sin\varphi\); since \(1 - \cos\varphi \le \sin\varphi\) on \([0, \pi/2]\),
\[
\Delta \le c_0\,\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}),
\qquad
c_0 = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \text{RAFE} \le \theta, \\ 2 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
\tag{26.6}\]
the first case because \(\text{RAFE} \le \theta\) forces \(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}'\boldsymbol{a} \ge 0\) and hence \(\varphi \le \pi/2\) (Salcher et al. 2026b; Stöckl and Hanke 2026). The RAFE therefore bounds the Sharpe-ratio shortfall and equals, up to \(2\gamma\), the certainty-equivalent loss. The squared-Sharpe decomposition is the same statement read in squares: \(\theta^2 - SR(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})^2 = \theta^2\sin^2\varphi\), the squared Sharpe ratio of the part of the truth the forecast points away from.

26.1.3 The RMSE as a special case
The usual score replaces \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) in Equation 26.4 by something simpler. Salcher et al. (2026b) order the simplifications as a nested sequence,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{RAFE}^2 &= (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})
&&\text{the investor's metric,}\\
\text{RAFE-CC}_\rho^2 &= (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\rho^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}),
\quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\rho = \boldsymbol{D}_\sigma\big[(1-\rho)\boldsymbol{I} + \rho\,\boldsymbol{\iota}\boldsymbol{\iota}'\big]\boldsymbol{D}_\sigma
&&\text{every correlation set to } \rho,\\
\text{RAFE-CC}_0^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{(\hat{\mu}_i - \mu_i)^2}{\sigma_i^2}
&&\text{correlations ignored,}\\
\text{RAFE-CV}^2 &= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{\mu}_i - \mu_i)^2
&&\text{one volatility for all,}\\
N\cdot\text{RMSE}^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{\mu}_i - \mu_i)^2
&&\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{I} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.7}\]
Each step discards something the optimizer uses. Setting the correlations to a constant removes the information about which combinations of assets are cheap to hold; setting them to zero treats a government bond and the credit index of the same region as unrelated, so that an error that cancels in the portfolio is charged twice; setting the variances equal makes a one-percent error on US_government cost the same as one on US_equity, although the first is a far larger move in Sharpe units; and \(\sigma = 1\) removes the scale altogether. In their simulation the correlation between the error measure and the tangency portfolio’s shortfall falls from 0.77 for the RAFE to 0.42 for the RMSE, and on their empirical data from 0.68 to 0.11 (Salcher et al. 2026b): heavy tails and time-varying moments widen the gap, because the RMSE loses almost all of its explanatory power under them and the RAFE keeps most of its. Kandel and Stambaugh (1996) had made the point from the other side, that an \(R^2\) too small to pass a statistical test can move an allocation a great deal, Cenesizoglu and Timmermann (2012) document the same disconnect on return-prediction models, and Section 27.1 draws the consequence for how a forecaster should be trained.

26.1.4 The covariance channel
When \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is estimated too, the plug-in position is \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\gamma\) and a second error enters, the estimated precision matrix measured in true risk units, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{C}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\), which equals \(\boldsymbol{I}_N\) when the estimate is right. The position in risk units is \(\gamma\boldsymbol{v} = \hat{\boldsymbol{C}}\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\), and Equation 26.3 gives, path by path, \(2\gamma\,\text{loss} = \|\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}\hat{\boldsymbol{a}} - \boldsymbol{a}\|^2\). Normalizing to unit length and applying the triangle inequality to \(\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}/\|\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\| - \boldsymbol{a}/\theta\) separates the two errors in the Sharpe-ratio shortfall,
\[
\Delta \le c_0\,\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}) + \theta\cdot\text{C-RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}),
\qquad
\text{C-RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) = \big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2} - \boldsymbol{I}_N\big\|_2 ,
\tag{26.8}\]
with \(\|\cdot\|_2\) the spectral norm, the largest relative eigenvalue error of the inverse (Salcher et al. 2026b). The covariance error is multiplied by \(\theta\): errors in risk cost most where the opportunity set is best. The expectation of the same identity is the result of Kan and Zhou (2007) that Section 8.1 quoted as Equation 8.6. Under normality \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) are independent, \((T-1)\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) is Wishart, and the two moments of the inverse are known,
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\big] = \alpha_N\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1},
\quad
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\big] = \beta_N\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1},
\qquad
\alpha_N = \frac{T-1}{T-N-2},
\quad
\beta_N = \frac{(T-1)^2(T-2)}{(T-N-1)(T-N-2)(T-N-4)} ,
\tag{26.9}\]
both above one and both unbounded as \(N/T \to 1\). Taking the expectation of the mean term over \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) first gives \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}'\boldsymbol{\mu}] = \alpha_N\theta^2/\gamma\); the variance term gives \(\beta_N\,\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}]/\gamma^2 = \beta_N(\theta^2 + N/T)/\gamma^2\), because the sample mean has covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/T\). Subtracting from \(2\gamma\,CE^* = \theta^2\) and adding and subtracting \(\theta^2\) and \(N/T\),
\[
2\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\text{loss}]
= \underbrace{\frac{N}{T}}_{\text{mean noise}}
\;+\;\underbrace{(1 - 2\alpha_N + \beta_N)\,\theta^2}_{\text{inversion error}}
\;+\;\underbrace{(\beta_N - 1)\frac{N}{T}}_{\text{noise, amplified}} ,
\tag{26.10}\]
which is Equation 8.6 rearranged (Salcher et al. 2026a). The first term is the mean channel of Equation 26.4. The second is the cost of inverting a noisy matrix with the true mean in hand, and since \(1 - 2\alpha_N + \beta_N = (\alpha_N - 1)^2 + (\beta_N - \alpha_N^2)\) it collects a leverage bias and a direction error. The third is the interaction: the noise in the forecast, multiplied by the inverse that over-reacts to it. The substitution design of Table 8.3, which holds one input at its truth and estimates the other, measures the first two terms and attributes the third to neither, because it vanishes when either input is true. A long-only constraint caps every term, which is Jagannathan and Ma (2003)’s shrinkage again and the reason the Sharpe shortfalls of Section 8.3 are smaller than the unconstrained ones below. Heavier tails raise \(\alpha_N\) and \(\beta_N\), since the constants of Equation 26.9 grow with the kurtosis for elliptical returns, so the covariance channel is priced faster in \(N/T\) than the normal case says (Salcher et al. 2026a).

26.1.5 An upper bound from the forecast’s information
The measures above price a forecast that exists. A bound prices one that could. For a single asset let \(r_{t+1} = m_t + e_{t+1}\) with \(m_t\) the conditional mean the forecast would deliver, \(\operatorname{Var}(m_t) = R^2\sigma^2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(e_{t+1}) = (1 - R^2)\sigma^2\), where \(R^2\) is the forecast’s explanatory power in the sense of Equation 16.2 and \(S_0 = \mu/\sigma\) the asset’s unconditional Sharpe ratio. The conditional tangency position holds \(m_t/(\gamma\sigma_e^2)\), and its average conditional squared Sharpe ratio, the ceiling Campbell and Thompson (2008) compute, is
\[
\theta_c^2 = \frac{\mathbb{E}[m_t^2]}{\sigma_e^2}
= \frac{\mu^2 + R^2\sigma^2}{(1 - R^2)\,\sigma^2}
= \frac{S_0^2 + R^2}{1 - R^2} ,
\tag{26.11}\]
using \(\mathbb{E}[m_t^2] = \mu^2 + \operatorname{Var}(m_t)\). The multivariate version replaces squares by quadratic forms: with \(\boldsymbol{m}_t\) the conditional mean vector and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e\) the conditional covariance matrix,
\[
\theta_c^2 = \mathbb{E}\big[\boldsymbol{m}_t'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e^{-1}\boldsymbol{m}_t\big]
= \boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \operatorname{tr}\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{m}_t)\big) ,
\tag{26.12}\]
the squared Sharpe ratio of the unconditional tangency portfolio under the residual covariance plus the information the forecast adds in every direction. No strategy built on the forecast can exceed \(\theta_c\) on average; it is the statistical limit of what the information allows. The bound is tight for an investor who holds the conditional tangency position every month, with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e\) known and no constraint, and slack for every restrained use of the forecast, a long-only tilt inside a band, a position on the sign of the forecast only, or a rule that averages the forecast over groups, each of which discards part of \(\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{m}_t)\) on purpose and pays \(1/T\) for every dimension it keeps (Salcher et al. 2026a). Its sample counterpart on \(T\) months inherits the inflation of Equation 8.5, so the bound is estimated with the same error as everything else in this chapter.

title: 26  The Cost of Forecast Error
section: 26.2 Measuring the Error in the Investor’s Units
text:
26.2 Measuring the Error in the Investor’s Units

26.2.1 Two functions and a worked box
The measures are a few lines each. The long-only tangency and minimum-variance programs and the Sharpe ratio under given moments are those of Section 8.2, repeated by name; the Bayes-Stein estimator is Equation 6.4 as Section 6.2 wrote it.

gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(structure(gmv_qp(S), fallback = TRUE))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  structure(setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu)), fallback = FALSE)
}
sharpe_of <- function(w, mu, S) as.numeric(sum(w * mu) / sqrt(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)

bayes_stein <- function(R) {                      # @eq-06-bayes-stein, chapter 6
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); Tw <- nrow(X); n <- ncol(X)
  m    <- colMeans(X)
  V    <- stats::cov(X) * (Tw - 1) / (Tw - n - 2)
  Vinv <- solve(V); iota <- rep(1, n)
  m0   <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Vinv %*% m) / as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Vinv %*% iota)
  d    <- m - m0
  v    <- (n + 2) / ((n + 2) + Tw * as.numeric(t(d) %*% Vinv %*% d))
  list(mu = setNames((1 - v) * m + v * m0, colnames(X)), mu0 = m0, v = v)
}


# @eq-26-rafe: the forecast error in risk units, monthly.
rafe <- function(mu_hat, mu, Sigma) {
  e <- mu_hat - mu
  sqrt(as.numeric(t(e) %*% solve(Sigma, e)))
}
rmse <- function(mu_hat, mu) sqrt(mean((mu_hat - mu)^2))

# @eq-26-loss-identity: 2 gamma times the certainty-equivalent loss of any position w,
# under the moments (mu, Sigma). gamma cancels when w is a plug-in position at gamma = 1.
ce_loss2 <- function(w, mu, Sigma) {
  d <- w - solve(Sigma, mu)
  as.numeric(t(d) %*% Sigma %*% d)
}
# @eq-26-cos: the Sharpe-ratio shortfall of a position against the maximum, annualized.
sharpe_shortfall <- function(w, mu, Sigma) {
  sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(mu) %*% solve(Sigma, mu))) - sharpe_of(w, mu, Sigma)
}







NoteWorked: the first sixty months against the full-sample truth






m60 <- colMeans(zoo::coredata(Re)[1:60, ])            # the sample mean of the first window
e60 <- m60 - mu
w60 <- solve(S, m60)                                   # plug-in position, gamma = 1, Sigma known
wk  <- list(rafe = rafe(m60, mu, S), rmse = rmse(m60, mu),
            cos  = as.numeric(t(m60) %*% solve(S, mu)) /
                   sqrt(as.numeric(t(m60) %*% solve(S, m60)) * theta2),
            loss = ce_loss2(w60, mu, S), short = sharpe_shortfall(w60, mu, S))
stopifnot(abs(wk$loss - wk$rafe^2) < 1e-12,                             # @eq-26-rafe
          abs(wk$short - sqrt(12 * theta2) * (1 - wk$cos)) < 1e-12)     # @eq-26-cos
round(unlist(wk), 4)
#>   rafe   rmse    cos   loss  short 
#> 0.2884 0.0025 0.6843 0.0832 0.3478

Substituting the first window’s sample mean and the full-sample moments into Equation 26.4 and Equation 26.5,
\[
\text{RAFE}^2 = (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})
= 0.0832
\quad\text{against}\quad
N\cdot\text{RMSE}^2 = 0.000100,
\]
\[
\cos\varphi = \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}'\boldsymbol{a}}{\|\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}\|\,\|\boldsymbol{a}\|} = 0.684,
\qquad
\Delta = \theta(1 - \cos\varphi) = 1.102 \times 0.316 = 0.348
\le c_0\,\text{RAFE} = 0.999 ,
\]
in annualized units. The certainty-equivalent loss at \(\gamma = 1\) is \(\text{RAFE}^2/2 = 0.0416\) a month against an optimum of \(\theta^2/2 = 0.0506\): with the covariance matrix known, the forecast error costs 82% of the attainable certainty equivalent. The expected \(\text{RAFE}^2\) on sixty months is \(N/T = 0.267\); this window came in below it.




26.2.2 Three forecasts of the mean on rolling windows
Section 6.3 re-estimated three vectors on rolling sixty-month windows, the sample mean, the Bayes-Stein estimate and the equilibrium return, and Section 8.2 measured the Sharpe gap of the portfolios built on the first. Here the same three forecasts are scored. The equilibrium needs the market-weight proxy of Section 6.2, repeated with its stated assumption.

eq_ids     <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
region_of  <- setNames(sim_assets$region, sim_assets$asset_id)
eq_classes <- grep("_equity$", colnames(Re), value = TRUE)
cap_region <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% eq_ids) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = paste0(region_of[asset], "_equity")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(cap = sum(market_cap), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = class, values_from = cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
cap_mat <- as.matrix(cap_region[, eq_classes])
W_eq <- t(vapply(seq_along(dates), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) dates[1] - 31 else dates[i - 1]
  j <- max(which(cap_region$date <= cutoff))
  cap_mat[j, ] / sum(cap_mat[j, ])
}, numeric(length(eq_classes))))
colnames(W_eq) <- eq_classes

block <- c(equity = 0.40, government = 0.40, credit = 0.15, commodity = 0.05)   # ASSUMPTION, chapter 6
W16 <- matrix(0, Tn, N, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Re)))
for (r in sub("_equity$", "", eq_classes)) {
  s <- W_eq[, paste0(r, "_equity")]
  W16[, paste0(r, "_equity")]     <- block[["equity"]]     * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_government")] <- block[["government"]] * s
  W16[, paste0(r, "_credit")]     <- block[["credit"]]     * s
}
W16[, "GLOBAL_commodity"] <- block[["commodity"]]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W16) - 1) < 1e-10), identical(colnames(W16), colnames(Re)))
delta16 <- mean(rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re))) / stats::var(rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re)))   # @eq-06-delta

The design is that of Salcher et al. (2026b): a training window supplies the forecast and the estimated covariance matrix, and the window that follows supplies the realization against which both are scored. They use sixty training and thirty-six test months on twelve industries; on sixteen series a thirty-six month test window has \(N/T = 0.44\) and a covariance matrix too poorly estimated to whiten with, so the test window here is sixty months too. For every window and forecast we record the RMSE, the RAFE whitened by the realized covariance matrix of the test window, the paper’s measure, and the RAFE whitened by the covariance matrix estimated on the training window, the measure available in real time and the sample Mahalanobis distance that Stöckl and Hanke (2026) show enters the corrected mean. Two rules convert each forecast into a position, the unconstrained plug-in direction \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) that Equation 26.4 and Equation 26.8 price and the long-only tangency portfolio the register holds, and each rule’s shortfall is its Sharpe ratio under the test-window moments against what its own perfect-foresight version attains there.

win <- 60L; test <- 60L
starts <- seq_len(Tn - win - test + 1L)
X <- zoo::coredata(Re)

roll <- lapply(starts, function(s) {
  tr <- s:(s + win - 1L); te <- (s + win):(s + win + test - 1L)
  m_tr <- colMeans(X[tr, ]); V_tr <- stats::cov(X[tr, ])
  m_te <- colMeans(X[te, ]); V_te <- stats::cov(X[te, ])
  wm   <- colMeans(W16[tr, , drop = FALSE])
  fc <- list(sample      = m_tr,
             bayes_stein = bayes_stein(X[tr, ])$mu,
             equilibrium = setNames(delta16 * as.numeric(V_tr %*% wm), colnames(Re)))   # @eq-06-equilibrium
  stopifnot(all(vapply(fc, function(f) identical(names(f), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))
  ceiling_u  <- sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(m_te) %*% solve(V_te, m_te)))       # perfect foresight, unconstrained
  ceiling_lo <- sharpe_of(tan_qp(m_te, V_te), m_te, V_te)                  # perfect foresight, long only
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fc), function(k) {
    w_u  <- solve(V_tr, fc[[k]])
    w_lo <- tan_qp(fc[[k]], V_tr)
    w_k  <- solve(V_te, fc[[k]])                                           # covariance known
    tibble::tibble(
      start = dates[te[1]], forecast = k,
      rmse       = rmse(fc[[k]], m_te),
      rafe_real  = rafe(fc[[k]], m_te, V_te) * sqrt(12),
      rafe_est   = rafe(fc[[k]], m_te, V_tr) * sqrt(12),
      short_u    = ceiling_u  - sharpe_of(w_u,  m_te, V_te),
      short_lo   = ceiling_lo - sharpe_of(w_lo, m_te, V_te),
      loss_known = 12 * ce_loss2(w_k, m_te, V_te))                        # @eq-26-rafe, to be checked
  }))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

stopifnot(nrow(roll) == 3L * length(starts),
          max(abs(roll$loss_known - roll$rafe_real^2)) < 1e-9)            # the identity, window by window
c(windows = length(starts), first_test_month = fmt_model(min(roll$start)))
#>                   windows          first_test_month 
#>                     "253" "January of model year 6"

The last assertion is Equation 26.4 holding on data: with the covariance matrix taken as known, the certainty-equivalent loss equals the squared RAFE on every one of the 253 windows, to machine precision. The Sharpe-ratio shortfall is where the error measures can be compared.

pts <- roll |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(short_u, short_lo), names_to = "rule", values_to = "shortfall") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(rmse, rafe_real, rafe_est), names_to = "measure", values_to = "error") |>
  dplyr::mutate(rule    = c(short_u = "unconstrained plug-in", short_lo = "long-only tangency")[rule],
                measure = c(rmse = "RMSE", rafe_real = "RAFE, realized covariance",
                            rafe_est = "RAFE, estimated covariance")[measure],
                forecast = c(sample = "sample mean", bayes_stein = "Bayes-Stein",
                             equilibrium = "equilibrium")[forecast])

cors <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  pts |> dplyr::group_by(forecast, rule, measure) |>
    dplyr::summarise(r = stats::cor(error, shortfall), .groups = "drop"),
  pts |> dplyr::group_by(rule, measure) |>
    dplyr::summarise(r = stats::cor(error, shortfall), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(forecast = "all three, pooled"))

Read Table 26.1 row by row. For the unconstrained plug-in the order is the one Equation 26.4 predicts, on every forecast and pooled: the RMSE is nearly uncorrelated with the shortfall, 0.09 pooled, while the RAFE under the realized covariance matrix correlates 0.55 and under the estimated one 0.56. The paper’s 0.68 on industry data is in the same place. For the long-only tangency the picture is different in one respect. The RAFE in the investor’s own estimated units still dominates the RMSE for every forecast, 0.64 against 0.49 for the sample mean, but the RAFE under the realized covariance matrix falls below the RMSE for the sample mean and for Bayes-Stein, 0.37 against 0.49, while for the equilibrium the two are 0.16 and 0.16. The reason is the constraint: a long-only position is \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) projected onto the simplex in the metric of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), the matrix the investor held, and the measure that explains its shortfall is the one in that metric. Equation 26.4 does not cover constrained positions and Salcher et al. (2026b) report them only across strategies; here the effect is visible within one.

26.2.3 The covariance channel by simulation
Equation 26.10 is an expectation under normality, and chapter 8 measured the two channels by substitution with a long-only rule. Here the unconstrained plug-in is drawn from a normal distribution with this market’s moments, a few hundred times per window length, and the three terms are checked against the draws in certainty-equivalent and in Sharpe units.

set.seed(1602)
L <- chol(S)
draw_months <- function(Tw, mu, L) matrix(rnorm(Tw * length(mu)), Tw) %*% L + matrix(mu, Tw, length(mu), byrow = TRUE)
alpha_n <- function(Tw, n) (Tw - 1) / (Tw - n - 2)
beta_n  <- function(Tw, n) (Tw - 1)^2 * (Tw - 2) / ((Tw - n - 1) * (Tw - n - 2) * (Tw - n - 4))
Ts <- c(36L, 60L, 120L, 240L, 372L, 1000L); B <- 300L

mc <- lapply(Ts, function(Tw) {
  d <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
    Xb <- draw_months(Tw, mu, L); m <- colMeans(Xb); V <- stats::cov(Xb)
    w_both <- solve(V, m); w_mean <- solve(S, m); w_cov <- solve(V, mu)
    c(rafe2      = rafe(m, mu, S)^2,
      loss_both  = ce_loss2(w_both, mu, S), loss_mean = ce_loss2(w_mean, mu, S), loss_cov = ce_loss2(w_cov, mu, S),
      short_both = sharpe_shortfall(w_both, mu, S), short_mean = sharpe_shortfall(w_mean, mu, S),
      short_cov  = sharpe_shortfall(w_cov, mu, S))
  }, numeric(7))
  tibble::tibble(T = Tw, stat = rownames(d), value = rowMeans(d))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::mutate(f_mean = N / T,
                f_inv  = (1 - 2 * alpha_n(T, N) + beta_n(T, N)) * theta2,
                f_amp  = (beta_n(T, N) - 1) * N / T,
                f_both = f_mean + f_inv + f_amp,                            # @eq-26-kz-split
                cov_share_ce = 1 - loss_mean / loss_both,
                cov_share_sr = 1 - short_mean / short_both)
stopifnot(identical(mc$T, Ts),
          all(abs(mc$rafe2 - mc$f_mean) / mc$f_mean < 0.05),               # E[RAFE^2] = N / T
          all(abs(mc$loss_both - mc$f_both) < pmax(0.1 * mc$f_both, 0.005)),   # @eq-26-kz-split, within sampling error
          all(abs(mc$loss_mean - mc$rafe2) < 1e-12),                       # the identity, draw by draw
          all(mc$short_mean > mc$short_cov))                               # in Sharpe units the mean channel leads

The simulation and the algebra agree to the second decimal: the mean channel averages 0.274 at sixty months against \(N/T = 0.267\), and the full loss 0.853 against the 0.845 of Equation 26.10. What the table adds to Table 8.3 is the third term. At sixty months the inversion error with the true mean in hand is only 0.100, the number a substitution design reports as the covariance channel, but the amplification of the mean’s noise by the inverse is 0.479, larger than the mean channel itself. In Sharpe units the ranking is the familiar one, the mean channel 0.53 against the covariance channel 0.15, because the Sharpe ratio does not see the length of a position and the amplification mostly lengthens it: \(\beta_N\) scales the whole of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\), and a scaled direction has the same Sharpe ratio. Section 26.3 returns to this.

26.2.4 The bound on the term-spread forecast
Section 16.2 found one signal that survived out of sample, the term spread of Fama and French (1989), and Section 16.3 turned it into a banded tilt around equal weighting. Equation 26.11 says what the forecast could have earned at most. The forecast is rebuilt here as chapter 16 built it: the spread read off the curve at each month end, the predictive regression of Equation 16.1 fit on an expanding window after a burn-in of 120 months, and the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of Equation 16.3 against the expanding historical mean.

cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(series == "US_Slope") |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)                    # last weekly row on or before each month end
stopifnot(all(cv$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[i_last] < 8))
term_lag <- as.numeric(xts::lag.xts(xts::xts(-cv$value[i_last], order.by = dates), 1))   # known at t - 1

burn <- 120L; oos <- seq.int(burn + 1L, Tn)
stopifnot(model_year(dates[oos[1]]) == 11L)
ols_fc <- function(y, x, m) {                             # fit strictly before m, forecast m
  tr <- which(!is.na(x) & seq_along(y) < m)
  b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, x[tr]), y[tr])$coefficients
  unname(b[1] + b[2] * x[m])
}
Fm <- sapply(colnames(Re), function(s) vapply(oos, function(m) ols_fc(X[, s], term_lag, m), numeric(1)))
Mm <- sapply(colnames(Re), function(s) vapply(oos, function(m) mean(X[seq_len(m - 1L), s]), numeric(1)))
Y  <- X[oos, ]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(Fm), colnames(Re)), !anyNA(Fm), nrow(Fm) == length(oos))

r2_os <- function(y, f, f0) 1 - sum((y - f)^2) / sum((y - f0)^2)      # @eq-16-r2os
r2 <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s) r2_os(Y[, s], Fm[, s], Mm[, s]), numeric(1))

# The equal-weight policy as one asset: its forecast is the average forecast.
y_p <- rowMeans(Y); f_p <- rowMeans(Fm); m_p <- rowMeans(Mm)
r2_p  <- r2_os(y_p, f_p, m_p)
s0_p  <- mean(y_p) / stats::sd(y_p)                                   # unconditional, monthly
bound_p <- sqrt((s0_p^2 + max(r2_p, 0)) / (1 - max(r2_p, 0))) * sqrt(12)   # @eq-26-bound1
round(c(median_r2 = median(r2), positive = sum(r2 > 0), policy_r2 = r2_p,
        policy_sharpe = s0_p * sqrt(12), bound_one_asset = bound_p), 4)
#>       median_r2        positive       policy_r2   policy_sharpe bound_one_asset 
#>          0.0052         10.0000          0.0043          0.6491          0.6888


vol60 <- zoo::rollapply(Re, 60, stats::sd, align = "right", fill = NA)
band  <- 0.5 / N
kappa <- band / (0.5 / sqrt(12))                          # @eq-16-tilt
w_policy <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
W_term <- t(vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i) {
  m  <- oos[i]
  s  <- Fm[i, ] / as.numeric(vol60[m - 1L, ]); s <- s - mean(s)
  tl <- pmin(pmax(kappa * s, -band), band)
  w  <- w_policy + tl - mean(tl); w <- pmax(w, 0); w / sum(w)
}, numeric(N)))
Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(W_term), colnames(Re)))
sr_arith <- function(r) mean(r - rf[oos]) / stats::sd(r - rf[oos]) * sqrt(12)
tilt <- c(policy = sr_arith(rowSums(Rm) / N), tilt = sr_arith(rowSums(W_term * Rm)))
stopifnot(abs(tilt[["policy"]] - s0_p * sqrt(12)) < 1e-12,
          bound_p > tilt[["policy"]],
          tilt[["tilt"]] - tilt[["policy"]] < bound_p - tilt[["policy"]])
round(tilt, 3)
#> policy   tilt 
#>  0.649  0.679

The forecast is weak and the bound is close. The equal-weight policy, treated as one asset whose forecast is the average of the sixteen, has an out-of-sample \(R^2\) of 0.43% and an unconditional Sharpe ratio of 0.649 over the 252 out-of-sample months; Equation 26.11 with these numbers,
\[
\theta_c = \sqrt{\frac{0.0351 + 0.0043}{1 - 0.0043}} \times \sqrt{12}
= 0.689 ,
\]
allows a timer of the policy at most 0.040 of Sharpe ratio on top of it. The tilt of Equation 16.9 realized 0.679, 0.029 above the policy, inside the bound. Campbell and Thompson (2008) made the point that an \(R^2\) of this size is economically meaningful, and Equation 26.11 says how meaningful: a few hundredths of a Sharpe ratio. The one-asset bound is the right ceiling for a timer of the policy and a loose one for the tilt, which reads the forecast cross-sectionally; the multivariate ceiling of Equation 26.12 is higher, but reaching it needs the unconstrained conditional tangency position every month with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e\) known, and the tilt keeps one dimension of that information inside a band and pays \(1/T\) for it (Salcher et al. 2026a). The distance to the ceiling is the price of restraint, paid because Section 8.3 showed what the unconstrained position costs when its inputs are estimated.

26.3 Which Channel Costs More

The answer depends on the unit, and both answers are right. In the certainty equivalent the covariance channel costs more than the mean channel at thirty-six and sixty months, 68% of the loss at sixty, and less at 120, 44%, because the Wishart constants of Equation 26.9 approach one as \(N/T\) shrinks while the mean channel falls only as \(1/T\). In Sharpe units the mean channel costs more at every window, with the covariance channel at 13% at sixty months. Chopra and Ziemba (1993)’s ten-to-one is a Sharpe-unit statement; the certainty equivalent of an unconstrained investor charges the covariance error for the leverage it induces, which the Sharpe ratio does not see and a long-only constraint does not allow. For the register’s rules, long only and rebalanced monthly, the Sharpe reading is the relevant one, and it agrees with Table 8.3.

26.3.2 Where the shortfall is largest
The rolling measurement above cannot reach the last two episodes, because a sixty-month test window has to end inside the sample. Against the full-sample truth it can: for every sixty-month estimation window ending at \(t\), the RAFE of its sample mean and the shortfall of the two rules under the truth are one number each, and the windows can be sorted by the episode their last month falls in.

ends <- seq.int(win, Tn - 1L)
ceiling_lo_truth <- sharpe_of(tan_qp(mu, S), mu, S)
top_truth <- names(which.max(tan_qp(mu, S)))                # the series the true tangency portfolio holds most of
by_end <- lapply(ends, function(e) {
  Xw <- X[(e - win + 1L):e, ]; m <- colMeans(Xw); V <- stats::cov(Xw)
  tibble::tibble(end = dates[e], rafe = rafe(m, mu, S) * sqrt(12),
                 short_u  = sharpe_shortfall(solve(V, m), mu, S),
                 short_lo = ceiling_lo_truth - sharpe_of(tan_qp(m, V), mu, S),
                 top_neg  = m[[top_truth]] < 0)                            # that series' estimated mean below zero
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
rates_neg <- mean(by_end$top_neg[in_episode(by_end$end, "rates_shock")])
other_neg <- mean(by_end$top_neg[!in_episode(by_end$end, "rates_shock")])

ep <- sim_episodes
in_any <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(ep$episode, function(k) in_episode(by_end$end, k)))
ep_tab <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ep)), function(i) {
    idx <- in_episode(by_end$end, ep$episode[i])
    tibble::tibble(episode = ep$label[i], windows = sum(idx), rafe = mean(by_end$rafe[idx]),
                   short_u = mean(by_end$short_u[idx]), short_lo = mean(by_end$short_lo[idx]))
  }),
  tibble::tibble(episode = "outside every episode", windows = sum(!in_any), rafe = mean(by_end$rafe[!in_any]),
                 short_u = mean(by_end$short_u[!in_any]), short_lo = mean(by_end$short_lo[!in_any])))
stopifnot(all(ep_tab$windows > 0),
          ep_tab$episode[which.max(ep_tab$short_u)]  == "credit crisis",
          ep_tab$episode[which.max(ep_tab$short_lo)] == "rates shock")

A window that ends inside the credit crisis produces the worst unconstrained portfolio, a shortfall of 0.92 against 0.49 for a window that ends outside every episode, and its RAFE of 1.70 is the measure saying so in advance of the portfolio. The long-only rule is hurt most by a window ending in the rates shock, 0.30 against 0.17. The series the true tangency portfolio holds most of is US_government, and its estimated mean is negative in 45% of the windows ending in the rates shock against none of the others; a long-only rule excludes a series whose mean it estimates below zero, and here it excludes the one the truth holds most of. The equity bear market produces a RAFE as large as the credit crisis, 1.72, and a smaller shortfall, which Equation 26.5 explains: the RAFE reads the length of the error and the shortfall its angle, and errors of the same length in different directions cost different amounts of Sharpe ratio.

26.3.3 The register, ranked by what it estimates
The register of Section 25.3 holds five strategies on the sixty-month window, and they can be ordered by how much they estimate: equal weighting estimates nothing, inverse volatility \(N\) volatilities, minimum variance the covariance matrix, minimum CVaR the lower tail of the whole return distribution, and the tangency portfolio the covariance matrix and the mean vector together. Figure 8.1 showed that the Sharpe gap, promised minus realized, follows that order for the four of them that chapter 8 ran. The shortfall of Salcher et al. (2026b) is a different quantity: each strategy’s own perfect-foresight Sharpe ratio on the out-of-sample months, with its weights solved on the moments of those months and held, minus what the rolling strategy realized there.

sweep <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", frequency == "months", basis == "gross", window == 60)
oos_r <- seq.int(121L, Tn)
stopifnot(sweep$n_periods[1] - 1L == length(oos_r), model_year(dates[oos_r[1]]) == 11L)
m_o <- colMeans(X[oos_r, ]); V_o <- stats::cov(X[oos_r, ]); Rt <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos_r, colnames(Re)]
sharpe_realized <- function(r, rf) {                       # as the register computes it
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
es_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |> add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95))
pf <- list(equal_weight = w_policy,
           inverse_vol  = (1 / sqrt(diag(V_o))) / sum(1 / sqrt(diag(V_o))),
           min_variance = gmv_qp(V_o),
           min_cvar     = extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re[oos_r, ], es_spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)],
           max_sharpe   = tan_qp(m_o, V_o))
stopifnot(all(vapply(pf, function(w) identical(names(w), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))

reg <- tibble::tibble(strategy = names(pf), estimates = seq_along(pf),
                      perfect_foresight = vapply(pf, function(w) sharpe_realized(as.numeric(Rt %*% w), rf[oos_r]), numeric(1))) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(sweep, strategy, label, realized = sharpe), by = "strategy") |>
  dplyr::mutate(shortfall = perfect_foresight - realized,
                se = sqrt((1 + (realized / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / length(oos_r)) * sqrt(12),   # @eq-25-se
                in_se = shortfall / se)
stopifnot(!anyNA(reg$realized),
          reg$in_se[reg$strategy == "max_sharpe"] > 1, all(abs(reg$in_se[reg$strategy != "max_sharpe"]) < 1),
          abs(reg$shortfall[reg$strategy == "equal_weight"]) < 1e-6,          # estimates nothing, loses nothing
          reg$strategy[which.max(reg$shortfall)] == "max_sharpe",
          reg$shortfall[reg$strategy == "min_cvar"] < 0,                      # the exception
          all(reg$shortfall[reg$strategy %in% c("inverse_vol", "min_variance")] < 0.05))

The order holds at both ends and breaks in the middle. Equal weighting has a shortfall of exactly zero, because a rule that estimates nothing has nothing to get wrong; inverse volatility loses 0.035 and minimum variance’s shortfall is -0.002, the covariance channel on sixteen well-estimated series, which Table 8.3 found nearly closed; and the tangency portfolio, the one rule that estimates the mean, loses 0.42, from a perfect-foresight 0.97 to a realized 0.55. The exception is minimum CVaR, whose shortfall is -0.19: the rolling strategy realized more than its own perfect-foresight version. The perfect-foresight portfolio minimizes expected shortfall, not variance, and the portfolio that minimizes the lower tail over 252 months at once is not the one with the highest Sharpe ratio over them, whereas the rolling version, re-solved on sixty months at a time, tracks the volatility clustering that Section 4.3 measured. A negative shortfall is not estimation paying off; it is the perfect-foresight benchmark of a non-Sharpe objective being the wrong ceiling, which Salcher et al. (2026b) note for their diversification rules too. Against the error bar of Equation 25.2 that Section 25.3 attaches to each realized Sharpe ratio, the tangency portfolio’s shortfall is 1.9 standard errors and every other strategy’s less than one. Section 27.1 asks whether a forecast trained on the RAFE rather than the RMSE narrows the one shortfall that is, and Section 28.1 asks what to do when the error is in the model rather than in its parameters.

title: 26  The Cost of Forecast Error
text:
Key Takeaways

For a mean-variance investor the cost of a wrong mean forecast is an identity: the certainty-equivalent loss is \(\text{RAFE}^2/(2\gamma)\), the squared Mahalanobis distance between forecast and truth under \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) (Salcher et al. 2026b, 2026a).
The Sharpe-ratio shortfall is \(\theta(1 - \cos\varphi)\), bounded by \(c_0\,\text{RAFE}\); the RMSE is the RAFE with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{I}\). For the unconstrained plug-in the RAFE correlates 0.55 with the realized shortfall and the RMSE 0.09.
For a long-only position the measure that explains the shortfall is the RAFE in the covariance metric the position was built in; whitened by the realized covariance matrix it falls below the RMSE for two of the three forecasts.
The covariance channel has three terms, Equation 26.10: the mean’s noise \(N/T\), the inversion error on the signal, and the amplification of the noise by the inverse. In certainty-equivalent units it is the larger channel at thirty-six and sixty months; in Sharpe units the mean channel is the larger at every window, which is Chopra and Ziemba (1993)’s reading.
A forecast with out-of-sample \(R^2\) allows at most \(\theta_c^2 = (S_0^2 + R^2)/(1 - R^2)\). For the term spread on the equal-weight policy the bound allows 0.040 of Sharpe ratio and the tilt took 0.029.
The register’s shortfalls follow the order of estimation at both ends, zero for equal weighting and 0.42 for the tangency portfolio, with minimum CVaR the exception, whose perfect-foresight benchmark minimizes a tail rather than maximizes a Sharpe ratio.

title: 26  The Cost of Forecast Error

Exercises

Replace the two position rules of the rolling measurement by the long-only minimum-variance portfolio of Equation 9.3, which uses no forecast, and correlate its shortfall with the RAFE and with the C-RAFE of Equation 26.8, computed as the spectral norm of \(\boldsymbol{V}_{\text{te}}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{V}_{\text{tr}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{V}_{\text{te}}^{1/2} - \boldsymbol{I}\). Which measure explains a rule that estimates only \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)?
Add the two intermediate measures of Equation 26.7, RAFE-CC\(_0\) with the correlations set to zero and RAFE-CV with one volatility for all, to the rolling frame for the unconstrained rule. Where do they sit between the RMSE and the RAFE, and which of the two simplifications costs more explanatory power on this market?
Using Equation 26.10 with this market’s \(\theta^2\) and \(N = 16\), find the window length at which the covariance channel’s share of the certainty-equivalent loss falls below one half, and the length at which the amplification term alone falls below the inversion error. How do the two change for \(N = 50\)?
From Equation 26.11, how much Sharpe ratio could a forecast with an out-of-sample \(R^2\) of one percent, and of five percent, add to the equal-weight policy? Compare the answers with the standard error of Equation 25.2 on 252 months.

title: 27  Decision-Aware Forecasting
text:
27.1 Two Losses for One Forecast
Should a return forecaster be trained on mean squared error at all? The investor who uses the forecast does not pay for its error in squared percentage points but in the units of the decision it feeds, and Stöckl and Hanke (2026) show that for a mean-variance investor those units are known exactly: the certainty equivalent lost to a forecast error is the error measured in risk units, so the forecast can be corrected in those units after the fact, with an intensity that follows from the number of assets and the length of the sample alone. The general form of the question is the operations-research one, where Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) propose training a predictor on the regret of the decision it induces rather than on its own accuracy; the finance case is the one in which that regret has a closed form.
This chapter sits on neither side of the horizon axis of Section 3.1: it is about estimation, and the same corrections apply to a long-run mean and to a conditional one. We first derive the mismatch between the statistical loss and the decision loss and three answers to it, then implement each on the sixteen class series in excess of the bill, scored out of sample from the first month of model year 11, and finally ask which of the three buys most on this market and where each fails.

title: 27  Decision-Aware Forecasting
text:
27.1.1 The statistical loss and the decision loss
Let \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) be the vector of expected excess returns on \(N\) assets, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) their covariance matrix, and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) a forecast of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) from any source, a sample mean or the predictive regression of Section 16.1. A forecaster is trained and judged on the statistical loss
\[
L_{\text{stat}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})
= (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}),
\tag{27.1}\]
the squared error summed over assets. The investor of Section 3.1 with risk aversion \(\gamma\) maximizes the certainty equivalent \(CE(\boldsymbol{w}) = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\), attains \(CE^* = \boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/(2\gamma)\) at \(\boldsymbol{w}^* = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/\gamma\), and holds the plug-in position \(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\gamma\) when handed the forecast. Expanding \(CE(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}) = \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/\gamma - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/(2\gamma)\) and subtracting it from \(CE^*\) leaves a perfect square:
\[
CE^* - CE(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})
= \frac{1}{2\gamma}\,
  (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})
= \frac{\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^2}{2\gamma}.
\tag{27.2}\]
The quadratic form is the squared risk-adjusted forecast error of Salcher et al. (2026b), and Section 26.1 derives it and the bound it places on the Sharpe-ratio gap; we take it from there. In the language of Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022), Equation 27.2 is the regret of the mean-variance decision, and their proposal to train on regret instead of on accuracy is, for this decision, the proposal to train on Equation 27.2 instead of on Equation 27.1.
The two losses are quadratic forms in the same error under two metrics, the identity and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), and they rank forecasts differently. In the eigenbasis of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_N\) and eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{u}_j\), the error \(\boldsymbol{e} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}\) has \(L_{\text{stat}} = \sum_j (\boldsymbol{u}_j'\boldsymbol{e})^2\) while \(2\gamma\) times the decision loss is \(\sum_j (\boldsymbol{u}_j'\boldsymbol{e})^2/\lambda_j\): the same squared error costs \(\lambda_1/\lambda_N\) times more in the least volatile direction of the universe than in the most volatile one, and that ratio is the condition number Section 7.1 measured.

ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE)
unit_cost <- function(u) as.numeric(t(u) %*% solve(S, u))   # 2 gamma times the decision loss of a unit error
cost_top <- unit_cost(ev$vectors[, 1]); cost_bottom <- unit_cost(ev$vectors[, N])
c(top = cost_top, bottom = cost_bottom, log10_ratio = log10(cost_bottom / cost_top))
#>         top      bottom log10_ratio 
#>      91.079 1158322.436       4.104

On the sixteen classes a unit error along the first eigenvector costs 91 in the units of Equation 27.2 and the same error along the last costs 1.2e+06, a ratio of \(10^{4.1}\). A forecaster that minimizes Equation 27.1 spends its accuracy where the variance is large; the optimizer needs it where the variance is small, because \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) places its largest weights there, the mechanism of Best and Grauer (1991) in Section 8.1. That a forecaster should be trained on the loss its user bears is an old point (Granger 1969; Elliott and Timmermann 2008); the mean-variance case adds that the loss is known in closed form. A forecaster trained on Equation 27.1 can be reconciled with a decision scored by Equation 27.2 in three places: after the forecast, by correcting its output in risk units and leaving the model alone, the post-optimal moment correction of Stöckl and Hanke (2026); between forecast and decision, by acting on fewer of its dimensions, which Salcher et al. (2026a) price; and inside the training loop, by replacing the loss with the certainty equivalent of the portfolio the forecast implies, the parametric policy of Section 18.1 taken one step further.

27.1.2 Correcting the mean in risk units
Take the setting of Kan and Zhou (2007): excess returns independent \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) over \(T \geq N + 1\) months, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) the sample mean and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) the unbiased sample covariance matrix, so that \((T-1)\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) is Wishart and independent of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\). In risk units, with \(\boldsymbol{m} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{m}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), the forecast is \(\hat{\boldsymbol{m}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{I}/T)\) and its risk, the expected squared RAFE, is the trace of that covariance:
\[
\mathbb{E}\,\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^2 = \frac{N}{T}.
\tag{27.3}\]
Each of the \(N\) dimensions costs \(1/T\), the variance of an estimated Sharpe ratio, whatever signal it carries; this \(N/T\) is what inflates the promised Sharpe ratio in Equation 8.5.
The correction is Stein estimation in these units. Fix a target in advance as \(\boldsymbol{P}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) with \(\boldsymbol{P}\) idempotent of rank \(r\); the two targets used here are zero, \(\boldsymbol{P} = \boldsymbol{0}\), and the grand mean, \(\boldsymbol{P} = \boldsymbol{\iota}\boldsymbol{\iota}'/N\), \(\boldsymbol{P}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \bar{\mu}\boldsymbol{\iota}\) with \(\bar{\mu}\) the average of the sixteen sample means. Whiten the forecast with any square root of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\), shrink its residual from the target by a James-Stein factor, and map back. Stöckl and Hanke (2026) show that the square root cancels and the estimated covariance matrix enters through one scalar, the sample Mahalanobis length of the residual:
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c
= \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \frac{c}{T}\,\frac{(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}{\hat{q}},
\qquad
\hat{q} = \big((\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\big)'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\big((\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\big).
\tag{27.4}\]
For the grand mean this reads \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c = \bar{\mu}\boldsymbol{\iota} + \big(1 - c/(T\hat{q})\big)(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \bar{\mu}\boldsymbol{\iota})\): the deviation of each sample mean from the average is scaled down by a factor that depends on how long that deviation is in estimated risk units. The risk follows from two facts. First, with \(q\) the same quadratic form under the true \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), the ratio \(\psi = q/\hat{q}\) satisfies \((T-1)\psi \sim \chi^2_{T-N}\) and is independent of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), a property of the Wishart distribution, so the feasible corrector is the oracle corrector with its constant randomly rescaled to \(c\psi\). Second, conditional on \(\psi\), the identity of Stein (1981) turns the cross term between the error and the shrinkage direction into the divergence of that direction, which for an idempotent \(\boldsymbol{R} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) is \((\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R} - 2)/\|\boldsymbol{R}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}\|^2\) with \(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R} = N - r\). Taking the expectation over \(\psi\) gives the exact risk,
\[
\mathbb{E}\,\text{RAFE}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^2
= \frac{N}{T} - \frac{\tau_P}{T^2}\Big[2c\,(N - r - 2)\,\mathbb{E}\psi - c^2\,\mathbb{E}\psi^2\Big],
\quad
\mathbb{E}\psi = \frac{T-N}{T-1},\;
\mathbb{E}\psi^2 = \frac{(T-N)(T-N+2)}{(T-1)^2},
\tag{27.5}\]
where \(\tau_P = \mathbb{E}\|\boldsymbol{R}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}\|^{-2}\) is finite whenever \(N - r \geq 3\). Everything about \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) that matters is in the two moments of \(\psi\), and they depend on \(N\) and \(T\) only. The bracket is a concave quadratic in \(c\), positive on \(0 < c < 2(N-r-2)(T-1)/(T-N+2)\) and largest at
\[
c_f = (N - r - 2)\,\frac{T-1}{T-N+2},
\tag{27.6}\]
a function of \(N\), \(T\) and the target’s rank alone: no tuning, no validation window. It exceeds the oracle constant \(N - r - 2\) because \(\psi\) has mean below one, so the feasible corrector shrinks less at the same \(c\). For the grand mean the risk is below \(N/T\) for every \(N \geq 4\) and \(T \geq N + 1\): the corrected mean dominates the sample mean, the input of every plug-in rule in this book, whenever the sample is longer than the number of assets.
The lineage matters because the result is easy to mistake for an old one. Stein (1956) showed that the sample mean of three or more normal means is inadmissible; James and Stein (1961) gave the estimator and, for an unknown covariance matrix, the constant \((N-2)/(T-N+2)\), which is Equation 27.6 with \(r = 0\) divided by \(T - 1\); Efron and Morris (1975) moved the target to the grand mean; and Jorion (1986) brought the idea into portfolio choice as the Bayes-Stein estimator of Section 6.1, whose target is the expected return of the minimum-variance portfolio. What Equation 27.5 adds is that the target projection need not be orthogonal in risk units: the grand mean’s is symmetric only if \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\iota} \propto \boldsymbol{\iota}\), which no covariance matrix with a 4.4-fold spread of volatilities comes near, and the proof uses only \(\boldsymbol{R}^2 = \boldsymbol{R}\) and \(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R} = N - r\). The Bayes-Stein target depends on \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), and the theorem does not cover it. Two further things it says. The zero target rescales the forecast and leaves the direction of the plug-in position unchanged, so its gain is in the certainty equivalent and not in the Sharpe ratio; a target of rank one moves the direction. And the theorem ranks the corrected mean against the sample mean, not against rules that use no mean, such as \(1/N\) or minimum variance, whose gap to the optimum is a population quantity rather than an estimation error.

27.1.3 Using less of the forecast
The second answer keeps the forecast and acts on fewer of its dimensions. Salcher et al. (2026a) start from the same identity. With \(\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}\) the truth in risk units and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{b}} = \boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{\eta}\) the forecast, an investor who acts only on the projection \(\boldsymbol{Q}\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\) onto a \(k\)-dimensional subspace loses \(\|(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{Q})\boldsymbol{a}\|^2 + \|\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{\eta}\|^2\) on every path, because the cross term carries \((\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{Q})\boldsymbol{Q} = \boldsymbol{0}\); in expectation, with the isotropic error of the sample mean,
\[
2\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\text{loss}]
= \underbrace{\|(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{Q})\boldsymbol{a}\|^2}_{\text{signal discarded}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{k}{T}}_{\text{noise retained}} .
\tag{27.7}\]
A dimension is worth acting on if and only if its squared Sharpe ratio exceeds \(1/T\), the squared standard error of an estimated Sharpe ratio (Jobson and Korkie 1981; Lo 2002). Shrinkage of the kind in Equation 27.4, or the two-fund scalar of Kan and Zhou (2007) and the combination with \(1/N\) of Tu and Zhou (2011), is a soft reduction: it pays the price on every one of the \(N\) dimensions whether or not the dimension carries signal, and loses to a hard reduction whenever the signal is concentrated on a few. The familiar rules are fixed cells of the grid spanned by the number of covariance dimensions estimated and the number of forecast dimensions acted on: the plug-in rule of Section 8.1 keeps \(N\) and \(N\), minimum variance the level alone inside a basis of \(N\), \(1/N\) of DeMiguel et al. (2009) one and one, the decile sort of Fama and French (1993) the sign of the ranking and no covariance matrix, the parametric tilt of Brandt et al. (2009) a slope inside a basis of two, and covariance shrinkage (Ledoit and Wolf 2004) every forecast dimension with the other side reduced. None sets its granularity from what the forecast can deliver.
The cell that moves does. Order the assets by the forecast, let \(\rho\) be the cross-sectional rank correlation between the forecast and the next month’s return in risk units, the information coefficient of Grinold (1989), and suppose the true profile is linear in the rank. Then the slope of that profile in risk units is \(\tau^2 = \rho^2/(1 - \rho^2)\), cutting the ranking into \(G\) equal groups and acting on the group averages discards about \(N\tau^2/G^2\) of signal and retains \(G/T\) of noise, and the loss is minimized at
\[
G^* = \left(\frac{2\,N\,T\,\rho^2}{1 - \rho^2}\right)^{1/3}.
\tag{27.8}\]
The cube root is the rate Cattaneo et al. (2020) derive for the number of characteristic-sorted portfolios, but the price per group here is \(1/T\) regardless of how many assets the group averages, because averaging lowers the noise of a portfolio’s mean and its risk in the same proportion; \(G^*\) is therefore small, and it falls to one group, which is \(1/N\), when the forecast cannot rank.

27.1.4 The decision loss inside the training loop
The third answer changes the loss the forecaster is trained on. Let \(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t)\) be a forecaster with parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) and conditioning variables \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\), and let \(\boldsymbol{w}(\cdot)\) be the map from a forecast to a weight vector: the plug-in map, or the clipped tilt of Equation 16.9. The decision-aware estimator maximizes the sample certainty equivalent of the portfolio the forecast implies,
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
= \arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\Big[r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^2\Big],
\qquad
r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \boldsymbol{w}\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t)\big)'\boldsymbol{r}_{t+1},
\tag{27.9}\]
and the parametric policy of Brandt et al. (2009) in Equation 18.2 is the special case in which the forecast is the weight itself, \(\boldsymbol{w}(f) = f\); Bertsimas and Kallus (2020) call this prescriptive rather than predictive analytics, and Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) give the loss its name. The connection to the first answer is exact in one case. With the plug-in map, a known \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) and \(\boldsymbol{r}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_t + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t+1}\), the expected certainty equivalent of month \(t\) is \([\boldsymbol{\mu}_t'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_t - (f_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t)'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(f_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t)]/(2\gamma)\) by the algebra of Equation 27.2, so that
\[
\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;\mathbb{E}\,CE
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;\mathbb{E}\,\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t\big)'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t\big):
\tag{27.10}\]
the decision-trained forecaster is the least-squares forecaster with its errors reweighted by \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), generalized least squares in the metric the optimizer uses. That is also why the third answer generalizes beyond mean-variance: nothing in Equation 27.9 uses the quadratic form. Replace the certainty equivalent by any utility, the plug-in map by any map with clipping, constraints or costs, and the forecaster by any model of Gu et al. (2020), and only the closed form of Equation 27.10 is lost.
What is also lost is precision. A certainty equivalent realized over \(T\) months carries the noise of a Sharpe ratio, whose standard error is of order \(\sqrt{(1 + SR^2/2)/T}\) (Lo 2002), and a tuning parameter chosen by that criterion is a further estimated quantity whose cost none of the displays above contains; Salcher et al. (2026a) make the same point for a number of groups chosen from the window. Each answer therefore comes with the condition under which it does not help. The correction of Equation 27.4 drops every deviation from the target when \(c_f \geq T\hat{q}\), which happens when \(T\) is small relative to \(N\); the corrected mean is then the grand mean, the tangency rule becomes minimum variance, and the correction cannot do better than a rule that never looked at the mean. The rule of Equation 27.8 returns one group when the forecast cannot rank, and buys nothing when the forecast’s cross-sectional content is small to begin with. And the loop of Equation 27.9 can choose worse on both counts when the certainty equivalent it tunes on is noisier than the gain it chases. One of the three partially falsifies its own prediction on this market, and the implementation says which.

title: 27  Decision-Aware Forecasting
text:
27.2 Three Corrections on Sixteen Classes

27.2.1 The corrected mean in a few lines
Equation 27.4 and Equation 27.6 are a function of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), \(N\), \(T\) and the target, with the positive part of the factor taken as implementations do.

correct_mean <- function(R, target = c("grand", "zero"), c = NULL) {
  target <- match.arg(target)
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu <- colMeans(X); S <- stats::cov(X)
  r   <- if (target == "grand") 1L else 0L                 # rank of the target projection
  Pmu <- if (target == "grand") rep(mean(mu), N) else rep(0, N)
  d   <- mu - Pmu                                          # (I - P) mu_hat
  q   <- as.numeric(t(d) %*% solve(S, d))                  # its length in estimated risk units
  if (is.null(c)) c <- (N - r - 2) * (T - 1) / (T - N + 2) # c_f of @eq-27-constant
  h   <- max(1 - c / (T * q), 0)                           # the James-Stein factor, positive part
  list(mu = setNames(Pmu + h * d, colnames(X)), factor = h, c = c, q = q, N = N, T = T)
}

cm_full <- correct_mean(Re)
round(c(c_f = cm_full$c, Tq = cm_full$T * cm_full$q, factor = cm_full$factor), 4)
#>     c_f      Tq  factor 
#> 13.4721 22.8625  0.4107

On the full sample of 372 months, Equation 27.6 with \(N = 16\) and \(r = 1\) is
\[
c_f = (16 - 1 - 2)\,\frac{371}{358} = 13.47,
\qquad
1 - \frac{c_f}{T\hat{q}} = 1 - \frac{13.47}{22.86} = 0.411,
\]
so that even on thirty-one model years the deviation of each sample mean from the grand mean is kept at 41% of its size. The Bayes-Stein estimator of Section 6.2 is the natural comparison and is copied here unchanged.

bayes_stein <- function(R) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu   <- colMeans(X)
  S    <- stats::cov(X) * (T - 1) / (T - N - 2)   # Jorion's unbiased scaling
  Sinv <- solve(S); iota <- rep(1, N)
  mu0  <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% mu) / as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% iota)
  d    <- mu - mu0
  v    <- (N + 2) / ((N + 2) + T * as.numeric(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d))
  list(mu = setNames((1 - v) * mu + v * mu0, colnames(X)), mu0 = mu0, v = v)
}
bs_full <- bayes_stein(Re)

Bayes-Stein shrinks 53% of the way toward the minimum-variance mean, the corrected mean 59% of the way toward the grand mean, and only the second has the exact risk of Equation 27.5 behind it; exercise 2 checks it by simulation.
