27.2.2 Four means in the tangency rule
The correction is scored where Section 8.2 scored the sample mean: the long-only tangency portfolio on rolling windows, as the quadratic program of that chapter, so that the register of Section 25.3 is reproduced, with the same estimated covariance matrix for every mean.

gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(structure(gmv_qp(S), fallback = TRUE))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  structure(setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu)), fallback = FALSE)
}
# The register's Sharpe ratio: compounded, in excess of the bill. The certainty
# equivalent is annualized from monthly excess returns at the chapter's gamma.
sharpe_realized <- function(r, rf) {
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
ce_annual <- function(e) 12 * mean(e) - gamma / 2 * 12 * stats::var(e)

oos <- seq.int(121L, Tn)                        # the months the register scores
stopifnot(model_year(dates[oos[1]]) == 11L, model_year(dates[120]) == 10L)

Each window supplies five fully invested rules: the tangency portfolio on the sample mean, on Bayes-Stein and on the corrected mean, equal weighting and minimum variance. One assertion inside the loop states the theory’s claim about the zero target: its unconstrained position is a scalar multiple of the sample mean’s in every window, so the long-only tangency rule, which is invariant to that scalar, cannot see it.

run_rules <- function(win) {
  lapply(oos, function(m) {
    X  <- Re[(m - win):(m - 1L), ]
    Xm <- zoo::coredata(X); V <- stats::cov(Xm); mh <- colMeans(Xm)
    cm_g <- correct_mean(X, "grand"); cm_0 <- correct_mean(X, "zero"); bs <- bayes_stein(X)
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(solve(V, cm_0$mu), cm_0$factor * solve(V, mh))))   # same direction
    means <- list(sample = mh, bayes_stein = bs$mu, corrected = cm_g$mu)
    rules <- c(lapply(means, tan_qp, S = V),
               list(equal_weight = setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re)), min_variance = gmv_qp(V)))
    stopifnot(all(vapply(rules, function(w) identical(names(w), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))
    tibble::tibble(
      date = dates[m], rule = names(rules), factor = cm_g$factor,
      total  = vapply(rules, function(w) sum(w * zoo::coredata(R)[m, ]), numeric(1)),
      excess = vapply(rules, function(w) sum(w * zoo::coredata(Re)[m, ]), numeric(1)))
  }) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |> dplyr::mutate(window = win)
}
roll <- dplyr::bind_rows(run_rules(60L), run_rules(120L))

res_means <- roll |>
  dplyr::group_by(window, rule) |>
  dplyr::summarise(sharpe = sharpe_realized(total, rf_by_month[as.character(date)]),
                   ce = ce_annual(excess), vol = stats::sd(excess) * sqrt(12), .groups = "drop")

Down the Sharpe columns of Table 27.2 the correction works as a direction: on sixty-month windows the tangency portfolio earns 0.546 on the sample mean, the register’s figure, 0.699 on Bayes-Stein and 0.728 on the corrected mean, and on 120 months 0.702, 0.816 and 0.899; the assertions above would fail the render if the order did not hold at both windows. What the corrected mean converges to is in the last row: it stays below minimum variance’s 0.828 and 0.902, and on 27% of the sixty-month windows and 17% of the 120-month ones it is minimum variance, because the factor is zero and a tangency portfolio on a constant mean is Equation 9.3; the theorem ranks the corrected mean against the sample mean and says nothing about a rule that never estimated one.
Across the certainty-equivalent columns the ranking changes, and the reason is the length rather than the direction. Equal weighting has the highest certainty equivalent of the five at both windows, 3.76% against 2.94% for the corrected tangency at sixty months, because a fully invested tangency portfolio with a volatility of 4.8% is far below the risk an investor with \(\gamma = 5\) would choose, and the certainty equivalent charges for that while the Sharpe ratio cannot see it. The unconstrained position that Equation 27.5 prices, whose length is its own choice, is left to exercise 1: the correction lowers its certainty-equivalent loss and leaves the covariance channel of Equation 8.6 untouched.

27.2.3 Granularity on the term-spread tilt
The second answer needs a forecast with a cross-section, and the one forecast in Section 16.3 that survived out of sample is the term spread, rebuilt here exactly as there: the US slope read off the weekly curve at each month end, lagged once, and an expanding regression of each series’ excess return on it from the first month of model year 11. The other six predictors of that chapter’s elastic net are built beside it for the third answer.

cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(series %in% c("US_Level", "US_Slope", "US_IG_Spread", "US_HY_Spread")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)
stopifnot(all(cv$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[i_last] < 8))
curve <- xts::xts(cbind(level = cv$US_Level[i_last], term = -cv$US_Slope[i_last],
                        ig = 100 * cv$US_IG_Spread[i_last], hy = 100 * cv$US_HY_Spread[i_last]),
                  order.by = dates)
P    <- cumprod(1 + R)
mom  <- xts::lag.xts(P, 1) / xts::lag.xts(P, 12) - 1
turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
colnames(turb) <- "turb"
common <- merge(curve, turb); stopifnot(identical(zoo::index(common), dates))
common_lag <- xts::lag.xts(common, 1); mom_lag <- xts::lag.xts(mom, 1); rev_lag <- xts::lag.xts(Re, 1)
pairs_of <- function(s) {
  data.frame(date = dates, y = as.numeric(Re[, s]), mom = as.numeric(mom_lag[, s]),
             rev = as.numeric(rev_lag[, s]), zoo::coredata(common_lag))
}
ols_fc <- function(d, v, m) {
  tr <- which(!is.na(d[[v]]) & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)
  b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d[[v]][tr]), d$y[tr])$coefficients
  unname(b[1] + b[2] * d[[v]][m])
}
F_term <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s); vapply(oos, function(m) ols_fc(d, "term", m), numeric(1))
}, numeric(length(oos)))
dimnames(F_term) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re))
stopifnot(!anyNA(F_term))

The forecast becomes a weight through the tilt of Equation 16.9, with the same band \(\delta = 1/(2N)\) and scale, and the reduction is inserted where Equation 27.7 says it belongs: after the forecast has been put into volatility units and demeaned, before it is clipped. Four cells come from one function: every magnitude is chapter 16’s tilt; three rank groups replaces each forecast by the average of its tercile; the sign keeps top minus bottom at the largest tilt the band allows, the long-short sort of Fama and French (1993) around the policy; equal weighting discards the forecast.

vol60 <- zoo::rollapply(Re, 60, stats::sd, align = "right", fill = NA)
band  <- 0.5 / N
kappa <- band / (0.5 / sqrt(12))
w_policy <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))

tilt_from <- function(F, idx, reduce = identity) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(F), colnames(Re)), nrow(F) == length(idx))
  W <- t(vapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
    m  <- idx[i]
    s  <- F[i, ] / as.numeric(vol60[m - 1L, ])   # volatility units, known at m - 1
    s  <- reduce(s - mean(s))                    # relative view, then the reduction
    tl <- pmin(pmax(kappa * s, -band), band)
    w  <- w_policy + tl - mean(tl); w <- pmax(w, 0); w / sum(w)
  }, numeric(N)))
  dimnames(W) <- list(as.character(dates[idx]), colnames(Re))
  stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W) - 1) < 1e-12), all(W >= 0))
  W
}
steps <- function(G) function(s) {                         # group averages
  if (G <= 1L) return(s * 0)
  stats::ave(s, ceiling(rank(s, ties.method = "first") * G / length(s)))
}
sign_only <- function(s) {                                 # top third +band, bottom third -band
  g <- ceiling(rank(s, ties.method = "first") * 3 / length(s))
  (band / kappa) * (as.numeric(g == 3L) - as.numeric(g == 1L))
}

cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(Re)
score_W <- function(W, idx) {
  Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[idx, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  Em <- zoo::coredata(Re)[idx, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(Re)), nrow(W) == nrow(Rm))
  r <- rowSums(W * Rm); e <- rowSums(W * Em)
  drifted <- W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + r)
  trade   <- abs(W[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(W), , drop = FALSE])
  cost    <- c(as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate), 0)
  c(sharpe = sharpe_realized(r, rf_by_month[as.character(dates[idx])]),
    ce = ce_annual(e), ce_net = ce_annual(e - cost),
    turnover = 12 * mean(c(rowSums(trade) / 2, 0)))
}

The cell that moves needs the information coefficient. At each out-of-sample month the regression is fit on the months before it, its fitted values are ranked against the realized returns of those months, both in volatility units, and the Spearman correlations are averaged: the ranking ability an investor standing at that month could measure. Equation 27.8 then gives the number of groups, rounded and capped at 8.

ic_of <- function(m) {
  tr <- seq.int(61L, m - 1L)
  Fhat <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
    d  <- pairs_of(s); ok <- which(!is.na(d$term) & seq_len(Tn) < m)
    b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d$term[ok]), d$y[ok])$coefficients
    b[1] + b[2] * d$term[tr]
  }, numeric(length(tr)))
  V60 <- zoo::coredata(vol60)[tr - 1L, ]; Y60 <- zoo::coredata(Re)[tr, ]
  mean(vapply(seq_along(tr), function(i)
    stats::cor(Fhat[i, ] / V60[i, ], Y60[i, ] / V60[i, ], method = "spearman"), numeric(1)))
}
ic      <- vapply(oos, ic_of, numeric(1))
G_star  <- (2 * N * (oos - 1L) * ic^2 / (1 - ic^2))^(1 / 3)
G_rule  <- pmax(1L, pmin(N %/% 2L, as.integer(round(G_star))))

# The same coefficient on the forecasts actually made, over the register's months.
V60_oos <- zoo::coredata(vol60)[oos - 1L, ]; Y_oos <- zoo::coredata(Re)[oos, ]
ic_oos  <- mean(vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
  stats::cor(F_term[i, ] / V60_oos[i, ], Y_oos[i, ] / V60_oos[i, ], method = "spearman"), numeric(1)))
G_oos   <- (2 * N * length(oos) * ic_oos^2 / (1 - ic_oos^2))^(1 / 3)
stopifnot(ic_oos < min(ic))
c(ic_window_mean = mean(ic), ic_realized = ic_oos, G_star_mean = mean(G_star), G_at_realized = G_oos)

The forecast cells all stand above equal weighting, by 0.017 to 0.031 in Sharpe ratio and by 13 to 25 basis points of certainty equivalent net of costs, the order of gain Section 16.3 found. Among themselves they are indistinguishable: the spread across the four forecast cells is 0.013 in Sharpe ratio and 9 basis points of certainty equivalent, against a standard error of the Sharpe ratio over these months of about 0.22 by the formula of Lo (2002). The information coefficient on the estimation windows averages 0.110, so Equation 27.8 asks for 4 to 5 groups, and the rule’s cell earns 0.644, inside the same spread. The coefficient realized on the forecasts actually made is 0.030, lower than on any estimation window, and at that value the formula gives 1.9 groups: the number read from fitted values overstates what the forecast delivers, at no visible cost here because nothing in the granularity has one. The sign cell trades 37% a year against 21% for the full vector and still matches it after costs. This is the second condition of the theory: a forecast whose cross-sectional content is a near-common shift, the term spread lifting every bond series together, leaves Equation 27.7 little to discard and little to retain, and the band of Equation 16.9, not the granularity, sets what the forecast is worth.

27.2.4 Tuning the elastic net on the certainty equivalent
The third answer is tried on the forecaster of Section 16.2 that lost: the elastic net of Zou and Hastie (2005) on seven predictors, which chose its penalty by five-fold cross-validated squared error on contiguous blocks, re-tuned once a year. Here the same folds and grid of penalties serve two criteria: the pooled out-of-fold squared error across the sixteen series, the loss of Equation 27.1, and the certainty equivalent of the tilt of Equation 16.9 built from the out-of-fold forecasts over the training months, the loss of Equation 27.9 with the tilt as the map. The penalty is the only parameter the loop chooses; the coefficients are refit inside glmnet at whichever penalty each criterion selects.

en_vars  <- c("mom", "rev", "term", "ig", "hy", "level", "turb")
D  <- lapply(colnames(Re), pairs_of); names(D) <- colnames(Re)
ok <- stats::complete.cases(D[[1]][, en_vars])
stopifnot(all(vapply(D, function(d) identical(stats::complete.cases(d[, en_vars]), ok), logical(1))))
lam_grid <- 10^seq(-1, -5, length.out = 33)     # decreasing, as glmnet expects
Y <- zoo::coredata(Re)

tune_both <- function(m) {
  tr   <- which(ok & seq_len(Tn) < m)
  fold <- ceiling(seq_along(tr) / (length(tr) / 5))
  oof  <- array(NA_real_, c(length(tr), N, length(lam_grid)))
  for (j in seq_len(N)) {
    X <- as.matrix(D[[j]][tr, en_vars]); y <- D[[j]]$y[tr]
    for (f in 1:5) {
      i   <- fold != f
      fit <- glmnet::glmnet(X[i, ], y[i], alpha = 0.5, lambda = lam_grid)
      oof[!i, j, ] <- as.matrix(stats::predict(fit, newx = X[!i, , drop = FALSE], s = lam_grid))
    }
  }
  mse <- vapply(seq_along(lam_grid), function(k) mean((oof[, , k] - Y[tr, ])^2), numeric(1))
  ce  <- vapply(seq_along(lam_grid), function(k) {
    F <- oof[, , k]; colnames(F) <- colnames(Re)
    ce_annual(rowSums(tilt_from(F, tr) * Y[tr, ]))
  }, numeric(1))
  list(lam_mse = lam_grid[which.min(mse)], lam_ce = lam_grid[which.max(ce)],
       null_mse = which.min(mse) == 1L)     # TRUE when the null model minimizes the CV error
}

retune <- oos[(oos - oos[1]) %% 12L == 0L]
tunes  <- lapply(retune, tune_both); names(tunes) <- retune
lam_path <- tibble::tibble(date = dates[retune],
                           mse = vapply(tunes, `[[`, numeric(1), "lam_mse"),
                           ce  = vapply(tunes, `[[`, numeric(1), "lam_ce"))
null_mse <- vapply(tunes, `[[`, logical(1), "null_mse")

The cross-validated squared error is minimized by the null model, every coefficient at zero and the forecast equal to the training mean, in 17 of the 21 re-tunings, and by a penalty next to it in the rest: judged by Equation 27.1, the best elastic net on seven predictors and sixteen series is no elastic net, the conclusion Section 16.3 reached by a longer route. The certainty-equivalent criterion selects a smaller penalty in 17 of the 21 re-tunings and wanders over 4 orders of magnitude from one year to the next, which is what a criterion estimated with the noise of a Sharpe ratio looks like when the surface it searches is flat.

fc_en <- function(which_lam) {
  lam <- NA_real_
  out <- vapply(oos, function(m) {
    if (m %in% retune) lam <<- tunes[[as.character(m)]][[which_lam]]
    tr <- which(ok & seq_len(Tn) < m)
    vapply(seq_len(N), function(j) {
      fit <- glmnet::glmnet(as.matrix(D[[j]][tr, en_vars]), D[[j]]$y[tr], alpha = 0.5, lambda = lam_grid)
      as.numeric(stats::predict(fit, newx = as.matrix(D[[j]][m, en_vars]), s = lam))
    }, numeric(1))
  }, numeric(N))
  out <- t(out); dimnames(out) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re)); out
}

F_ce   <- fc_en("lam_ce")
F_mean <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s)
  vapply(oos, function(m) mean(Y[seq_len(m - 1L), s]), numeric(1)), numeric(length(oos)))
dimnames(F_mean) <- dimnames(F_mse)

r2_os <- function(F) 1 - sum((Y[oos, ] - F)^2) / sum((Y[oos, ] - F_mean)^2)
res_train <- tibble::tibble(
  forecast = c("elastic net, tuned on squared error", "elastic net, tuned on the certainty equivalent",
               "historical mean"),
  mse  = c(mean((Y[oos, ] - F_mse)^2), mean((Y[oos, ] - F_ce)^2), mean((Y[oos, ] - F_mean)^2)),
  r2os = c(r2_os(F_mse), r2_os(F_ce), 0)) |>

Table 27.4 is the result the chapter was built to show. The forecast tuned on the certainty equivalent has the worse mean squared error, an out-of-sample \(R^2\) of -7.7% against the expanding mean where the squared-error forecast has -0.5%, and the better portfolio: a Sharpe ratio of 0.717 against 0.597 and a certainty equivalent net of costs of 4.41% against 3.53%, 88 basis points a year. Trained on the loss the decision bears, the forecaster gives up accuracy in the directions the optimizer does not use and keeps it where the tilt acts, Equation 27.10 in a case where no closed form exists. Two qualifications belong beside the number: the decision-trained net turns the portfolio over 87% a year, 7 times the 13% of the squared-error net, because the penalty it chooses lets the forecasts move; and the Sharpe-ratio advantage of 0.120 is inside the standard error of 0.22. The prediction is confirmed in sign and not established in significance, which on 252 months is as much as any forecast comparison in this book can say.

title: 27  Decision-Aware Forecasting
text:
27.3 What Each Answer Buys







Figure 27.1: Every rule of this chapter and every line of the register, scored on the same months with sixty-month estimation windows, in the register’s Sharpe ratio, from one data frame. The dashed line is equal weighting.




Figure 27.1 puts the three answers on one axis with the register of Section 25.3. In the Sharpe ratio added to the rule it corrects, the first answer buys most: the corrected mean lifts the sixty-month tangency portfolio by 0.18, from the register’s 0.546 to 0.728, at 120 months by 0.20, and the corrected tangency portfolio is the best forecast-based rule in the figure. The third answer buys 0.12 over the same forecaster tuned on squared error, which makes the decision-trained net the best of the tilts at 0.717, 67 basis points of net certainty equivalent above equal weighting. The second answer buys the 0.03 that the term spread was already worth in Section 16.3 and nothing beyond it. In certainty equivalent the first two change places: the training loop adds 88 basis points net to its forecaster where the corrected mean adds 43 to a fully invested tangency rule whose length is not its own to choose.
Each fails somewhere. The corrected mean does not beat the rules that use no mean: the register’s minimum variance stands at 0.829 and its best line, Minimum CVaR, at 0.893, above every forecast-based rule in the figure, and on 27% of the sixty-month windows the correction concedes the point by collapsing onto minimum variance itself; the covariance channel of Equation 8.6 it leaves untouched is where that rule’s advantage lives. Granularity fails to matter: four ways of acting on the term spread land within 0.013 of one another, the rule’s choice of 4 to 5 groups rests on an information coefficient measured in sample that the realized forecasts do not reach, and with sixteen assets and a band of 3.1 percentage points there is too little cross-section for Equation 27.7 to decide anything. And the training loop, the answer that generalizes furthest, is the one whose own prediction is only partially borne out: it delivers a forecast with a worse squared error and a better portfolio, but it chooses its penalty from a criterion so noisy that the choice moves by orders of magnitude between years, trades 7 times as much, and leaves a Sharpe-ratio gain the sample cannot distinguish from zero. The decision loss is the right teacher and a far noisier one than squared error.
For the plug-in rules of Section 9.3 and Section 8.3 the reading is short. The sixty-month tangency portfolio’s 0.546 was never the price of using an estimated mean; it was the price of using the sample mean, and Equation 27.4 recovers 64% of the distance to minimum variance without touching the covariance matrix, with a constant that needed no tuning. What remains is the covariance matrix’s share, which Section 26.1 separates from the mean’s, and the part no estimator can recover: on this market the level direction that minimum variance trades carries most of what there is to earn, and the decision-aware forecaster changes which loss that arithmetic is done in, not the arithmetic. Section 28.1 asks what to do when the model behind the loss is itself in doubt, and the resampled frontiers of Section 28.3 put the same estimation error back on the picture of Section 9.3.

title: 27  Decision-Aware Forecasting
text:
Key Takeaways

A mean-variance investor pays for forecast error in the metric \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), not the identity (Equation 27.2): on the sixteen classes the same squared error costs \(10^{4.1}\) times more in the least volatile direction than in the most (Salcher et al. 2026b; Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022).
Shrinking the sample mean toward the grand mean in estimated risk units has an exact risk; the best constant is \((N - 3)(T - 1)/(T - N + 2)\), a function of \(N\) and \(T\) alone, and the corrected mean dominates the sample mean whenever \(T > N\) (Stöckl and Hanke 2026; James and Stein 1961; Stein 1981). On sixty-month windows it lifts the tangency portfolio’s Sharpe ratio from 0.55 to 0.73 and collapses onto minimum variance, which stays ahead, in 27% of the windows.
Every dimension of a forecast acted on costs \(1/T\) whatever it carries, so the familiar rules are cells of a granularity grid and the number of rank groups worth forming is \((2NT\rho^2/(1 - \rho^2))^{1/3}\) from the information coefficient (Salcher et al. 2026a; Cattaneo et al. 2020). On the term spread every granularity earns the same few basis points: the band of the tilt, not its resolution, sets the value.
Tuning the elastic net’s penalty on the certainty equivalent of the tilt it implies instead of on squared error gives a forecast with a worse \(R^2_{\text{OS}}\) and a better portfolio, 88 basis points net a year, inside the sampling error of the Sharpe ratio and at 7 times the turnover (Brandt et al. 2009; Bertsimas and Kallus 2020).
None of the three answers beats the register’s rules that use no mean. The correction prices the mean channel; the covariance channel of Equation 8.6 is where the rest of the plug-in rule’s loss lives.

title: 28  Robustness and Model Uncertainty
text:
28.1 Parameter Uncertainty and Model Uncertainty
What should an investor do when the doubt is not about the values of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) but about whether the model that produced them is the right one? Garlappi et al. (2007) posed that question for the mean-variance investor and answered it with the decision rule of Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989): hold on to every model the data cannot rule out, and choose the portfolio whose worst case over that set is best. The answer turns out to be a shrinkage toward the minimum-variance portfolio, which places the whole of this chapter on the strategic axis of Section 3.1: a robust policy is still a policy, set once from unconditional beliefs and held, with the ambiguity about those beliefs built into the weights rather than into a signal.
We first separate parameter uncertainty, a distribution over the inputs that Section 8.1 and Section 26.1 price, from model uncertainty, a set of models with no distribution over it, and derive the multi-prior portfolio, the robust worst case over a Kullback–Leibler ball, and the resampled frontier; we then implement all four devices on the sixteen classes, including random portfolios as a picture of the feasible set rather than as the solver of Section 13.1; and we run the robust portfolios out of sample against the register.

title: 28  Robustness and Model Uncertainty
text:
28.1.1 Two kinds of not knowing
Every chapter since Section 6.1 has treated the inputs of Markowitz (1952) as estimates. A sample mean carries the standard error of Equation 6.1, a sample covariance the error Section 7.1 measures, and the plug-in rule of Equation 8.2 pays for both. Section 26.1 turns that error into a cost in the investor’s units and Section 27.1 corrects the forecast for the decision it feeds. All of this is parameter uncertainty: the model is taken as true, and what is unknown is a vector of numbers inside it, about which the investor holds a distribution — the sampling distribution of the estimator, or a posterior. The natural tool is then to average. The Bayesian investor maximizes expected utility under the predictive distribution, and for the mean-variance problem that is a shrinkage of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) toward a prior center with an intensity set by the posterior precision (Jorion 1986; Black and Litterman 1992), or, once the estimation risk in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) is admitted, a scaled-down position in the risky assets (Kan and Zhou 2007).
Model uncertainty is a different object. The investor entertains a set of models and has no distribution over the set: not because the prior is diffuse, but because there is no prior. Knight (1921) separated the two as risk and uncertainty, and Ellsberg (1961) showed experimentally that people treat them differently, preferring a bet with known odds to one with unknown odds even when no probability assignment makes the second worse. Averaging over the set requires exactly the weights the investor does not have. The rule Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989) derived from axioms replaces the average with the worst case: evaluate each portfolio by the lowest expected utility any model in the set assigns to it, and pick the portfolio that does best under that evaluation.
The two need different tools because they produce different objects: a distribution over the inputs has a mean, and a set of models has a boundary, on which the worst case sits. What follows derives what the boundary does to the weights.

28.1.2 The multi-prior portfolio
Garlappi et al. (2007) keep the covariance matrix and put the ambiguity in the mean. The set of models is a confidence ellipsoid around the sample mean,
\[
\max_{\boldsymbol{w}} \; \min_{\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathcal{E}(\varepsilon)}
\; \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
\qquad
\mathcal{E}(\varepsilon) = \left\{\boldsymbol{\mu} :
(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) \leq \varepsilon \right\},
\tag{28.1}\]
with \(\gamma\) the risk aversion of Equation 3.12. The inner problem has a closed form. Its Lagrangian in \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) has first-order condition \(\boldsymbol{w} = 2\lambda\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\), so the worst mean lies in the direction of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\), and substituting into the constraint, which binds, fixes the distance:
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{*}(\boldsymbol{w})
= \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}}}\;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu}^{*}(\boldsymbol{w})
= \boldsymbol{w}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}} .
\tag{28.2}\]
Nature marks the portfolio’s expected return down by \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) standard deviations, and the outer problem becomes
\[
\max_{\boldsymbol{w}} \;
\boldsymbol{w}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
- \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}
- \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}} ,
\tag{28.3}\]
a mean-variance objective with a second, linear penalty on volatility. With a risk-free asset and no budget constraint the solution is proportional to \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), as in Equation 9.5. Writing \(\boldsymbol{w} = k\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and \(C = \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\), the objective is \(kC - \sqrt{\varepsilon C}\,k - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}k^2 C\), and the first-order condition gives
\[
\boldsymbol{w}^{*} = \frac{1}{\gamma}
\left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{C}}\right)^{+}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} .
\tag{28.4}\]
Since \(\sqrt{C}\) is the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio of Equation 9.6, the ambiguity-averse investor holds the same risky portfolio as the plug-in investor and scales it down by one minus the ratio of \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) to that Sharpe ratio, holding nothing risky once the ellipsoid is wide enough to contain a mean at which the best Sharpe ratio is zero.
Fully invested, with \(\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w} = 1\), the budget constraint enters with a multiplier and the first-order condition reads \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - (\gamma + \sqrt{\varepsilon}/\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} = \lambda\boldsymbol{\iota}\). Define the effective risk aversion \(\gamma^{*} = \gamma + \sqrt{\varepsilon}/\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}\). Solving for \(\boldsymbol{w}\) and eliminating \(\lambda\) with the budget gives, with \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) the scalars of Equation 9.6,
\[
\boldsymbol{w}^{*} = \boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mv}} + \frac{1}{\gamma^{*}}\,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\!\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \frac{B}{A}\boldsymbol{\iota}\right),
\qquad
\gamma^{*} = \gamma + \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}^{*}}} .
\tag{28.5}\]
The robust portfolio is the ordinary mean-variance portfolio of an investor whose risk aversion has been raised from \(\gamma\) to \(\gamma^{*}\). The second term is the speculative component, which carries no net weight because \(\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \tfrac{B}{A}\boldsymbol{\iota}) = B - B = 0\), and its shrinkage factor relative to the plug-in investor is \(\gamma/\gamma^{*} = 1 / (1 + \sqrt{\varepsilon}/(\gamma\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}^{*}}))\). As \(\varepsilon \to \infty\) the factor goes to zero and \(\boldsymbol{w}^{*} \to \boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mv}}\): the investor who trusts nothing about the means holds the one portfolio of Equation 9.3 that needs none. Because \(\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}^{*}}\) depends on the answer, Equation 28.5 is a fixed point. The two components are \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)-orthogonal, so \(\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}^{*}} = 1/A + D/\gamma^{*2}\) with \(D = C - B^2/A\), and \(\gamma^{*}\) solves one scalar equation; under a long-only constraint the same iteration runs with a quadratic program in place of the closed form.
The size of the ellipsoid is a confidence level. Under normality, \(T(T-N)/((T-1)N)\) times the quadratic form in Equation 28.1 with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) replaced by \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) follows an \(F\) distribution with \(N\) and \(T-N\) degrees of freedom, so
\[
\varepsilon(p) = \frac{N\,(T-1)}{T\,(T-N)}\; F^{-1}_{N,\,T-N}(p)
\tag{28.6}\]
is the radius of the ellipsoid that contains the true mean with probability \(p\). The set of models is a confidence region, which is a sampling object, and the radius grows with \(N\) and shrinks with \(T\) exactly as the standard error of Equation 6.1 does. The multi-prior portfolio is a parameter-uncertainty device that uses a worst case where the Bayesian uses an average, and the comparison with Equation 6.4 is direct: Bayes–Stein moves the estimate toward a common mean by a factor set by the posterior precision; Equation 28.5 moves the portfolio toward minimum variance by a factor set by the radius. Both end in the same place as the sample shrinks. The decision-aware corrections of Section 27.1 change the forecast so that the decision it feeds costs less; the multi-prior rule leaves the forecast alone and changes the decision.

28.1.3 Robust optimization over a set
The inner problem of Equation 28.1 is one instance of robust optimization: specify an uncertainty set for the inputs and optimize the worst case over it. Goldfarb and Iyengar (2003) define the set through a factor model, with intervals for the factor loadings and for the covariance of the factors, and show that the worst-case mean-variance problem is a second-order cone program, convex and solvable with the machinery of Section 13.1. Tütüncü and Koenig (2004) take box sets for \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) and solve the saddle point directly. The set does the work: a box is a per-asset haircut on every long position, an ellipsoid is the volatility penalty of Equation 28.3. The scenario appendix of Appendix H is the same idea applied to the factors of the modeled market rather than to its moments, and Appendix C records which of these formulations the package’s solvers can carry.

28.1.4 The Kullback–Leibler ball
A worst case over means leaves every other feature of the model intact. The robust control approach of Hansen and Sargent (2008) widens the set to every distribution within a fixed relative entropy of a reference model \(p\),
\[
\mathcal{Q}(\eta) = \left\{ q : \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)
= \sum_t q_t \log\frac{q_t}{p_t} \leq \eta \right\},
\tag{28.7}\]
so that an alternative model may move tails, correlations and skewness as well as means. For a portfolio \(\boldsymbol{w}\) with realized returns \(x_t = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}_t\) under \(p\), the worst case for the expected return is again a Lagrangian problem, now in the probabilities: minimizing \(\sum_t q_t x_t\) subject to the entropy constraint gives the first-order condition \(x_t + \tfrac{1}{\theta}(\log(q_t/p_t) + 1) = \lambda\), whose solution is the exponential tilt
\[
q_t^{*} = \frac{p_t\, e^{-\theta x_t}}{\sum_s p_s\, e^{-\theta x_s}},
\qquad \theta = \theta(\eta) \;\text{ such that }\; \mathrm{KL}(q^{*}\,\|\,p) = \eta .
\tag{28.8}\]
Nature reweights the sample toward the months in which the portfolio did badly, with an intensity \(\theta\) that rises with the radius, and the worst-case mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_q = \sum_t q^{*}_t \boldsymbol{r}_t\) marks down most the assets whose bad months coincide with the portfolio’s. The same tilt expressed through the multiplier gives the multiplier preference of Anderson et al. (2003),
\[
\min_{q \in \mathcal{Q}(\eta)} \mathbb{E}_q[x]
= \max_{\theta > 0}\left\{ -\frac{1}{\theta}\log \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[e^{-\theta x}\right]
- \frac{\eta}{\theta} \right\},
\tag{28.9}\]
whose first term is the certainty equivalent of an investor with exponential utility and absolute risk aversion \(\theta\). Robustness and risk aversion are therefore nearly indistinguishable from outside, and Maenhout (2004) derives robust portfolio rules in which the preference for robustness enters exactly as Equation 28.5 found: as an increase in effective risk aversion. The two sets are related exactly when the reference model is Gaussian: the relative entropy between \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) and \(\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu} - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu} - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\), so a ball of radius \(\eta\) restricted to shifts in the mean is the ellipsoid of Equation 28.1 with \(\varepsilon = 2\eta\). On the empirical distribution the ball is larger, and Section 28.2 shows what the extra room buys. Anderson et al. (2003) calibrate \(\eta\) by the probability that the sample would be mistaken for the worst-case model, the counterpart of Equation 28.6.
Between the average and the worst case lies the smooth ambiguity model of Klibanoff et al. (2005), in which the investor holds a second-order distribution \(\pi\) over the models and evaluates a portfolio as \(\mathbb{E}_\pi\!\left[\phi\!\left(\mathbb{E}_q[u(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r})]\right)\right]\) with \(\phi\) concave. A linear \(\phi\) recovers the Bayesian average, and the limit of infinite concavity recovers the maxmin rule, so ambiguity aversion becomes a parameter rather than a switch; this chapter traces that parameter through Equation 28.6.

28.1.5 Resampling, and what kind of uncertainty it treats
Michaud (1989) proposed to replace the frontier by its average over resampled inputs: draw \((\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_b, \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_b)\) from the sampling distribution, solve the frontier on each draw, and average the weights rank by rank,
\[
\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_k = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}
\boldsymbol{w}_k\!\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_b, \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_b\right),
\qquad k = 1, \dots, K ,
\tag{28.10}\]
where \(k\) indexes the frontier portfolios from minimum variance to maximum return (Michaud and Michaud 2008). The result is a frontier of more diversified portfolios that move less when the sample changes, which is the property the block bootstrap of Section 9.3 showed the tangency portfolio lacks. It is an average over parameter draws and therefore a parameter-uncertainty device: every draw comes from the same model, and no draw asks what happens if that model is wrong. Scherer (2002) adds the critique that it is not the Bayesian answer either, since the expectation of an optimizer is not the optimizer of an expectation, and that averaging long-only weights pulls every portfolio toward the center of the simplex regardless of what the data say. Measuring it beside the maxmin rules shows the difference between averaging and guarding.

title: 28  Robustness and Model Uncertainty
section: 28.2 Four Robustifications on the Sixteen Classes
text:
28.2 Four Robustifications on the Sixteen Classes
The quadratic programs below are those of Section 8.2, written out so that the loops of this chapter run in seconds; the PortfolioAnalytics specification is kept beside them as the check. Risk aversion is \(\gamma = 3\) throughout, the default of Stöckl (2020), and every number is annualized from monthly moments.

qp_simplex <- function(Dmat, dvec, nm) {       # max d'w - w'Dw/2 on the simplex
  n <- length(dvec)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = Dmat * 1e4, dvec = dvec * 1e4,
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), nm)
}
gmv_qp <- function(S) qp_simplex(2 * S, rep(0, ncol(S)), colnames(S))
mv_qp  <- function(mu, S, gamma) qp_simplex(gamma * S, mu, names(mu))   # eq. 03 utility
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {                     # min y'Sy s.t. y'mu = 1, y >= 0; w = y / sum(y)
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(gmv_qp(S))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu))
}
target_qp <- function(mu, S, target) {          # one frontier point
  n <- length(mu)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), mu * 1e2, diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, target * 1e2, rep(0, n)), meq = 2)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), names(mu))
}
p_vol <- function(w, V = S) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% V %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w, m = mu) sum(m * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w) p_ret(w) / p_vol(w)
turnover <- function(w1, w2) sum(abs(w1[names(w2)] - w2)) / 2

w_gmv <- gmv_qp(S)
w_tan <- tan_qp(mu, S)
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
w_pa <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(
  Re, add.objective(base_spec, type = "risk", name = "var"), optimize_method = "ROI"))
stopifnot(max(abs(w_pa[colnames(Re)] - w_gmv)) < 1e-4)


28.2.1 The resampled frontier
Each draw resamples the 372 months in twelve-month blocks, as Section 9.3 does, so that the serial dependence a naive bootstrap would destroy is kept (Künsch 1989; Politis and Romano 1994). On each draw we solve the long-only frontier at 25 equally spaced targets between the draw’s own minimum-variance return and its highest mean, and average the weights by rank as Equation 28.10 prescribes. The resampled tangency portfolio is the average of the draws’ tangency portfolios.

set.seed(1602)
block_index <- function(n, block = 12L) {
  starts <- sample.int(n - block + 1L, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE)
  as.vector(outer(0:(block - 1L), starts, "+"))[seq_len(n)]
}
frontier_of <- function(m, V, K = 25L) {
  lo <- sum(gmv_qp(V) * m); hi <- max(m)
  targets <- lo + (hi - lo) * seq(0, 0.995, length.out = K)   # the vertex itself is degenerate
  t(vapply(targets, function(tg) target_qp(m, V, tg), numeric(length(m))))
}

K <- 25L; B <- 200L
fr_sample <- frontier_of(mu, S, K)
boot <- lapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(Re)[block_index(Tn), ]
  m <- colMeans(X); V <- stats::cov(X)
  list(W = frontier_of(m, V, K), tan = tan_qp(m, V))
})
W_res     <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(boot, `[[`, "W")) / B
tan_draws <- t(vapply(boot, function(b) b$tan, numeric(N)))
w_res_tan <- colMeans(tan_draws)[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(W_res), identical(colnames(W_res), colnames(Re)),
          abs(sum(w_res_tan) - 1) < 1e-8)








Figure 28.1: The sample frontier, two hundred block-bootstrap frontiers and their rank-by-rank average, the resampled frontier of Equation 28.10. Every point is evaluated at the full-sample moments. The resampled frontier lies inside the sample frontier because averaging long-only weights diversifies them.

The resampled tangency holds 9 classes where the sample tangency holds 4, and the two are 13% of the portfolio apart. The block bootstrap of Section 9.3 measured how far a draw moves the tangency portfolio; here the mean distance of a draw’s tangency from the sample tangency is 21%, and from the resampled tangency 23%. The resampled portfolio is the arithmetic mean of the draws, which minimizes their squared distance and not the trading distance, so it is not a portfolio the draws cluster around any more tightly. What it does is diversify: it pays 2.1% of the in-sample Sharpe ratio for that, and no point on the resampled frontier reaches the sample tangency’s ratio, which is Scherer (2002)’s point that the averaged frontier is dominated at the moments it was averaged under. Whether it is dominated at the moments that follow is the question of Section 28.3.

28.2.2 Random portfolios as a picture of the feasible set
Section 13.3 used random_portfolios() as a solver and measured it at a fraction of the attainable optimum. Here it is a different instrument: a sample from the feasible set, drawn three ways, so that the frontier can be seen against the set it is the edge of. The sample engine of rp_sample() perturbs weights one at a time under the full constraint list; the simplex engine of rp_simplex() draws uniformly on the simplex and then biases the draw toward its faces, edges and vertices through the fev argument, with \(q = 2^{\text{fev}}\) concentrating the weights into fewer assets as it grows; rp_grid() lays a grid over the box and normalizes.

set.seed(1602)
rp_s <- rp_sample(base_spec, permutations = 2000)
rp_x <- rp_simplex(base_spec, permutations = 2000, fev = 0:5)
rp_g <- rp_grid(base_spec, permutations = 2000, normalize = TRUE)
c(sample = nrow(rp_s), simplex = nrow(rp_x), grid = nrow(rp_g))
#>  sample simplex    grid 
#>    1999    2004   65535


cloud <- function(W, kind, extra = NA_integer_) {
  stopifnot(ncol(W) == N)
  colnames(W) <- names(base_spec$assets); W <- W[, colnames(Re)]
  tibble::tibble(kind = kind, layer = "cloud", fev = extra,
                 vol  = sqrt(rowSums((W %*% S) * W)) * sqrt(12),
                 ret  = as.numeric(W %*% mu) * 12,
                 dist = rowSums(abs(W - rep(w_tan, each = nrow(W)))) / 2,
                 n_pos = rowSums(W > 1e-6))
}
clouds <- dplyr::bind_rows(cloud(rp_s, "sample"),
                           cloud(rp_x, "simplex", rep(0:5, each = nrow(rp_x) / 6L)),
                           cloud(rp_g, "grid"))
stopifnot(nrow(rp_x) %% 6L == 0L)

Figure 28.2: The same feasible set sampled three ways, at the full-sample moments, with the long-only frontier drawn over each cloud and the member of each cloud nearest to the tangency portfolio marked. The grid engine in sixteen dimensions returns every equal-weighted subset of the classes, of which two thousand are drawn for the picture.




Nothing a cloud contains comes within 15% of the tangency portfolio in trading distance, and the best member of the best cloud reaches 92% of its Sharpe ratio: the frontier is the edge of the set, and a sample of the set does not reach its edge. The three engines sample it differently. The simplex draws spread across the interior at fev = 0, where every portfolio holds all 16 classes, and move to the faces as fev rises, reaching a median of 2 positions at fev = 5. The grid engine in sixteen dimensions has two levels per asset, so its 65,535 portfolios are exactly the equal-weighted subsets of the classes, which is why its cloud is a lattice. That is a useful picture of the feasible set and a poor search of it, which is the finding of Section 13.3 seen from the other side.






Noterandom_portfolios() ignores a factor-exposure constraint



A factor-exposure constraint bounds \(\boldsymbol{B}'\boldsymbol{w}\), the portfolio’s loading on a set of factors. Take the betas of the sixteen classes on their equal-weighted average, the single factor of Section 5.2, and cap the portfolio beta below the tangency portfolio’s.

mkt  <- rowMeans(zoo::coredata(Re))
beta <- apply(zoo::coredata(Re), 2, function(x) stats::cov(x, mkt) / stats::var(mkt))
beta_tan <- sum(w_tan * beta)
spec_fe <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = beta, lower = 0.2, upper = 0.4)

set.seed(1602)
rp_fe   <- random_portfolios(spec_fe, permutations = 2000, rp_method = "sample")
rp_fe_x <- rp_simplex(spec_fe, permutations = 2000, fev = 0:5)
violates <- function(W) { e <- as.numeric(W %*% beta); mean(e < 0.2 | e > 0.4) }
c(generated = nrow(rp_fe), sample_violating = violates(rp_fe), simplex_violating = violates(rp_fe_x))
#>         generated  sample_violating simplex_violating 
#>           158.000             1.000             0.992


fe_spec <- spec_fe |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")
w_fe_random <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, fe_spec, optimize_method = "random",
                                                 rp = rp_fe, maxSR = TRUE, trace = FALSE))
w_fe_roi    <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, fe_spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE))
c(tangency = beta_tan,
  random = sum(w_fe_random[colnames(Re)] * beta), ROI = sum(w_fe_roi[colnames(Re)] * beta))
#> tangency   random      ROI 
#>   0.4884   0.4993   0.4000

The documentation says which constraints the generators check — leverage, box, group, position limit and leverage exposure — and factor exposure is not among them. The audit confirms it: of the 158 portfolios the default call keeps after the budget elimination described in Section 13.2, 100% breach the bound, as do 99% of the simplex draws, and the grid engine honors only the box by its own account. Nor does the objective catch it: constrained_objective() penalizes budget, box, group, position, diversification and turnover violations and has no term for factor exposure, so optimize_method = "random" returns a portfolio with a beta of 0.50 against a cap of 0.4, without a warning, while ROI returns one at the cap exactly. A factor-exposure constraint is a linear constraint and belongs on the convex path of Appendix C.



28.2.3 The multi-prior portfolio
Equation 28.5 and Equation 28.4 are closed forms, and glPF() in Stöckl (2020) implements the same problem. We write the derivation out, check it against a direct maximization of Equation 28.3, and compare it with the package.

gamma <- 3
A <- as.numeric(t(rep(1, N)) %*% solve(S, rep(1, N)))
Bs <- as.numeric(t(rep(1, N)) %*% solve(S, mu))
C <- as.numeric(t(mu) %*% solve(S, mu))
D <- C - Bs^2 / A
eps_of <- function(p, T_ = Tn, N_ = N) N_ * (T_ - 1) / (T_ * (T_ - N_)) * stats::qf(p, N_, T_ - N_)

mp_closed <- function(eps, gamma) {           # eq. 28-fully-invested, weights of any sign
  w_mv <- solve(S, rep(1, N)) / A
  spec_dir <- solve(S, mu - (Bs / A) * rep(1, N))
  phi <- if (eps == 0) 1 / gamma else
    stats::uniroot(function(phi) phi * (gamma + sqrt(eps) / sqrt(1 / A + phi^2 * D)) - 1,
                   c(0, 1 / gamma), tol = 1e-12)$root
  list(w = setNames(as.numeric(w_mv + phi * spec_dir), names(mu)), shrink = phi * gamma)
}
robust_objective <- function(w, eps, gamma) {
  sg <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w))
  sum(w * mu) - sqrt(eps) * sg - gamma / 2 * sg^2
}

eps_half <- eps_of(0.5)
mp <- mp_closed(eps_half, gamma)
brute <- optim(mp$w[-N], function(v) -robust_objective(c(v, 1 - sum(v)), eps_half, gamma),
               method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 2000))
w_brute <- c(brute$par, 1 - sum(brute$par))
w_glpf  <- uncertaintymeasures::glPF(mu = mu, Sigma = S, gamma = gamma,
                                     epsilon = list(eps_half), rf = FALSE)$w
c(shrinkage = mp$shrink,
  gap_brute = max(abs(mp$w - w_brute)), gap_glPF = max(abs(mp$w - w_glpf)),
  objective_gap_glPF = robust_objective(mp$w, eps_half, gamma) - robust_objective(w_glpf, eps_half, gamma))
#>          shrinkage          gap_brute           gap_glPF objective_gap_glPF 
#>  0.217151683605830  0.000000000001159  0.077023618629827  0.000004213097561

At the median radius \(\varepsilon(0.5) = 0.043\) the shrinkage factor \(\gamma/\gamma^{*}\) is 0.22: the speculative component of Equation 28.5 is cut to about a fifth before the ellipsoid has reached even odds of containing the true mean. The derived weights agree with the direct maximization to 1e-12. glPF() returns the same weights at \(\varepsilon = 0\) and, at this radius, weights that differ by up to 0.077 and attain a lower value of Equation 28.3, so the chapter keeps the derived solution.
Under the long-only constraint of every portfolio in this book the closed form is gone and the fixed point remains: solve the quadratic program of Equation 3.12 at \(\gamma^{*}\), read off \(\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}\), update \(\gamma^{*}\), repeat.

mp_long_only <- function(mu, S, eps, gamma, tol = 1e-8, maxit = 200L) {
  w <- mv_qp(mu, S, gamma); g_star <- gamma
  for (i in seq_len(maxit)) {
    g_star <- gamma + sqrt(eps) / sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w))
    w_new  <- mv_qp(mu, S, g_star)
    if (max(abs(w_new - w)) < tol) { w <- w_new; break }
    w <- w_new
  }
  structure(w, gamma_star = g_star, iterations = i)
}

p_grid <- c(0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, 0.9999)
trace <- lapply(p_grid, function(p) mp_long_only(mu, S, eps_of(p), gamma))
W_mp  <- do.call(rbind, trace)
mp_tab <- tibble::tibble(p = p_grid, eps = eps_of(p_grid),
                         gamma_star = vapply(trace, attr, numeric(1), "gamma_star"),
                         to_gmv = apply(W_mp, 1, turnover, w2 = w_gmv),
                         to_plugin = apply(W_mp, 1, turnover, w2 = W_mp[1, ]))
mp_tab
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>       p    eps gamma_star to_gmv to_plugin
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>

#> 2 0.5   0.0431       16.1  0.265     0.687

Figure 28.3: Weights of the long-only multi-prior portfolio as the radius of the ellipsoid grows, from the plug-in portfolio at \(\varepsilon = 0\) toward the minimum-variance portfolio. Classes never held above two percent are pooled.




The distance to the minimum-variance portfolio falls monotonically, from 93% of the portfolio at the plug-in solution to 14% at \(p = 0.9999\), where the effective risk aversion has reached 31 from 3. The largest move happens first: between \(p = 0\) and \(p = 0.5\) the portfolio travels 69% of its weight, because at \(\varepsilon = 0\) the plug-in investor with \(\gamma = 3\) holds an all-equity portfolio that Section 9.3 showed to be the least well determined point on the frontier, and the first increment of doubt removes most of it.
Stöckl (2022) turns Equation 28.6 into a time series by replacing the confidence level with the \(p\)-value of the turbulence of Equation 5.6: a month far from the estimated mean, in the metric of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\), is evidence that the mean is poorly known, and the ellipsoid widens. OSminimax_one() computes that radius and the scale factor of Equation 28.4 out of sample.

library(uncertaintymeasures)
mm    <- OSminimax_one(Re, s.k = 1, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)
eps_t <- as.numeric(mm$epsilon)
turb  <- as.numeric(OSturbulence(Re, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb)
disp  <- sqrt(rowMeans(zoo::coredata(Re)^2))          # the month's cross-sectional dispersion
ok  <- !is.na(eps_t); fin <- ok & is.finite(eps_t)
amb <- c(rank_cor_turbulence = stats::cor(eps_t[ok], turb[ok], method = "spearman"),
         r2_log_dispersion   = summary(stats::lm(log(eps_t[fin]) ~ log(disp[fin])))$r.squared,
         share_nothing_risky = mean(as.numeric(mm$sturb)[ok] == 0))
round(amb, 3)
#> rank_cor_turbulence   r2_log_dispersion share_nothing_risky 
#>               1.000               0.497               0.319

The radius is a monotone transform of the month’s turbulence, with a rank correlation of 1.00, and 50% of the variation in its logarithm is the logarithm of the month’s cross-sectional dispersion alone. In 32% of the months the radius exceeds the squared Sharpe ratio and Equation 28.4 holds nothing risky. A time-varying ambiguity of this kind is therefore largely a volatility-timing rule: it widens the set of models when the month was volatile, and Kritzman and Li (2010) show what such a rule buys as a risk signal. Whether it also measures something volatility does not is the question Stöckl (2022) asks of the equity premium, and it cannot be settled on a modeled market.

28.2.4 The Kullback–Leibler ball
The reference model is the empirical distribution of the 372 months. For a portfolio, Equation 28.8 is a one-dimensional root in \(\theta\); the robust portfolio maximizes the tilted mean less the variance penalty, a concave problem, by Newton steps in which the curvature of the worst-case mean is \(\theta\) times the covariance under the tilt.

Xm <- zoo::coredata(Re)
kl_tilt <- function(w, eta, X = Xm) {
  x <- as.numeric(X %*% w)
  q_of  <- function(th) { a <- -th * x; a <- a - max(a); q <- exp(a); q / sum(q) }
  kl_of <- function(th) { q <- q_of(th); q <- q[q > 0]; sum(q * log(q * length(x))) }
  theta <- if (eta <= 0) 0 else
    stats::uniroot(function(th) kl_of(th) - eta, c(0, 5000), tol = 1e-10)$root
  q <- q_of(theta)
  list(q = q, theta = theta, mu_q = setNames(as.numeric(t(X) %*% q), colnames(X)))
}

kl_robust <- function(eta, gamma, X = Xm, tol = 1e-8, maxit = 100L) {
  m0 <- colMeans(X); V <- stats::cov(X); n <- length(m0)
  J <- function(w) sum(kl_tilt(w, eta, X)$q * as.numeric(X %*% w)) -
    gamma / 2 * as.numeric(t(w) %*% V %*% w)
  w <- mv_qp(m0, V, gamma); j_old <- J(w)
  for (i in seq_len(maxit)) {
    tl <- kl_tilt(w, eta, X)
    Xc <- sweep(X, 2, tl$mu_q) * sqrt(tl$q)
    Cq <- crossprod(Xc)                                  # covariance under the tilt
    w_new <- qp_simplex(gamma * V + tl$theta * Cq,
                        tl$mu_q + tl$theta * as.numeric(Cq %*% w), names(m0))
    step <- 1; j_new <- J(w_new)
    while (j_new < j_old - 1e-12 && step > 1e-4) {      # damp a step that overshoots
      step <- step / 2; w_new <- w + step * (w_new - w); j_new <- J(w_new)
    }
    if (max(abs(w_new - w)) < tol) { w <- w_new; break }
    w <- w_new; j_old <- j_new
  }
  tl <- kl_tilt(w, eta, X)
  structure(w, theta = tl$theta, mu_q = tl$mu_q, iterations = i)
}

etas <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.2)
kl   <- lapply(etas, kl_robust, gamma = gamma)
w_plugin <- mv_qp(mu, S, gamma)

The ball does to the portfolio what the ellipsoid did: the distance to minimum variance falls as the radius grows, to 7% at \(\eta = 0.2\). The route is different. Nature’s mark-down is not proportional to \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}\) as in Equation 28.2 but to each class’s covariance with the months in which the portfolio lost most. EU_equity, a class the plug-in portfolio holds, is marked down by 13 percentage points a year at \(\eta = 0.05\), and the classes with the longest left tails of Section 4.3 are marked down beyond what their covariance implies, which the fourth exercise measures. Even the smallest radius moves the portfolio by more than half its weight, because the plug-in portfolio at \(\gamma = 3\) is the all-equity corner that Equation 28.5 also abandoned first. For the application the radius is set by the Gaussian correspondence \(\eta = \varepsilon/2\), so that the two robust portfolios guard against sets of the same size and differ only in their shape.

title: 28  Robustness and Model Uncertainty
text:
28.3 Robustness Out of Sample
The six portfolios are re-estimated on every sixty-month window and held for the month that follows, from January of model year 11, the first month the register of Section 25.3 scores, with the metrics computed as that register computes them. The resampled tangency uses 100 draws per window with a small ridge on each draw’s covariance, since five twelve-month blocks can coincide; the multi-prior portfolio uses \(\varepsilon(0.5)\) of Equation 28.6 at \(T = 60\), and the ball \(\eta = \varepsilon(0.5)/2\). The certainty equivalent is \(\bar{r} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\hat{\sigma}^2\) at \(\gamma = 3\), annualized, in excess of the bill.

win <- 60L
ends <- seq.int(120L, Tn - 1L)
oos_start <- d[121]
stopifnot(model_year(oos_start) == 11L, model_year(d[120]) == 10L)
eps_app <- eps_of(0.5, win, N); eta_app <- eps_app / 2
Rm <- zoo::coredata(R); Rem <- zoo::coredata(Re)

set.seed(1602)
rules <- lapply(ends, function(e) {
  X <- Rem[(e - win + 1L):e, , drop = FALSE]
  m <- colMeans(X); V <- stats::cov(X)
  tans <- t(vapply(seq_len(100L), function(b) {
    Xb <- X[block_index(win), , drop = FALSE]; Vb <- stats::cov(Xb)
    tan_qp(colMeans(Xb), Vb + diag(1e-6 * mean(diag(Vb)), N))
  }, numeric(N)))
  out <- list(
    max_sharpe   = tan_qp(m, V),
    resampled    = colMeans(tans),
    multi_prior  = mp_long_only(m, V, eps_app, gamma),
    kl_robust    = kl_robust(eta_app, gamma, X),
    min_variance = gmv_qp(V),
    equal_weight = setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
  )
  stopifnot(all(vapply(out, function(w) identical(names(w), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))
  out
})

score <- function(rule) {
  eop <- NULL; gross <- turn <- numeric(length(ends))
  for (j in seq_along(ends)) {
    w  <- as.numeric(rules[[j]][[rule]])
    rt <- Rm[ends[j] + 1L, ]
    turn[j]  <- if (is.null(eop)) NA_real_ else 0.5 * sum(abs(w - eop))
    gross[j] <- sum(w * rt)
    eop <- w * (1 + rt) / (1 + gross[j])                 # drift to the next rebalance
  }
  rfo <- rf[ends + 1L]; n <- length(gross)
  ann_return <- prod(1 + gross)^(12 / n) - 1
  ann_rf     <- prod(1 + rfo)^(12 / n) - 1
  x <- xts::xts(gross, order.by = d[ends + 1L])
  tibble::tibble(strategy = rule,
                 sharpe = (ann_return - ann_rf) / (stats::sd(gross) * sqrt(12)),
                 ce = 12 * mean(gross - rfo) - gamma / 2 * 12 * stats::var(gross),
                 ann_turnover = mean(turn, na.rm = TRUE) * 12,
                 max_drawdown = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(x)),
                 ann_vol = stats::sd(gross) * sqrt(12))
}
oos <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(rules[[1]]), score))

register <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", window == win, frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
oos$register <- register$sharpe[match(oos$strategy, register$strategy)]

The register rows reproduce to within 5e-05 for the two strategies fitted on excess returns and within 0.001 for minimum variance, which the register fits on total returns. By Sharpe ratio the order is Minimum variance, Multi-prior, p = 0.5, Equal weight, KL ball, eta = eps/2, Tangency, Resampled tangency.
Each robustification buys something different. The two maxmin portfolios move the tangency portfolio part of the way to minimum variance, and the data pay for the distance traveled: the multi-prior portfolio raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.55 to 0.65, cuts turnover from 0.82 to 0.50 of the portfolio a year and the drawdown from 20% to 16%, and the ball of the same size does slightly less of each. Neither reaches minimum variance, which needs no mean at all and finishes first of the six here, as it finishes ahead of every rule that estimates a mean in every cell of the register Section 8.3 reads. The resampled tangency buys nothing here: averaging over draws moves weight away from US_government, which anchors the tangency portfolio, from 57% on average to 47%, and the result is more volatile, has a lower Sharpe ratio than the plug-in portfolio it was meant to stabilize, a larger drawdown, and a turnover of 0.73, because the average of a hundred unstable answers is itself re-estimated every month. Equal weighting has the highest certainty equivalent at \(\gamma = 3\), as DeMiguel et al. (2009) would predict, and the lowest turnover; it is the one rule here that guards against model uncertainty by holding no model.
The lesson is the one Equation 28.5 states: a worst case over means is an increase in risk aversion, and what it buys is what a higher risk aversion buys, in proportion to the size of the set. The set is a confidence region, and on sixty months of sixteen classes the region is already wide enough at even odds to move most of the way to the portfolio that ignores the means.

title: 28  Robustness and Model Uncertainty
text:
Key Takeaways

Parameter uncertainty is a distribution over the inputs and is treated by averaging; model uncertainty is a set of models with no distribution over it and is treated by a worst case (Gilboa and Schmeidler 1989). The first produces shrinkage of the estimate, the second shrinkage of the portfolio.
The multi-prior investor of Garlappi et al. (2007) holds the mean-variance portfolio of an investor with effective risk aversion \(\gamma^{*} = \gamma + \sqrt{\varepsilon}/\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}\), and converges to minimum variance as the ellipsoid grows. Its radius Equation 28.6 is a confidence level, which makes it a parameter-uncertainty device in a model-uncertainty frame.
A Kullback–Leibler ball around the empirical distribution reweights the sample toward the portfolio’s bad months (Hansen and Sargent 2008); with a Gaussian reference it is the ellipsoid with \(\varepsilon = 2\eta\). The worst case marks down the classes with the worst tails rather than the most volatile.
Resampling averages over parameter draws. On this market the resampled tangency portfolio is more diversified in sample and dominated out of sample; it is not a robust portfolio in the sense of this chapter (Scherer 2002).

random_portfolios() is a picture of the feasible set and not a search of it, and it ignores a factor-exposure constraint at generation and in the objective; a bound on factor exposure belongs on the convex path.

title: 28  Robustness and Model Uncertainty
text:
Exercises

Rerun the rolling exercise of Section 28.3 with the multi-prior portfolio at \(p = 0.1\), \(0.5\) and \(0.9\). Report the Sharpe ratio, the turnover and the mean trading distance from the minimum-variance portfolio at each level. At which level does the multi-prior portfolio stop being distinguishable from minimum variance?
The resampled frontier of Equation 28.10 averages by rank. Compute the expected return of its highest-ranked portfolio and compare it with the highest sample mean among the sixteen classes. Explain, using the long-only constraint, why the two must differ, and what that implies for the right end of a resampled frontier.
Fix the trap of the callout by hand: generate two thousand portfolios with rp_sample() under spec_fe, discard those whose beta lies outside \([0.2, 0.4]\), and compare the best surviving Sharpe ratio with the ROI solution. How many survive, and how much of the optimum does the best one reach?
Replace the empirical reference of the ball with a Gaussian one: compute the worst-case mean of Equation 28.2 at \(\varepsilon = 2\eta\) for the plug-in portfolio and compare it, class by class, with the tilted mean of Equation 28.8 at \(\eta = 0.05\). Which classes are marked down more by the tilt than by the ellipsoid, and what feature of their distribution from Section 4.3 explains the difference?

title: Appendix A — Data Description
text:
A.1 Class Series
This appendix documents the modeled market in full. Chapter 2 (Section 2.2) introduces it and says why the book runs on it; chapter 4 (Section 4.2) measures its properties. Here we record what each shipped object contains, how it was constructed, and what it cannot support. Everything below is computed from the objects as they ship in tidypm, so the appendix cannot drift from the data.
The dataset is modeled and contains no real data. Factor models for government bonds, credit, equities and commodities were estimated by historical simulation on market data from 1992 to 2022; the factors were replayed, the idiosyncratic components drawn afresh, and the asset paths reassembled, so that no series is the history of a real security. The market therefore runs on its own calendar, model years 1 to 31, read with the tools of Section 2.2.1. Its stress episodes are named for what happens in them and ship as sim_episodes. And because every series is the output of a factor model, the market can be re-run with its factors shocked, which a history cannot, and Appendix H does so.
The return tables and the exchange rates cover model years 1 to 31 exactly. The weekly bill and the curve start one week before the first weekly return, and the capitalizations extend past both ends of the sample, so that a lagged capitalization exists for the first return.
The allocation universe is the sixteen risky class series in sim_class_returns_monthly: five currencies, each with a government bond, a credit and an equity series, plus one global commodity index. The five money-market series ship beside them in sim_money_market_monthly and are not part of the universe, for the reason given in Section 2.4. Both tables carry date, class, return (a simple total return in decimal) and index (a total-return index with base 100 one period before the first observation).
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
M  <- as_xts_pm(sim_money_market_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
d  <- zoo::index(R)
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, ncol(M) == 5L,
          identical(d, zoo::index(M)),
          all(d == sim_riskfree_monthly$date))

# The index is the compounded return series, in both tables.
rebuilt <- dplyr::bind_rows(sim_class_returns_monthly, sim_money_market_monthly) |>
  dplyr::group_by(class) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rebuilt = 100 * cumprod(1 + return)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(max(abs(rebuilt$rebuilt - rebuilt$index)) < 1e-8)

c(months = nrow(R), first_model_year = min(model_year(d)),
  last_model_year = max(model_year(d)))

Weighting. Equity class series are value-weighted on the market capitalization of the previous weekly observation, so no portfolio is formed with information it could not have had; government, credit, money-market and commodity series are equally weighted across their instruments, because no capitalization exists for them. The portfolio is rebalanced weekly, and the monthly return is the compounded weekly one, so the monthly series is a weekly-rebalanced portfolio observed at month ends rather than a monthly-rebalanced one.
The money market is a duration asset. Each *_money_market series is the 0.25-year point on a Nelson–Siegel curve fitted to 2-, 5- and 10-year yields, marked to market. The US series tracks the bill closely but is not the bill:

  correlation          = stats::cor(mm, rf))

section: A.3 Risk-Free Rate and Exchange Rates
text:
A.3 Risk-Free Rate and Exchange Rates
sim_riskfree_monthly and sim_riskfree_weekly are a three-month Treasury bill carried onto the model’s grid: rate_annual is the quoted annual rate and return the simple return over one period. The bill enters the model as an input, and it is the risk-free rate everywhere in the book (Section 3.1).

c(annualized = ann_ret(rf), negative_months = sum(rf < 0),
  min_rate = min(sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual),
  max_rate = max(sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual))
#>      annualized negative_months        min_rate        max_rate 
#>         0.02262         1.00000        -0.00010         0.06190

sim_fx_monthly and sim_fx_weekly hold, for the four non-US regions, the value of one unit of local currency in dollars (rate, weekly only) and its return fx_return. Like the bill, the exchange rates enter the model as inputs. The quote direction matters: a positive fx_return means the local currency appreciated against the dollar, which is a gain for an unhedged dollar investor holding the local asset. Subtracting fx_return from an unhedged local return gives the hedged return, which is how the book hedges (Section 4.3).

sim_fx_monthly |>
  dplyr::group_by(region) |>
  dplyr::summarise(ann_vol = ann_vol(fx_return),
                   ann_return = ann_ret(fx_return), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   region ann_vol ann_return
#>   <chr>    <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 CH      0.103     0.0122 
#> 2 EU      0.0953   -0.00907
#> 3 JP      0.101    -0.00171
#> 4 UK      0.0915   -0.0142

sim_curve_weekly holds the drivers of the bond block: Nelson–Siegel level, slope and curvature for each region, plus an investment-grade and a high-yield credit spread per region. Chapter 22 (Section 22.1) decomposes bond returns on them.

sort(unique(sim_curve_weekly$series))
#>  [1] "CH_Curvature" "CH_HY_Spread" "CH_IG_Spread" "CH_Level"     "CH_Slope"    
#>  [6] "EU_Curvature" "EU_HY_Spread" "EU_IG_Spread" "EU_Level"     "EU_Slope"    
#> [11] "JP_Curvature" "JP_HY_Spread" "JP_IG_Spread" "JP_Level"     "JP_Slope"

sim_marketcap_weekly holds the market capitalization of the 123 equities on the weekly grid, which is what a capitalization-weighted benchmark needs (Section 24.3, Section 21.2).
sim_esg_changes_quarterly holds changes in an ESG rating of the equities: the quarter end (date), the instrument (asset) and an integer esg_change. It carries changes only, no starting level, and the changes have no effect on the returns.
